cards.q: What does `type(3.0)` return?

<class 'str'>

cards.q: What is the result of `7 // 2`?
cards.x: `//` is floor division: it divides and rounds down to a whole number.

cards.x: `%` is modulo: the remainder after division.

cards.q: What is the result of `2 ** 3`?
cards.x: `**` is exponentiation.

wrong: "Hi " . name
"Hi %name"
concat("Hi", name), joining the pieces together

wrong: Yes, always — any character can change in place

cards.x: len() counts characters in a string or items in a collection.

A missing default route
A duplicate MAC

cards.q: If two routers will not become OSPF neighbors, check...

cards.x: Any mismatch in these Hello parameters prevents adjacency.
wrong: The VLAN database, checking that the trunk allows the right VLANs through
The STP root
The DHCP scope

decks.title: Security Concepts
decks.summary: CIA, AAA, controls, zero trust, and change management. (Domain 1.0)

cards.q: What does the CIA triad stand for?
cards.a: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
cards.x: The three core goals of information security.
wrong: Control, Identity, Access
Cipher, Integrity, Authentication
Confidentiality, Identity, Accountability

cards.q: Encryption primarily protects which CIA goal?
cards.a: Confidentiality
cards.x: Hashing protects integrity; redundancy protects availability.
wrong: Integrity
Availability
Non-repudiation

cards.q: Hashing primarily protects which goal?
cards.a: Integrity
cards.x: A changed file produces a different hash.
wrong: Confidentiality
Availability
Authorization

cards.q: What does non-repudiation mean?
cards.a: The sender cannot deny having sent it
cards.x: Digital signatures provide non-repudiation.
wrong: Data cannot be read by unauthorised people
The service stays available during an attack
Users can reset passwords whenever they forget them

cards.q: What are the parts of AAA?
cards.a: Authentication, Authorization, Accounting
cards.x: Prove who you are, decide what you can do, log what you did.
wrong: Access, Audit, Alert
Authorization, Availability, Audit — the three As
Authenticate, Allow, Archive

cards.q: Control categories (SY0-701)?
cards.a: Technical, managerial, operational, physical
cards.x: Technical = firewall; managerial = policy; operational = guard rotation; physical = locks.
wrong: Preventive, detective, corrective — by control function
Hardware, software, people — the things themselves
Strong, medium, weak — how tough each one is

cards.q: A security camera is primarily which control type?
cards.a: Detective
cards.x: Types: preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating, directive.
wrong: Preventive
Corrective
Directive

cards.q: What is a compensating control?
cards.a: An alternative control when the primary isn’t feasible
cards.x: Example: isolating a legacy system that cannot be patched.
wrong: A backup control that duplicates the first exactly
A control that pays for damage after an incident
A detective control, spotting problems after they happen

cards.q: What is the core idea of zero trust?
cards.a: Never trust, always verify, every request
cards.x: Control plane (policy engine/administrator) and data plane (policy enforcement point).
wrong: Trust everything inside the firewall
Trust verified users forever
Block all traffic

cards.q: What is a gap analysis?
cards.a: Comparing current posture to a desired standard
cards.x: Often measured against frameworks like NIST CSF or ISO 27001.
wrong: A penetration test, actively exploiting weaknesses found
A risk transfer, handing the risk to an insurer
A vulnerability scan, listing weaknesses without exploiting them

cards.q: Why is an alert from a honeypot treated as high-fidelity, unlike an alert from a production IDS?
cards.a: No legitimate user ever touches a honeypot, so any interaction is almost certainly malicious
cards.x: Honeynets, honeyfiles, and honeytokens are related deception tech.
wrong: Because a honeypot blocks the attacker automatically

cards.q: Why does change management matter to security?
cards.a: Unreviewed changes cause outages and vulnerabilities
cards.x: Approval, impact analysis, test results, and a backout plan.
wrong: It speeds up releases by removing review steps
It removes the need for regular patching
It mainly tracks budget approval for IT purchases

decks.title: Threat Actors & Social Engineering
decks.summary: Who attacks, why, and how people get tricked. (Objectives 2.1, 2.2)

cards.q: Which threat actor has the most resources and persistence?
cards.a: Nation-state
cards.x: Often behind APTs (advanced persistent threats).
wrong: Unskilled attacker
Hacktivist
Insider

cards.q: Which actor is motivated by ideology or causes?
cards.a: Hacktivist
cards.x: Defacements and DDoS are common tactics.
wrong: Organized crime
Nation-state
Shadow IT

cards.q: What is shadow IT?
cards.a: Systems or apps used without IT approval
cards.x: Creates unmanaged risk and data leakage.
wrong: Dark web hacking
A type of malware
Encrypted backups

cards.q: What is phishing?
cards.a: Fraudulent messages that trick users into acting
cards.x: Spear phishing targets individuals; whaling targets executives.
wrong: Brute-forcing passwords, guessing them again and again
Scanning ports to find open services
Sniffing Wi-Fi traffic on public networks

cards.q: How does vishing differ from smishing?
cards.a: Vishing uses voice calls; smishing uses SMS text messages — both are phishing by another channel
cards.x: Smishing is via SMS; phishing is via email.
wrong: Vishing uses video calls with a cloned face; smishing uses voice calls — the attacker deepfakes a video call for vishing and reads a script over the phone for smishing
Vishing is malware spread through email; smishing is malware spread through SMS
Vishing targets VPN logins; smishing targets voicemail boxes

cards.q: A caller claims to be from IT, says there is a security incident, and asks for your password to “verify your account”. Which technique is this?
cards.a: Pretexting — inventing a believable scenario to extract information or access
cards.x: Example: posing as IT support needing your password.
wrong: Tailgating, following someone through a door
Typosquatting, registering a lookalike domain

cards.q: How does a watering hole attack differ from a spear-phishing email?
cards.a: A watering hole compromises a site the target group already visits instead of contacting the victim directly
cards.x: Targets a community rather than one person.
wrong: A watering hole floods the group’s website with traffic

A watering hole registers a lookalike of the group’s own domain

cards.q: A user types “gooogle.com” and lands on a fake login page that steals their password. What is this attack called?
cards.a: Typosquatting — registering lookalike domains to catch mistyped URLs
cards.x: Also called URL hijacking; used for phishing and malware.
wrong: DNS poisoning, corrupting the resolver cache entries — the resolver sends gooogle.com visitors to the attacker’s server, so the mistyped domain never matters

Brute-forcing URLs to find hidden pages

cards.q: Finance gets an urgent email from the “CEO” asking for a wire transfer to a new supplier account. No malware is attached. What is this attack?
cards.a: Business email compromise (BEC) — a hijacked or spoofed business email requesting fraudulent payments
cards.x: Verify payment changes out of band, by phone.
wrong: Spam filtering, blocking junk mail before delivery

cards.q: An attacker waits by the office entrance and slips in behind an employee who just badged in. What is this called?
cards.a: Tailgating (piggybacking) — following an authorised person through a secured door
cards.x: Mitigated by access control vestibules (mantraps) and training.
wrong: Shoulder surfing, watching passwords over a shoulder
Dumpster diving, searching discarded papers for secrets
Pretexting, inventing a scenario to extract information — the attacker claimed to be a delivery courier with a package, and the employee held the door open for them

cards.q: Which is the most effective defence against social engineering?
cards.a: Security awareness training plus verification procedures
cards.x: Technical filters help, but people are the target.
wrong: A next-generation firewall with SSL inspection
Faster patching of every endpoint and server
Longer password requirements for all staff

cards.q: What is an attack surface?
cards.a: Every point where an attacker could get in
cards.x: Reduce it by removing unused services, ports, and accounts.
wrong: A defaced website, its homepage replaced by hackers
A firewall rule, blocking one entry point at a time
A DDoS target only, flooded until it stops responding

decks.title: Malware & Attack Indicators
decks.summary: Malware types and signs of compromise. (Objective 2.4)

cards.q: Which malware self-replicates across networks without user action?
cards.a: Worm
cards.x: A virus needs a host file and user action to spread.
wrong: Virus
Trojan
Logic bomb

cards.q: Which malware disguises itself as legitimate software?
cards.a: Trojan
cards.x: Remote access Trojans (RATs) give attackers control.
wrong: Worm
Rootkit
Adware

cards.q: Which malware encrypts files and demands payment?
cards.a: Ransomware
cards.x: Offline, tested backups are the key recovery control.
wrong: Spyware
Keylogger, recording every keystroke typed
Bloatware

cards.q: Which malware hides deep in the OS to conceal itself?
cards.a: Rootkit
cards.x: Kernel rootkits can evade normal tools; reimaging is often safest.
wrong: Worm
Adware
Logic bomb

cards.q: A disgruntled admin plants code that deletes the customer database the day their account is deactivated. What is this malware called?
cards.a: A logic bomb — malicious code that triggers on a condition or date
cards.x: Often planted by insiders.
wrong: A DDoS tool, flooding servers with junk traffic
A phishing kit, ready-made fake login pages
A self-spreading worm, copying itself across networks — the code spreads to every machine it can reach and deletes the database on each one the day the admin leaves

cards.q: Why does fileless malware evade traditional antivirus that scans files on disk?
cards.a: It runs in memory using legitimate tools, leaving no binary on disk for the scanner to find
cards.x: Leaves few files on disk; EDR behaviour monitoring helps.
wrong: Because it has no payload and does nothing harmful
Because it only spreads through USB flash drives — the malware lives on removable media, so a disk scanner on the workstation never sees its files
Because it hides inside browser adverts

cards.q: An attacker rents out thousands of compromised home routers to flood a target. What is that rented network called?
cards.a: A botnet — a network of compromised machines under an attacker’s command, used for DDoS, spam, and credential stuffing
cards.x: Used for DDoS, spam, and credential stuffing. Controlled via C2.
wrong: A cluster of firewalls sharing one policy
A pool of servers behind a load balancer — thousands of rented home routers share one public address, so the flood looks like legitimate load-balanced traffic
A distributed vulnerability scanning platform

cards.q: What is credential stuffing?
cards.a: Trying leaked username/password pairs on other sites
cards.x: Password reuse makes it work. MFA stops most of it.
wrong: Guessing one password across many accounts at once
Stealing cookies, hijacking logged-in browser sessions
Phishing, tricking users with leaked passwords

cards.q: What is password spraying?
cards.a: A few common passwords tried against many accounts
cards.x: Avoids lockouts. Detect by failures spread across accounts.
wrong: Trying many passwords on one account until one works
Rainbow tables, precomputed hashes for fast cracking
Keylogging, recording every keystroke a user types

cards.q: What is an indicator of compromise (IoC)?
cards.a: Evidence that a system may have been breached
cards.x: Examples: known-bad hashes, C2 IPs, impossible travel, odd account lockouts.
wrong: A vulnerability score, rating how bad the breach already is
A firewall rule, allowing only known-good traffic through
A patch note, describing what an update fixes

cards.q: What does "impossible travel" suggest?
cards.a: Account compromise: logins from far-apart places too quickly
cards.x: A key identity threat detection signal.
wrong: A VPN gateway rotating the user's exit IP
A DNS resolver returning the wrong region
Normal behaviour for a frequently travelling user

cards.q: A trusted software update is poisoned at the vendor, and every customer who installs it is compromised. What is this attack?
cards.a: A supply chain attack — compromising a vendor or update channel to reach its customers
cards.x: Examples: SolarWinds (2020), the xz Utils backdoor (2024).
wrong: Stealing delivery trucks full of hardware shipments

DDoS on a warehouse, flooding its ordering systems

decks.title: Cryptography & PKI
decks.summary: Symmetric, asymmetric, hashing, certificates. (Objective 1.4)

cards.q: Symmetric encryption uses…
cards.a: One shared key for encryption and decryption
cards.x: Fast; AES is the standard. Key distribution is the hard part.
wrong: A public and private key pair, two keys together
No key; the algorithm itself is secret
A hash and a salt, for storing passwords safely

cards.q: Asymmetric encryption uses…
cards.a: A public/private key pair
cards.x: RSA and elliptic curve (ECC). Slower, used for key exchange and signatures.
wrong: One shared key used by both sides
A hash function and a salt
A one-time pad shared in advance

cards.q: To send someone a confidential message with asymmetric crypto, encrypt with…
cards.a: The recipient’s public key
cards.x: Only the recipient’s private key can decrypt it.
wrong: Your private key
Your public key
The recipient’s private key

cards.q: To digitally sign a message, you use…
cards.a: Your private key
cards.x: Anyone verifies with your public key: integrity, authentication, non-repudiation.
wrong: Your public key
The recipient’s public key
A shared symmetric key

cards.q: Which is a current recommended symmetric cipher?
cards.a: AES-256
cards.x: DES and 3DES are deprecated.
wrong: DES
RC4
3DES

cards.q: Why is MD5 unsuitable for security?
cards.a: It is vulnerable to collisions
cards.x: Use SHA-256 or SHA-3.
wrong: It is too slow
It is encryption, not hashing — it scrambles data reversibly
It needs a key

cards.q: What does a salt do in password hashing?
cards.a: Adds random data so identical passwords hash differently
cards.x: Defeats precomputed rainbow tables.
wrong: Encrypts the password before it is hashed
Speeds up hashing so logins are faster
Shortens the hash so it takes less storage

cards.q: What does key stretching do?
cards.a: Makes each hash deliberately slow
cards.x: PBKDF2, bcrypt, and Argon2 slow brute force.
wrong: Makes keys longer on disk
Splits keys
Rotates keys

cards.q: What issues and signs digital certificates?
cards.a: A Certificate Authority (CA)
cards.x: Trust chains from the root CA through intermediates to the leaf.
wrong: A DNS server
A registration authority only
A web browser

cards.q: How is a revoked certificate checked quickly?
cards.a: OCSP (often with OCSP stapling)
cards.x: The client asks the CA's OCSP responder about one certificate; stapling lets the server attach a fresh signed response. CRLs are the older list-based method. Since 2025 some public CAs (for example Let's Encrypt) have dropped OCSP in favour of CRLs for privacy reasons.
wrong: DNSSEC, signing DNS records to prove authenticity
A CSR, a certificate signing request
SAN lookup, checking the certificate name list

cards.q: What is a CSR?
cards.a: A certificate signing request sent to a CA
cards.x: Contains the public key and subject details; the private key stays with you.
wrong: A revoked cert list, certificates that are no longer valid
A private key backup, stored somewhere safe offline
A self-signed cert, signed by its own owner

cards.q: What is perfect forward secrecy?
cards.a: Ephemeral keys per session, useless for past sessions
cards.x: Provided by ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE/ECDHE). TLS 1.3 removed the static RSA and static Diffie-Hellman key exchanges that lacked forward secrecy.
wrong: Long-lived keys that are never rotated
Encrypting keys twice, double-wrapping them for extra safety
Storing keys offline, locked away in a safe place forever

cards.q: What is post-quantum cryptography?
cards.a: Algorithms designed to resist attacks by quantum computers
cards.x: NIST standardised ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) in 2024.
wrong: Encryption using quantum computers
A faster AES
A hashing method

puzzles.prompt: Hashing protects integrity. Tamper with the message by changing just one character.
puzzles.x: Any change produces a completely different digest, so comparing hashes detects tampering.

puzzles.x: One bit, 128 in decimal. AES-256 has 2^256 possible keys, far beyond any brute force.

decks.title: Identity & Access Management
decks.summary: MFA, SSO, federation, and access models. (Objective 4.6)

cards.q: What are the MFA factor categories?
cards.a: Something you know, have, or are
cards.x: Two passwords are still one factor.
wrong: Username, password, PIN — three secrets you memorise
Email, SMS, call — three channels for receiving codes
Device, network, app — three things you might own

cards.q: Which MFA method resists phishing best?
cards.a: FIDO2 / passkeys (hardware or platform authenticators)
cards.x: SMS codes can be intercepted via SIM swapping.
wrong: SMS codes, texted to the registered mobile phone number
Email codes, sent to the registered inbox address
Security questions, like the name of your first pet

cards.q: What is SSO?
cards.a: One login grants access to many applications
cards.x: Reduces password fatigue; protect the IdP heavily.
wrong: One password per app, memorised separately
A shared admin account used by the whole team
A VPN, tunnelling logins back to the office network

cards.q: What is SAML used for?
cards.a: XML-based federated web SSO
cards.x: IdP issues assertions to a service provider.
wrong: Encrypting disks
Authorising APIs only
Routing email

cards.q: OAuth 2.0 is primarily for…
cards.a: Delegated authorization
cards.x: OpenID Connect adds authentication (an ID token) on top of OAuth.
wrong: Authentication: proving who the user is
Encryption
Password hashing

cards.q: Which access control model uses labels and clearances?
cards.a: Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
cards.x: Used in military systems; users cannot change permissions.
wrong: DAC, where owners decide who gets access
RBAC, where roles decide who gets access
ABAC, where labels and clearances decide access

cards.q: Which model lets the data owner set permissions?
cards.a: Discretionary Access Control (DAC)
cards.x: Typical of NTFS file shares.
wrong: MAC, where owners decide who gets access
RBAC, where job roles decide who gets access
Rule-based, where fixed rules decide every request

cards.q: Which model grants permissions based on job function?
cards.a: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
cards.x: Assign users to roles; assign permissions to roles.
wrong: DAC, where data owners set their own permissions
MAC, where roles and clearances decide access
ABAC, where job attributes decide who gets access

cards.q: Which model evaluates attributes like department, time, and device?
cards.a: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)
cards.x: Most granular and flexible; common in cloud IAM policies.
wrong: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
Discretionary Access Control (DAC)
Mandatory Access Control (MAC)

cards.q: What does PAM (privileged access management) provide?
cards.a: Vaulting, just-in-time elevation, session recording
cards.x: Reduces standing privilege.
wrong: Password complexity only, longer passwords for admins

Email filtering, blocking phishing aimed at admins

cards.q: What is account provisioning and deprovisioning?
cards.a: Creating accounts at hire, removing access at exit
cards.x: Orphaned accounts after leavers are a common finding.
wrong: Password resets, helping users who have forgotten theirs
MFA enrolment, registering authenticator apps for every user
Backing up accounts, copying user profiles for safekeeping

cards.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
cards.a: Only the access needed to do the job
cards.x: Pair it with regular access reviews to catch privilege creep.
wrong: Give admins everything, full rights from day one
Remove all access, nobody can do anything
Share accounts, one login for the whole team

cards.q: When is the OAuth authorization code flow (with PKCE) used?
cards.a: Whenever a user signs in through a browser: web, mobile and single-page apps
cards.x: RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice, 2025) recommends the authorization code flow with PKCE for all clients. The implicit and resource-owner password grants are deprecated.
wrong: Only for machine-to-machine calls with no user present
Only for input-constrained devices such as smart TVs
Only when the app collects the user's password itself

cards.q: When is the OAuth client credentials grant used?
cards.a: Machine-to-machine communication, no user involved
cards.x: A service authenticates as itself to call an API.
wrong: User login on a website, signing in personally each time
Smart TV login, typing a code from the screen
Password resets, helping users who forgot theirs

cards.q: When is the OAuth device authorization flow used?
cards.a: Input-constrained devices like smart TVs
cards.x: The user approves on a second device by entering a code.
wrong: Web servers, hosting sites and APIs

Email servers, sending and receiving messages

cards.q: What is PKCE for in OAuth?

cards.x: A per-request secret (the code verifier) proves the token request came from the same client that started the flow. RFC 9700 now recommends PKCE for confidential clients too, not only public ones.
wrong: Encrypting passwords, scrambling them before storage
Faster logins, skipping the password step entirely
Blocking bots, stopping automated traffic at the edge

cards.q: OIDC vs SAML: when to choose which?
cards.a: OIDC for modern apps and APIs (JSON/JWT); SAML for legacy enterprise web SSO (XML)
cards.x: Both are federation protocols; OIDC is lighter and mobile-friendly.
wrong: SAML for mobile apps and APIs; OIDC for legacy enterprise SSO
OIDC only for on-premises Windows domain logons
They are identical protocols with different names

cards.q: Kerberos vs SAML vs OIDC: where does each fit?
cards.a: Kerberos on-prem Windows; SAML/OIDC for web federation
cards.x: Kerberos needs direct KDC connectivity, which the internet does not provide.
wrong: Kerberos for web SSO, browsers talking directly to the KDC
SAML for file shares, logging into network folders
OIDC for Windows logon, signing into the desktop

cards.q: What happens in the Kerberos AS exchange?
cards.a: The client authenticates and receives a TGT
cards.x: The TGT is encrypted so only the client can use it.
wrong: The server sends its password across the network
A service ticket is issued for the file server
The user is logged out and must start again

cards.q: What happens in the Kerberos TGS exchange?
cards.a: Presents its TGT, receives a service ticket
cards.x: One TGT yields many service tickets without re-entering credentials.
wrong: The KDC is bypassed entirely, no tickets needed
The password is sent again in clear text
A new TGT is issued, replacing the old one

cards.q: What is the Kerberos authenticator?
cards.a: A timestamp encrypted with the session key, proving the client holds the ticket
cards.x: It prevents replay without resending the password.
wrong: A hash of the user's password sent to the service
An X.509 certificate presented by the client
A second ticket-granting ticket for the same service

cards.q: What is RADIUS used for?
cards.a: Centralised AAA for network access
cards.x: UDP-based; it encrypts only the password, not the whole packet.
wrong: Web single sign-on across SaaS applications
Signing and encrypting email messages
Issuing certificates to network devices

cards.q: What is TACACS+ and how does it differ from RADIUS?
cards.a: Cisco AAA for device admin, TCP-based
cards.x: RADIUS combines authentication and authorization; TACACS+ keeps them distinct.
wrong: A Wi-Fi standard, how wireless clients connect
Identical to RADIUS but over UDP
A VPN protocol, tunnelling traffic to the office

cards.q: RADIUS or TACACS+ for router admin logins?
cards.a: TACACS+: per-command authorization on network devices
cards.x: Use RADIUS for network access (802.1X); TACACS+ for device administration.
wrong: RADIUS always, for every kind of login
Neither; use Telnet, it is simpler and much faster
Both are wrong, use local accounts instead

cards.q: What is MFA fatigue and how do you stop it?
cards.a: Attackers spam push approvals until the user accepts; stop it with number matching or phishing-resistant MFA
cards.x: FIDO2/passkeys eliminate the approve-prompt entirely.
wrong: Users forget passwords after too many forced resets; stop it with longer reset intervals
Too many password complexity rules; stop it by removing special-character requirements
Login pages slow down under load; stop it with a CDN in front of the IdP

cards.q: What is SCIM?
cards.a: Automated user provisioning across SaaS apps
cards.x: Powers joiner-mover-leaver automation from the identity provider.
wrong: A firewall rule, blocking or allowing SaaS logins
A backup format, how copies are stored on disk
A VPN client, tunnelling traffic to the office

cards.q: What is the main risk of SSO?
cards.a: One compromised credential unlocks every connected app
cards.x: Protect the IdP with phishing-resistant MFA, conditional access, and monitoring.
wrong: Slower logins, waiting longer at every sign-in
Too many passwords, one for each application you use
Weaker encryption, easier for attackers to break

decks.title: Security Architecture
decks.summary: Secure design, cloud, IoT/OT, and data protection. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: What are the three data states?
cards.a: At rest, in transit, in use
cards.x: Encrypt at rest (disk), in transit (TLS); in use is protected by secure enclaves.
wrong: Public, private, secret — the classification levels
Hot, warm, cold — how often data is accessed
Raw, processed, archived — the pipeline stages

cards.q: What does tokenization do?
cards.a: Replaces sensitive data with a non-sensitive token
cards.x: Common for card numbers; the mapping lives in a vault.
wrong: Encrypts the data with AES so it can be decrypted later

cards.q: What does data masking do?
cards.a: Hides part of the data, e.g. ****-1234
cards.x: Used for display and non-production environments.
wrong: Deletes data, removing it from the disk entirely
Encrypts data, scrambling it with a secret key
Backs data up, copying it somewhere safe

cards.q: What does DLP do?

cards.x: Endpoint, network, and cloud DLP.
wrong: Blocks all email, nothing gets in or out
Encrypts disks, scrambling everything stored locally
Scans outbound files for malware

cards.q: What is the key risk with ICS/SCADA systems?
cards.a: Old systems, hard to patch, uptime critical
cards.x: Segment OT from IT networks.
wrong: Too much encryption, slowing everything down
Too many updates, breaking things every week
They are always cloud hosted, never on-premises

cards.q: What is infrastructure as code’s security benefit?
cards.a: Consistent, reviewable, repeatable configuration
cards.x: Scan templates for misconfigurations before deployment.
wrong: It removes the need for access control on the pipeline
It makes servers run faster in production
It replaces logging, since every change is in git

cards.q: What does a WAF protect?
cards.a: Web applications, at Layer 7
cards.x: Blocks SQL injection, XSS, and similar attacks.
wrong: Wireless networks, at Layer 2
DNS resolvers, at Layer 7
Physical servers, at the hardware level

cards.q: Why should a new IPS first run in IDS (monitor-only) mode before it starts blocking?
cards.a: To tune out false positives — blocking inline on untuned rules can drop legitimate traffic and cause outages
cards.x: Signature, anomaly, and behavioural detection.
wrong: Because an IPS cannot block until it has an IDS licence
Because IDS mode is only for wireless, never for wired networks

decks.title: Security Operations

cards.x: SOAR adds automated response playbooks.
wrong: Because the SIEM encrypts logs instead of inspecting them

cards.x: XDR extends this across network, cloud, and identity.

wrong: A tabletop is a live failover to the recovery site

decks.title: Application & AI Security

cards.q: A login form builds its query by pasting the username straight into the SQL string. An attacker logs in as admin without a password. Which flaw did they exploit?
cards.a: SQL injection — malicious SQL smuggled in through unsanitised input and run by the database

wrong: Cross-site scripting — the login page reflects the username back into the page, so a script in the username runs in the next visitor’s browser

cards.q: A comment field on a forum lets an attacker store a script that runs in every visitor’s browser. What vulnerability is this?

cards.x: Fix with output encoding and a Content Security Policy.
wrong: Forging requests from a victim, using their logged-in session — the comment field submits a transfer request as the victim, so the forum spends the victim’s money

cards.q: A victim visits a malicious page while logged into their bank, and the page silently submits a transfer request. Which attack is this?

cards.x: Fix with anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies.
wrong: Injecting script that runs in other users’ browsers — the malicious page stores a script in the bank’s comment field, and it runs for every visitor afterwards

cards.x: Mitigated by memory-safe languages, ASLR, and DEP.
wrong: Because memory-safe languages do not use buffers

Because buffer overflows only happen in SQL databases

cards.q: What is input validation?
cards.a: Checking input type, length, and format
cards.x: Validate on the server; client-side checks are easily bypassed.
wrong: Encrypting input, scrambling it before it is stored

Hashing input, turning it into a fixed digest

cards.q: What is code signing for?
cards.a: Proving software came from the publisher unaltered
cards.x: Protects the supply chain and users.
wrong: Encrypting the code so it cannot be read

cards.q: What is SAST vs DAST?

cards.x: Use both in CI/CD.
wrong: Two names for the same scan

cards.x: HSMs (network appliances or PCIe cards) serve many systems; TPMs anchor one machine's boot integrity and disk encryption.
wrong: HSM: a chip on one motherboard; TPM: a shared network appliance

cards.x: You cannot "decrypt" a hash — you can only recompute and compare.

cards.a: On a defined schedule and immediately on suspected compromise or staff departure

wrong: Only when the key expires

cards.x: ECC suits mobile and constrained devices.
wrong: RSA: factoring-based keys are stronger bit for bit than any curve

cards.x: Unlike encryption it hides the existence of the message, not just its content.

cards.q: Obfuscation vs encryption?
cards.a: Obfuscation only makes data hard to read; encryption makes it unreadable without the key
cards.x: Security by obscurity is not a control.
wrong: They are the same thing
Obfuscation is stronger because attackers cannot see the algorithm
Encryption only hides data; obfuscation removes it

cards.q: What problem does a digital signature NOT solve?
cards.a: Confidentiality: a signed message is still readable by anyone
cards.x: Signatures prove origin and integrity, not secrecy — encrypt as well if needed.
wrong: Integrity: detecting whether the message changed after it was signed
Authenticity: proving who sent it
Non-repudiation: the sender cannot deny it

cards.q: HMAC: what does it add over a plain hash?
cards.a: A secret key, so only key holders can create or verify the tag
cards.x: Proves both integrity and authenticity of a message.
wrong: Faster hashing for large messages
A longer digest that resists collisions better than the plain hash
Encryption of the message contents

cards.q: What is key derivation (e.g. HKDF)?
cards.a: Generating multiple working keys from one master secret
cards.x: TLS derives separate encryption and MAC keys per direction from the handshake secret.
wrong: Copying a key to a backup HSM
Replacing a compromised key
Publishing a public key to a directory so others can derive it

cards.q: Why use ephemeral keys in a handshake?
cards.a: Each session gets fresh keys
cards.x: This is the mechanism behind perfect forward secrecy.
wrong: They are cheaper to generate than long-term keys
They never expire during the session
They need no randomness to create

cards.q: A developer hard-codes an AES key in the mobile app. What is wrong?
cards.a: Anyone who downloads the app can extract the key and decrypt everything
cards.x: Keys belong in a keystore, HSM, or derived per device — never in shipped code.
wrong: The key is too short: AES keys in mobile apps must be at least 4096 bits
AES is broken and should not be used
Mobile apps are not allowed to encrypt data

decks.title: Core Security Concepts
decks.summary: CIA, AAA, zero trust, physical security, and design principles. (Domain 1.1–1.3)

cards.q: Ransomware encrypts the file server. Which CIA goals are attacked?
cards.a: Availability first, then confidentiality if data is also stolen
cards.x: Double extortion adds a confidentiality breach to the availability loss.
wrong: Integrity only, because files are modified
None, because no data leaves the network
Confidentiality only, because the encrypted files can no longer be read

cards.q: A database shows wrong account balances but no outage. Which goal failed?
cards.a: Integrity: the data is present and reachable but untrustworthy
cards.x: Backups restore availability; only verified clean copies restore integrity.
wrong: Confidentiality: keeping information away from unauthorised eyes
Authentication: the database never checked who changed the balances
Accountability: nobody logged who changed the balances

cards.q: A DDoS takes the web shop offline during a sale. Which goal?
cards.a: Availability
cards.x: Mitigate with CDN absorption, scrubbing, and rate limiting.
wrong: Confidentiality
Integrity
Authentication

cards.q: An attacker sniffs unencrypted HTTP logins at a café. Which goal?
cards.a: Confidentiality
cards.x: HTTPS everywhere is the fix; HSTS enforces it.
wrong: Availability
Integrity
Accounting

cards.q: RAID, clustering, and generators protect which CIA goal?
cards.a: Availability
cards.x: Redundancy at every layer: power, network, systems, sites.
wrong: Confidentiality
Integrity
Authentication

cards.q: Checksums and version control protect which goal?
cards.a: Integrity
cards.x: They detect unauthorised change, not eavesdropping.
wrong: Confidentiality
Availability
Authorisation

cards.q: Authentication vs authorization vs accounting?
cards.a: Prove identity, grant permissions, log actions
cards.x: You authenticate to the VPN, are authorized to the finance share, and accounting records the access.
wrong: Grant permissions, prove identity, log actions
Prove identity, log actions, grant permissions
Log actions, prove identity, grant permissions

cards.q: What does the accounting part of AAA enable?
cards.a: Audit trails, billing, and forensic reconstruction
cards.x: Without accounting you cannot prove who did what.
wrong: Faster logins, because sessions can be cached and replayed securely
Stronger password enforcement
Encryption of traffic between users

cards.q: A badge opens the door but the log shows no entry. Which AAA failed?
cards.a: Accounting: authentication and authorization worked, the record did not
cards.x: Gaps in accounting blind incident response.
wrong: Authentication: the badge never proved who held it
Authorization: the badge was valid but the door should not have opened
Integrity: the log entries were altered afterwards

cards.q: Zero trust vs the old castle-and-moat model?
cards.a: No implicit trust by network location; verify every request continuously
cards.x: A compromised laptop inside the LAN gets no free pass.
wrong: Trust devices on the LAN; verify remote ones
Trust is based on network location alone
Zero trust keeps the perimeter but moves it from the data centre to the cloud edge

cards.q: What is microsegmentation in zero trust?
cards.a: Dividing the network into tiny isolated zones with per-zone policy
cards.x: Limits lateral movement: breaching one segment does not open the rest.
wrong: Placing guests on a separate VLAN
Routing traffic faster through the core by removing internal firewalls
Merging subnets to simplify policy

cards.q: What does "continuous validation" mean in zero trust?
cards.a: Re-check identity, device health, and context throughout the session
cards.x: A stolen session token alone should not grant lasting access.
wrong: Authenticate once at login, then trust the session until it times out
Re-authenticate users once a year
Check device health only at enrolment

cards.q: Policy engine vs policy administrator vs enforcement point?
cards.a: The engine decides; the administrator acts on the decision; the enforcement point allows or blocks the connection
cards.x: These are the NIST SP 800-207 logical components: the policy administrator configures the policy enforcement point according to the policy engine's decision.
wrong: They are one component with three names
The enforcement point decides; the engine applies the decision
The administrator decides; the engine logs the decision

cards.q: What does "assume breach" change in design?
cards.a: You build detection, segmentation, and least privilege as if attackers are already inside
cards.x: Backups, monitoring, and blast-radius limits become primary controls.
wrong: Monitoring is no longer needed
The perimeter firewall is removed
Strong passwords and perimeter firewalls become the main controls

cards.q: Why does zero trust still need strong identity?
cards.a: Identity becomes the perimeter
cards.x: Weak identity collapses the whole model.
wrong: Identity is optional once devices are trusted
The network location still grants trust
Passwords alone count as strong identity

cards.q: A row of concrete posts blocks the lobby entrance. What are they?
cards.a: Bollards: anti-ram barriers against vehicle attacks
cards.x: Rated by crash standards; part of perimeter physical security.
wrong: Planters
Speed bumps that slow vehicles at the entrance
Flag poles

cards.q: What is a mantrap (access control vestibule)?
cards.a: Two interlocked doors: the second opens only after the first closes and you authenticate
cards.x: Defeats tailgating and piggybacking.
wrong: A revolving door that admits one person at a time after a badge swipe
A turnstile that counts staff in and out
A guarded reception desk

cards.q: Why would a facility install a Faraday cage room?
cards.a: To block all radio signals
cards.x: Protects against wireless exfiltration and eavesdropping.
wrong: To boost Wi-Fi signal strength
To protect equipment from power surges
To keep the room at a stable temperature

cards.q: What attack does a cable lock on a laptop prevent?
cards.a: Opportunistic theft of the device itself
cards.x: It does not stop a determined thief with cutters — layer it with encryption.
wrong: Remote network attacks
Malware infection
Tailgating by someone following staff into the office

cards.q: Where should CCTV cameras go first?
cards.a: Entries, exits, server rooms, and other chokepoints
cards.x: Coverage of high-value areas beats blanket coverage of hallways.
wrong: Car parks only
Every hallway and stairwell, evenly spaced across the building
Break rooms and kitchens

cards.q: Visitor logs and escort policies enforce what?
cards.a: Accountability for non-employees inside secure areas
cards.x: Know who was where, when — and never leave visitors unescorted near sensitive zones.
wrong: Faster visitor check-in
Guest Wi-Fi access
Building occupancy limits set by fire regulations

cards.q: Fingerprint, iris, face, voice: what are these?
cards.a: Biometric authentication factors (something you are)
cards.x: They authenticate identity; they do not replace authorization.
wrong: Knowledge factors (something you know)
Possession factors (something you have), stored on the device
Location factors (somewhere you are)

cards.q: FAR vs FRR in biometrics?
cards.a: False Acceptance Rate vs False Rejection Rate
cards.x: Lowering one raises the other; tune to the risk.
wrong: FAR counts rejections; FRR counts acceptances
Two measures of how fast matching runs
Two measures of cost per enrolment

cards.q: What is CER (crossover error rate)?
cards.a: The point where FAR equals FRR
cards.x: Use it to compare biometric systems objectively.
wrong: The point where FAR is lowest
The rate at which enrolment fails
The average of FAR and FRR

cards.q: Why can’t you revoke a compromised fingerprint?
cards.a: Biometrics are permanent: you cannot issue a new fingerprint
cards.x: Use biometrics for convenience, pair with a revocable factor for high security.
wrong: You can: a new fingerprint template is issued, just like a new password
Fingerprints change every few years
You can revoke it by re-enrolling the same finger

cards.q: Smart card vs hardware token: what do they prove?
cards.a: Possession: something you have
cards.x: Combine with a PIN (knowledge) for true multi-factor.
wrong: Knowledge: something you know
Inherence: something you are
Location: somewhere you are

cards.q: What is defense in depth?
cards.a: Layered controls so one failure does not mean breach
cards.x: If phishing beats training, MFA and EDR still stand in the way.
wrong: One strong perimeter firewall
More complex password rules
Patching faster than attackers can exploit new vulnerabilities

cards.q: What is separation of duties?
cards.a: Splitting critical tasks so no single person can complete fraud alone
cards.x: The person who approves payments cannot also issue them.
wrong: Rotating staff through critical tasks
One trusted administrator for all systems
Sharing one admin account between two people so they can check each other

cards.q: What is implicit deny in access control?
cards.a: Default stance: deny everything not explicitly allowed
cards.x: The safe default behind allow-listing and firewall rules.
wrong: Allow everything not explicitly denied
Deny every request, including those an explicit rule allows
Prompt the user to decide each time

cards.q: Why enforce job rotation?
cards.a: It exposes fraud and removes single points of knowledge
cards.x: Someone covering a role may spot what the regular hid.
wrong: To cover staff holidays
To reduce training costs
To keep employees motivated by giving them varied work

cards.q: Why require mandatory vacations?
cards.a: Fraud that needs constant cover unravels when the person is away
cards.x: A classic anti-fraud control in finance roles.
wrong: To stop staff building up large leave balances the company must pay out
To improve staff morale
Because labour law requires it

cards.q: What is dual control (two-person rule)?
cards.a: Two authorized people required to complete a sensitive action
cards.x: Used for key ceremonies, safe combinations, and large transfers.
wrong: Two passwords required for one account, typed by the same person
Two firewalls in series
Two backup copies of the data

cards.q: "Need to know" limits what?
cards.a: Access to information: only those who require it for their role
cards.x: Classification plus need-to-know equals least privilege for data.
wrong: Network bandwidth per user
The hours of the day when each role is allowed to log in
Which meetings staff can join

cards.q: A policy says screens lock after 5 idle minutes. What kind of control is this?
cards.a: A technical preventive control against unattended access
cards.x: It stops someone using an unattended session; badges, clean-desk rules and disk encryption add further layers.
wrong: A detective control that records idle sessions
A physical control enforced by facilities staff
A corrective control that restores sessions after they are locked

decks.title: SOC Analyst Fundamentals
decks.summary: Triage, logs, alerts, and phishing analysis.

cards.q: What does SOC Tier 1 typically do?
cards.a: Alert triage: validate, enrich, escalate
cards.x: Tier 2 investigates deeper; Tier 3 hunts and handles major incidents.
wrong: Write and tune the SIEM's correlation rules for new threats
Reverse-engineer malware samples
Lead threat hunts and major incidents

cards.q: Windows Event ID 4625 means…
cards.a: A failed logon
cards.x: 4624 = successful logon; 4672 = special privileges assigned.
wrong: A successful logon
A new service was installed
An account was locked out

cards.q: Windows Event ID 4624 means…
cards.a: A successful logon
cards.x: Logon type 10 is RemoteInteractive (RDP).
wrong: A failed logon
An account was locked out
A user account was created

cards.q: Windows Event ID 1102 means…
cards.a: The security audit log was cleared
cards.x: A strong indicator of anti-forensics.
wrong: A user logged off
A service was started
The audit policy was changed to stop logging failures

cards.q: Windows Event ID 4720 means…
cards.a: A user account was created
cards.x: Unexpected accounts are a persistence indicator.
wrong: A user's password was reset
A member was added to a security group
A user account was disabled

cards.q: Which email header field shows the path a message took?
cards.a: Received
cards.x: Read Received headers bottom to top.
wrong: Subject
Reply-To
X-Mailer

cards.q: What do SPF, DKIM, and DMARC do?
cards.a: Authenticate email senders and set a policy for failures
cards.x: SPF = allowed servers; DKIM = signature; DMARC = alignment and policy.
wrong: Encrypt email between mail servers so that messages cannot be read in transit
Filter spam by scoring keywords
Scan attachments for known malware

cards.q: Your SOC gets 10,000 alerts a day and analysts start ignoring them. What is this called, and what is the fix?
cards.a: Alert fatigue — analysts overwhelmed by noisy alerts miss real ones; fix by tuning detections, suppressing known-good, and automating enrichment
cards.x: Tune detections, suppress known-good, automate enrichment.
wrong: The SIEM silently dropping events once it passes its licence limit — when the queue fills up, the oldest alerts vanish before any analyst ever sees them
Analysts working too many overnight shifts
Log storage filling up and losing old alerts

cards.q: What is Sysmon?
cards.a: A free Microsoft tool that logs detailed process, network, and file events
cards.x: Event ID 1 = process creation with the full command line.
wrong: A log forwarder that ships Windows events to a SIEM unchanged
A built-in task manager for running processes
A packet capture tool for Windows hosts

cards.q: What is a sandbox in malware analysis?
cards.a: An isolated environment to safely run suspicious files
cards.x: Observe behaviour: files dropped, registry keys, network calls.
wrong: A network share where analysts keep copies of samples for later review
A copy of production data for testing
A decoy system that lures attackers

cards.q: What does a file hash lookup (e.g. VirusTotal) tell you?
cards.a: Whether the exact file is known to be malicious
cards.x: A single changed byte changes the hash, so absence proves little.
wrong: Who wrote the file and when it was compiled
Whether any variant of the malware family is present
That the file is safe if no engine flags it

cards.q: What does "true positive" mean for an alert?
cards.a: The alert fired and the activity was malicious
cards.x: Track TP/FP rates to measure detection quality.
wrong: The alert fired, but investigation showed the activity was benign
A real attack happened and no alert fired
A test alert generated during a drill

cards.q: A server runs Telnet, FTP, and an old SMB version. What is the FIRST hardening step?
cards.a: Disable unneeded services and close unused ports
cards.x: Reduce the attack surface before patching: if nothing is listening, nothing can be exploited.
wrong: Put a new firewall in front of the server
Change every account password on the server
Enable detailed logging on the server and keep the services running

cards.q: What is OS hardening?
cards.a: Securing an OS by removing defaults, closing ports, and applying baselines
cards.x: Use CIS Benchmarks or STIGs as the starting template.
wrong: Installing antivirus on the host
Encrypting the system disk
Taking regular backups of the host so it can be rebuilt after an attack

cards.q: BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS — what do they have in common?
cards.a: Full-disk encryption for Windows, macOS, and Linux
cards.x: Protects data at rest if the device is lost or stolen.
wrong: Host firewalls for each operating system
VPN clients built into each operating system
Malware scanners built into Windows, macOS and Linux

cards.q: EDR vs traditional antivirus: what is the key difference?
cards.a: EDR records behaviour and enables response; AV mostly matches signatures
cards.x: AV asks "is this known bad?"; EDR asks "what did this process just do?"
wrong: AV records behaviour and responds; EDR matches signatures
EDR runs without any agent on the endpoint
They differ only in licence cost

cards.q: Why does Security+ prefer application allow-listing over block-listing?
cards.a: Default-deny: only approved software runs, stopping unknown malware
cards.x: Block-listing chases an infinite list of badness.
wrong: It is cheaper to buy and run than any block-listing or antivirus product
Users find it less restrictive
It never needs updating once deployed

cards.q: What is a host-based firewall’s job vs a network firewall’s?
cards.a: Controls traffic on that single machine, even off the corporate network
cards.x: Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security is the common example.
wrong: It replaces antivirus on the endpoint
It encrypts all traffic leaving the machine, even on untrusted networks
It filters traffic for the whole subnet

cards.q: A kiosk PC must boot the same clean image every restart. Which control?
cards.a: Reboot-to-restore or write-protected baseline image
cards.x: Prevents persistence of any change, malicious or accidental.
wrong: Stronger local administrator passwords on the kiosk
Full-disk encryption on the kiosk
Application allow-listing alone

cards.q: Patch Tuesday is monthly, but a critical RCE under active exploitation is published two days later. What now?
cards.a: Out-of-band emergency patching per the patch management policy
cards.x: Microsoft's Patch Tuesday is the second Tuesday of each month. Criticality and active exploitation override the normal cadence.
wrong: Wait for next month's Patch Tuesday and patch then
Disconnect affected servers from the internet until next month's cycle
Reinstall the operating system on affected hosts

cards.q: What does "secure baseline" mean in hardening?
cards.a: An approved, locked-down configuration every system is compared against
cards.x: Drift from baseline triggers remediation.
wrong: The vendor's factory default configuration
The newest available operating system version with default settings
An encrypted backup of a known-good system

cards.q: Why disable Autorun/AutoPlay on Windows hosts?
cards.a: USB-borne malware would otherwise execute on insert
cards.x: A classic initial-access vector; disable via GPO.
wrong: It slows down boot and logon times
It uses too much memory on older hosts and slows down logons
It conflicts with printer drivers

cards.q: What is a CMDB used for in security operations?
cards.a: A single inventory of assets, owners, and configurations
cards.x: You cannot protect or patch what you do not know exists.
wrong: A vault for storing and rotating service account passwords
A tool that blocks malware on endpoints
A system that encrypts backups

cards.q: Why tag assets (e.g. "crown-jewel", "pci-scope")?
cards.a: So controls, monitoring, and incident priority follow asset value
cards.x: Tagging drives data classification and handling rules.
wrong: To track physical items such as desks and chairs for the facilities team
To document assets for insurance claims
To slow attackers who scan the network

cards.q: Data is labelled Public, Internal, Confidential. What is this?
cards.a: Data classification driving handling and protection requirements
cards.x: Classification decides encryption, sharing, and retention rules.
wrong: A backup tiering scheme
A firewall zone naming policy
A retention schedule saying how long each type of document is kept

cards.q: A decommissioned drive held customer PII. How must it be disposed?
cards.a: Sanitised (purged or destroyed) per NIST SP 800-88
cards.x: Clear, Purge or Destroy according to the media and its sensitivity; a delete or quick format is not enough for PII.
wrong: Quick-formatted once, then resold
Deleted file by file, then donated
Stored in a locked cupboard indefinitely in case it is needed

cards.q: What is the difference between wiping and degaussing?
cards.a: Wiping overwrites data; degaussing scrambles magnetic media with magnets
cards.x: Degaussing ruins HDDs and tapes but does nothing to SSDs or flash.
wrong: They are the same process with different names
Wiping is physical; degaussing is software
Degaussing encrypts data so it can be recovered later

cards.q: Why does asset inventory matter for vulnerability management?
cards.a: You can only scan and patch the assets you know exist
cards.x: Unknown assets are unpatched assets.
wrong: It is mainly needed to pass audits, not to find vulnerabilities
It frees disk space on the scanner
It makes scans run faster on Wi-Fi

cards.q: What does NAC check before letting a device on the network?
cards.a: Identity plus health: patched, AV current, compliant configuration
cards.x: Non-compliant devices are quarantined or remediated.
wrong: The user's job title and department, read from the HR system
The device's purchase date and warranty
The time of day the device connects

cards.q: 802.1X in one sentence?
cards.a: Port-based authentication: a device must authenticate before the switch port opens
cards.x: Uses EAP, commonly with RADIUS, on wired and WPA2/3-Enterprise wireless.
wrong: A shared Wi-Fi password for the whole office
A RADIUS server that stores every network password
An encryption cipher for switch ports

cards.q: Agent-based vs agentless NAC?
cards.a: An installed agent reports deep health; agentless probes with less detail
cards.x: Agentless suits BYOD and IoT that cannot run agents.
wrong: Agents are always better, because they never need updating once installed
Agentless works without any network connection
Agentless sees more detail than an installed agent

cards.q: Pre-admission vs post-admission NAC?
cards.a: Check before access vs continuously monitor after access is granted
cards.x: Post-admission catches a healthy device that later becomes compromised.
wrong: Pre-admission checks guests only; staff skip it
Post-admission needs no agent or monitoring
Post-admission checks run first, before access is granted

cards.q: Endpoint DLP vs network DLP: what is the difference?
cards.a: Endpoint DLP watches the device; network DLP inspects egress traffic
cards.x: Cloud DLP (CASB) covers SaaS. Layer them.
wrong: Endpoint DLP is cheaper, so network DLP is unnecessary once it is deployed
Network DLP is faster, so endpoint DLP is unnecessary
They conflict and cannot run together

cards.q: An engineer emails 500 SSNs to a personal address. Which control should catch it?
cards.a: DLP with PII patterns on email egress
cards.x: Tune patterns so legitimate work is not blocked.
wrong: Antivirus on the mail server
The email archiving system
Full-disk encryption on the engineer's laptop

cards.q: What does DNS filtering block?
cards.a: Resolution of known-malicious domains: phishing, C2, malware delivery
cards.x: Stops the connection before it starts, for any protocol.
wrong: Spam and phishing emails, before they are delivered to users' inboxes
Slow websites that waste bandwidth
Pop-up advertisements in browsers

cards.q: Why filter DNS instead of only filtering web URLs?
cards.a: DNS covers every protocol and app
cards.x: Malware using its own resolver (DoH) is the bypass to watch for.
wrong: DNS filtering is cheaper than URL filtering
URLs cannot be filtered over HTTPS
Browsers do not use DNS for web traffic

cards.q: A web filter blocks "gambling" and "adult" categories. What is it filtering by?
cards.a: URL/content category set by policy
cards.x: Also used for bandwidth and liability control.
wrong: The destination IP address
The hash of each downloaded file
The size of each packet

cards.q: What does JML stand for in identity lifecycle?
cards.a: Joiner, Mover, Leaver: provision, adjust, deprovision access with role changes
cards.x: Automate it from the HR system to kill orphaned accounts.
wrong: Join, Manage, Lock: three stages of account security
Java Management Layer: a framework for directory services
Joiner, Member, Leaver: provision, group, remove

cards.q: An employee is terminated Friday at 5pm. When should access be revoked?
cards.a: Immediately at termination, automated from HR
cards.x: Orphaned accounts are a top insider-threat vector.
wrong: On Monday morning, when IT is back
After 30 days, once the handover and knowledge transfer are complete
Never; keep it open for forensics

cards.q: Rank by phishing resistance: SMS codes, authenticator app, hardware key
cards.a: Hardware key > authenticator app > SMS
cards.x: SMS falls to SIM swapping; push alone suffers MFA fatigue.
wrong: SMS > authenticator app > hardware key
All three are equally phishing-resistant
Authenticator app > hardware key > SMS

cards.q: What does SSO give the security team besides convenience?
cards.a: One place to enforce MFA, login policy, and deprovisioning
cards.x: But it becomes a single point of failure — harden the IdP.
wrong: Faster network connections, because sessions are cached at the edge
Lower licence costs for every app
It removes passwords entirely

cards.q: SAML vs OIDC in one line each?
cards.a: SAML: XML-based SSO for enterprise apps; OIDC: modern JSON/REST SSO on OAuth2
cards.x: Both let one identity provider vouch for you to many apps.
wrong: SAML: JSON/REST SSO on OAuth2; OIDC: XML-based enterprise SSO
SAML is for Wi-Fi logins; OIDC is for VPNs
OIDC is for disk encryption; SAML for web logins

cards.q: What is privileged access management (PAM)?
cards.a: Vaulting, rotating and just-in-time issuing of admin credentials
cards.x: No standing domain-admin passwords; check out access per session.
wrong: Giving every IT employee admin rights
A password manager for personal logins
Disabling all admin accounts permanently

cards.q: Why run periodic access reviews (recertification)?
cards.a: To remove accumulated, unneeded permissions
cards.x: Managers attest their team’s access is still required.
wrong: To cancel unused software licences
To meet a requirement for joining the corporate Wi-Fi
To speed up sign-ins for users

cards.q: A service account password has not changed in 4 years. What is the risk?
cards.a: Long-lived, rarely monitored credentials are ideal attacker persistence
cards.x: Rotate, vault, and scope service accounts to least privilege.
wrong: It will expire soon and break the service
Its age proves the password is strong
There is no risk if nobody logs in with it

cards.q: What is just-in-time (JIT) admin access?
cards.a: Elevated rights granted for a limited window, then auto-revoked
cards.x: Removes standing privilege without slowing real work.
wrong: Permanent admin rights for on-call staff
Admin rights granted on weekends only
A shared admin password that is checked out by email when needed

cards.q: An audit finds 40 enabled accounts for departed staff. What is the FIRST fix?
cards.a: Disable them now
cards.x: A process failure, not just a cleanup task.
wrong: Delete the audit logs that list them
Email the former employees to confirm
Leave them until the next quarterly review

decks.title: Threat Actors & Attack Vectors

cards.q: APT vs opportunistic attacker: what is the difference?
cards.a: APTs are resourced, patient, targeted; opportunistic actors spray broadly

Testing tools for later sale

cards.q: Name the three insider threat types.

wrong: Admin, user and guest insiders

cards.x: They run ransomware-as-a-service like a business.

Research curiosity and finding new vulnerabilities
National defence

cards.q: What is the risk of shadow IT?
