wrong: Exempt the legacy order system from scanning and record it as an accepted risk
Scan it more aggressively
Stop scanning it entirely

cards.q: Mean time to remediate criticals has climbed from 9 to 41 days over two quarters, while closed-ticket counts look great. What is the most defensible read?
cards.a: The program is optimising easy wins: track ageing and exposure-weighted metrics
cards.x: When MTTR climbs while closures look good, the team is closing easy findings. Leadership needs aging and exposure-weighted metrics, not counts.
wrong: The program is improving, because the closed-ticket count is the best measure of remediation work
Metrics do not matter
The remediation team is too slow and needs replacing

decks.title: Security Architecture: Cloud & Virtualization Scenarios
decks.summary: Shared responsibility, IaC, containers, and cloud controls as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: A junior admin makes an S3 bucket public “temporarily” to share a build, and access logs show anonymous GETs for three days before anyone notices. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Restrict the bucket to private immediately, scope exactly what was accessed from the logs, and trigger the breach-notification process with legal if customer data was involved
cards.x: A public bucket is a finding; anonymous downloads make it a breach. Remediation is instant, but the logs decide whether notification duties trigger.
wrong: Make it private and close the ticket, since three days is a short window and the build was not sensitive
Treat public buckets as a normal way to share builds
Discipline the junior admin and move on

cards.q: A developer runs company workloads in a personal AWS account “because procurement is slow”. The account has no CloudTrail and no SSO. What is the most defensible move?
cards.a: Migrate the workloads into the organization with SSO, SCPs and logging, and fix the procurement bottleneck
cards.x: Shadow cloud has no logging, no guardrails, no offboarding — work that lives outside the organization boundary is invisible to security.
wrong: Approve it as a pilot and leave it running in the personal account until procurement catches up
Treat it as the developer's personal problem
Block his corporate card

cards.q: A CSPM scan flags 300 security groups open to 0.0.0.0/0 across 12 accounts. The app teams say “some of those are needed”. What is the most defensible approach?
cards.a: Triage before touching anything: classify by exposure, narrow the needed rules, and remove the rest
cards.x: Blindly deleting 300 rules is an outage; ignoring them is exposure. The defensible path is classify, narrow, and control.
wrong: Delete all 300 rules at once and let the app teams raise tickets for whatever breaks afterwards
Leave them until something bad happens
Open a ticket per rule and wait

cards.q: Friday’s deploy went fine, but Monday’s Terraform plan shows 40 resources drifted from code after a weekend hotfix. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Reconcile the hotfix into code and re-apply so the state matches
cards.x: Drift is debt with a timer: the longer hotfixes live outside code, the more the next deploy surprises you. Codify it or lose the audit trail.
wrong: Ignore the drift, since the hotfix works and the next planned deploy will overwrite it anyway
Delete the resources and redeploy from code
Disable Terraform plans

cards.q: A serverless function processes payments with an IAM role that has AdministratorAccess “because the docs example did”. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Scope the role to exactly the APIs the function calls, per function, with no wildcards
cards.x: Ephemeral code with standing admin privilege is the worst of both worlds: tiny blast radius only if the role is tiny. Scope it to the function’s actual calls.
wrong: Keep admin, because serverless functions are short-lived and an attacker cannot keep a foothold in them
Leave it; functions are too small to be attacked
Add more permissions to be safe

cards.q: The container registry allows pushing unsigned images, and production deploys whatever is tagged latest. What is the most defensible control?
cards.a: Require signed images and enforce an admission policy so only signed images run in production
cards.x: Unsigned images in prod mean anyone with push access owns the cluster. Signing plus admission control makes the registry a gate, not a shelf.
wrong: Pin production to specific version tags instead of latest, and trust any image pushed to the internal registry
Leave it; signing slows developers down
Treat internal images as trusted

cards.q: A pen test shows the web app is vulnerable to SSRF, and the cloud metadata service still runs in IMDSv1 mode. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Enforce IMDSv2, which requires a session token, and fix the SSRF
cards.x: SSRF to 169.254.169.254 is the classic cloud credential theft: IMDSv2 breaks the one-request theft by requiring a PUT for the token first.
wrong: Block 169.254.169.254 in the application code only, and keep IMDSv1 for compatibility with older tools
Keep IMDSv1 behind the firewall
Treat SSRF as low severity

cards.q: The CI system deploys to Kubernetes with a cluster-admin service account. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Replace it with a namespace-scoped role granting only the verbs the pipeline needs
cards.x: Automation with cluster-admin is standing privilege that never sleeps: a compromised pipeline token becomes a cluster takeover. Scope the role to the job.
wrong: Keep cluster-admin but rotate the service account token every month and alert on unusual use
Keep it; CI needs admin to work
Treat service accounts as untouchable

cards.q: The company runs AWS, Azure, and GCP, and nobody can list all production assets in one place. What is the most defensible first step?
cards.a: Aggregate into one inventory with consistent tagging via a CSPM or CMDB
cards.x: Multi-cloud without a single asset view is three blind spots. Tagging standards plus aggregation turn sprawl into an inventory.
wrong: Let each cloud team keep its own asset list, and merge the three lists into a spreadsheet each quarter
Rely on the cloud bills to show assets
Treat visibility as a nice-to-have

cards.q: EU customers learn their data sits in a US region, and the contracts promise EU residency. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Migrate the data to an EU region and document the residency control
cards.x: Data residency is decided by contracts and regulators, not latency. When the contract says EU, the region choice is compliance, not convenience.
wrong: Keep the data in the US region but encrypt it, since encryption makes its physical location irrelevant
Explain that the cloud is global
Ask customers not to worry

cards.q: Development, staging, and production all live in one AWS account to “keep billing simple”. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Separate accounts under the organization with SCP guardrails
cards.x: One account means one failure domain: a dev mistake can delete prod, and you cannot tell whose spend is whose. Accounts are the cloud’s cheapest isolation.
wrong: Keep one account but separate environments with tags and IAM conditions on every resource
Keep one account for simplicity
Accept the risk for simpler billing

cards.q: CloudTrail is disabled in two regions “to save on storage costs”. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Re-enable it everywhere immediately — audit logging is not an optional line item
cards.x: The regions without trails are the regions attackers will find. Logging is the cheapest control in the building; cutting it is not savings.
wrong: Leave it, since attackers mainly target the primary region where all production workloads run
Treat storage costs as a fair trade-off
Enable it only after an incident

cards.q: API keys are committed in the mobile app’s repo and also baked into the container image. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Rotate every exposed key now, move secrets to a vault injected at runtime, and add secret scanning to CI
cards.x: A committed secret is a public secret: rotation closes the window, but only vault-at-runtime plus scanning keeps it closed.
wrong: Leave the keys in place, since the repository is private and the image is in a private registry
Rotate them at the next release
Obfuscate the keys in the code

cards.q: The golden image pipeline broke two years ago, so every new VM starts from a 2023 base and gets patched at boot. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Rebuild the pipeline: a minimal hardened base, monthly rebuilds, and scanning before deploy
cards.x: Images rot: every manual patch at boot is an untested, unaudited snowflake. Build once, scan it, deploy it everywhere.
wrong: Keep patching at boot, since the end state is the same as a fresh image and it avoids pipeline work
Drop golden images as outdated
Keep the 2023 base

cards.q: A SaaS vendor you depend on announces a breach exposing customer data you store with them. What remains YOUR responsibility?
cards.a: Your users, access controls, data classification, sharing settings, and your own incident response
cards.x: Shared responsibility does not end at the vendor’s breach notification: your half of the model is still yours. Review your side, rotate keys, audit sharing.
wrong: Nothing, because the vendor's breach is the vendor's responsibility under the shared responsibility model
Migrate to a new vendor immediately
Sue the vendor

cards.q: The lift-and-shift migration kept the on-prem flat firewall rules “for compatibility”. What is the most defensible redesign?
cards.a: Rebuild with tiered security groups and subnets for web, app and data
cards.x: Lift-and-shift carries the old weaknesses along: compatibility with a bad design is not a reason to keep it. Segment in the cloud’s own primitives.
wrong: Keep the flat rules for compatibility and add a cloud firewall in front of the whole environment
Rely on the provider to segment it
Keep the flat network for speed

cards.q: A cryptominer is found on a production VM, and the bill spiked 40%. What is the most defensible first action?
cards.a: Isolate the instance, preserve it for forensics, rotate any credentials it could reach
cards.x: Mining is a symptom of compromise, not a billing problem: the instance is evidence, and the attacker’s keys are still valid until rotated.
wrong: Terminate the instance immediately to stop the cost, and raise a ticket to check the other instances
Treat it as a cost problem only
Increase the budget and pay the bill

cards.q: An internal API has no authentication “because it is only reachable internally”. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Add authentication and authorisation anyway; internal reachability is not a control
cards.x: The perimeter is porous: once an attacker is inside, unauthenticated “internal” APIs are free moves. Authenticate every API.
wrong: Leave it, since only internal systems can reach it and the perimeter firewall blocks outside access
Add authentication only after an attack
Treat internal APIs as trusted

cards.q: A cross-account role trusts “*” as the principal for “flexibility”. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Scope the trust policy to the specific account and role, and require an external ID for third-party access
cards.x: A wildcard principal is an open door with a welcome mat: trust policies must name exactly who may assume the role, and external IDs stop confused-deputy attacks.
wrong: Keep the wildcard but add a condition requiring MFA, so only authenticated callers can assume the role
Assume the wildcard only covers your accounts
Treat trust policies as advisory

cards.q: The entire platform runs in one region; the DR plan says “we will figure it out”. What is the most defensible architecture?
cards.a: At minimum multi-AZ for resilience, with a tested cross-region plan only if the RTO/RPO justify the cost
cards.x: Region choice is a business decision expressed in RTO/RPO: multi-AZ survives datacenter loss, cross-region survives regional loss, and both need testing.
wrong: Keep one region, since major cloud providers are designed never to lose a whole region
Leave DR plans to banks
Treat multi-region as wasted spend

cards.q: Compliance requires dedicated cryptographic hardware, but the team proposes KMS. What is the most defensible choice?
cards.a: If the requirement is dedicated, single-tenant HSMs under your exclusive control, use CloudHSM
cards.x: AWS KMS runs on FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs, but they are multi-tenant; when the auditor requires dedicated hardware boundaries, only a dedicated HSM satisfies it.
wrong: KMS is always sufficient, because its HSMs are FIPS validated and that is what every standard asks for
Dedicated hardware is always better
Treat compliance requirements as suggestions

cards.q: Three-year-old IAM users with console access and no MFA belong to people who left. What is the most defensible program fix?
cards.a: Deprovision immediately and institute quarterly access reviews with automated deprovisioning on HR events
cards.x: Orphaned accounts are standing invitations: the fix is joiner-mover-leaver automation so access dies when employment does.
wrong: Disable console access for the old users but keep their access keys in case automation depends on them
Leave them in case the people return
Treat dormant accounts as harmless

cards.q: Cloud backups live in the same account as production, and ransomware just encrypted both. What is the most defensible redesign?
cards.a: A separate backup account with Object Lock immutability
cards.x: A backup an attacker can delete is a copy, not a recovery plan. Immutability plus a separate account puts recovery outside the blast radius.
wrong: Back up hourly within the same account so that a recent copy is always available after an attack
Keep same-account backups for simplicity
Encrypt the backups with a stronger key

cards.q: The API gateway fronts 200 microservices with a single shared API key. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Per-client credentials with scopes, rotation and per-key rate limiting
cards.x: A shared key means one leak revokes everyone or revokes nobody: per-client keys make compromise survivable.
wrong: Keep the shared key but rotate it every year and limit it to internal IP ranges
Use no keys for internal APIs
Keep one shared key for simplicity

cards.q: A production app authenticates to AWS with a static access key baked into the AMI, and the key is two years old. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Replace it with an IAM role attached to the instance
cards.x: Static keys are standing credentials that never expire on their own: roles for compute give the same access with no secret to steal, and rotation is automatic.
wrong: Rotate the static access key every year and store it in an environment variable instead of the AMI
Leave it, since private AMIs are safe
Move the key into the application config file

resources.title: NIST SP 800-210 — General Access Control Guidance for Cloud Systems

decks.title: Security Architecture: Network Design Scenarios
decks.summary: Segmentation, zero trust, VPN choices, and secure topologies as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: After a breach, the forensics team reports the attacker crossed from a phishing laptop to the domain controllers in 40 minutes on a flat /16. What is the most defensible architectural fix?
cards.a: Segment into tiered networks with firewall-enforced flows between user, server and DC tiers
cards.x: Lateral movement speed is a network-design metric: flat networks are a single failure domain. Segmentation turns a 40-minute domain takeover into a contained host.
wrong: Keep the flat network but deploy EDR to every host, so that lateral movement is detected and blocked by the agents
Shorten password expiry for all domain accounts
Add a second domain controller for resilience

cards.q: A vendor needs access to one database for a week. The current answer is a full-tunnel VPN to the whole network. What is the most defensible alternative?
cards.a: Per-application access via ZTNA or a jump host with scoped credentials and session recording, time-boxed to the engagement
cards.x: A week of full-network VPN for one database is standing over-privilege: grant the application, not the network, and expire it automatically.
wrong: Keep the full-tunnel VPN but disable the vendor's account at the end of the week by hand
Give the vendor a domain admin account for the week
Open the firewall to the vendor's office IP

cards.q: Thirty branches run expensive MPLS; the proposal is SD-WAN with internet underlay. What is the most defensible evaluation?
cards.a: Compare an encrypted overlay with centralised policy and monitoring against the MPLS cost and risk
cards.x: The transport decision is threat-model plus cost: unencrypted SD-WAN is just the internet, while MPLS bought you a private path you are giving up.
wrong: Keep MPLS, because a private carrier circuit is always more secure than any encrypted overlay on the internet
Move to SD-WAN without encryption, since it is cheaper
Leave branch security to local staff

cards.q: Remote staff still use a legacy VPN concentrator, and helpdesk sees weekly credential-phishing reports. What is the most defensible direction?
cards.a: Migrate to ZTNA with device posture checks and phishing-resistant MFA
cards.x: VPN credentials are a single phishable secret guarding the whole network: ZTNA shrinks the blast radius to the one application.
wrong: Require longer VPN passwords that change every 60 days, with a lockout after three failed attempts
Run more phishing training for remote staff
Treat the VPN as zero trust already

cards.q: The OT network that runs the factory floor is routable from the corporate LAN “for convenience”. What is the most defensible architecture?
cards.a: Isolate OT behind a DMZ or data diode with only required flows, and monitor the boundary
cards.x: IT/OT convergence without a boundary puts production lines one phishing email from the helpdesk: the diode or firewall makes the crossing deliberate.
wrong: Keep it routable but add an antivirus product to every engineering workstation on the OT network
Leave it; OT systems are not targeted
Keep the convenience and monitor later

cards.q: Guest Wi-Fi shares a VLAN with the point-of-sale terminals. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Separate SSID on its own VLAN with client isolation and a captive portal
cards.x: A guest device on the POS VLAN is a PCI failure and a pivot away from card data: segmentation is the control, not hoping guests behave.
wrong: Keep the shared VLAN but require a guest password that changes every week at reception
Rely on the POS encryption
Leave it; guests are trusted visitors

cards.q: Two hundred employees share one WPA2 pre-shared key, and the password is on a sticky note in the break room. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Move to enterprise 802.1X with per-user or per-device credentials
cards.x: Shared keys fail twice: you cannot tell who connected, and one departure forces a building-wide rotation. Per-user credentials fix both.
wrong: Switch to WPA3-Personal with a new shared password that is changed every quarter
Change the sticky-note password monthly
Keep the PSK, which is fine for offices

cards.q: An employee plugs in a personal travel router to “get better Wi-Fi”. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Remove it, scan for rogue devices with WIDS, and enforce port security plus 802.1X so unauthorized devices cannot join
cards.x: Rogue APs bridge your secured network to an uncontrolled one: detection finds them, 802.1X and port security keep them off.
wrong: Ask the employee to remove it, and send a reminder to all staff that personal routers are not allowed
Leave it, since better Wi-Fi helps productivity
Ignore it; rogue access points are harmless

cards.q: The new IPS is inline and immediately starts blocking legitimate payroll traffic. What is the most defensible deployment?
cards.a: Run in detect-only mode first, tune out false positives, then enable blocking in stages
cards.x: Inline blocking with untuned signatures is a self-inflicted outage: the defensible rollout is IDS-mode tuning, then staged prevention.
wrong: Keep blocking, because an IPS that blocks immediately proves that it is working, and add payroll exceptions as complaints arrive
Disable the IPS permanently
Let payroll wait until tuning is done

cards.q: The DMZ web server has a direct rule to the internal database on 1433. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Remove it: the web tier talks to an app tier, and only the app tier reaches the database on required ports
cards.x: A compromised web server with a direct DB path is game over: tiering means each layer only reaches the next, never skips.
wrong: Keep the rule but restrict it to the web server's IP address and log every connection to the database
Leave it, since direct access is faster
Trust the DMZ, since it is firewalled

cards.q: The jump server — the only path into the server VLAN — has no MFA and keeps a shared admin password. What is the most defensible hardening?
cards.a: Enforce MFA, per-admin accounts, session recording, and source allow-listing
cards.x: A bastion concentrates all admin access: without MFA and individual accountability, one phished password owns every server.
wrong: Rotate the shared admin password every month and limit the jump server to office hours only
Leave it, since the bastion is internal
Require MFA only for remote users

cards.q: IPv6 is enabled by default on all hosts but no firewall rules or monitoring cover it. What is the most defensible posture?
cards.a: Either manage it — firewall rules, RA guard, monitoring — or disable it where unused
cards.x: Attackers love the protocol you forgot: IPv6 tunnels and rogue RAs bypass IPv4-only controls. Managed or off, never ignored.
wrong: Leave IPv6 enabled and unmonitored, since attackers rarely use it inside corporate networks
Leave it; IPv6 is the future
Disable IPv6 everywhere, including where it is needed

cards.q: The SOC sees DNS queries to random-looking domains every 30 seconds from a finance workstation. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Isolate the host, force DNS through the internal resolvers, and inspect the queries
cards.x: DNS is the covert channel that firewalls wave through: periodic random domains are the tell. Force DNS through your resolvers and watch.
wrong: Treat it as Windows telemetry or update checks, which often query many generated domain names
Block the workstation's internet access permanently
Treat DNS as always benign

cards.q: There is no packet capture or flow data at the internet edge — “the firewall logs are enough”. What is the most defensible addition?
cards.a: Full packet capture or at minimum NetFlow plus an NDR sensor at the edge
cards.x: Firewall logs are the bouncer’s diary: for forensics you need the actual traffic. Capture at the chokepoint before you need it.
wrong: Keep relying on the firewall logs, which already record every allowed and denied connection at the edge
Skip capture as too expensive
Assume cloud traffic has no edge to capture

cards.q: VoIP phones share the data VLAN with workstations. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: A dedicated voice VLAN with 802.1X authentication for the phones
cards.x: Mixed voice and data means eavesdropping and toll fraud ride the same wire: a voice VLAN with authentication separates them.
wrong: Keep voice on the data VLAN but turn on SRTP encryption for every call, which makes separation unnecessary
Treat voice as low risk
Treat voice VLANs as overkill

cards.q: The entire datacenter hangs off one core switch with no redundancy. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Build a redundant core and distribution design with no single points of failure
cards.x: Redundancy belongs where failure hurts most: one core switch means one failed power supply away from a total outage.
wrong: Buy a spare core switch and keep it boxed in the data centre, ready to swap in after a failure
Accept the risk; switches rarely fail
Leave redundancy to hyperscalers

cards.q: All branch traffic backhauls through headquarters, and video calls crawl. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Local internet breakout with SASE policy enforcement
cards.x: Hairpinning SaaS traffic through HQ made sense in 2010: split-tunnel with cloud-delivered security keeps policy without the trombone.
wrong: Keep backhauling through headquarters, since central inspection is more secure, and upgrade the HQ link
Accept slower calls at every branch
Block internet at branches entirely

cards.q: A MAC-flooding attack crashes the access switch’s CAM table, turning it into a hub. What is the most defensible mitigation?
cards.a: Port security with MAC limits, sticky learning, and violation shutdown
cards.x: CAM exhaustion is physics: limit addresses per port and shut violators down. The switch stops being a switch only if you let it.
wrong: Replace the switch with a larger model that has a bigger CAM table, so flooding takes longer to work
Ignore it; MAC flooding is theoretical
Leave it; hubs are fine internally

cards.q: Cameras, badge readers, and HVAC controllers sit on the user LAN. What is the most defensible placement?
cards.a: Dedicated IoT VLAN with internet-only access and no path to the LAN
cards.x: IoT devices are unpatchable by design: the VLAN contains them, and no-LAN rules keep a Mirai moment from becoming your moment.
wrong: Keep them on the user LAN, but change all default passwords and update firmware where available
Treat IoT devices as low risk
Give them full LAN access, since they need it

cards.q: Management interfaces (iDRAC, switch admin) are reachable from the user LAN. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Move them to an out-of-band management network, reachable only via the bastion
cards.x: An iDRAC on the user LAN is a backdoor with a web UI: one compromised laptop away from bare-metal control. Isolate the management plane.
wrong: Keep them on the user LAN but set long, unique passwords on every management interface
Treat out-of-band management as legacy
Rely on nobody knowing the IPs

cards.q: The firewall has 4,000 rules, and nobody knows what half of them do. What is the most defensible cleanup?
cards.a: Audit by hit counts, remove the unused, document the rest with owners and expiry
cards.x: Firewall rules accrete like sediment: unused rules are unreviewed allow-lists. Measure, prune, and give every rule an owner and a reason.
wrong: Leave the rule base alone, since the firewall works and removing rules might break an application
Treat more rules as more security
Assume the rules document themselves

cards.q: Server-to-server traffic inside the datacenter is completely uninspected. What is the most defensible addition?
cards.a: Microsegmentation or host-based firewalls on the servers
cards.x: East-west is where ransomware lives: encrypt and policy the lateral paths, not just the front door.
wrong: Rely on the perimeter firewall, since traffic between servers inside the data centre is trusted
Treat microsegmentation as too complex
Assume servers never attack servers

cards.q: A second ISP is proposed “for redundancy” but both circuits enter through the same conduit. What is the most defensible design?
cards.a: Diverse physical paths into the building, ideally with diverse providers
cards.x: Redundancy that shares a failure mode is theater: path diversity is the actual control.
wrong: Add the second ISP as proposed, because two separate contracts with two SLAs give the redundancy needed
Rely on one ISP with a strong SLA
Assume the shared conduit will not be cut

cards.q: The honeypot sits in the production VLAN and keeps alerting on the backup server’s scans. What is the most defensible placement?
cards.a: An isolated decoy segment with no production traffic
cards.x: Decoys only work when every touch is suspicious: production noise ruins the signal, and entrapping legitimate users creates liability.
wrong: Keep it in production and add the backup server to an allow list so its scans stop alerting
Place honeypots in every VLAN
Treat the backup server as the attacker

cards.q: NAC is deployed in monitor mode and has been “almost ready” for two years. What is the most defensible push?
cards.a: Define the enforcement policy, pilot enforcement on one VLAN, then expand
cards.x: NAC only works when it can say no: the blockers are always exceptions and politics, so pilot small and enforce deliberately.
wrong: Keep NAC in monitor mode, since visibility alone meets the requirement and enforcement is too disruptive
Spend another year tuning before enforcing
Abandon NAC

resources.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — Security and Privacy Controls

decks.title: Security Architecture: Data Protection Scenarios
decks.summary: Classification, encryption, keys, and DLP as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: The company has no data classification — every file gets the same handling. What is the most defensible first step?
cards.a: Define classes with handling rules, then label data and apply controls per class
cards.x: Protection without classification is guesswork: you cannot encrypt “everything” sensibly. Classes tell each system what it is protecting and how hard.
wrong: Encrypt every file with the same company-wide key, so every document gets the same strong protection
Treat classification as bureaucracy
Treat all data as public

cards.q: Application logs containing customer PII are shipped to a third-party analytics vendor. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Mask or tokenize PII in the pipeline before it leaves
cards.x: Logs are data too: once PII flows to a vendor, your breach surface includes their breach surface. Scrub at the boundary.
wrong: Rely on the vendor's privacy policy and data processing agreement, which already cover personal data
Treat logs as not real data
Add a consent notice to the logs

cards.q: The payment page still negotiates TLS 1.0 for “old clients”. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Disable TLS 1.0/1.1 and weak ciphers, in stages with compatibility monitoring
cards.x: Protocol negotiation lets the attacker pick the weakest option: the server must remove the weak options, not hope clients choose well.
wrong: Keep TLS 1.0 for old clients and show them a banner recommending that they upgrade their browser
Keep it, since TLS 1.0 is fine internally
Prioritise old clients over security

cards.q: The database uses transparent encryption, but the keys sit in a config file next to the database. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Move keys to a KMS or HSM with access controls and audit
cards.x: A key beside the data is decoration: whoever reads the disk reads the key. Separate the key, control access to it, log every use.
wrong: Keep the keys in the config file but restrict the file's permissions to the database service account
Rely on TDE alone
Leave it; nobody knows the file is there

cards.q: A laptop with the full HR database is stolen from a car, unencrypted, no MDM. What is the most defensible program fix?
cards.a: Full-disk encryption on all endpoints plus MDM with remote wipe
cards.x: Stolen hardware is a when, not an if: encryption makes the theft a hardware loss, not a breach. MDM adds the wipe for the window.
wrong: Report the theft to the police and focus on recovering the laptop before deciding on any other changes
Treat HR data as low sensitivity
Assume laptops are rarely stolen

cards.q: DLP blocks the R&D team’s legitimate file shares daily, so they moved to personal drives. What is the most defensible tuning?
cards.a: Tune policies by data classification and user context with allowlisted workflows
cards.x: A DLP that blocks real work teaches circumvention: precision policies plus approved paths keep both security and productivity.
wrong: Block more aggressively and discipline anyone caught using personal drives to get around DLP
Disable DLP for R&D
Allow personal drives as the workaround

cards.q: The new system must store card numbers for recurring billing. What is the most defensible design?
cards.a: Tokenise with the payment processor so card numbers never reach your systems
cards.x: The best way to protect card data is not to have it: tokenization removes PANs from your scope entirely. Encryption still leaves you holding the keys.
wrong: Encrypt the card numbers in the database with AES-256 and store the key in a separate key vault
Hash the card numbers
Store them in plaintext behind the firewall

cards.q: Encryption keys have not been rotated in five years and the admin who created them left. What is the most defensible program fix?
cards.a: Scheduled rotation with versioned keys and automated re-encryption
cards.x: Keys age like passwords: rotation limits the blast radius of a compromise nobody noticed. Automate it so it actually happens.
wrong: Leave the keys as they are, since rotating them risks making old data unreadable
Treat keys as never expiring
Trust the departed admin

cards.q: Backup tapes go offsite unencrypted in a courier van. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Encrypt backups before they leave the building, with keys managed separately
cards.x: Offsite media is in the wild: unencrypted tapes make the courier a breach vector. Encrypt first, then transport.
wrong: Keep the tapes unencrypted but use a bonded courier with tracked, locked cases for every shipment
Skip encryption because tapes are obsolete
Skip encryption because it slows restores

cards.q: An employee emails a spreadsheet of SSNs to a personal address “to work from home”. What is the most defensible layered response?
cards.a: DLP and email encryption gateway to catch it, plus an approved remote-access path
cards.x: People exfiltrate through the easiest hole: block the bad path AND provide the good one, or the workaround just moves.
wrong: Ask the employee to delete the email from the personal account and remind them of the policy
Treat SSNs in email as normal
Treat DLP monitoring as spying

cards.q: Engineers sync laptops to a personal cloud drive with no policy. What is the most defensible control?
cards.a: Approved sync with DLP, device posture checks, and admin-controlled sharing
cards.x: Shadow sync puts company data under personal accounts: bring it under policy with technical controls, not just a memo.
wrong: Publish a policy memo banning personal cloud sync and ask managers to remind their teams
Leave sync to each user
Block all sync tools

cards.q: Decommissioned drives are sold to a recycler without wiping “to save time”. What is the most defensible process?
cards.a: Sanitize per NIST 800-88 — clear, purge, or destroy based on media and classification — with certificates of destruction
cards.x: Resale without sanitization is a breach with extra steps: the buyer gets your data free. Sanitization level follows the data’s classification.
wrong: Quick-format the drives before sale, which removes the file tables so the data can no longer be found
Trust the recycler to wipe them
Treat old drives as worthless

cards.q: The public website’s certificate expires at 3 AM on a holiday, and renewal is a manual ticket. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Automate issuance and renewal with ACME, plus expiry alerting
cards.x: Manual certificate processes expire at the worst possible hour: automation plus expiry alerting makes renewal boring.
wrong: Buy the longest-validity certificate available and set a calendar reminder a month before it expires
Rely on a calendar reminder
Accept occasional outages

cards.q: An internal app uses a self-signed certificate, and users are trained to click through the warning. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Issue from an internal CA trusted by managed devices, or automate with ACME
cards.x: Click-through training is anti-training: every bypassed warning teaches users that warnings do not matter. Proper certs restore the signal.
wrong: Keep the self-signed certificate and explain in security training that this warning is expected
Leave it; self-signed is fine internally
Treat warnings as useful practice

cards.q: The mobile app ships with a hardcoded database password used by 50,000 installs. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Rotate the credential immediately, scope the replacement to least privilege, audit usage, and move secrets to runtime injection with CI scanning
cards.x: Shipped secrets are public secrets: rotation closes the window, the audit tells you if it was used, and CI scanning keeps it from recurring.
wrong: Move the password into native code in the next release so it is much harder to extract
Accept that it is too late
Assume users will not decompile the app

cards.q: Analytics needs customer data, but privacy objects to sharing raw PII. What is the most defensible technique?
cards.a: Anonymize or aggregate so records cannot be linked to individuals
cards.x: Masking keeps format but not privacy: true anonymization removes linkability. The technique follows the use case — analytics rarely needs real names.
wrong: Hash the customer names and email addresses, which makes the records anonymous for analysis
Share the raw data with trusted analysts
Refuse analytics on privacy grounds

cards.q: The company keeps every email and file for ten years “just in case”. What is the most defensible policy?
cards.a: A retention schedule per data type, with a legal-hold process
cards.x: Hoarding is liability: every retained byte is discoverable, breachable, and storable at cost. Retention is a schedule, not a sentiment.
wrong: Keep everything, since storage is cheap and old records may help in future disputes
Delete everything every year
Treat legal holds as optional

cards.q: A third-party analytics SDK in the mobile app is caught sending contact lists to its servers. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Remove or replace the SDK, audit what it sent, and disclose as required
cards.x: Your app’s permissions become the SDK’s permissions: vet SDKs like vendors, minimize their data, and monitor their traffic.
wrong: Ask the SDK vendor to stop collecting contacts in its next version, and keep it in the app meanwhile
Treat contact lists as not sensitive
Rely on users having agreed

cards.q: USB drives are allowed on all workstations with no policy. What is the most defensible control?
cards.a: Block by default, allow only approved encrypted drives for defined roles
cards.x: Uncontrolled USB is a two-way hole: data walks out, malware walks in. Allowlist the need, encrypt the media, log the use.
wrong: Rely on antivirus to scan USB drives when they are inserted
Allow USB for convenience
Assume nobody uses USB

cards.q: Sensitive documents are found on the shared printer daily. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Secure print with badge release at the printer
cards.x: Paper is data: the fix is making the printer hold the job until the human arrives, not hoping people hurry.
wrong: Email the people who leave documents behind, and post a reminder above the printer
Treat printers as no security issue
Remove all printers

cards.q: A vendor screen-share session exposed the full customer database to their support tech. What is the most defensible control?
cards.a: Least-privilege views for support plus DLP on collaboration tools
cards.x: Support access should be scoped to the problem: full-table views for a password reset is overexposure by design.
wrong: Rely on the vendor's NDA, which covers anything its staff see during support sessions
Give vendors full access to help
Treat screen shares as temporary

cards.q: The only copy of the master encryption key is with an admin who just resigned. What is the most defensible recovery design?
cards.a: M-of-N key recovery with split knowledge across several custodians
cards.x: Single key holders are single points of failure and single points of coercion: split custody means the keys survive people.
wrong: Ask the departing admin to hand the key to their manager, who becomes the new sole holder
Keep one key holder for simplicity
Treat the key as needing no recovery plan

cards.q: The messaging app offers “encrypted” chats, but the provider holds the keys. What is the most defensible read?
cards.a: That is transport and storage encryption, not end-to-end: the provider can read the chats
cards.x: Who holds the keys decides who can read: provider-held keys mean provider access. E2EE is the only design where the provider cannot.
wrong: It is end-to-end encryption, since the messages are encrypted in transit and at rest
Assume the provider never looks
Treat E2EE as marketing

cards.q: A leaked board deck is traced by its unique watermark to one recipient. What made that possible?
cards.a: Forensic watermarking — per-recipient invisible marks that identify the source of a leak
cards.x: Watermarks do not prevent leaks; they attribute them. The deterrent is knowing the copy is traceable to you.
wrong: Digital rights management, which stopped the deck from being forwarded and logged the attempt
The leaker confessed
The deck's metadata contained the author's name

cards.q: Passwords are hashed with MD5 “because it is fast”. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Migrate to Argon2, bcrypt or scrypt with unique salts, rehashing at next login
cards.x: Password hashing must be slow by design: MD5 falls to GPUs in hours. Salts stop rainbow tables; work factors stop brute force.
wrong: Add a single company-wide salt to the MD5 hashes, which stops rainbow tables
Keep MD5, since it is a hash
Treat speed as a feature

resources.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — Security and Privacy Controls

decks.title: Security Architecture: Resilience & Recovery Scenarios
decks.summary: Backups, DR, RTO/RPO, and HA as exam-style scenarios. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: The only backup sits on the same SAN as production. What is the most defensible redesign?
cards.a: 3-2-1: three copies, two different media, one offsite
cards.x: A backup sharing fate with production is a copy, not a recovery plan. The offsite copy is what survives fire, flood, and ransomware.
wrong: Add a second SAN in the same rack that mirrors the first, so a disk or controller failure cannot lose data
Keep it on the same SAN for faster restores
Keep one copy, since it already exists

cards.q: The contract demands RPO of one hour, but backups run nightly. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Increase backup frequency (or add replication) to meet the one-hour RPO
cards.x: RPO is the maximum data loss the business accepts: nightly backups guarantee up to 24 hours of loss. The schedule must satisfy the contract.
wrong: Keep nightly backups, since they are the industry norm, and explain the gap in the next service review
Treat the RPO as aspirational
Renegotiate the contract down

cards.q: Ransomware encrypted production and the online backups in the same night. What is the most defensible redesign?
cards.a: Immutable or offline copies — air-gapped, Object Lock, or tape — that no compromised credential can delete
cards.x: Online backups live in the blast radius: ransomware hunts them first. Immutability puts recovery outside the attacker’s reach.
wrong: Back up more often, so that the latest online copy is newer than the encryption, and keep backups on the network
Keep backups online, since offline restores are too slow
Pay the ransom faster

cards.q: The DR plan was written three years ago and has never been tested. What is the most defensible program?
cards.a: Tabletop exercises, then simulations, then full failover tests on a cadence
cards.x: Plans rot: staff, systems, and vendors all changed. Testing graduates from discussion to simulation to real failover, on schedule.
wrong: Have the plan reviewed and signed off again by the leadership team, since it is well written
Avoid testing, which could cause outages
Keep it for natural disasters only

cards.q: A cold site is chosen to meet a two-hour RTO. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: Cold sites cannot meet a two-hour RTO: use a hot or warm site, or change the RTO
cards.x: Cold means empty building: procuring and restoring in two hours is fiction. The site type must match the RTO the business signed.
wrong: Keep the cold site, because it is cheaper and the team can restore quickly if equipment is ordered in advance
Renegotiate the RTO after a disaster
Two hours is plenty for a cold site

cards.q: The generator has never been load-tested; it “starts fine”. What is the most defensible program?
cards.a: Monthly load tests under real building load
cards.x: Untested generators are the classic outage multiplier: the test must prove it carries the actual load, not just turns over.
wrong: Run it off-load for five minutes each week, since a generator that starts reliably will carry the load
Test it during the next real outage
Assume generators are reliable

cards.q: The UPS holds ten minutes but the generator needs twenty to take load. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Size the UPS to bridge the generator's start time with margin
cards.x: Power resilience is a chain: the UPS covers exactly the generator’s start time plus margin. A ten-minute bridge over a twenty-minute gap is an outage.
wrong: Keep ten minutes of UPS runtime, since generators start faster under real outage conditions
Treat ten minutes as the standard
Use the UPS for surge protection only

cards.q: The company has one ISP and the SLA promises 99.99% uptime. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: Add a diverse second path, ideally a second provider with a separate building entry
cards.x: Carrier SLAs pay credits, not continuity: real availability comes from diverse paths, ideally diverse providers and entries.
wrong: Rely on the 99.99% SLA, since the carrier is contractually obliged to keep the link up
One good ISP is enough
Treat 99.99% as easy for one provider

cards.q: The load balancer is a single instance in front of everything. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: HA pair or anycast — the front door cannot be a single point of failure
cards.x: Every request crosses the load balancer: its failure is everyone’s failure. Redundant balancers with health checks fix it.
wrong: Keep a single load balancer but monitor it closely and keep a spare configuration ready to deploy
Keep one for simplicity
Replace it with DNS round-robin

cards.q: The database runs on a single master with no replica. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: Add replication or clustering matched to the RPO
cards.x: The replica is the RPO made real: without it, recovery means restoring from last night’s backup and losing the day.
wrong: Rely on nightly backups, which can restore the single master if it fails
Treat masters as reliable
Replicas only serve read traffic

cards.q: Backups complete nightly and report success, but nobody has ever restored one. What is the most defensible program?
cards.a: Scheduled restore tests — a backup without a tested restore is a prayer
cards.x: Success reports measure the write, not the read: restores fail on corruption, missing keys, and wrong procedures. Test the read.
wrong: Rely on the nightly success reports, which confirm every job wrote its data without errors
Assume restores always work
Avoid restore tests to protect production

cards.q: The array runs RAID 5 across twelve 12TB drives. What is the most defensible concern?
cards.a: Rebuild time and unrecoverable read error risk: move to RAID 6/10 or erasure coding
cards.x: RAID 5 rebuilds read every surviving disk: with huge drives the rebuild takes days, and one bad sector ends it. RAID 6/10 or erasure coding fits.
wrong: Add a hot spare, so that a failed drive is replaced automatically and the array rebuilds without risk
Treat RAID 5 as the standard
Bigger drives make RAID 5 safer

cards.q: Planned datacenter failover is set, but DNS TTLs are 24 hours. What is the most defensible preparation?
cards.a: Lower TTLs well before the cutover
cards.x: DNS caching obeys the TTL you published yesterday: cutover speed is decided before the event, not during it.
wrong: Lower the TTLs during the failover itself, once the new site is confirmed to be working
Ignore TTLs, since DNS changes are instant
Leave the TTLs, since they do not matter

cards.q: Nobody knows the graceful shutdown order, and the last outage corrupted the database. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: A documented, tested runbook that sets the shutdown and startup order
cards.x: Ungraceful shutdowns corrupt state: the runbook makes the order explicit and rehearsed, not improvised at 3 AM.
wrong: Pull the power faster during outages so the database has less time to write partial transactions
Treat it as bad luck
Treat all shutdowns as the same

cards.q: The DR strategy is “we are in the cloud”. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: A region is not a DR plan: replicate and test recovery to another region or provider
cards.x: Cloud regions fail too: without replication and tested procedures, “we are in the cloud” is a hope with a logo.
wrong: Rely on multi-AZ deployment within one region, which already counts as disaster recovery
Clouds do not fail
Treat DR as legacy thinking

cards.q: Tape backups rotate to a storage room in the same building. What is the most defensible change?
cards.a: True offsite rotation — different facility, tested retrieval — because the building is the shared failure
cards.x: Fire, flood, and theft do not respect floors: offsite means a different risk zone, and retrieval must be proven, not assumed.
wrong: Keep the tapes in the same building, since the storage room is fireproof and on a different floor
Skip offsite rotation; tapes are obsolete
Assume the room protects the tapes

cards.q: A breach hits at midnight and nobody knows who notifies customers or regulators. What is the most defensible preparation?
cards.a: A crisis communication plan with named owners, templates, and legal review
cards.x: Notification duties have clocks: the plan names who decides, who writes, and who calls, before the midnight call happens.
wrong: Leave it to the PR team, which handles all external communications and can decide on the night
Say nothing and hope
Let the CEO decide live

cards.q: Only one engineer knows how to restore the backups, and she is on vacation. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Cross-training plus tested runbooks — the bus factor of one is an outage waiting for a holiday
cards.x: Recovery cannot depend on one person’s memory: document the procedure, train a second pair of hands, test together.
wrong: Rely on the engineer being reachable by phone on holiday, and pay her for any time she spends
Skip documentation as overhead
Cancel her vacations

cards.q: Sales promises 99.9% uptime on a single-server deployment. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: 99.9% allows about 9 hours of downtime a year, including maintenance, which one server cannot deliver
cards.x: Availability math is unforgiving: promises must follow architecture. Redundancy, not optimism, delivers the nines.
wrong: Accept the promise, since nighttime maintenance does not count toward the availability figure
Treat the nines as marketing
Single servers are reliable enough

cards.q: Snapshots are the only “backup” — same array, same site. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: Snapshots are not backups: copy to separate media at a separate site
cards.x: A snapshot is a pointer, not a copy: array failure, ransomware, or site loss takes snapshots with it. Separate media, separate site.
wrong: Snapshots count as backups, because they can restore any file to an earlier point in time quickly
Same-array snapshots are fine
Snapshots beat offsite backups

cards.q: The DR plan was last updated before the cloud migration. What is the most defensible maintenance?
cards.a: Review and test the plan after every architecture change
cards.x: DR plans rot with every migration: the review cadence must follow the change cadence, or the plan is fiction.
wrong: Update the plan after the next incident, when the gaps are known from real experience
Treat the plan as timeless
The cloud made DR obsolete

cards.q: After ransomware, the CFO asks whether to just pay. What is the most defensible answer?
cards.a: Restore from clean, verified backups; payment is a legal and business decision, not a shortcut
cards.x: Paying buys uncertainty: decryptors fail, data is already stolen, and payers get re-targeted. Tested backups are the answer.
wrong: Pay, because it is faster than restoring and the insurer will reimburse the ransom
Pay in instalments
Assume insurance covers it

cards.q: The alternate site’s configs are six months stale. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Continuous config replication or IaC-driven rebuilds
cards.x: Failover to stale configs fails differently but equally: the recovery site must track production, automatically.
wrong: Update the alternate site's configs during the failover, once production is confirmed to be down
Treat stale configs as close enough
DR sites do not need current configs

cards.q: Every change window lacks a rollback plan “because rollbacks are admitting failure”. What is the most defensible standard?
cards.a: Every change ships with a tested backout plan
cards.x: Changes fail: the question is whether failure is a 10-minute rollback or a 10-hour incident. Backout plans are mandatory.
wrong: Fix forward on every change, since rollbacks waste time and good engineers rarely need them
Treat rollbacks as failure
Good changes need no backout

cards.q: The same root cause has caused three outages this year, and each post-mortem recommended the same fix. What is the most defensible read?
cards.a: The lessons-learned process is broken: actions need owners, deadlines and verification
cards.x: Repeat incidents are a management failure, not a technical one: track every action item to closure or the post-mortem was theater.
wrong: The engineers are careless and need retraining on change procedures
Bad luck
The post-mortems themselves are the fix

resources.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 — Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems

decks.title: Security Concepts: Scenarios
decks.summary: Zero trust, control types, AAA, and physical controls in real decisions.

cards.q: Your company still trusts anything inside the office network: no MFA on internal apps, flat VLANs, file shares open to everyone. The CEO asks where a zero-trust migration should start. What is the most defensible first move?
cards.a: Strong identity everywhere first — MFA on every account and app, before touching the network
cards.x: Identity is the new perimeter: without strong authentication, network segmentation just rearranges who the attacker impersonates. MFA kills the credential-reuse path that flat networks invite.
wrong: Rebuild the network into many VLANs first, since segmentation is the foundation of zero trust
Buy a NAC appliance and call it zero trust
Put a bigger firewall at the internet edge

cards.q: The branch office runs a ten-year-old time-clock system that cannot do MFA and cannot be patched. Finance will not fund a replacement this year. What is the most defensible approach?
cards.a: Compensating controls: isolate it on its own segment, allow access only via jump host, and monitor it heavily
cards.x: When the ideal control is impossible, compensating controls reduce the risk to an acceptable level: isolation plus monitoring contains what patching and MFA would have prevented.
wrong: Leave it on the main network, since it works and has never been attacked in ten years
Disconnect it and use paper timesheets
Open it to the internet for the vendor

cards.q: The board wants 'defense in depth' but the budget covers one project. The CISO proposes adding a second firewall behind the first from the same vendor. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: Defense in depth means different layers of different control types, not two identical boxes
cards.x: Two identical firewalls fail identically to the same exploit. Real depth layers different control types — preventive, detective, corrective — across network, endpoint, identity, and data.
wrong: Two firewalls are defense in depth, as long as both have their signatures updated every day
Spend it on the most expensive firewall
One enterprise-grade layer is enough

cards.q: An engineer proposes hiding the admin panel at a random URL instead of fixing its broken authentication. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Obscurity is not a control: fix the authentication
cards.x: Security through obscurity fails the moment the secret leaks — and scanners find 'hidden' paths in minutes. It can supplement real controls but never replace them.
wrong: Hiding the URL is a valid primary control if the path is long and random enough
Remove the admin panel entirely
Keep the URL secret and leave the authentication

cards.q: The new SSO rollout covers authentication but nobody planned where the logs go. What is the most defensible gap to close?
cards.a: The accounting leg of AAA: SSO events must feed the SIEM with alerting
cards.x: AAA is authentication, authorization, and accounting: without accounting, you cannot detect misuse of valid credentials — the exact scenario SSO centralizes.
wrong: SSO replaces the need for logging, because every login is already verified with MFA at the IdP
Export logs quarterly for auditors
Leave logs to the IdP vendor

cards.q: The firewall rulebase is ten years old, 3,000 rules, nobody knows what half of them do. What is the most defensible rebuild principle?
cards.a: Default deny with explicit, documented allows
cards.x: Implicit deny is the safe default: everything not explicitly permitted is blocked. A decade of accumulated allows is how attackers walk through 'enterprise' firewalls.
wrong: Migrate all 3,000 rules as they are, to be safe, and review them after the migration
Default allow with blocks for known-bad IPs
Remove the firewall and use host firewalls

cards.q: A developer who writes code also deploys it straight to production. What is the most defensible separation?
cards.a: Split build and deploy: a different person or pipeline approval releases changes
cards.x: Separation of duties means no single person can both create and release a change — it blocks both fraud and the 'oops, it worked on my laptop' outage.
wrong: Give the developer a second account used only for deploys, so that build and deploy are separate identities
Trust senior developers with both
Have the developer email before deploying

cards.q: The payroll administrator has processed every pay run alone for six years and resists vacations. What is the most defensible control?
cards.a: Mandatory vacation: someone else runs payroll for two consecutive weeks
cards.x: Mandatory vacations are a detective control — fraud that needs the perpetrator present to sustain itself breaks when they are gone.
wrong: Let her keep working, since six years of reliable payroll runs proves she can be trusted
Give her a bonus instead
Move payroll to a new hire

cards.q: Wire transfers above $50,000 need two-person approval, but the CFO can override alone 'in emergencies'. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: No unilateral overrides: emergencies use a pre-defined second approver, because the override is the attack path
cards.x: Dual control fails the moment one person can bypass it — social engineers and fraudsters both aim straight at the exception process.
wrong: Keep the CFO override, because emergencies need speed and the CFO is the most senior approver
Raise the threshold to $500,000
Remove approvals to speed things up

cards.q: The 'assume breach' principle is adopted. A sales laptop is stolen from a hotel. What is the most defensible response?
cards.a: Treat it as compromised: wipe it, rotate its credentials and tokens, and review its access
cards.x: Assume breach means acting as if the attacker already has access: a wipe command may never arrive, but rotated credentials are useless to a thief either way.
wrong: Remote-wipe it and close the incident, since the wipe removes all data from the device
Do nothing, since it had disk encryption
Wait to see if anything happens

cards.q: A vendor RFP asks for the 'policy engine, policy administrator, and policy enforcement point' of your zero-trust design. What is the most defensible way to answer?
cards.a: Describe the three roles: the engine decides, the administrator configures, the enforcement point allows or blocks
cards.x: NIST SP 800-207 splits the job: the policy engine evaluates trust, the administrator pushes configuration, and enforcement points (agents, gateways) carry out allow/deny.
wrong: Explain that one appliance performs all three functions, and name the product used
They are three brand names for a firewall
Zero trust has no such components

cards.q: Users authenticate once in the morning and stay trusted all day, including on the finance system. What is the most defensible tightening?
cards.a: Step-up authentication and session re-validation on sensitive actions
cards.x: Continuous validation is a zero-trust pillar: a session hijacked at 10 AM inherits the morning's trust unless sensitive actions re-verify.
wrong: Log everyone out every hour, so that a stolen session token is valid for at most sixty minutes
Longer sessions improve productivity
One MFA prompt a year is enough

cards.q: Firewall change requests are approved by email from whoever is online. What is the most defensible approval control?
cards.a: Signed, ticketed approvals from a named approver
cards.x: Non-repudiation means the approver cannot later deny it: approvals need identity, timestamp, and a record — 'whoever was online' is none of those.
wrong: Approval by email from a manager is enough, since email shows who approved and when
Verbal approval is faster
Approvals slow security down

cards.q: The badge reader opens the door but the audit log shows no entry for a visitor who was inside. Which AAA element failed, and what is the fix?
cards.a: Accounting failed: the reader authenticated but did not log
cards.x: AAA breaks into three legs: the badge authenticated, the door authorized, but accounting (the record) failed. An access event nobody can reconstruct is a gap.
wrong: Authentication failed, so the visitor badges should be replaced
Authorisation failed, so the door rules should be reprogrammed
Nothing failed, since the visitor was escorted

cards.q: A penetration test finds the guest Wi-Fi can reach the finance VLAN. What is the most defensible design principle violated?
cards.a: Segmentation with implicit deny between trust zones
cards.x: Network segmentation enforces least privilege at the network layer: the guest zone's default route should be the internet, never internal segments.
wrong: The firewall is misconfigured, so the guest network should bypass it entirely
Guests sometimes need finance access
Wi-Fi is inherently insecure

cards.q: The company wants to roll out biometrics for the data center. What is the most defensible enrollment caution?
cards.a: Biometrics cannot be revoked: protect templates and never use them as the only factor
cards.x: You get ten fingers and two eyes for life — a compromised biometric is compromised forever. Treat templates as high-value data and never as a single factor.
wrong: Fingerprints cannot be guessed, so a single biometric factor is enough for the data centre
Store templates in a shared folder
Biometrics replace passwords entirely

cards.q: Job rotation is proposed for the SOC but analysts fear losing expertise. What is the most defensible implementation?
cards.a: Rotate through roles with documented handovers and overlap
cards.x: Rotation is both a security control and a resilience practice: it prevents single-person dependency and exposes processes that only work in one person's head.
wrong: Keep everyone in their specialty, since expertise matters more than rotation for SOC analysts
Rotate people out of the company
Rotate executives only

cards.q: A file share contains 'salary_2024_final_FINAL.xlsx' visible to the whole company. What is the most defensible classification fix?
cards.a: The data owner classifies it, and access is limited to those with a need to know
cards.x: Classification starts with the data owner — the business side that understands the data's value — and 'need to know' limits access to those with a legitimate purpose.
wrong: IT decides how sensitive it is, since IT manages the file share and its permissions
Leave it visible for transparency
Rename the file to hide it

cards.q: The new office has a side door propped open for smokers, bypassing the badge reader. What is the most defensible physical fix?
cards.a: A mantrap or turnstile with enforced badging on every entry
cards.x: Physical access control fails at the weakest door: tailgating defeats a $50,000 reader in seconds. Enforce badging at all entries, no exceptions.
wrong: Put up a sign asking people to close the door, and remind smokers in the next staff meeting
Remove the badge reader
Allow front-door access only at weekends

cards.q: Honeytokens are proposed: fake credentials planted in the environment. What is the most defensible deployment?
cards.a: Place them where no legitimate user or process would ever touch them
cards.x: Deception works when false positives are near zero: a honeytoken in a real workflow pages you about your own staff. Put it in attacker-only territory.
wrong: Plant them in the CEO's inbox, since attackers always target executives first
Tell all staff where they are
Use them instead of the SIEM

cards.q: The risk team asks whether a screen-lock policy is preventive or detective. What is the most defensible classification, and why does it matter?
cards.a: Preventive: it stops unauthorized use before it happens
cards.x: Controls are classified by function (preventive/detective/corrective) and nature (technical/administrative/physical): a gap analysis that finds only detective controls has found a real gap.
wrong: Detective, because it notices that a user has gone idle and records the event
The distinction is only academic
All controls are preventive

cards.q: CCTV footage is reviewed only after incidents. What is the most defensible upgrade path?
cards.a: Monitored alarming on motion in restricted areas plus retained footage
cards.x: Cameras nobody watches are forensic, not protective: pair recording with real-time alerting on the zones that matter.
wrong: Install more cameras so that every area is covered and footage is kept for longer
Rely on cameras as a deterrent
Delete old footage to save disk

cards.q: The change advisory board rubber-stamps firewall changes in bulk every Friday. What is the most defensible reform?
cards.a: Real review: risk assessment per change, testing evidence, and a backout plan
cards.x: Change management is a preventive control: unreviewed changes are how outages and backdoors ship. Every change needs risk review and a rollback plan.
wrong: Approve changes faster to help the business, and review any that cause problems afterwards
Skip the CAB for security changes
Disband the CAB

cards.q: An intern asks why the company bothers with 'least privilege' when everyone is trusted. What is the most defensible explanation?
cards.a: Trust is not the issue: credentials get stolen, and least privilege limits the damage
cards.x: Least privilege assumes credentials will be stolen: the damage is bounded by what the account could reach. 'Trusted' staff get phished too.
wrong: Trusted staff do not need access controls, since controls exist to stop malicious employees
Least privilege slows work too much
Admins are exempt

cards.q: The data center installed bollards, a mantrap, and badge readers — but the loading dock door is on a shared code. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Individual badges on every entry, including the loading dock
cards.x: Accountability requires attribution: a shared code authenticates 'someone with the code', which is no authentication at all for incident response.
wrong: Change the shared dock code every month and give it only to the delivery team
Shared codes are fine for docks
Remove the dock door

decks.title: Cryptography & PKI: Scenarios
decks.summary: Algorithm choices, certificate lifecycles, and key management under pressure.

cards.q: Two services need to exchange large files securely over the internet. What is the most defensible design?
cards.a: TLS 1.2+ with strong ciphersuites
cards.x: Use proven protocols: TLS gives confidentiality, integrity, and authentication in one maintained standard. Custom crypto is where breaches are born.
wrong: A custom encryption protocol built by the team, so attackers cannot know how it works
Base64-encode the files before sending them
Plain FTP on a non-standard port

cards.q: The app stores passwords with unsalted SHA-256 'because it is fast'. What is the most defensible correction?
cards.a: Switch to bcrypt, Argon2, or scrypt
cards.x: Fast hashes are built for attackers: rainbow tables and GPUs chew through SHA-256. Password hashing must be deliberately slow and unique per password.
wrong: Keep SHA-256 but add one company-wide salt to every password before hashing it
Encrypt the passwords with AES instead
Move the hashes to a separate database table

cards.q: Two companies with no prior relationship must agree on a shared secret over a public channel. What is the most defensible mechanism?
cards.a: Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman with authentication — forward-secret key agreement
cards.x: DH lets two parties derive a shared secret over a public channel; ephemeral keys plus authentication add forward secrecy and MITM resistance.
wrong: Exchange a pre-shared key by email, encrypted with a password sent by text message
Use the same password on both sides
Unauthenticated Diffie-Hellman

cards.q: Log files must prove they were not tampered with in transit to the SIEM. What is the most defensible mechanism?
cards.a: HMAC with a shared key — integrity plus authenticity of the sender
cards.x: A plain hash proves nothing about who sent it; HMAC binds the integrity check to a secret only the sender holds.
wrong: An MD5 checksum sent alongside each log batch, which the SIEM recomputes and compares
A password-protected zip of the logs
Trust the internal network

cards.q: The public website's certificate expires on launch day and nobody noticed. What is the most defensible program?
cards.a: Automated issuance and renewal with expiry alerting
cards.x: Certificate expiry is a solved operational problem: automation renews, monitoring alerts. A launch-day outage from an expired cert is a process failure.
wrong: Buy the longest-validity certificate available and give one person a calendar reminder to renew it
A shared calendar reminder
One person renewing every certificate by hand

cards.q: The company needs certificates for forty subdomains of one domain. What is the most defensible choice?
cards.a: A wildcard certificate, understanding that one compromised key affects all forty subdomains
cards.x: Wildcards trade operational simplicity for blast radius: scope the risk deliberately, protect the private key accordingly, and prefer SAN certs for distinct names.
wrong: Forty individual certificates managed by hand in a spreadsheet, renewed one at a time
One certificate shared across unrelated domains
Self-signed certificates for all forty

cards.q: The internal HR portal uses a self-signed certificate and staff click through warnings daily. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Deploy an internal CA, distribute its root to managed devices, and issue proper certificates
cards.x: Warning fatigue is the real vulnerability: staff trained to click through cert warnings will click through a real MITM too. Internal PKI removes the warnings legitimately.
wrong: Tell staff the warnings are expected for this portal, and add a note to the security awareness training
Move the portal to the public internet
Configure browsers to hide certificate errors

cards.q: Encrypted backups need key recovery if the admin leaves, but no single person should hold the keys. What is the most defensible design?
cards.a: M-of-N key recovery: key split so any M of N custodians can reconstruct it
cards.x: Escrow must survive both departure and compromise: M-of-N means no single custodian can abuse the keys, and the organization cannot be locked out by one absence.
wrong: Give the CEO a copy of every backup key, stored in a safe in the CEO's office
Email the keys to the whole team
No escrow; hope nobody leaves

cards.q: TLS 1.0 is still enabled 'for legacy clients'. What is the most defensible action?
cards.a: Disable it: segment the legacy clients and give them a migration path
cards.x: TLS 1.0 has known weaknesses (BEAST and more). Keeping it for a handful of clients exposes everyone negotiating down to it.
wrong: Keep TLS 1.0 enabled for compatibility, since only a handful of clients still negotiate it
Enable SSL 3.0 as well for the oldest clients
Move the legacy clients to plain HTTP

cards.q: Database backups of 4 TB must be encrypted. What is the most defensible approach?
cards.a: AES-256 for the data, with the data key wrapped asymmetrically or by a KMS
cards.x: Symmetric ciphers handle bulk data; asymmetric handles key distribution. RSA-encrypting 4 TB directly is absurd; hybrid is the standard pattern.
wrong: RSA-encrypt the whole 4 TB backup directly with the backup server's public key
XOR the data with a long password
Compress it, which also encrypts it

cards.q: Release builds must prove they came from the build pipeline. What is the most defensible mechanism?
cards.a: Sign artifacts with a pipeline-held key and verify the signature before deploy
cards.x: Code signing gives authenticity and integrity: the deploy trusts the signature, not the network path the artifact traveled.
wrong: Publish SHA-256 checksums of each build on the intranet for ops to compare before deploying
Trust anything from the build server
Email the binaries to operations

cards.q: How should the company detect certificates fraudulently issued for its domains?
cards.a: Monitor Certificate Transparency logs for your domains and alert on unexpected issuance
cards.x: CT logs make all public issuance visible: monitoring them catches misissued or attacker-obtained certificates for your names.
wrong: Check the website's certificate manually each morning and compare its fingerprint with yesterday's
Leave CT monitoring to the CA
Buy more certificates to crowd out fakes

cards.q: Payment-card keys need the strongest protection for PCI. What is the most defensible storage?
cards.a: A hardware security module — tamper-resistant, FIPS-validated key operations
cards.x: HSMs perform crypto inside hardened hardware that resists extraction; software keystores cannot make the same assurance to an auditor.
wrong: A config file readable only by the payment service account, on an encrypted disk
Keep keys on the app server
Split the key across two config files

cards.q: The board asks about quantum computers breaking encryption. What is the most defensible strategy?
cards.a: Crypto agility: inventory where each algorithm is used, prefer hybrid post-quantum options where available, plan migration
cards.x: Panic-migrating is as bad as ignoring it: agility — the ability to swap algorithms — plus an inventory is the defensible posture while standards settle.
wrong: Double every key length now, which is enough to stay ahead of any quantum computer
Ignore it; quantum is decades away
Migrate everything to untested algorithms now

cards.q: File deduplication uses SHA-256 hashes to skip identical uploads. What is the most defensible security caveat?
cards.a: Hashes confirm integrity, but dedup leaks whether a file already exists
cards.x: Content-defined storage has a side channel: an attacker can probe for the existence of files. Integrity hashing is fine; the dedup oracle needs handling.
wrong: SHA-256 is broken for this use, so the dedup system must switch to MD5 for speed
Dedup is a form of encryption
There is no caveat

cards.q: Executives want 'encrypted email' for board materials. What is the most defensible deployment?
cards.a: S/MIME or PGP with managed keys and a clear key-recovery story
cards.x: Real email encryption needs key management: issuance, revocation, recovery, and training. A banner changes nothing about who can read the message.
wrong: Mark the subject line CONFIDENTIAL so mail gateways apply the right protection
BCC the board members
Use personal Gmail accounts

cards.q: Encryption keys are rotated 'when someone remembers'. What is the most defensible rotation program?
cards.a: Scheduled rotation plus event-driven rotation (staff departure, suspected compromise), automated
cards.x: Rotation limits the value of a stolen key: schedule it like patching, trigger it like incident response, and automate both.
wrong: Rotate keys daily by hand, so no key is ever used for more than one day
Keys never need rotation
Rotate only when auditors ask

cards.q: The app encrypts session tokens with AES-CBC and no MAC. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Switch to an authenticated mode such as AES-GCM, or add an HMAC (encrypt-then-MAC)
cards.x: CBC without integrity lets attackers tamper with ciphertext and learn plaintext through error oracles. Authenticated encryption is the standard.
wrong: Switch to ECB mode, which has no IV and so cannot be attacked through padding errors
Keep CBC as it is
Encrypt twice with CBC

cards.q: A partner proposes 'Diffie-Hellman' for a new integration with no mention of authentication. What is the most defensible objection?
cards.a: Unauthenticated DH is MITM-trivial: require authenticated ECDHE
cards.x: DH without authentication lets an attacker sit in the middle of both handshakes. The fix is authenticating the exchange, not abandoning DH.
wrong: Accept it, because Diffie-Hellman with a 4096-bit group is strong enough to stop interception
Accept it; DH is unbreakable
Reject DH as obsolete

cards.q: API keys are committed to the repo 'temporarily' and end up in container images. What is the most defensible practice?
cards.a: A secrets manager or vault with runtime injection, plus secret scanning in CI
cards.x: Committed secrets are compromised secrets: repos are copied, images are shared, and 'temporary' lasts years. Inject at runtime from a vault.
wrong: Keep them in the private repository but rotate them once a year
Base64-encode them in the repo
Private repos make it fine

cards.q: The security team wants revocation checking that does not phone home for every user. What is the most defensible mechanism?
cards.a: OCSP stapling: the server presents a fresh revocation proof with the handshake
cards.x: Stapling gives clients revocation status without per-user OCSP queries — no privacy leak, no extra round trip, no soft-fail downgrade pressure.
wrong: Have every client download the full CRL every hour, so that no per-user lookup is ever needed
Disable revocation checking
Treat revocation as unimportant

cards.q: The password-reset flow generates tokens with MD5 of the timestamp. What is the most defensible fix?
cards.a: Replace it with a long token from a cryptographically secure random generator
cards.x: Reset tokens must be unguessable: MD5-of-timestamp is predictable to anyone who knows roughly when it was issued. Use the OS random source.
wrong: Add a secret salt to the MD5 of the timestamp, so attackers cannot reproduce the token
Keep MD5, since it is a hash
Make tokens shorter for usability

cards.q: Laptops have OS passwords but no disk encryption. What is the most defensible upgrade?
