tracks.title: CySA+
tracks.tagline: SOC analyst skills: detection, vulnerability management, and incident response, aligned to CS0-004.

decks.title: SOC Foundations
decks.summary: SOC tiers, alert triage, SIEM basics, and core analyst metrics. (Domain 1.0)

cards.q: What is the primary role of a Tier 1 SOC analyst?
cards.a: Triage incoming alerts and escalate confirmed incidents
cards.x: Tier 1 filters noise and does initial investigation; Tier 2 performs deep analysis and Tier 3 does threat hunting.
wrong: Write and tune the SIEM correlation rules
Reverse-engineer malware samples pulled from escalated incidents
Lead threat hunts based on new intelligence

cards.q: What distinguishes a true positive from a false positive?
cards.a: A true positive is an alert for a real malicious event
cards.x: A false negative — a missed attack — is the most dangerous outcome.
wrong: A true positive is any alert rated critical severity
A true positive is an alert the SOAR closed automatically
A true positive is a real attack the SIEM failed to alert on

cards.q: What is alert fatigue?
cards.a: Analysts become desensitized by excessive false positives and risk missing real threats
cards.x: Solved through tuning, correlation, and SOAR automation.
wrong: The SIEM drops events once the licensed volume is exceeded
Analysts get worn down by long overnight shifts, whatever the quality of the alerts they see
Attackers flood the SOC with alerts to cover a real intrusion

cards.q: What does a SIEM do?
cards.a: Collects, normalizes, and correlates logs to detect security events
cards.x: It provides central visibility; it does not block traffic inline.
wrong: Inspects traffic inline at the perimeter and drops malicious packets before they arrive
Stores logs encrypted for compliance only
Replaces EDR agents on endpoints

cards.q: Which data sources typically feed a SIEM?
cards.a: Firewalls, IDS/IPS, EDR, servers, identity systems, and cloud audit logs
cards.x: Breadth of telemetry determines detection quality.
wrong: Antivirus detections only, since they are the highest-fidelity events
Email gateway logs and web proxy logs only
NetFlow records only, because they cover every host

cards.q: What is log normalization?
cards.a: Converting logs from different formats into a common schema
cards.x: Normalization enables correlation across vendors and products.
wrong: Compressing older logs so that more months of history fit on the same disk
Encrypting logs in transit to the collector
Removing duplicate events before storage

cards.q: What is the difference between an event and an incident?
cards.a: An event is any observable occurrence; an incident is a confirmed policy or security violation
cards.x: Only incidents trigger the formal incident response process.
wrong: They are synonyms in the NIST terminology
An incident is any observable occurrence; an event is a confirmed violation
An event always requires breach notification

cards.q: What is the alert queue in SOC workflow?
cards.a: The prioritized list of alerts analysts work through
cards.x: Prioritized by severity, asset criticality, and threat intel context.
wrong: The list of firewall change requests waiting for the security team's approval
The schedule of scans and backup jobs
The list of systems awaiting patches

cards.q: What is mean time to detect (MTTD)?
cards.a: The average time from compromise to detection
cards.x: Lower MTTD limits attacker dwell time.
wrong: The average time from patch release to deployment
The average time from detection to containment
The average time to restore from backup

cards.q: What is mean time to respond (MTTR)?
cards.a: The average time from detection to containment or remediation
cards.x: A key SOC efficiency metric tracked over time.
wrong: The average time from the initial compromise until the SOC first detects it
The average time to provision a new account
The average time a ticket waits in the queue

cards.q: What is dwell time?
cards.a: How long an attacker remains undetected in the environment
cards.x: Industry averages are measured in days to weeks; hunting reduces it.
wrong: How long a user's session stays active before the identity provider times it out
How long the SIEM retains searchable logs
How long an alert waits before triage

cards.q: What is a runbook?
cards.a: A documented step-by-step procedure for handling a specific alert type
cards.x: Runbooks ensure consistent Tier 1 response.
wrong: An inventory of privileged accounts, their owners and when each was last reviewed
A diagram of the network topology and zones
A report of the latest vulnerability scan

cards.q: What is a playbook?
cards.a: A broader conditional response plan linking multiple runbooks, tools, and decisions
cards.x: SOAR platforms automate playbooks.
wrong: A single fixed checklist for one alert type
A catalogue of the SOC's detection rules
A rota of which analysts are on shift and who is on call for each tier of escalation

cards.q: What is ticket enrichment?
cards.a: Automatically adding context to a ticket
cards.x: Enrichment speeds up triage decisions.
wrong: Merging duplicate tickets into one
Routing tickets to the next free analyst
Closing tickets that match a known false positive

cards.q: How do severity and priority differ in triage?
cards.a: Severity is the technical impact of the event; priority is the response order
cards.x: A compromised domain controller outranks a compromised print server.
wrong: They are identical labels in most SIEMs
Priority is the technical impact; severity is the response order
Severity applies only to malware alerts

cards.q: What is the typical SOC escalation path?
cards.a: Tier 1 triage → Tier 2 investigation → Tier 3 hunting and IR → management
cards.x: The path is defined in the incident response plan.
wrong: Tier 3 hunting → Tier 1 triage → Tier 2 investigation → management
Analyst → management → legal, skipping tiers
Each analyst escalates directly to the CISO

cards.q: What is a baseline in security monitoring?
cards.a: A profile of normal behavior used to spot anomalies
cards.x: Deviations from baseline trigger investigation.
wrong: The minimum configuration every server must meet
A backup copy of a known-good system image
The default-deny rule at the end of a firewall policy

cards.q: Why does asset criticality matter in alert triage?
cards.a: More important systems raise an alert’s response priority
cards.x: A domain controller alert outranks a print server alert.
wrong: It sets the SIEM licensing cost per asset
It decides which analyst tier handles the alert
None, because severity alone decides the response order for every alert

cards.q: How do IDS and IPS differ in SOC workflow?
cards.a: An IDS alerts for analyst review; an IPS blocks inline
cards.x: Poorly tuned IPS rules can disrupt legitimate business traffic.
wrong: They are the same appliance running in two different licensing modes
An IDS blocks inline; an IPS only alerts
An IPS cannot generate logs for the SIEM

cards.q: What is continuous monitoring?
cards.a: The ongoing collection and analysis of security telemetry
cards.x: Required by frameworks such as NIST CSF; not a once-a-year audit.
wrong: An annual penetration test of critical systems by an external firm
A quarterly review of user access rights
A yearly audit against a control framework

cards.q: What is Zero Trust Network Architecture (ZTNA)?
cards.a: Access granted per user, device, and application after verification, instead of trusting anything inside the network
cards.x: ZTNA replaces implicit trust with explicit verification on every access request.
wrong: A firewall rule that blocks all inbound traffic by default, so nothing from outside the network can ever reach an internal system
A VPN that gives remote users full access to the internal network
A network design that trusts all devices already connected to the corporate LAN

cards.q: What is secure access service edge (SASE)?
cards.a: Network and security functions such as SWG, CASB, and ZTNA delivered from the cloud
cards.x: Remote workers get the same controls as office workers.
wrong: A hardware appliance that inspects traffic at the data-centre perimeter only
A backup service that replicates cloud data to on-premises storage
A protocol for encrypting traffic between two branch offices

cards.q: What does privileged access management (PAM) do?
cards.a: Vaults and rotates administrator credentials and controls privileged sessions
cards.x: Stolen admin credentials are the fastest path to domain compromise.
wrong: Grants every user administrator rights so work is never blocked
Stores passwords in a shared spreadsheet the team can access
Disables multi-factor authentication for service accounts

cards.q: Which logging concepts matter to a SOC analyst?
cards.a: Ingestion, configuration, integrity and security, time synchronization, and retention
cards.x: A wrong clock or a tampered log makes evidence unusable.
wrong: Compression, deduplication, and colour-coding of log files
How many analysts are on shift and which queue each one works
The brand of the SIEM and the size of its licence

cards.q: Why does operational technology (OT) need different handling from IT?
cards.a: Availability beats confidentiality, and patching or scanning can halt a production line
cards.x: OT includes industrial control systems and SCADA; monitor it with the same discipline, not the same playbook.
wrong: OT systems are never connected to any network, so they need no monitoring and no security controls
OT uses the same patching windows as office laptops
OT has no logging, so analysts ignore it

decks.title: Vulnerability Scanning Basics
decks.summary: Scan types, CVSS fundamentals, and remediation concepts. (Domain 2.0)

cards.q: What is vulnerability scanning?
cards.a: Automated discovery of known weaknesses in systems
cards.x: It finds flaws; penetration testing exploits them to prove impact.
wrong: Exploiting weaknesses to prove an attacker could gain access
Encrypting data on systems with known flaws
Blocking IP addresses linked to known exploits

cards.q: How do credentialed and non-credentialed scans differ?
cards.a: Credentialed scans authenticate and see configuration detail; non-credentialed scans show the attacker’s external view
cards.x: Credentialed scans find missing patches; non-credentialed scans find exposed services.
wrong: They produce identical results on patched systems
Non-credentialed scans see configuration detail; credentialed scans show the external view
Credentialed scans need written legal approval from the vendor

cards.q: What is an agent-based vulnerability scan?
cards.a: A lightweight agent on the host reports vulnerabilities continuously
cards.x: Works well for remote, roaming, or intermittently offline assets.
wrong: An analyst manually tests each host against a checklist, one system at a time
A network scan launched from a central appliance
A scan that needs no software on the target

cards.q: What is CVSS?
cards.a: An open standard for scoring vulnerability severity from 0.0 to 10.0
cards.x: CVSS v3.1 has base, temporal and environmental metric groups; CVSS v4.0 (2023) uses base, threat, environmental and supplemental.
wrong: The public catalogue of vulnerabilities known to be actively exploited in the wild
A numbering scheme that gives each flaw a unique ID
A model of exploitation probability over 30 days

cards.q: What does a CVSS score of 9.8 indicate?
cards.a: Critical severity
cards.x: Scores of 9.0–10.0 are critical, but score alone does not equal organizational risk.
wrong: High severity
Medium severity
Low severity

cards.q: What is a CVE?
cards.a: A unique public identifier for a known vulnerability, such as CVE-2021-44228
cards.x: Format CVE-YYYY-NNNN, where the sequence number has four or more digits. CVEs let tools and teams refer to the same flaw.
wrong: A severity score from 0.0 to 10.0 that NIST assigns to each newly published flaw
A probability that a flaw will be exploited soon
A vendor patch identifier for a known flaw

cards.q: What is the NVD?
cards.a: NIST’s database of CVEs with CVSS scores and references
cards.x: The primary US source analysts consult for vulnerability details.
wrong: MITRE's master list of CVE identifiers, published without any severity scores
CISA's catalogue of actively exploited flaws
FIRST's model of exploitation probability

cards.q: What is a false positive in vulnerability scanning?
cards.a: A reported vulnerability that does not actually exist
cards.x: Validate findings before committing to patching sprints.
wrong: A real vulnerability that the scan failed to report in its results
A correctly identified vulnerability
A vulnerability with no available patch

cards.q: What is a false negative in vulnerability scanning?
cards.a: A real vulnerability the scan failed to detect
cards.x: False negatives are more dangerous than false positives.
wrong: A finding reported twice by two scanners
A reported vulnerability that does not exist
A finding on a system outside the scan scope

cards.q: What is vulnerability remediation?
cards.a: Fully fixing the root cause, usually by patching or reconfiguring
cards.x: Remediation is preferred over temporary workarounds.
wrong: Adding a compensating control around the system while the flaw itself stays in place
Formally accepting the risk with an expiry date
Suppressing the finding in the scanner

cards.q: What is vulnerability mitigation?
cards.a: Reducing exposure without fully fixing the flaw, for example with compensating controls
cards.x: Used when patching is not immediately possible.
wrong: Removing the root cause entirely, by patching the software or reconfiguring the system so the flaw is gone
Formally accepting the risk with owner sign-off
Re-running the scan to confirm the finding

cards.q: What is a vulnerability exception (risk acceptance)?
cards.a: Formal documented acceptance of a vulnerability’s risk by an owner
cards.x: Exceptions require sign-off and an expiry date.
wrong: Excluding a host from all future scans
Suppressing a finding as a false positive
Delaying a patch until the next scheduled maintenance window without telling the owner

cards.q: What is patch management?
cards.a: The process of testing and deploying updates on a schedule
cards.x: Includes rollback planning for failed patches.
wrong: Updating antivirus signatures daily
Applying every vendor update to production the moment it is released, without testing
Removing unsupported software from servers

cards.q: What is a maintenance window?
cards.a: A scheduled period for disruptive changes such as patching
cards.x: Minimizes business impact of reboots and outages.
wrong: The period during which backup copies must be retained before they can be deleted
The hours when the SOC is fully staffed
The term of a vendor support contract

cards.q: How does a vulnerability assessment differ from a penetration test?
cards.a: An assessment finds and reports weaknesses; a pentest exploits them to prove impact
cards.x: CySA+ focuses primarily on the assessment and analysis side.
wrong: They are the same activity under different names
A pentest finds and reports; an assessment exploits to prove impact
An assessment needs no authorisation; a pentest does

cards.q: What is configuration compliance scanning?
cards.a: Checking systems against secure baselines such as CIS Benchmarks
cards.x: Finds drift from approved configurations.
wrong: Scanning each host for open ports and listening services only
Testing the strength of user passwords
Checking software licences for compliance

cards.q: What is a CIS Benchmark?
cards.a: Consensus-based secure configuration guidance for platforms and applications
cards.x: Used as audit baselines for hardening.
wrong: A score that rates vulnerability severity
A vendor's published list of which product versions are still supported with security patches
A government law that mandates hardening

cards.q: What does scan scope mean?
cards.a: The defined set of assets included in a vulnerability scan
cards.x: Scanning outside scope can be disruptive or unauthorized.
wrong: The plug-ins enabled in the scanner
How deep the scanner probes each host, from a light ping sweep to full plug-in checks
The time window the scan runs in

cards.q: Why are scans often scheduled during off-hours?
cards.a: Scanning can degrade performance or crash fragile systems
cards.x: Legacy and OT systems are especially sensitive to scan traffic.
wrong: Scanners are licensed only for off-hours use
Results are more accurate when traffic is low
Regulations require all vulnerability scans to run outside business hours

cards.q: What is vulnerability chaining?
cards.a: Combining multiple lower-severity flaws into a serious exploit path
cards.x: Prioritize findings with attack-path context, not just single scores.
wrong: Running several scanners against one host
Linking every finding for the same CVE across hosts into a single grouped ticket
Linking firewall rules into a single policy

cards.q: How do internal and external vulnerability scans differ?
cards.a: Internal scans see what a compromised host would see; external scans see the attacker’s view from outside
cards.x: Run both: each reveals what the other cannot.
wrong: Internal scans are always credentialed and external scans are always agentless, and the two kinds never overlap in practice
They produce identical results, so one is a backup
External scans see patch levels; internal scans see only exposed services

cards.q: How do passive and active scans differ?
cards.a: Passive scans listen without sending probes; active scans send traffic and get fuller answers
cards.x: Passive scanning is safe for fragile systems such as OT.
wrong: Passive scans need credentials; active scans do not
Active scans are silent and undetectable
Passive scans crash fragile systems; active scans never do

cards.q: What is security baseline scanning?
cards.a: Checking system configuration against a standard such as PCI DSS, CIS Benchmarks, or ISO 27000
cards.x: It catches misconfigurations that CVE scanning misses.
wrong: Scanning for known CVEs only
Testing password strength on user accounts
Measuring how fast the network responds to scan traffic

cards.q: Which tools are used for network scanning and mapping?
cards.a: Angry IP Scanner and Masscan for discovery, Nmap for probing, and Metasploit for validating exploitability
cards.x: Maltego and Recon-ng add link analysis and OSINT reconnaissance.
wrong: Burp Suite, ZAP, and Nikto, which probe running web applications for injection flaws, broken authentication, and misconfigurations
ScoutSuite, Prowler, Trivy, and Checkov
Atomic Red Team and Caldera

cards.q: Which tools scan web applications and cloud infrastructure?
cards.a: Burp Suite, ZAP, and Nikto for web apps; ScoutSuite, Prowler, Trivy, and Checkov for cloud and IaC
cards.x: Nessus, Nuclei, and OpenVAS are the general vulnerability scanners.
wrong: Wireshark, tcpdump, and Zeek, which capture and analyse network traffic to find suspicious connections and protocol anomalies
MISP, OpenCTI, and OTX
Joe Sandbox and Cuckoo Sandbox

cards.q: What is breach attack simulation (BAS)?
cards.a: Safely running real adversary techniques against your own defenses to prove whether detections fire
cards.x: Atomic Red Team and Caldera are the common BAS tools.
wrong: A penetration test performed without authorisation
A scanner that only checks for missing patches
A backup test that restores systems from snapshots

decks.title: SIEM Correlation & SOAR
decks.summary: Correlation rules, tuning, automation playbooks, and threat intel integration. (Domain 1.0)

cards.q: What is event correlation in a SIEM?
cards.a: Linking related events across sources into a single incident view
cards.x: Example: failed logins followed by a successful login and data exfiltration.
wrong: Compressing related events to save storage
Removing events older than the retention period so searches stay fast and cheap
Encrypting events before they are indexed

cards.q: What is a correlation rule?
cards.a: Logic that fires an alert when a defined pattern of events occurs
cards.x: Example: five failed logins in two minutes from one source.
wrong: A firewall rule that allows or blocks traffic based on source, destination and port
A parser that maps raw logs to fields
A retention rule for a log source

cards.q: What is aggregation in SIEM processing?
cards.a: Combining similar events into one to reduce alert volume
cards.x: Prevents alert storms from repeated identical events.
wrong: Splitting one combined alert back into the separate raw events that produced it
Encrypting event payloads at rest
Deleting raw logs after parsing

cards.q: What is a SIEM use case?
cards.a: A defined detection scenario mapped to a specific threat
cards.x: Example: impossible-travel detection for compromised accounts.
wrong: A licensing tier that sets how many events per second the SIEM may ingest
A dashboard showing alert volume by source
A log source onboarded to the SIEM

cards.q: How do you tune a noisy detection rule?
cards.a: Adjust thresholds, add allowlists, and require additional corroborating events
cards.x: Measure the false positive rate before and after tuning.
wrong: Disable the rule until it can be rewritten
Lower the rule's severity so it is ignored
Increase log retention so the rule has more historical data to compare each event against

cards.q: What is SOAR?
cards.a: Security orchestration, automation, and response: automated playbooks that act on alerts
cards.x: It enriches, contains, and tickets without manual clicks.
wrong: Security operations and response: a SIEM that blocks traffic inline
A threat intelligence platform for sharing IOCs
An endpoint agent that isolates infected hosts

cards.q: What can SOAR automate during triage?
cards.a: Enrichment, ticket creation, IP blocking, account disablement, and evidence collection
cards.x: Humans should still approve high-impact destructive actions.
wrong: Final decisions on whether an incident is a reportable breach under the applicable regulations
Approval of security budgets and tooling
Writing new detection rules from scratch

cards.q: What is a SOAR playbook trigger?
cards.a: The alert condition that starts a sequence of automated actions
cards.x: Example: a phishing alert triggers URL detonation and mailbox search.
wrong: An analyst manually reviewing the alert and then choosing which playbook to run
A scheduled job that runs the playbook nightly
The final action that closes the ticket

cards.q: What is the main risk of fully automated SOAR response?
cards.a: Automated containment can disrupt legitimate business activity
cards.x: Use human-in-the-loop approval for destructive actions like network isolation.
wrong: Automation is slower than manual triage
SOAR cannot integrate with the firewalls, EDR and ticketing tools already in place
Automated actions are never logged

cards.q: What does threat intelligence feed integration add to a SIEM?
cards.a: Automatic matching of observed indicators against known-bad IOCs
cards.x: Known threats get triaged faster with less analyst effort.
wrong: Behavioural baselining of every user and host so that deviations raise an alert
More log sources for the SIEM to ingest
Automatic blocking of every external IP

cards.q: What is the difference between an IOC and an IOA?
cards.a: An IOC is an artifact of compromise such as a hash or IP; an IOA is a behavior pattern
cards.x: IOAs survive attacker infrastructure changes better than IOCs.
wrong: They are identical terms from different vendors
IOCs are behaviour patterns; IOAs are hashes and IPs
IOAs apply only to network traffic

cards.q: What are STIX and TAXII?
cards.a: Standards for sharing threat intelligence: STIX is the format, TAXII the transport
cards.x: They enable machine-readable intel sharing between organizations.
wrong: STIX is the transport; TAXII is the data format
Two SIEM query languages
Two scoring systems for threat severity

cards.q: What is log retention and why does it matter to analysts?
cards.a: How long logs are kept; it determines the forensic lookback window
cards.x: Compliance often mandates a year or more of retention.
wrong: How fast the SIEM indexes new logs
How many log sources the SIEM can parse
How long alerts are allowed to wait in the triage queue before they must be picked up

cards.q: What is EPS in SIEM sizing?
cards.a: Events per second: the ingest rate the SIEM must handle
cards.x: Under-licensing EPS causes dropped events and blind spots.
wrong: Encrypted packets per second: the volume of TLS traffic the SIEM must decrypt
Endpoints per sensor in the deployment
Errors per search in the SIEM

cards.q: What is a parser in SIEM architecture?
cards.a: Code that extracts fields from raw logs into the SIEM’s schema
cards.x: A parser is needed for each log source type.
wrong: A correlation rule that links events from several sources into a single alert
An agent that forwards logs from hosts
A dashboard that charts parsed fields

cards.q: How do agent and agentless log collection differ?
cards.a: An agent is software on the host forwarding logs; agentless collection has the SIEM pull
cards.x: Agents provide richer endpoint telemetry.
wrong: They produce identical telemetry
Agentless collection always gives richer endpoint data
Agents can only read logs, never forward them

cards.q: What is UEBA?
cards.a: User and entity behavior analytics: baselining normal behavior to flag anomalies
cards.x: Effective against insider threats and compromised accounts.
wrong: User and endpoint backup automation
A rule engine that matches events against signatures of known-bad activity only
A threat intelligence sharing standard

cards.q: What is a watchlist in a SIEM?
cards.a: A custom list of entities such as IPs, users, or domains to alert on
cards.x: Useful for VIP accounts and known-bad infrastructure.
wrong: A list of approved applications that users are allowed to run on managed devices
A list of suppressed alerts treated as noise
A schedule of upcoming patch windows

cards.q: Scenario: the SIEM fires “multiple failed VPN logins followed by a success from a new country.” What is the likely assessment?
cards.a: Likely account takeover via brute force; force a password reset and review session activity
cards.x: Corroborate with impossible-travel logic and MFA logs.
wrong: Normal travel: the user is on a business trip and logged in after mistyping the password
A vulnerability scanner testing VPN logins
A VPN outage causing repeated failures

cards.q: Scenario: an alert fires for a known-malicious IP communicating with a workstation. What is the efficient SOAR-driven response?
cards.a: Auto-isolate the host, block the IP at the perimeter, enrich the ticket
cards.x: Automation handles containment while the analyst investigates scope.
wrong: Close it as a likely false positive
Email the user to ask what they were doing, then decide on containment once they reply
Wait for Tier 2 before taking any action

cards.q: Which tools analyse network packets?
cards.a: Wireshark and tcpdump capture and dissect traffic; Snort and Suricata are signature IDS; Zeek logs connections, DNS, and files
cards.x: CyberChef decodes and parses encoded payloads in the browser.
wrong: Nessus, Nuclei, and OpenVAS, which scan hosts systematically for known CVEs and report missing patches, weak credentials, and misconfigurations
Burp Suite, ZAP, and Nikto
MISP, OpenCTI, and OTX

cards.q: Which platforms aggregate threat intelligence?
cards.a: AlienVault OTX, MISP, and OpenCTI
cards.x: They feed indicators and context into the SIEM automatically.
wrong: Wireshark, tcpdump, and Zeek
Joe Sandbox and Cuckoo Sandbox
AbuseIPDB, WHOIS, and GEO-IP

cards.q: How do analysts check whether a file is malicious?
cards.a: Extract strings, check the hash on VirusTotal, match YARA rules, or detonate it in a sandbox such as Joe Sandbox or Cuckoo Sandbox
cards.x: Never detonate a suspicious file on a production workstation.
wrong: Run it on the analyst’s own laptop and watch what happens
Check the file size and extension only, because malicious files always use an unusual extension and a suspicious size that gives them away
Ask the user who received it whether it looks safe

cards.q: What file formats must a SOC analyst be able to read?
cards.a: JSON and XML for APIs and logs, YAML for configuration, and EVTX for Windows event logs
cards.x: EVTX is the Windows event log format.
wrong: Only CSV, because all security tools export CSV
Only PDF, because reports are always PDFs
Only plain text, because logs never use structured formats

cards.q: What is an AI hallucination in security operations?
cards.a: A confident, plausible, wrong AI output — such as an invented indicator or log line that never existed
cards.x: Verify every AI-assisted finding against the raw evidence.
wrong: A model that refuses to answer a question, staying silent instead of guessing when it does not know the answer
A model that runs too slowly to be useful in triage
A model that flags every event as malicious

cards.q: What should AI usage policies in a SOC cover?
cards.a: Which tools are approved, what data may be pasted into them, and when a human must verify the output
cards.x: Legal or regulatory compliance constrains what may be sent to a model.
wrong: Which analysts are allowed to use a keyboard
How many alerts each analyst must close per hour
Which vendor the SIEM was bought from, since the vendor contract decides what the SOC is allowed to automate

cards.q: How do SOAR platforms integrate with other tools?
cards.a: APIs connect the SIEM to firewalls, EDR, and ticketing; webhooks push events in real time; plug-ins extend the platform
cards.x: Integration is what turns a playbook into an automated response.
wrong: By emailing screenshots between tools, with analysts copying alert details from one console into another by hand for every alert
They cannot integrate; each tool works in isolation
By replacing the SIEM entirely

decks.title: Threat Hunting & Telemetry Analysis
decks.summary: Hunting hypotheses, network, endpoint, and email analysis techniques. (Domain 1.0)

cards.q: What is threat hunting?
cards.a: Proactive, hypothesis-driven searching for threats that evaded automated detection
cards.x: It assumes breach and hunts beyond existing alerts.
wrong: Triaging alerts raised by the SIEM
Running scheduled antivirus scans
Applying vendor patches to vulnerable hosts as soon as the weekly scan reports them

cards.q: What is a hunting hypothesis?
cards.a: An educated guess about attacker behavior to test against telemetry
cards.x: Example: “attackers use WMI for lateral movement in this environment.”
wrong: A confirmed incident that is waiting for the containment team to isolate the affected hosts
An IOC received from a threat feed
A compliance requirement to review logs

cards.q: What are the steps of the threat hunting loop?
cards.a: Hypothesize, investigate, uncover, and inform or improve
cards.x: Findings feed back into new detections and hypotheses.
wrong: Detect, contain, eradicate, recover
Scan, prioritise, patch, verify
Collect, normalise, correlate, alert, and then close the ticket

cards.q: What is intel-driven threat hunting?
cards.a: Starting from threat reports and known actor TTPs
cards.x: Map the hunt to MITRE ATT&CK techniques.
wrong: Searching telemetry for statistical outliers without any lead
Reviewing alerts the SIEM already raised
Scanning hosts for known vulnerabilities

cards.q: What is data-driven threat hunting?
cards.a: Exploring telemetry for anomalies without a specific intelligence lead
cards.x: Uses clustering and outlier analysis on large datasets.
wrong: Starting from a published threat report on a named actor and searching for that actor's known TTPs
Following an IOC from a threat feed
Reviewing alerts closed as false positives

cards.q: What network evidence indicates C2 beaconing?
cards.a: Regular, low-volume callbacks at fixed intervals, often with slight jitter
cards.x: Look for periodicity in NetFlow and DNS logs.
wrong: Occasional very large downloads from many different external hosts at random times
Slow page loads on many internal hosts
Bursts of traffic during backup windows

cards.q: What does DNS tunneling look like in logs?
cards.a: Long encoded subdomains with high query volume to rarely seen domains
cards.x: Data is exfiltrated inside DNS queries.
wrong: Many queries to popular, well-known domains such as CDNs and software update services
Repeated DHCP requests from one host
A single query that returns NXDOMAIN

cards.q: What is NetFlow analysis used for?
cards.a: Determining who talked to whom, when, and how much — without payload content
cards.x: Reveals lateral movement and exfiltration patterns.
wrong: Reading the full payload of every session to see exactly what data was sent and received
Decrypting TLS traffic for inspection
Blocking traffic from known-bad addresses

cards.q: What endpoint artifacts suggest process injection?
cards.a: Unexpected parent-child process relationships, such as Word spawning PowerShell
cards.x: EDR telemetry is the primary source for this analysis.
wrong: A process running from C:\Windows\System32
A scheduled update by the vendor's updater
A user opening several spreadsheets at once, each starting a new instance of Excel

cards.q: What is living-off-the-land (LotL)?
cards.a: Attackers using legitimate system tools like PowerShell, WMI, and PsExec to evade detection
cards.x: Requires behavior-based detection rather than signature matching.
wrong: Attackers relying only on custom malware they compiled
Attackers working from compromised home networks
Attackers hiding in unused cloud regions

cards.q: Which email headers help investigate phishing?
cards.a: Return-Path, the Received chain, and SPF, DKIM, and DMARC results
cards.x: They reveal spoofing and the true sending infrastructure.
wrong: The subject line and display name
The message size, the attachment names and the Importance header
The X-Priority and Importance headers

cards.q: What is URL detonation?
cards.a: Safely opening a suspicious link in a sandbox to observe its behavior
cards.x: A standard step in phishing email triage.
wrong: Blocking the URL at the proxy without analysis
Rewriting the link so that every click is first routed through the web proxy's filter
Checking the URL against a reputation list only

cards.q: What indicates a successful phishing compromise?
cards.a: Credential entry on a lookalike domain, followed by impossible travel or new mailbox rules
cards.x: Check for auto-forwarding rules created by the attacker.
wrong: The user reporting the email to the security team after opening the attachment preview
The message landing in the junk folder
A bounce message for one recipient

cards.q: How do attackers abuse mailbox rules for persistence?
cards.a: Creating auto-forwarding rules or rules that delete security alerts
cards.x: Hunt for recently created or modified inbox rules after phishing.
wrong: Changing the mailbox's display language and time zone so alerts arrive at odd hours
Adding a new email signature
Archiving messages older than a year

cards.q: What is memory forensics used for?
cards.a: Finding fileless malware, injected code, and encryption keys in RAM
cards.x: Memory is volatile: capture it before rebooting.
wrong: Recovering deleted emails from the mail server so investigators can read them
Recovering data from old backup tapes
Reviewing firewall rule changes

cards.q: What is the order of volatility?
cards.a: Collect the most volatile evidence first: CPU cache and RAM before disk
cards.x: Rebooting destroys the most valuable forensic evidence.
wrong: Disk first, then RAM, then network state
Archived backups first, then live systems
Any order, as long as each item is hashed

cards.q: What is timeline analysis in forensics?
cards.a: Ordering artifacts by timestamp to reconstruct the attack sequence
cards.x: Super-timelines combine disk, log, and registry timestamps.
wrong: Drawing a network diagram that shows every host the attacker touched
Ranking findings by CVSS score
Listing affected hosts alphabetically

cards.q: What is file carving?
cards.a: Recovering deleted files from unallocated disk space
cards.x: Useful when attackers delete logs or tools.
wrong: Splitting a large disk image into smaller files so it is easier to transfer
Encrypting a disk image for transport
Hashing each file on a seized disk

cards.q: Scenario: EDR shows rundll32.exe with no command line making external connections. What is the assessment?
cards.a: Highly suspicious; rundll32 is a common living-off-the-land loader
cards.x: Legitimate rundll32 use almost always has a visible command line.
wrong: Normal; rundll32 often runs without arguments
A signed driver update fetching files from the vendor's download servers
A false positive caused by EDR telemetry gaps

cards.q: Scenario: DNS logs show 10,000 queries to random-looking subdomains of a single domain in one hour. What is the assessment?
cards.a: Likely DNS tunneling or exfiltration — block the domain and inspect the source host
cards.x: The entropy and volume pattern is the key indicator.
wrong: Normal CDN behaviour for a busy site
A misconfigured printer retrying failed lookups against a domain it can no longer reach
Windows telemetry checking for updates

cards.q: An attacker rotates domains and IPs faster than you can block them. According to the Pyramid of Pain, what should you pivot to detecting instead?
cards.a: Their tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs)
cards.x: TTPs cost the attacker far more to change than a hash or an IP, so detections built on them last longer.
wrong: The file hashes of their malware, since a hash stays the same every time the same file is used
The email addresses they send phishing from, because attackers rarely change their sending accounts
The countries their servers sit in, since infrastructure moves slowly between regions

cards.q: What three factors determine confidence in a threat intelligence report?
cards.a: Timeliness, relevance, and accuracy
cards.x: Low confidence does not mean discard it — it means verify before acting.
wrong: Cost, vendor, and licence type
Severity, asset value, and patch availability
Length, formatting, and the number of indicators listed

cards.q: What is the difference between an atomic and a behavioral indicator of compromise?
cards.a: An atomic IoC is a single fact such as a hash or IP; a behavioral IoC is a pattern of activity
cards.x: Atomic indicators expire fast; behavioral ones last.
wrong: Atomic IoCs describe behaviour; behavioral IoCs are hashes and IPs
They are the same thing under different names
Atomic IoCs apply only to email; behavioral IoCs only to network traffic

cards.q: What is STRIDE in threat modeling?
cards.a: Spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, and elevation of privilege
cards.x: Walk each component through all six categories.
wrong: A SIEM query language for threat hunting
A scoring system for vulnerability severity, rating each flaw from zero to ten like CVSS does for published CVEs
A framework for ranking firewall rules

cards.q: A finance officer gets an urgent wire-transfer request that looks like it comes from the CEO, but the reply-to is a lookalike domain. What is this, and what is the key check?
cards.a: Business email compromise — verify it through a second channel first
cards.x: The display name matches the executive, but the reply-to domain gives it away.
wrong: A credential-stuffing attack — the attacker is testing passwords stolen from another breach
A watering-hole attack — the attacker compromised a website the finance team visits daily
A DNS cache-poisoning attack — the attacker altered DNS records so the CEO's mail goes to them

cards.q: Lookalike domains of your brand keep appearing, such as rnicrosoft.com. What defensive practice counters typosquatting?
cards.a: Defensively register the obvious lookalike domains and monitor for newly registered ones
cards.x: You cannot stop others registering domains, but you can own the obvious variants.
wrong: Block all external DNS queries so no employee can ever reach a lookalike domain by mistake
Rotate the company's real domain name every quarter so lookalikes go stale quickly
Disable URL shorteners in email, since they hide the real destination behind a trusted link

decks.title: Vulnerability Prioritization & Response
decks.summary: EPSS, KEV, risk-based prioritization, and remediation workflows. (Domain 2.0)

cards.q: What is EPSS?
cards.a: The Exploit Prediction Scoring System: the estimated probability a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days
cards.x: Prioritize high-EPSS flaws over high-CVSS flaws with no exploit activity.
wrong: A severity score from 0.0 to 10.0 that NIST assigns to each CVE based on its impact and attack vector
CISA's catalogue of actively exploited flaws
A standard for sharing exploit code between vendors

cards.q: Why is CVSS alone insufficient for prioritization?
cards.a: It measures severity, not likelihood of exploitation or asset context
cards.x: Combine CVSS with EPSS, KEV status, and asset criticality.
wrong: CVSS scores are assigned by vendors and are too often wrong to be trusted
CVSS covers only operating-system flaws
CVSS cannot be calculated without a vendor

cards.q: What is the CISA KEV catalog?
cards.a: The list of vulnerabilities known to be actively exploited in the wild
cards.x: US federal agencies must remediate KEV entries by binding deadlines.
wrong: A list of products certified as secure by CISA
NIST's full database of CVEs with scores
A list of the flaws with the highest predicted probability of exploitation in the next 30 days

cards.q: How do you prioritize a CVSS 9.8 with no known exploit versus a CVSS 7.5 listed in KEV?
cards.a: Remediate the KEV-listed flaw first: known exploitation beats theoretical severity
cards.x: Risk equals likelihood times impact, not score alone.
wrong: The 9.8 first: higher severity always wins
Whichever CVE was published first
Both together in the next scheduled maintenance window, since either could be exploited

cards.q: How do remediation, mitigation, and acceptance differ?
cards.a: Remediation fixes the root cause; mitigation reduces exposure; acceptance formally documents the risk
cards.x: The choice depends on feasibility, cost, and risk appetite.
wrong: They are synonyms for fixing the flaw
Mitigation fixes the root cause; remediation reduces exposure
Acceptance means closing the finding without a record

cards.q: When is mitigation preferred over remediation?
cards.a: When no patch exists or the system cannot yet be patched, such as legacy equipment
cards.x: Deploy compensating controls until remediation is possible.
wrong: Whenever the CVSS score is below 7.0
Whenever a patch is available but untested
Whenever the asset owner would prefer not to reboot the server during business hours

cards.q: What is a compensating control for an unpatchable server?
cards.a: Network segmentation, IPS signatures, or restricted access around the vulnerable system
cards.x: Document it in the risk exception with an expiry date.
wrong: Raising the finding's priority in the scanner so the server owner patches it sooner
Running the scanner more often on that server
Marking the finding as a false positive

cards.q: What is vulnerability validation?
cards.a: Confirming a scanner finding is real and exploitable before acting on it
cards.x: Validation eliminates false positives before remediation work begins.
wrong: Running the same scan a second time
Asking the vendor to confirm whether the flaw exists before any further work is done
Checking the CVSS score in the NVD

cards.q: What role does penetration testing play in vulnerability management?
cards.a: It validates exploitability and finds scanner blind spots
cards.x: Pentesting complements scanning; it does not replace it.
wrong: It replaces vulnerability scanning for internet-facing systems
It is only needed for compliance audits
It produces CVSS scores for each finding

cards.q: What is continuous vulnerability management?
cards.a: Ongoing cycles of discovery, prioritization, and remediation
cards.x: Modern programs scan continuously, not annually.
wrong: One full scan per year before the audit
Scanning only newly deployed servers
An annual penetration test of key systems, followed by a remediation sprint

cards.q: What is threat-informed prioritization?
cards.a: Weighting vulnerabilities by active threat intelligence relevant to your sector
cards.x: Example: prioritizing CVEs that ransomware groups are currently exploiting.
wrong: Ranking findings by CVSS base score only
Patching the oldest CVEs first
Patching only the flaws the vendor itself rates as critical, in the order they were released

cards.q: What is a remediation SLA?
cards.a: A deadline for fixing vulnerabilities based on severity, such as criticals within 15 days
cards.x: SLA compliance is tracked as a core security metric.
wrong: A vendor agreement for the scanning tool's support response times and availability
An uptime guarantee for the scanner service
A cyber-insurance policy covering vulnerabilities

cards.q: What is a vulnerability exception workflow?
cards.a: Request, risk assessment, owner approval, expiry date, and periodic review
cards.x: Exceptions must expire; otherwise accepted risk accumulates silently.
wrong: Marking a finding as a false positive in the scanner so it no longer appears in reports
Moving the host out of the scan scope
Raising a change request to patch the host

cards.q: What is the risk of indefinite vulnerability exceptions?
cards.a: Accepted risk accumulates until it becomes breach material
cards.x: Review exceptions at least quarterly.
wrong: Scanners stop reporting the excepted hosts
Auditors reject any exception older than a year
Vendors stop releasing patches for systems that have an accepted exception

cards.q: What is configuration drift?
cards.a: Systems gradually diverging from their secure baselines over time
cards.x: Compliance scanning detects drift between audits.
wrong: Increasing network latency between sites
Malware that changes system settings at random
Clock skew between servers and the domain controller that breaks Kerberos authentication

cards.q: Why run both authenticated and unauthenticated scans?
cards.a: Authenticated scans find missing patches and misconfigurations; unauthenticated scans find exposed services
cards.x: Each shows a different view of the attack surface.
wrong: Unauthenticated scans are required by law; authenticated are optional
They produce identical results, so one is a backup
Authenticated scans find exposed services; unauthenticated find missing patches

cards.q: Scenario: a scanner flags Log4Shell on 200 hosts, threat intel shows active exploitation, and 10 hosts are internet-facing. What is the priority order?
cards.a: Patch internet-facing hosts first, then internal hosts ordered by EPSS, KEV status, and asset criticality
cards.x: Exposure plus exploitability drives the order, not alphabetical lists.
wrong: All 200 hosts simultaneously in one change window
Internal hosts first, because they hold the sensitive data, then the internet-facing ones
Hosts ordered alphabetically by hostname

cards.q: What is a vulnerability disclosure program?
cards.a: An official channel for researchers to report flaws to the vendor
cards.x: It is distinct from a bug bounty, which pays for reports.
wrong: A program that pays researchers for every valid report
A public list of the vulnerabilities the vendor has already patched in released versions
A vendor's schedule for monthly security updates

cards.q: What is coordinated vulnerability disclosure?
cards.a: The reporter and vendor agree the timing, so a fix can ship before details go public
cards.x: It protects users during the window between discovery and patching.
wrong: The researcher publishes the flaw and a working exploit immediately so users can protect themselves
The vendor keeps the flaw secret indefinitely
Details go only to government agencies, never the public

cards.q: Which metrics show vulnerability program health?
cards.a: Mean time to remediate by severity, percentage of criticals past SLA, and scan coverage
cards.x: Report trends over time, not just raw counts.
wrong: The number of scanning tools licensed and the number of plug-ins each one has enabled
The total number of findings per scan
The number of analysts on the team

cards.q: What are the three types of security controls?
cards.a: Administrative (policies, procedures, training), technical (firewalls, encryption, access controls), and physical (locks, badges, guards)
cards.x: A vulnerability program uses all three types.
wrong: Preventative, detective, and corrective only, which describe what a control does rather than what kind of control it is, so they miss the type distinction
Hardware, software, and network only
Internal, external, and cloud only

cards.q: What are the four control functions?
cards.a: Preventative, detective, responsive, and corrective
cards.x: The patch is preventative, the scan is detective, the IPS signature is responsive, the rebuild is corrective.
wrong: Accept, transfer, avoid, and mitigate
Scan, prioritise, patch, and verify
Identify, protect, detect, and respond

cards.q: What is the difference between inherent risk and residual risk?
cards.a: Inherent risk is the risk before controls; residual risk is what remains after controls
cards.x: Risk appetite is how much risk the organisation is willing to accept.
wrong: They are the same measure, just calculated at different times in the audit cycle
Inherent risk is the risk after controls; residual risk is the risk before them
Residual risk is always zero once a control is in place

cards.q: What are the four risk management strategies?
cards.a: Accept, transfer, avoid, and mitigate
cards.x: Accept means taking the risk knowingly, with an owner and an expiry.
wrong: Scan, patch, verify, and report
Prevent, detect, respond, and recover
Identify, assess, treat, and ignore

cards.q: How do SAST and DAST differ?
cards.a: SAST reads source code for flaws before it runs; DAST probes the running application
cards.x: Both feed vulnerability management from the application side.
wrong: SAST probes the running application over the network while DAST reads the source code for flaws before it runs
SAST is for networks; DAST is for endpoints
They are the same technique under two names

cards.q: What is a software bill of materials (SBOM)?
cards.a: A list of every component and version in a piece of software, built by software composition analysis (SCA)
cards.x: When the next Log4Shell lands, an SBOM answers in minutes whether you are affected.
wrong: A vendor invoice for software licences
A list of the vulnerabilities in a single CVE entry
A report of how many lines of code an application has

decks.title: Incident Response & Forensics
decks.summary: IR phases, containment and recovery, digital forensics, and legal considerations. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: What are the classic NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 incident response phases?
cards.a: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity
cards.x: Rev. 2's lifecycle is still the model most IR plans follow. SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (April 2025) superseded it and maps incident response to the NIST CSF 2.0 functions.
wrong: Identify; Protect; Detect; Respond; Recover
Preparation; Identification; Containment; Eradication; Recovery; Lessons
Detection; Response; Mitigation; Reporting; Recovery; Remediation; Lessons

cards.q: What happens during the preparation phase?
cards.a: Building the IR team, tooling, playbooks, and communication plans
cards.x: Tabletop exercises validate readiness before a real incident.
wrong: Isolating the first compromised host and taking a memory image before anything else
Writing the post-incident report
Notifying regulators of the breach

cards.q: What is the first priority when ransomware is confirmed on a host?
cards.a: Contain it: isolate the host from the network immediately
cards.x: Stop lateral spread before beginning detailed analysis.
wrong: Restore the host from the last known-good backup straight away
Power the host off to stop encryption
Run a full antivirus scan on the host

cards.q: What is the difference between short-term and long-term containment?
cards.a: Short-term containment isolates the threat now; long-term containment provides temporary clean systems
cards.x: It balances stopping spread against business disruption.
wrong: Short-term restores from backup; long-term rebuilds the network
Short-term is for malware; long-term is for insider threats
Short-term waits for evidence; long-term isolates the host

cards.q: What is eradication in incident response?
cards.a: Removing all attacker presence: malware, backdoors, and persistence mechanisms
cards.x: Verify eradication with clean scans before recovery.
wrong: Isolating the host from the network
Restoring data and systems from known-good backups so the business can operate again
Rebooting the server to clear memory

cards.q: What is recovery in incident response?
cards.a: Restoring systems to normal operation from known-good backups or images
cards.x: Monitor closely for reinfection after recovery.
wrong: Removing all malware, backdoors and persistence mechanisms the attacker left behind
Isolating the affected systems
Reviewing what went wrong and why

cards.q: What is the purpose of the post-incident lessons-learned review?
cards.a: Blameless analysis of what happened and how to improve people, process, and technology
cards.x: Findings feed playbook and control updates.
wrong: Identifying which employee caused the incident
Deciding whether to notify customers
Calculating the cost of the incident so it can be billed back to the responsible business unit

cards.q: What is digital forensics?
cards.a: The scientific collection and analysis of digital evidence
cards.x: Methodology preserves the evidence’s admissibility.
wrong: Restoring compromised systems to service
Searching telemetry for threats that evaded automated detection
Testing systems for exploitable flaws

cards.q: Evidence changes hands three times during an investigation, but nobody logs the transfers. What breaks, and what is the consequence?
cards.a: The chain of custody — the documented record of who handled evidence, when, and how; gaps can make evidence inadmissible in court
cards.x: An unbroken chain is required for evidence to be admissible.
wrong: The path the attacker took through the network
The order in which evidence must be collected — the volatile RAM is gathered first and the disk last, so the transfer log matters less than the collection order
The list of systems in scope for the investigation and who owns each one

cards.q: What is a forensic image?
cards.a: A bit-for-bit copy of storage media used for analysis
cards.x: The original media stays pristine and hashed.
wrong: A full system backup taken by the backup tool on its normal schedule
A logical copy of the user's files only
A screenshot of the running system

cards.q: What does write-blocking do in forensics?
cards.a: Hardware or software that prevents any writes to evidence media
cards.x: It preserves hash integrity of the original evidence.
wrong: A setting that speeds up imaging by skipping the hash verification step
Encrypts the evidence copy for transport
Wipes the destination drive before imaging

cards.q: What is legal counsel’s role in incident response?
cards.a: Protecting privilege, managing breach notification obligations, and liaising with law enforcement
cards.x: Engage legal early in significant incidents.
wrong: Writing the firewall rules that block the attacker
Analysing the malware sample
Leading technical containment

cards.q: What is the tension between evidence preservation and business continuity?
cards.a: Forensics wants systems frozen; the business wants them restored quickly
cards.x: Predefined criteria in the IR plan resolve the conflict.
wrong: There is none once backups exist
Forensics always takes priority over operations, however long the systems stay down
The business always decides without the IR plan

cards.q: How do you contain a compromised cloud account?
cards.a: Revoke sessions and access keys, block API access, and snapshot resources for forensics
cards.x: Cloud containment is typically faster than on-premises.
wrong: Delete the account and every resource in it so the attacker loses access immediately
Reset the console password only
Wait for the provider to detect the abuse

cards.q: What is the difference between an incident and a breach?
cards.a: A breach is confirmed unauthorized acquisition of data
cards.x: Breach determination triggers notification laws.
wrong: They are the same term
Any incident involving malware is a breach
An incident always requires notification; a breach does not

cards.q: Should analysts perform attack attribution?
cards.a: Generally avoid definitive attribution; focus on TTPs and remediation
cards.x: Attribution is difficult and rarely changes the response.
wrong: Always attribute first, because who the attacker is decides the containment steps
Always name the suspected country in the report
Only law enforcement may look at TTPs

cards.q: What is a war room in incident response?
cards.a: A centralized coordination space or channel with defined roles during major incidents
cards.x: Keeps communications structured under pressure.
wrong: The SOC's normal day-to-day monitoring floor where Tier 1 analysts work the queue
The data centre where affected servers sit
A sandbox for detonating malware samples

cards.q: What is an IR retainer?
cards.a: A pre-contracted external incident response firm for surge support
cards.x: It is far faster than procuring help mid-crisis.
wrong: An annual fee paid to outside legal counsel
A cyber-insurance deductible
A subscription to a commercial threat intelligence feed for the SOC

cards.q: Scenario: EDR quarantines malware on a finance workstation, and the user reports odd wire transfer instructions. What are the next steps?
cards.a: Treat as potential BEC plus compromise: isolate the host, check mailbox rules
cards.x: Correlate endpoint and email telemetry before deciding scope.
wrong: Reimage the workstation, since EDR quarantined the malware, and close the ticket
Treat the wire request as unrelated
Approve the transfer and monitor the account

cards.q: Scenario: logs show data staged in a zip on a server with a large outbound transfer at 2 AM. What is the phase and action?
cards.a: Likely exfiltration in progress: contain the host and preserve the archive as evidence
cards.x: Do not delete the staged data; it is evidence.
wrong: Delete the zip so the data cannot leave
Wait until business hours so IT can confirm whether the transfer was a scheduled backup job
Reboot the server to stop the transfer

cards.q: How do tabletop exercises and simulations differ?
cards.a: A tabletop talks through a scenario around a table; a simulation has the team actually work the incident in a controlled environment
cards.x: Both test who decides, who communicates, and whether the playbooks hold up.
wrong: A tabletop is a real incident; a simulation is a written plan
Simulations are only for executives; tabletops are only for analysts
They are the same exercise under two names

cards.q: What is a legal hold in incident response?
cards.a: Preserving relevant data when litigation or regulatory action is possible, stopping normal deletion, rotation, or overwriting
cards.x: Data integrity validation by hashing proves nothing changed in between.
wrong: A court order that stops the IR team from working
A backup schedule that keeps data for 90 days, which preserves copies but does not stop the normal deletion and rotation of the original evidence
A policy that deletes logs after 30 days

cards.q: When may a system be released from isolation?
cards.a: Only after verification that the threat is gone
cards.x: A host released too early is a reinfection waiting to happen.
wrong: As soon as containment starts, so the business is not disrupted
After 24 hours, regardless of verification
Only after the post-incident report is published

cards.q: What is root cause analysis (RCA) in incident response?
cards.a: Asking why the incident happened, not just what happened
cards.x: Corrective action development turns the answer into changes with owners and deadlines.
wrong: Listing every host the attacker touched
Calculating the cost of the incident
Writing the press release about the breach

decks.title: Attack Frameworks & Threat-Informed Defense
decks.summary: MITRE ATT&CK, the cyber kill chain, and the diamond model. (Domain 3.0)

cards.q: What is MITRE ATT&CK?
cards.a: A knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures
cards.x: Analysts map detections and incidents to its technique IDs.
wrong: A scoring system that rates the severity of vulnerabilities from 0 to 10
A list of the most critical web app risks
A catalogue of defensive countermeasures

cards.q: What is the difference between a tactic, technique, and procedure in ATT&CK?
cards.a: Tactic = the adversary's goal; technique = how it is achieved; procedure = a specific actor's implementation
cards.x: Example: Persistence (tactic) via Registry Run Keys (technique).
wrong: They are synonyms used interchangeably
A tactic is a tool; a technique is a goal; a procedure is a policy
A tactic is a single command; a procedure is a whole campaign

cards.q: What are the phases of the cyber kill chain?
cards.a: Reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives
cards.x: Breaking any link stops the attack.
wrong: Reconnaissance, initial access, execution, persistence, exfiltration
Identify, protect, detect, respond, recover
Preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery

cards.q: How does ATT&CK improve on the kill chain for analysts?
cards.a: It is non-linear and far more granular
cards.x: The kill chain is a useful model but too rigid alone.
wrong: It is simpler, with fewer stages to learn
It replaces every other model, including the kill chain
It covers malware only, not human operators

cards.q: What is the diamond model of intrusion analysis?
cards.a: A framework linking adversary, capability, infrastructure, and victim with analytic pivoting
cards.x: Pivoting across vertices enriches investigations.
wrong: A model that breaks every intrusion into tactics, techniques and procedures, with an ID for each
A seven-stage linear model of an intrusion
A scoring model for intelligence confidence

cards.q: Which ATT&CK tactic covers credential dumping such as LSASS access?
cards.a: Credential Access
cards.x: Technique T1003 covers OS credential dumping.
wrong: Privilege Escalation
Discovery
Defense Evasion

Longer context, more tokens in the window

cards.q: What is prompt caching?
cards.a: Reusing a processed prompt prefix across calls
cards.x: Put stable content (system prompt, docs) first so it can be cached.
wrong: Storing answers in a database, caching every reply
Browser caching, storing pages on the user’s machine
Compressing prompts, shrinking them before sending

cards.q: How should you handle HTTP 429 from an LLM API?
cards.a: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter
cards.x: 429 means rate limited. Respect retry-after headers.
wrong: Retry immediately in a loop, hammering the API
Switch API keys, rotating to a fresh credential
Ignore it, pretending the error never happened

cards.q: Where must API keys for an LLM live in a web app?
cards.a: On the server, never in browser code
cards.x: Anything shipped to the browser is public.
wrong: In the React bundle
In localStorage
In the URL

cards.q: How are LLM API costs usually charged?
cards.a: Per input and output token
cards.x: Output tokens are typically priced higher than input.
wrong: Per request only, a flat fee per call
Per hour, renting the model by time
Per user, charging for each seat monthly

cards.q: What is model routing?
cards.a: Easy tasks to small models, hard ones to large
cards.x: Balances cost, latency, and quality.
wrong: Network routing for AI, sending packets along the most efficient paths
Load balancing GPUs, sharing work across cards
Choosing a region, picking the nearest data centre

cards.q: Why set max output tokens?
cards.a: Caps cost and latency, prevents runaway responses
cards.x: Too low truncates answers, so check the stop reason.
wrong: Improves accuracy, fewer mistakes in answers
Required for streaming, tokens must flow continuously onward
Enables tools, letting the model call functions

cards.q: What is an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server?
cards.a: A standard way to expose tools and data to AI applications
cards.x: An open protocol; treat third-party servers as untrusted code.
wrong: A hosted GPU server that runs the model itself
A vector DB
A model host

cards.q: What does "grounding" a model output mean?
cards.a: Tying answers to supplied sources or tool results
cards.x: Reduces hallucination and enables citations.
wrong: Lowering temperature, making outputs more predictable
Training on more data, feeding it larger corpora
Using a smaller model, fewer parameters to run

decks.title: Fine-tuning & Evaluation
decks.summary: When to fine-tune, LoRA, and building evals.

cards.q: When is fine-tuning the right tool?
cards.a: Style, format, or narrow tasks prompting can’t do
cards.x: Try prompting and RAG first; they are cheaper to iterate on.
wrong: Adding fresh facts daily, updating the knowledge base
Fixing every bug, patching all the errors
Always first, before trying anything else

cards.q: What is LoRA?
cards.a: Training small low-rank adapters instead of all weights
cards.x: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning; QLoRA adds 4-bit quantisation.
wrong: A long-range radio, transmitting over many miles
A tokeniser, splitting text into small pieces
A loss function, measuring how wrong the predictions are

cards.q: What is quantisation?
cards.a: Storing weights in lower precision (e.g. 8-bit, 4-bit) to save memory
cards.x: Some quality loss, big savings on hardware.
wrong: Adding more parameters so the model can learn more from the same data
Encrypting weights
Splitting data

cards.q: What is an "eval" in AI engineering?
cards.a: A repeatable test set measuring model quality
cards.x: Run evals on every prompt or model change, like unit tests.
wrong: A marketing demo, showing the product off
A pentest, attacking the system for real
A benchmark only vendors run, for their own marketing

cards.q: What is LLM-as-a-judge?
cards.a: Using a model to grade outputs against a rubric
cards.x: Calibrate it against human grades; watch for bias.
wrong: A court case, a legal dispute before a judge
Human grading only, people scoring every answer by hand
A benchmark name, one test suite among many

cards.q: Why is benchmark contamination a problem?
cards.a: Test data leaked into training inflates scores
cards.x: Build private evals from your own use cases.
wrong: Benchmarks are too hard, nobody can pass them
It slows training, adding hours to every run
It breaks tokenisers, splitting text incorrectly

cards.q: What is catastrophic forgetting?
cards.a: Fine-tuning erodes previously learned general abilities
cards.x: Mitigate with adapters, mixed data, and low learning rates.
wrong: Losing the original training data after fine-tuning
A GPU crash
Context overflow

cards.q: What is a golden dataset?
cards.a: Curated inputs with expected outputs for regression testing
cards.x: Grow it from real failures in production.
wrong: The training set, the data the model learns from
A random sample, picked blindly from the dataset
Public benchmarks only, shared test sets for all teams to use

cards.q: What is distillation?
cards.a: Training a small model to imitate a larger one
cards.x: Cheaper inference at some quality cost.
wrong: Cleaning data, fixing messy datasets before training
Removing layers randomly, deleting parts of the network
Encrypting a model, scrambling its weights for safe storage

cards.q: Why log prompts and outputs in production?
cards.a: For debugging, evals, abuse detection, and audits
cards.x: Redact PII and control access to logs.
wrong: To retrain automatically, updating the weights every night
To retrain on every user conversation
For marketing, showing off the product in the prompt logs

decks.title: Agents & Orchestration
decks.summary: Agent loops, planning, memory, and safe autonomy.

cards.q: What is an AI agent?
cards.a: An LLM in a loop that chooses tools and actions toward a goal
cards.x: Observe, think, act, repeat until done.
wrong: A chatbot that answers questions from its training data
A cron job
A fine-tuned model

cards.q: Workflow vs agent?
cards.a: Fixed code paths vs the model deciding its steps
cards.x: Prefer the simplest workflow that works; add autonomy only when needed.
wrong: Workflows and agents are the same pattern
Agents are always better, whatever the task happens to be
Workflows use no LLM, just plain old code

cards.q: What is the orchestrator-worker pattern?
cards.a: A lead model delegating subtasks to workers
cards.x: Good for broad research; costs more tokens.
wrong: One model handles every step itself
Two models vote, the majority answer wins
Human-only orchestration, people assigning every subtask

cards.q: What is human-in-the-loop?
cards.a: Requiring human approval for high-impact actions
cards.x: e.g. sending money, deleting data, emailing customers.
wrong: Humans write every prompt, typing each one by hand
Humans train the model, adjusting weights themselves
No automation, everything done by hand

cards.q: Why give agents least-privilege credentials?
cards.a: A manipulated agent can only do limited damage
cards.x: Scope tokens per tool; sandbox code execution.
wrong: Agents run faster with fewer permissions to check
Required by APIs
Reduces token cost

cards.q: What is agent memory?
cards.a: Persisting useful information across steps or sessions
cards.x: Short-term = context; long-term = external store or files.
wrong: GPU RAM, memory on the graphics card
Model weights, the learned parameters inside
Browser cache, storing web pages on the user’s machine

cards.q: What is context engineering?
cards.a: Curating the context window at each step
cards.x: Too much noise degrades reasoning; summarise and prune.
wrong: Enlarging the model, adding more parameters to it
Writing CSS, styling web pages for browsers
Adding GPUs, more cards for faster computation

cards.q: Why sandbox agent code execution?
cards.a: Generated code may be buggy or malicious
cards.x: Isolated containers, no secrets, network egress controls.
wrong: It is faster, running code without any checks
Models require it, refusing to run otherwise
To save tokens, using fewer of them per call

cards.q: What is the "lethal trifecta" for agent data exfiltration?
cards.a: Private data access + untrusted content + a way to send data out
cards.x: Remove at least one leg to break the attack.
wrong: Model size, prompt length and temperature set too high
Speed, cost, quality
Prompt, model, output

cards.q: How do you evaluate an agent?
cards.a: Task success on realistic scenarios
cards.x: Inspect transcripts, not just final answers.
wrong: Token count only, how many tokens are used
Benchmark score only, one number from a test set
User vibes, whether people feel good about it

cards.q: What is a guardrail in an AI system?
cards.a: A check blocking unsafe inputs or actions
cards.x: Input filters, output validators, tool allow-lists, rate limits.
wrong: A bigger model, with many more parameters
A slower model, taking longer to answer
A new prompt style, wording requests more carefully

decks.title: AI Security (OWASP LLM Top 10)
decks.summary: Attacks on LLM apps and how to defend them.

cards.q: OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) #1?
cards.a: Prompt Injection
cards.x: Direct (user) and indirect (content) injection.
wrong: Sensitive Information Disclosure
Supply Chain
Excessive Agency

cards.q: What is sensitive information disclosure in LLM apps?
cards.a: Revealing PII, secrets, or confidential data
cards.x: Minimise data in context; filter outputs; control access.
wrong: Answering more slowly when sensitive topics come up
A hallucination, confident but fabricated output
A cost overrun, the bill growing out of control

cards.q: What is improper output handling?
cards.a: Passing model output unchecked into browsers, shells, or SQL
cards.x: Treat LLM output as untrusted user input: encode and validate.
wrong: Formatting errors in the model's markdown output
Long answers
Short answers

cards.q: What is system prompt leakage?
cards.a: Extracting hidden instructions from the system prompt
cards.x: Never put credentials or security logic in prompts.
wrong: A model crash, the whole service stopping unexpectedly
A lost API key, a credential leaked in public
A billing issue, charges higher than expected

cards.q: What is unbounded consumption?
cards.a: Abuse that drives up cost or exhausts resources
cards.x: Rate limits, quotas, max tokens, and budget alerts.
wrong: Too much RAM, memory usage growing unchecked daily
A large training set, millions of examples
Long context windows, huge prompts every time

cards.q: What is model or data supply-chain risk?
cards.a: Tampered models, datasets, or plugins
cards.x: Verify sources, pin versions, scan model files (e.g. prefer safetensors over pickle).
wrong: Slow downloads, files trickling in over many hours
Old GPUs, outdated cards running slowly
Expensive tokens, each API call costing more and more

cards.q: What is a jailbreak?
cards.a: Prompts crafted to bypass a model’s safety behaviour
cards.x: A form of prompt injection aimed at policies.
wrong: Rooting a phone to install apps
A GPU exploit
A network attack

cards.q: What is vector and embedding weakness (LLM08)?
cards.a: Attacks via poisoned or leaked embeddings
cards.x: Apply access control and integrity checks to vector stores.
wrong: Slow vector search, queries taking far too long
Large vectors, thousands of dimensions each
Wrong dimensions, mismatched vector sizes

cards.q: What is MITRE ATLAS?
cards.a: An ATT&CK-style knowledge base for AI attacks
cards.x: Use it for AI threat modelling.
wrong: A GPU vendor, selling graphics cards for AI training
A model benchmark, a test suite for models
An AI law, legislation regulating AI systems

cards.q: Best mitigation mindset for prompt injection?
cards.a: Assume success; limit a compromised model’s reach
cards.x: Least privilege, human approval, output validation, isolation.
wrong: Rely on careful prompt wording to refuse injected instructions
Keep the system prompt secret so attackers cannot read it
Raise the temperature so the model ignores injected text

cards.q: What is model inversion / extraction?
cards.a: Recovering training data or cloning a model via repeated queries
cards.x: Rate-limit, monitor query patterns, and avoid training on secrets.
wrong: Encrypting the model weights at rest
Fine-tuning
Distillation by the owner

decks.title: AI Governance & Risk
decks.summary: NIST AI RMF, EU AI Act, and responsible AI in practice.

cards.q: What are the NIST AI RMF core functions?
cards.a: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage
cards.x: Govern is cross-cutting; the Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) extends it.
wrong: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond
Plan, Build, Test, Deploy
Collect, Train, Serve

cards.q: What approach does the EU AI Act take?
cards.a: Risk-based tiers: unacceptable, high, limited, minimal risk
cards.x: Unacceptable-risk practices are banned; high-risk systems carry strict obligations.
wrong: Bans all AI, forbidding every use outright
Applies only to chatbots
Voluntary guidelines only, suggestions with no force

cards.q: Which ISO standard defines an AI management system?
cards.a: ISO/IEC 42001
cards.x: The AI counterpart to ISO 27001 for security management.
wrong: ISO 27001, the information security management standard
ISO 9001

cards.q: What is algorithmic bias?
cards.a: Systematically unfair outcomes for certain groups
cards.x: Often inherited from skewed training data.
wrong: A slow algorithm, taking hours to finish
A random error, unpredictable noise in outputs
A software bug only, a coding mistake somewhere in the code

cards.q: What is explainability?
cards.a: Showing why a model produced an output
cards.x: SHAP and LIME explain feature contributions for classic ML.
wrong: Model size, the parameter count shown in the explanation
Speed, how fast answers come back
Cost transparency, showing what each call costs

cards.q: What is a model card?
cards.a: Documentation of a model’s intended use, data, limits, and evaluations
cards.x: Datasheets do the same for datasets.
wrong: A GPU spec sheet
An API key card issued to each developer
A pricing page

cards.q: Why maintain an AI inventory?
cards.a: You cannot govern unknown AI systems
cards.x: Includes shadow AI: staff pasting data into public tools.
wrong: For licensing only, tracking who paid for what
For marketing, listing every model in the launch brochure
It is needed to calculate GPU budgets

cards.q: What is a key data-protection risk of public AI tools?
cards.a: Staff pasting confidential data into public tools
cards.x: Use approved enterprise tools with clear data policies.
wrong: Tools are too slow, answers taking minutes
Tools are expensive, the subscription costs too much
Public tools refuse to answer work questions

cards.q: Who should own AI risk in an organisation?
cards.a: Business leadership with a cross-functional governance group
cards.x: Security, legal, privacy, data science, and business owners together.
wrong: The IT helpdesk, which fields user reports about the AI tools
The vendor that supplies the model, under its contract
The data science team, since it builds and tunes the models

cards.q: What is red teaming an AI system?
cards.a: Adversarially probing for harmful or unsafe behaviour
cards.x: Do it before launch and after major changes.
wrong: Testing the model's accuracy on a benchmark
A DDoS test, flooding the servers with junk traffic
A cost audit, checking where the money goes
