decks.title: Think Like a Manager
decks.summary: How CISSP questions want you to reason.

cards.q: What is always the first priority in a CISSP answer?
cards.a: Human safety
cards.x: Life safety beats data, systems, and money every time.
wrong: Protecting data
Reducing cost
Catching the attacker

cards.q: Who is ultimately accountable for security in an organisation?
cards.a: Senior management
cards.x: Responsibility can be delegated; accountability cannot.
wrong: The CISO alone
The IT team
Every user equally

cards.q: CISSP answers favour which role’s viewpoint?
cards.a: A risk advisor to the business
cards.x: Pick answers that align security with business goals.
wrong: The hands-on engineer fixing systems directly
The attacker trying to break in
The auditor only, checking compliance after the fact

cards.q: What should come before choosing any control?
cards.a: Understanding the risk and the business requirements first
cards.x: Assess, then treat. Technology is rarely the first answer.
wrong: Buying a tool before assessing the risk
Writing code to build a custom fix
Blocking all traffic until someone complains

cards.q: What are the four canons of the ISC2 Code of Ethics, in order?
cards.a: Protect society; act honourably; serve principals competently; advance the profession
cards.x: When canons conflict, apply them in that order.
wrong: Serve the employer first; protect data; obey the law; teach others
Act legally; serve the employer; protect data; report breaches
Protect data; protect systems; protect users; protect yourself first — in that exact order

cards.q: What is due care vs due diligence?
cards.a: Due care: acting as a reasonable person would; due diligence: the research and checking behind it
cards.x: Memory aid: due diligence is knowing (investigating, planning, verifying); due care is doing (acting responsibly to protect assets). Failing at due care is negligence.
wrong: Two names for the same legal duty
Due care is the investigation; due diligence is the action taken
Due diligence is the fine paid after a breach

cards.q: What is the best "first step" in most CISSP scenarios?
cards.a: Gather facts and consult policy before acting
cards.x: Avoid drastic unilateral actions.
wrong: Shut down all systems immediately, before checking anything
Call the police before gathering any facts
Fire the suspect on the spot, without evidence

cards.q: How much should a control cost at most?
cards.a: No more than the asset’s value
cards.x: The usual exam rule: never spend more on a control than the asset is worth. More precisely, the annual cost of the control should be less than the reduction in ALE it delivers.
wrong: Any amount, whatever the cost to the business
Twice the asset value, to be extra safe
The whole IT budget, spent on this one control

cards.q: An attacker phishes past the firewall, but EDR blocks the payload and backups restore the data. Which principle saved the organisation?
cards.a: Defence in depth — multiple layered controls so one failure is never fatal
cards.x: Administrative, technical, and physical layers.
wrong: One strong perimeter firewall
Encrypting data everywhere as the main control — if the data is encrypted at rest and in transit, one control is enough to stop any attack
Hiding systems so attackers cannot find them

cards.q: What exam format does CISSP English use (2026)?
cards.a: CAT: 100-150 items in 3 hours, pass at 700/1000
cards.x: CAT = computerised adaptive testing.
wrong: 250 items in 6 hours, the old linear exam format
90 items in 90 minutes, like a short screening test
Hands-on labs only, with no multiple-choice questions

cards.q: Experience required for full CISSP certification?
cards.a: 5 years paid work in 2+ domains
cards.x: A degree or approved cert can waive 1 year. Otherwise pass as an Associate of ISC2.
wrong: 1 year in any IT role, no domain required
No experience, if you pass the exam
10 years across all eight domains

decks.title: Domain 1: Security & Risk Management (16%)
decks.summary: Governance, risk, legal, BCP, and personnel security.

cards.q: Quantitative vs qualitative risk analysis?
cards.a: Monetary values (ALE) vs ratings like high, medium, or low
cards.x: Most organisations blend both.
wrong: The same thing, both describing risk in words
Qualitative uses dollars and exact figures
Quantitative uses opinions only, never numbers

cards.q: What are the NIST RMF (SP 800-37) steps?
cards.a: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor
cards.x: Authorisation is the management decision to accept residual risk.
wrong: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Plan, Do, Check, Act
Scan, Patch, Verify

cards.q: What is residual risk?
cards.a: Risk remaining after controls are applied
cards.x: Total risk − controls = residual; management must accept it.
wrong: Risk before controls are ever applied
Transferred risk, handed off to an insurer
Risk that was avoided entirely, never accepted

cards.q: What is the goal of a Business Continuity Plan?
cards.a: Keep critical business functions running during a disruption
cards.x: DRP is the IT-focused subset that restores systems.
wrong: Restore IT systems after an outage
Prevent all incidents from ever happening
Punish attackers after an incident occurs

cards.q: What is MTD (maximum tolerable downtime)?
cards.a: Longest tolerable downtime before unacceptable damage
cards.x: RTO must be less than or equal to MTD.
wrong: The average repair time across all incidents
The data loss limit, measured in hours
The backup window each night for copying data to tape

cards.q: Which legal concept protects a trade secret?
cards.a: Keeping it secret with reasonable protections
cards.x: No registration; protection lasts while it stays secret.
wrong: Patent filing, which publishes the idea for all to see
Copyright registration, filed with the government office
Trademark — registering the name or logo for protection

cards.q: How long does a US utility patent generally last?
cards.a: 20 years from filing
cards.x: Copyright lasts life of author + 70 years; trademarks can renew indefinitely.
wrong: 70 years, like copyright after death
As long as the patent fees are paid, indefinitely
10 years from the filing date

cards.q: In a finance team, one person approves payments and a different person issues them. Which control is this?
cards.a: Separation of duties — splitting critical tasks so no single person can complete fraud alone
cards.x: Collusion is then required. Job rotation and mandatory vacations help detect fraud.
wrong: Giving everyone admin rights from their first day
Rotating shifts only, with no task split
Least privilege — giving each user only the minimum access they need, which also stops one person completing fraud alone

cards.q: What is a supply chain risk management (SCRM) control?
cards.a: Assessing and monitoring vendors, including their suppliers, on an ongoing basis
cards.x: Includes SBOMs, contract requirements, and right-to-audit clauses.
wrong: Blocking all vendor network access permanently
Paying suppliers late to keep the cash longer
Buying the cheapest option without checking the vendor

cards.q: What does ISO/IEC 27001 specify?
cards.a: Requirements for an organisation’s information security management system (ISMS)
cards.x: ISO 27002 provides the control guidance.
wrong: Encryption algorithms and the maths behind them
Cloud pricing and how providers charge customers
Network cabling and how to wire an office

cards.q: What is threat modelling with STRIDE?
cards.a: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Info disclosure, DoS, Elevation of privilege
cards.x: A Microsoft method for design-time threat analysis.
wrong: A risk formula that multiplies likelihood by impact to produce a dollar figure
A backup scheme for restoring data after a failure
A compliance law that sets fines for breaches

cards.q: Who must be involved when terminating an employee’s access?
cards.a: HR and IT together, revoking access at or before notification
cards.x: Collect assets and disable accounts promptly.
wrong: Only the manager, with no IT involvement
Only the employee, trusting them to comply
Nobody until a week later, after a handover

puzzles.prompt: Order the NIST Risk Management Framework steps.

puzzles.prompt: A risk has an ALE of $50,000. A control cuts it to $10,000 and costs $15,000 a year. What is the control’s annual value?

decks.title: Domain 1: GRC Deep Dive (16%)
decks.summary: BCP/DRP, control types, policy hierarchy, and personnel security.

cards.q: BCP vs DRP?
cards.a: BCP runs the business; DRP restores IT systems
cards.x: The DRP is the IT-focused subset of the wider business continuity effort.
wrong: BCP and DRP are the same plan
BCP restores servers; DRP runs the whole business
DRP is a legal document filed with regulators

cards.q: What does a BCP contain?
cards.a: BIA, recovery strategies, plan invocation, roles, communications, and maintenance
cards.x: It is owned by the business, not just IT.
wrong: Firewall rules, port lists, blocked addresses, and logs
Source code, repositories, build scripts, tests, and docs
Vendor invoices, contracts, payment terms, and receipts

cards.q: What does a DRP contain?
cards.a: System recovery procedures, RTO/RPO targets, backup and restore steps, alternate site details
cards.x: One DRP per critical system or site is common.
wrong: Marketing plans, campaigns, advertising budgets, and branding
Hiring procedures, interviews, onboarding, and probation reviews
Office floor plans, desk layouts, and meeting room bookings

cards.q: What does a Business Impact Analysis (BIA) identify?
cards.a: Critical functions, dependencies, MTD, RTO/RPO, and financial and operational impacts
cards.x: The BIA drives both BCP and DRP priorities.
wrong: Firewall vendors and which brand to buy
Employee salaries, the payroll the BIA must protect first
Software licences and how many seats are bought

cards.q: If backups run every 6 hours, what is the worst-case RPO?
cards.a: 6 hours — the RPO is the maximum tolerable data loss, and it is set by the backup frequency
cards.x: Shorten the backup interval to shrink the RPO; RTO is about restore speed, not data loss.
wrong: 0 hours — backups eliminate data loss entirely
6 hours is the RTO, not the RPO — the backup interval sets how fast you restore, while the RPO is fixed by the SLA

cards.q: What is a structured walkthrough (tabletop) DR test?
cards.a: The team talks through the plan step by step
cards.x: Cheap, discussion-based, and good for finding plan gaps.
wrong: A live failover to the recovery site in production
A code review of the recovery scripts and procedures
A pentest against the production network and servers

cards.q: What is a simulation DR test?
cards.a: The team practices recovery in a simulated scenario without failing over production
cards.x: More realistic than a walkthrough, still non-disruptive.
wrong: Shutting down production for a real, full failover test
A checklist review done on paper, ticking boxes
A phishing test emailed to all the staff

cards.q: What is a parallel DR test?
cards.a: Recovery runs alongside production, no cutover
cards.x: Close to real, but needs duplicate capacity.
wrong: Running two firewalls side by side instead
A load test hammering the production servers hard
A backup restore only, with no live systems

cards.q: Preventive vs detective vs corrective controls?
cards.a: Prevent incidents before they happen; detect them in progress; restore afterwards
cards.x: A firewall rule prevents; an IDS detects; antivirus quarantining malware, or patching an exploited flaw, corrects. (Restoring from backup is usually classed as a recovery control.)
wrong: All detect incidents, only the timing differs between them
Corrective comes first, before prevention or detection
Preventive fixes damage after the incident happens

cards.q: Deterrent vs preventive control?
cards.a: Deterrent discourages attack; preventive blocks it
cards.x: Deterrents rely on the attacker choosing not to act.
wrong: A deterrent and a preventive control are exactly the same
Deterrents block traffic at the firewall
Preventives only warn, never actually block

cards.q: What are recovery and compensating controls?
cards.a: Recovery restores operations; compensating substitutes when the primary is not feasible
cards.x: A compensating control must provide equivalent protection.
wrong: Two names for firewalls, nothing more than that
Both prevent incidents before they can happen
Recovery detects fraud after the money is gone

cards.q: Administrative vs technical vs physical controls?
cards.a: Policies and training; enforced by systems like firewalls and encryption; guards, locks, cameras
cards.x: CISSP calls these control categories; types are preventive/detective/corrective.
wrong: Same as the control types, just with new names
Only technical controls matter, the rest are paperwork
Physical means software that runs on the servers

cards.q: Policy vs standard vs procedure vs guideline?
cards.a: Policy: mandatory intent; standard: mandatory specifics; procedure: steps; guideline: optional advice
cards.x: Policy needs senior management sign-off.
wrong: All are optional, none of them binding on anyone
Guidelines are mandatory, exactly the same as a written policy, and just as binding
Procedures are high-level statements of intent

cards.q: An employee has refused to take leave for three years while handling all payments alone. Which fraud control is being evaded?
cards.a: Mandatory vacations — fraud that needs constant cover unravels when the person is away and someone else covers their duties
cards.x: A classic detective control against employee fraud.
wrong: Separation of duties — splitting the payment tasks between two people so no single employee can both approve and issue a payment
Job rotation — moving staff through different roles
Least privilege — giving each user only the access they need

cards.q: What is the security benefit of job rotation?
cards.a: Cuts fraud opportunity and knowledge silos
cards.x: Pairs with separation of duties and mandatory vacations.
wrong: Faster promotions, moving people up sooner
Lower training costs, spending less on courses
Shorter work weeks with the same pay
