decks.title: Domain 2: Asset Security (10%)
decks.summary: Classification, ownership, retention, and sanitisation.

cards.q: What is the first step in asset security?
cards.a: Identify and inventory assets
cards.x: You cannot protect what you don’t know you have.
wrong: Encrypt everything before doing anything else
Classify data into sensitivity levels first
Buy DLP to stop data leaving the network

cards.q: Who classifies data?
cards.a: The data owner
cards.x: Custodians implement the protection the owner specifies.
wrong: The custodian who looks after the systems
The user who works with the data daily
The auditor who checks compliance afterwards

cards.q: US government classification levels, highest first?
cards.a: Top Secret, Secret, Confidential, plus Unclassified at the bottom
cards.x: Commercial equivalents: confidential/proprietary, private, sensitive, public.
wrong: Secret, Top Secret, Confidential, in that order
Restricted, Private, Public, from highest to lowest
High, Medium, Low, the usual risk ratings

cards.q: What is data remanence?
cards.a: Residual data left on media after deletion
cards.x: Why sanitisation matters.
wrong: Data backups kept for disaster recovery purposes
Data classification into sensitivity levels for handling
Data in transit moving across the network

cards.q: Clearing vs purging vs destruction?
cards.a: Overwrite for reuse inside the organisation; stronger methods outside; destroy
cards.x: NIST SP 800-88 defines Clear, Purge, Destroy.
wrong: The same thing, just three names for wiping disks
Destruction is weakest, barely removing anything
Clearing is strongest, better than destroying it

cards.q: Does degaussing work on SSDs?
cards.a: No, SSDs are not magnetic
cards.x: Use cryptographic erase, vendor secure erase, or physical destruction.
wrong: Yes, always, on every kind of drive
Only on NVMe drives, never on SATA ones
Only when powered on and running hot

cards.q: What is a data retention policy for?
cards.a: Keeping data only as long as needed
cards.x: Over-retention increases breach impact and e-discovery costs.
wrong: Keeping everything forever, just in case
Deleting all data older than one year
Encrypting backups so nobody can read them

cards.q: Data controller vs data processor (GDPR)?
cards.a: Controller decides purpose; processor acts for it
cards.x: A cloud provider is typically a processor.
wrong: Same role, with identical duties under GDPR
Processor decides purpose and how to use it
Controller stores data only, never deciding anything

cards.q: What is scoping and tailoring a baseline?
cards.a: Selecting relevant controls, then adjusting them
cards.x: Start from a standard baseline like NIST SP 800-53.
wrong: Buying new controls to replace the old ones
Removing all controls and starting again from scratch
Auditing controls to check they still work

cards.q: What is pseudonymisation?
cards.a: Replacing identifiers with pseudonyms, so data can’t be linked without extra info
cards.x: Still personal data under GDPR; anonymised data is not.
wrong: Full anonymisation that can never be reversed
Encryption with a public key that anyone can use
Deleting the records once they are no longer needed

cards.q: What does DRM protect?
cards.a: Use of digital content after distribution
cards.x: Controls copying, printing, and forwarding.
wrong: Disk encryption, scrambling everything stored locally
Network perimeters, firewalls around the whole estate
Physical access, locks and guards on the doors

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: Domain 2: Asset Security Deep Dive (10%)
decks.summary: Data lifecycle, legal holds, DLP, and cloud data controls.

cards.q: What are the phases of the data lifecycle?
cards.a: Create, store, use, share, archive, destroy
cards.x: Protection must follow the data through every phase, not just storage.
wrong: Buy, sell, delete — the commercial lifecycle
Create, encrypt, forget — lock it and move on
Collect, analyse, publish — gather and share it

cards.q: Data owner vs steward vs custodian?
cards.a: Owner classifies; steward manages handling; custodian maintains systems
cards.x: The owner decides, the steward oversees daily handling, the custodian operates.
wrong: All three are the same job, really — one role with three different titles
Custodian classifies data and sets all the labels
Steward owns the servers and all the storage

cards.q: How do handling requirements differ by classification?
cards.a: Higher classes need marking, encryption, strict access
cards.x: Handling rules must be written, trained, and enforced.
wrong: All data is handled the same, whatever its classification says
Only public data is encrypted, nothing sensitive ever is
Classification labels are enough without handling rules

cards.q: What typically sets a data retention period?
cards.a: Law plus business need, whichever is longer
cards.x: Document the justification for each retention period.
wrong: Employee preference, whatever the staff would like
Disk capacity, however much storage is free
The auditor’s mood on the day they visit

cards.q: What is a legal hold (litigation hold)?
cards.a: Suspending destruction so relevant data is preserved
cards.x: Destroying data under a hold can be ruled spoliation of evidence.
wrong: A court order to encrypt everything at once
A backup schedule for nightly copies
A retention policy saying how long to keep company data

cards.q: Do backups fall under retention and legal holds?
cards.a: Yes: backups and archives must follow retention schedules, and holds extend to them
cards.x: A hold that misses backups is a failed hold.
wrong: Backups are exempt from every retention rule
Only live data counts, never copies or archives
Holds apply to email and chat only

cards.q: What does network DLP inspect?
cards.a: Data in motion at egress points
cards.x: It can block, quarantine, or encrypt on policy violation.
wrong: Inbound malware trying to get inside
Disk encryption, scrambling data stored locally
Password strength, how hard logins are to guess

cards.q: What does endpoint DLP control?
cards.a: USB drives, printing, clipboard, and local storage on endpoint devices
cards.x: Stops the "sneakernet" exfiltration path.
wrong: Network routing, moving packets between office networks
Cloud billing, working out what all the usage costs
CPU temperature, how hot the processor is running now

cards.q: How is DLP applied to cloud and SaaS?
cards.a: Cloud-native DLP or a CASB scanning uploads, sharing links, and collaboration apps
cards.x: Shadow IT discovery is a common CASB win.
wrong: It cannot be done, the cloud is out of reach
Only with on-prem tools, never cloud ones
By blocking the cloud entirely, for all staff

cards.q: What actions can DLP take on a violation?
cards.a: Block, quarantine, encrypt, or alert, according to the policy in force
cards.x: Start in monitor/alert mode before enforcing blocks.
wrong: Only delete the file, with no other action allowed
Only email the CEO and wait for a reply
Nothing until audit, months later at the earliest

cards.q: Who owns data stored in a SaaS application?
cards.a: The customer, who is the data owner, not the provider
cards.x: Contracts should state this explicitly, with return and deletion terms.
wrong: The SaaS vendor, since it hosts everything
Whoever pays most for the subscription
Nobody — once uploaded, it belongs to no one

cards.q: Why does data sovereignty force regulated workloads into specific cloud regions?
cards.a: Because data follows the laws of the country where it is stored, so the region must satisfy the applicable legal regime
cards.x: Storing EU data in a US region can put it under US law.
wrong: Because data centres in other regions are slower
Because encryption is illegal outside the home country
Because cloud providers charge extra for cross-border traffic, so keeping data in one region is a cost control rather than a legal requirement

cards.q: Data residency vs data sovereignty?
cards.a: Residency is where data is stored; sovereignty is whose laws apply
cards.x: You can meet residency and still fail sovereignty.
wrong: The same thing, both about where the data lives
Residency is about laws, not about location
Sovereignty is about disks and where they sit

cards.q: Which controls protect data in IaaS?
cards.a: Customer-managed keys (BYOK), storage encryption, and private network endpoints
cards.x: In IaaS you own the data and OS layers; the provider owns the hypervisor down.
wrong: The provider handles everything, the customer does nothing
Only firewalls, blocking bad traffic at the edge
Antivirus on VMs, scanning for known malware

cards.q: What do data discovery and classification tools do?
cards.a: Automatically scan stores to find and label sensitive data
cards.x: You cannot apply handling rules to data you have not found.
wrong: Delete old files to free up disk space
Compress databases to save on storage costs
Monitor CPU so the servers run smoothly

cards.q: A sales manager wants to email a spreadsheet of customer records to an outside marketing agency. The data has never been classified. What should the security manager do FIRST?
cards.a: Ask the data owner to classify the data and decide whether it may be shared
cards.x: Classification and the decision to share belong to the data owner. Encryption, DLP and labels are controls applied after that decision, not substitutes for it.
wrong: Encrypt the spreadsheet with a strong password and let the email go out
Block the email until DLP rules are deployed across the whole company
Have the database custodian label it Confidential and approve the transfer

cards.q: Leased SSDs that held regulated health data must be returned to the leasing company at the end of the contract. Which sanitisation approach is MOST appropriate?
cards.a: Purge them with cryptographic erase and verify the result
cards.x: Media leaving the organisation's control needs Purge, not Clear (NIST SP 800-88). Degaussing does nothing to flash memory, and formatting or deleting partitions leaves the data recoverable.
wrong: Degauss each drive with a strong degausser before shipping it back
Quick-format the drives and reinstall a clean operating system on them
Delete every partition and overwrite the drive's file allocation table

cards.q: The retention schedule deletes project email after three years. Legal counsel warns of a lawsuit about a four-year-old project whose email is due for deletion next week. What is the BEST action?
cards.a: Place the relevant records, backups included, under a legal hold
cards.x: A legal hold overrides the retention schedule. Destroying relevant records once litigation is reasonably anticipated can be ruled spoliation of evidence, and a hold that misses backups is incomplete.
wrong: Follow the approved retention schedule, since the policy was signed off
Delete the records now, before any hold is formally served on the company
Ask each employee to keep any email they personally think might matter

cards.q: A database administrator notices that a salary table is readable by every employee. Who should decide what the correct access to that table is?
cards.a: The data owner, such as the HR director accountable for the data
cards.x: The owner is accountable for the data and decides who may access it. The DBA is a custodian who implements that decision; the CISO sets the security program, not access to each data set.
wrong: The database administrator, who manages the database day to day
The CISO, who is responsible for the overall security program
The help desk team, which processes the company's access requests

cards.q: A company stores its EU customers' personal data in a cloud CRM. The CRM provider is breached. Under the GDPR, who remains accountable for the purposes and lawful basis of that processing?
cards.a: The company, because it is the data controller
cards.x: The controller decides why and how personal data is processed and stays accountable to regulators. The processor has its own duties, such as notifying the controller without undue delay, but a contract cannot transfer the controller's accountability.
wrong: The CRM provider, because it is the one physically holding the data
The CRM provider alone, because the contract shifts all liability to it
Nobody, because the breach happened outside the company's own systems

cards.q: Databases are encrypted at rest and every connection uses TLS, yet analysts routinely export sensitive query results to their own laptops. Which control BEST closes this gap?
cards.a: Endpoint DLP that blocks copying classified data to unmanaged storage
cards.x: Encryption at rest and in transit already cover those states. The gap is data in use on the endpoint, where endpoint DLP and handling rules apply.
wrong: Stronger TLS cipher suites on the links between clients and the database
Full-disk encryption on the database servers in the data centre
Longer retention for the database query logs, kept for later review

cards.q: A small firm adopts the NIST SP 800-53 moderate baseline. Several controls apply only to mainframes, which the firm does not have. What should it do with those controls?
cards.a: Scope them out and document why they do not apply
cards.x: Scoping removes controls that do not apply to the environment; tailoring adjusts the rest. Both must be justified in writing so the baseline remains defensible to auditors.
wrong: Implement every control anyway, so the baseline stays fully compliant
Abandon the baseline and write a custom control set from scratch
Mark them as implemented, since no mainframe exists that could fail them

cards.q: An EU company must keep customer data in the EU. A SaaS vendor offers EU-only hosting, but its support engineers in another country can view customer records. What is the PRIMARY concern?
cards.a: Remote access from abroad may count as a cross-border transfer
cards.x: Under the GDPR, making data accessible from a third country is a transfer even when the servers stay in the EU, so it needs a lawful transfer mechanism and safeguards.
wrong: Network latency for EU users when engineers connect to troubleshoot
Engineers abroad may not be trained on the latest product features
The EU data centre may cost more than the vendor's other regions

cards.q: Attackers got in through a forgotten test server that nobody patched or monitored. Which control would MOST likely have prevented this?
cards.a: An asset inventory with an accountable owner per asset
cards.x: You cannot patch, monitor or retire what you do not know exists. The inventory and ownership come before every other control on the asset.
wrong: A more capable next-generation firewall at the network perimeter
More frequent penetration tests of the production environment
A stronger password policy for all of the company's user accounts

cards.q: A research team needs patient data that can never be linked back to individuals, so that it falls outside data protection law. Which technique fits?
cards.a: Irreversible anonymisation, with the re-identification risk assessed
cards.x: Pseudonymised, encrypted or tokenised data can be re-linked by whoever holds the key or table, so it is still personal data. Only properly anonymised data leaves the scope of the GDPR.
wrong: Pseudonymisation, with the re-linking keys stored on a separate server
Encryption of the dataset, with the key held by the lead researcher
Tokenisation through the same vault the company uses for card numbers

cards.q: Printed reports containing confidential data keep turning up in a shared printer tray. The staff involved say they did not realise the reports were sensitive. Which control addresses the ROOT cause?
cards.a: Marking classified outputs, backed by handling training for staff
cards.x: The staff did not know the data was sensitive, so the fix is making classification visible on the output and teaching what each label requires. Physical measures only treat the symptom.
wrong: Moving the printer into a locked room that only managers can enter
Disabling printing for every user in the organisation permanently
Having the cleaning staff shred everything left in the tray each night

cards.q: A company keeps all customer data indefinitely in case it becomes useful one day. Which risk does this MOST increase?
cards.a: The impact of a breach and the cost of legal discovery
cards.x: Data that is kept can be stolen and must be produced in litigation. Retaining only what law and business need limits both.
wrong: The chance of losing data in a natural disaster at the main site
The time it takes the operations team to patch the database servers
The number of help desk calls about forgotten customer passwords

cards.q: A data owner wants assurance that the cloud provider itself cannot read the company's stored data. Which control BEST provides it?
cards.a: Encryption with customer-held keys kept outside the provider's control
cards.x: If the provider manages the keys, it can decrypt the data. Holding the keys yourself (external key management or hold-your-own-key) is what removes the provider's ability to read it; reports and contracts only describe intent.
wrong: The provider's default encryption at rest, which is enabled for every bucket
A clause in the service agreement promising staff will never look at data
A recent SOC 2 Type II report on the provider's internal security controls

cards.q: Backup tapes are sent offsite by courier every week. Which control BEST protects their confidentiality if a tape goes missing in transit?
cards.a: Encrypt the backups, keeping the keys separate from the tapes
cards.x: A bonded courier, tracking and chain-of-custody logs make loss less likely and easier to trace, but only encryption protects the contents once a tape is lost.
wrong: Use a bonded courier service with real-time tracking of every box
Label each tape clearly as Confidential before it leaves the site
Keep a signed chain-of-custody log for every tape that is shipped

cards.q: A sign-up form collects each customer's full date of birth, but the business only needs to confirm that the customer is 18 or older. What is the BEST change?
cards.a: Collect only a confirmation that the customer is 18 or older
cards.x: Data that is never collected cannot leak. Minimisation at the point of collection beats protecting an unnecessary field afterwards.
wrong: Encrypt the date-of-birth column in the customer database
Hash each date of birth before it is written to storage
Mask the date of birth everywhere it appears in the interface

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: Domain 3: Security Architecture & Engineering (13%)
decks.summary: Security models, secure design, crypto, and physical security.

cards.q: Bell-LaPadula enforces which goal?
cards.a: Confidentiality: no read up, no write down
cards.x: Military classification model.
wrong: Integrity, keeping data accurate and completely unaltered
Availability, keeping systems up and reachable
Non-repudiation, proving beyond doubt who did what

cards.q: Biba enforces which goal?
cards.a: Integrity: no read down, no write up
cards.x: The inverse of Bell-LaPadula.
wrong: Confidentiality, keeping secrets from unauthorised eyes always
Availability, keeping data reachable whenever users need it
Accountability, tracing every action back to a person

cards.q: Which model prevents conflicts of interest?
cards.a: Brewer-Nash (Chinese Wall)
cards.x: Access changes dynamically based on prior access.
wrong: Clark-Wilson, with its well-formed transactions
Biba, with its integrity levels and rules
Take-Grant, with its take and grant rights

cards.q: Clark-Wilson enforces integrity using…
cards.a: Well-formed transactions and separation of duties
cards.x: Users access data only through programs (the access triple).
wrong: Clearance levels, from Confidential up to Top Secret
Chinese walls between competing client teams
No read up, the confidentiality rule

cards.q: What is a trusted computing base (TCB)?
cards.a: Hardware, firmware, software enforcing the policy
cards.x: The reference monitor mediates all access and must be tamper-proof.
wrong: A backup server holding copies for recovery
A trusted vendor who supplies the equipment
A certificate chain proving identity step by step

cards.q: What does a TPM provide?
cards.a: Hardware root of trust for keys and boot
cards.x: Used by BitLocker to seal disk keys.
wrong: Faster CPUs for quicker encryption and hashing work
Network encryption for traffic in transit everywhere
Extra RAM for running more virtual machines at once

cards.q: What is Common Criteria?
cards.a: An international framework for evaluating security products, rated EAL1-7
cards.x: Protection profiles define requirements.
wrong: A cloud standard for hosting services securely worldwide
A crypto algorithm for encrypting data at rest
A privacy law that every company must obey

cards.q: Which fire suppression is best for data centres?
cards.a: Clean agents (e.g. FM-200) or pre-action sprinklers
cards.x: Pre-action fills pipes only after detection, reducing accidental water damage.
wrong: Wet pipe sprinklers, always full of pressurised water
Halon, the old gas now banned for ozone damage
Water hoses, aimed by the fire crew at flames

cards.q: Why must cryptographic code run in constant time, regardless of the secret value?
cards.a: To stop timing side-channel attacks — if execution time varies with the secret, an attacker can extract it from timing measurements
cards.x: Spectre and Meltdown exploited CPU speculative execution.
wrong: To stop phishing, tricking users with fake emails
To stop SQL injection — constant-time code keeps database queries from leaking secrets through the time each query takes to run, to an attacker watching response times
To stop brute force, guessing passwords again and again

cards.q: Secure design principle: "fail securely" means…
cards.a: On failure, the system defaults to a secure state
cards.x: Also: secure defaults, least privilege, zero trust, privacy by design.
wrong: Failing fast, crashing at the very first error
Failing open, letting everyone straight through the gate
Never failing, running perfectly forever without a fault

cards.q: What is the key length/strength trade-off of ECC vs RSA?
cards.a: ECC gives equal strength with much shorter keys
cards.x: 256-bit ECC ≈ 3072-bit RSA.
wrong: RSA is always stronger, whatever the key size is
Same key sizes for exactly the same strength
ECC needs longer keys than RSA to match it

cards.q: What does a CPTED approach use?
cards.a: Environmental design to deter crime: lighting, sightlines, and landscaping
cards.x: Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design.
wrong: Cameras only, watching every entrance all day
Guards only, patrolling the grounds all night long
Encryption, scrambling data so nobody can read it

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: Domain 4: Communication & Network Security (13%)
decks.summary: Secure network architecture, protocols, and channels.

cards.q: At which OSI layer does IPsec operate?
cards.a: Layer 3 (Network)
cards.x: TLS is usually placed at Layer 4-6 depending on the model used.
wrong: Layer 2, the data link layer
Layer 4, the transport layer
Layer 7, the application layer

cards.q: IPsec AH vs ESP?
cards.a: AH = integrity and authentication only; ESP also adds confidentiality
cards.x: ESP is what most VPNs use.
wrong: AH and ESP do exactly the same job
AH encrypts the whole packet for total secrecy
ESP has no integrity, encryption is all it does

cards.q: Two branch offices connect their gateways over the internet. Which IPsec mode do they use, and why not transport mode?
cards.a: Tunnel mode — it encrypts the whole packet, headers included, between gateways; transport mode protects only the payload and is for end hosts
cards.x: Site-to-site VPNs use tunnel mode.
wrong: Transport mode — it encrypts the whole packet between the two gateways, including the headers, so it is the right choice for site-to-site links
Tunnel mode — it encrypts headers only, leaving the payload in cleartext
Transport and tunnel mode are identical, so either works

cards.q: A zero trust design isolates every workload with its own policy, so breaching one server opens nothing else. What is this called?
cards.a: Micro-segmentation — fine-grained policies isolating individual workloads
cards.x: A zero trust building block, limits lateral movement.
wrong: VLANs only — separating traffic by switch port, which isolates every workload with its own policy just like micro-segmentation does
One big flat network, everything able to reach everything
A DMZ, a buffer zone for public servers

cards.q: What does EAP-TLS require?
cards.a: Certificates on both the client and the server
cards.x: Strongest common 802.1X method. PEAP needs only a server cert.
wrong: A shared password only, one password for all users
No certificates, just usernames and passwords
A server cert only, the client needs nothing

cards.q: What is converged networking (e.g. FCoE, iSCSI, VoIP)?
cards.a: Storage, voice, and other traffic over IP/Ethernet
cards.x: Convenient, but widens the attack surface of those services.
wrong: Using two ISPs so one can fail over to the other
Merging VLANs into one big broadcast domain
Wireless mesh, access points relaying for each other

cards.q: What is a CDN’s security benefit?
cards.a: Absorbs DDoS and shields origin servers
cards.x: Often combined with a WAF at the edge.
wrong: Encrypts databases stored on the servers
Replaces IAM for all user logins
Stops phishing emails reaching the inbox

cards.q: Which protocol secures DNS responses with signatures?
cards.a: DNSSEC
cards.x: Provides integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality. DoH/DoT add encryption.
wrong: DoH
SPF
LDAPS

cards.q: What is a bastion/jump host’s role?
cards.a: A single hardened, monitored entry point
cards.x: Increasingly replaced by ZTNA brokers.
wrong: A load balancer spreading traffic across servers
A DNS server resolving names to addresses
A backup host standing by for failover

cards.q: What does network segmentation mainly limit?
cards.a: Blast radius and lateral movement
cards.x: A PCI DSS scope-reduction technique too.
wrong: Bandwidth, how much data the links carry
Latency, how long packets take to arrive
Licence costs for network equipment

cards.q: What does ZTNA replace?
cards.a: Broad VPN access gives way to per-application, identity-aware access
cards.x: Zero Trust Network Access; users never land "on the network".
wrong: Firewalls entirely, removing every network control at once
MFA, the extra factor checked at login time
DNS, the service that resolves names to addresses

cards.q: What is a key risk of IoT devices on corporate networks?
cards.a: Weak, rarely patched devices becoming pivot points
cards.x: Put them on isolated segments with strict egress.
wrong: They use too much power for the building
They are too fast for the network switches to handle
They need IPv6 addresses to communicate

decks.title: Domain 5: Identity & Access Management (13%)
decks.summary: Identification, authentication, authorisation, and lifecycle.

cards.q: What is the order of access control steps?
cards.a: Identification, authentication, authorisation, accountability
cards.x: Claim identity, prove it, get permissions, get logged.
wrong: Authorisation first, then identification, then authentication
Authentication, identification, accounting, in that order
Auditing first, before anyone is identified

cards.q: Biometric Type I error is…
cards.a: False rejection (a valid user denied)
cards.x: Type II is false acceptance, the more serious security failure.
wrong: False acceptance, letting an impostor straight in
Crossover error, where the two rates meet
Failure to enrol, unable to register a user

cards.q: What is the Crossover Error Rate (CER)?
cards.a: The point where false rejection and false acceptance rates are equal
cards.x: Lower CER = more accurate biometric system.
wrong: Maximum error rate the system ever reaches in practice
Enrolment time, how long signing a user up takes
Throughput rate, how many users pass through per hour

cards.q: What is Kerberos’ trusted third party?
cards.a: The KDC (Key Distribution Center)
cards.x: Includes the Authentication Service and Ticket-Granting Service.
wrong: The CA, issuing certificates to everyone
The RADIUS server, checking network logins
The client, asking for its own ticket

cards.q: Kerberos’ main weakness?
cards.a: The KDC is a single point of failure
cards.x: Clock skew beyond 5 minutes (default) breaks authentication.
wrong: It uses plaintext passwords sent in clear over the network
It has no tickets, just usernames and passwords
It cannot use AES encryption

cards.q: What is federated identity?
cards.a: Trusting identities issued by another organisation’s IdP
cards.x: SAML, OIDC, and WS-Federation implement it.
wrong: A shared password used by everyone in the company together
A local account created on this system only
A VPN, tunnelling traffic to the office

cards.q: What is JIT (just-in-time) access?
cards.a: Elevated rights only when needed, briefly
cards.x: Eliminates standing privilege.
wrong: Faster logins, skipping the password step
Permanent admin rights, granted on day one
Automatic account creation for every new hire

cards.q: Why perform periodic access reviews?
cards.a: Removing privilege creep and orphaned accounts
cards.x: Managers recertify their team’s access.
wrong: To reset passwords, all of them at once every month
To comply with DNS rules and standards
To add users as quickly as possible

cards.q: What does NIST SP 800-63B advise on passwords?
cards.a: Favour length, screen breached lists, no forced rotation
cards.x: Change passwords only on evidence of compromise.
wrong: Force rotation every 30 days
Require special characters always, in all passwords
Maximum 8 characters, no longer passwords are ever allowed

cards.q: What is session management’s key control?
cards.a: Timeouts, secure tokens, and re-authentication for sensitive actions
cards.x: Invalidate sessions on logout and password change.
wrong: Longer sessions that never time out, ever
Shared sessions used by the whole team together, with one login for all
URL-based session IDs embedded in links

cards.q: What is a risk-based / conditional access policy?
cards.a: Adjusting requirements by device, location, and risk
cards.x: e.g. require MFA from unknown devices, block impossible travel.
wrong: Same rules for all users, whatever the context or risk
A password check with a fixed lockout policy
Blocking all remote access, for every user

cards.q: An employee moved from Finance to Sales six months ago and can still approve payments in the finance system. Which part of the identity lifecycle failed?
cards.a: The mover process, which should remove old rights at a role change
cards.x: When people change roles, access for the old role must be removed, not just new access added. Without that, privilege creep builds up; periodic access reviews are the safety net that catches it.
wrong: The leaver process, which handles staff who leave the company
Identity proofing, which verifies a person's identity at hire
Password policy, which sets the complexity of user passwords

cards.q: A system administrator is about to be dismissed for misconduct. When should the administrator's access be removed?
cards.a: As the dismissal is being communicated, or just before
cards.x: An unfriendly termination is the highest-risk moment: a privileged insider who has just been told could do serious damage. Coordinate HR and IT so access ends as the conversation starts.
wrong: At the end of the administrator's final scheduled working day
Once HR has completed all of the exit paperwork
Within the standard 24-hour deprovisioning window

cards.q: Employees should sign in to a new SaaS application with their corporate credentials, and the vendor must never store their passwords. What is the BEST approach?
cards.a: Federate through SAML or OIDC, with the corporate IdP as identity provider
cards.x: With federation the user authenticates to the company's own identity provider, and the SaaS application receives a signed assertion or token instead of the password.
wrong: Synchronise corporate password hashes into the SaaS vendor's directory
Create local SaaS accounts that reuse each employee's corporate password
Share a single service account through the company's password vault

cards.q: A SaaS application accepts SAML assertions from a customer's identity provider. What MUST the application verify before trusting an assertion?
cards.a: The IdP's signature, the audience and the time window
cards.x: An unsigned or unchecked assertion can be forged or replayed. The service provider validates the signature against the IdP's certificate, that the assertion is meant for it, and that it is within its time window.
wrong: That the user's browser sent it over an HTTPS connection
That the user's email address domain matches the company's
That the assertion arrived within one second of the login

cards.q: Attackers are phishing employees' one-time MFA codes and relaying them in real time. Which authenticator BEST resists this attack?
cards.a: FIDO2 security keys or passkeys bound to the real site
cards.x: FIDO2 authenticators sign a challenge tied to the genuine site's origin, so a look-alike phishing site gets nothing it can replay. Any code a user can read and type can be relayed.
wrong: SMS one-time codes sent to each employee's registered phone
Six-digit codes from a time-based authenticator app (TOTP)
One-time sign-in links sent to the employee's email address

cards.q: A hospital wants access to patient records to depend on the user's role, whether they are treating that patient, the time of day and where they are working. Which access control model fits BEST?
cards.a: Attribute-based access control (ABAC)
cards.x: ABAC evaluates policies over attributes of the subject, the resource, the action and the environment, which is exactly this combination. Static roles alone cannot express "treating this patient now".
wrong: Discretionary access control (DAC)
Role-based access control with fixed roles
Mandatory access control (MAC) with labels

cards.q: In a defence system, users cannot change permissions on anything they create, and access depends only on their clearance and the data's classification label. Which model is in use?
cards.a: Mandatory access control (MAC)
cards.x: In MAC the system enforces access by comparing clearances with labels, and users, even owners, cannot grant access themselves.
wrong: Discretionary access control (DAC)
Rule-based access control on a firewall
Attribute-based access control (ABAC)

cards.q: On a file share, each file's creator decides who else may open it. What is the PRIMARY risk of this arrangement?
cards.a: Owners can over-share with no central oversight
cards.x: This is discretionary access control. It is flexible, but access spreads at each owner's discretion, and malware running as the user inherits the same power.
wrong: Users cannot share files with colleagues who need them
Every access decision has to be approved by a central team
File labels must be assigned by a security administrator

cards.q: Six administrators share one root password for the production servers. What is the BEST improvement?
cards.a: Privileged access management with individual named accounts
cards.x: A shared credential destroys accountability: nobody can tell which administrator did what. PAM gives each person their own access, with check-out, rotation and recorded sessions.
wrong: Rotate the shared root password every month and tell everyone
Write the root password down and keep it in the office safe
Allow the shared root account to log in only during business hours

cards.q: An audit finds 40 active accounts belonging to contractors whose contracts ended months ago. What is the MOST effective long-term fix?
cards.a: Automatic deprovisioning from contract end dates, plus recertification
cards.x: Disabling the 40 accounts fixes today's finding only. Tying account lifecycle to an authoritative source of contract end dates, with managers recertifying access, stops it recurring.
wrong: Disable the 40 accounts by hand and close the audit finding
Shorten the password expiry period for all contractor accounts
Require multi-factor authentication on every contractor account

cards.q: After a virtualisation host's clock drifted by ten minutes, users of the domain controllers it runs suddenly cannot authenticate with Kerberos. What is the MOST likely cause?
cards.a: The clock skew exceeds Kerberos' tolerance, five minutes by default
cards.x: Kerberos tickets carry timestamps to prevent replay, so clients and the KDC must agree on the time. Synchronise the clocks to a reliable time source with NTP.
wrong: The ticket-granting tickets have all reached their maximum renewal age
The users' passwords expired at the same moment the clock drifted
The domain controllers lost their TLS certificates when time changed

cards.q: A company hires staff fully remotely and must issue them credentials for sensitive systems. Which identity proofing step is STRONGEST?
cards.a: Verify official ID authoritatively, with a supervised live check
cards.x: Strong proofing checks that the evidence is genuine and that the person presenting it is its owner (as in NIST SP 800-63A at IAL2 or higher). Emailed scans and social profiles prove neither.
wrong: Ask each new hire to email a scanned copy of their passport to HR
Send the first password to the personal email on the application
Confirm the hire's identity from their public social media profiles

cards.q: An application's service account was given domain administrator rights "to avoid permission errors". What should the security manager require?
cards.a: Only the rights it needs, on a managed, auto-rotated account
cards.x: A compromised service account inherits every right it holds. Grant only what the application needs, and use a managed service account so the credential rotates without a human knowing it.
wrong: Keep domain admin rights but give it a longer, stronger password
Keep domain admin rights but allow sign-in only from that server
Keep domain admin rights and review its activity logs once a year

cards.q: Customers use an online banking site on shared public kiosks, and sessions stay signed in after they walk away. Which control BEST reduces the risk?
cards.a: Session timeouts plus re-authentication for transfers
cards.x: Short timeouts limit how long an abandoned session can be reused, and re-authentication protects the actions that matter most even inside a live session.
wrong: Longer, more complex passwords required for every customer
A CAPTCHA challenge shown on the bank's sign-in page
Encrypting the session cookie with a stronger algorithm

cards.q: Attackers are deliberately locking out every user by submitting wrong passwords against all usernames. What is the BEST way to keep brute-force protection without enabling this?
cards.a: Progressive delays and risk checks, not hard lockouts
cards.x: Hard lockouts turn the defence into a denial-of-service tool. Throttling, IP and device reputation, and step-up challenges slow guessing without letting an attacker lock everyone out.
wrong: Turn off account lockout and failed-login throttling entirely
Lock each account permanently after three failed attempts
Force every user to change their password once a week

decks.title: Domain 6: Security Assessment & Testing (12%)
decks.summary: Audits, vulnerability assessment, pentesting, and metrics.

cards.q: Vulnerability assessment vs penetration test?
cards.a: Finding and ranking weaknesses vs actively exploiting them
cards.x: Pentests prove impact; both need authorisation.
wrong: Assessment and pentest are the same exercise
Pentest is passive, only reading and reporting
Assessments exploit every weakness they find

cards.q: First-party vs second-party vs third-party audit?
cards.a: Internal audit by own staff; customer audit; independent-firm audit
cards.x: First-party audits are internal; second-party audits are external but by an interested party; third-party audits are independent and carry the most weight.
wrong: First, second, and third-party audits are identical
Third-party is internal, done by the company staff
Second-party means on-site only, never done remotely

cards.q: SOC 1 vs SOC 2 vs SOC 3?
cards.a: Financial controls vs security/trust controls (detailed) vs public summary
cards.x: SOC 2 covers the Trust Services Criteria.
wrong: Three severity levels — low, medium, and high risk — applied to every finding
Three SIEM tiers: basic, standard, and premium
SOC 1, 2, and 3 are the same report

cards.q: What is synthetic transaction monitoring?
cards.a: Scripted simulated user activity testing availability
cards.x: Real user monitoring (RUM) observes actual users.
wrong: Fake log entries written to confuse the SIEM analysts
A pentest against the production systems
A load test only, hammering the servers hard

cards.q: What is fuzz testing?
cards.a: Feeding malformed input to find crashes
cards.x: Mutation fuzzing alters valid input; generation fuzzing builds from a spec.
wrong: Code review, reading every line by eye
Unit testing, checking each function alone
Static analysis, scanning code without running it

cards.q: What is misuse case testing?
cards.a: Testing how an attacker might abuse functionality
cards.x: The adversarial counterpart of use cases.
wrong: Load testing, flooding the login page with fake users
Usability testing, watching real users struggle with it
Regression testing, re-running old tests after every change

cards.q: What are KPIs vs KRIs?
cards.a: Performance indicators (past results) vs risk indicators (early warnings)
cards.x: Report both to leadership in business terms.
wrong: KPIs and KRIs track the same measures
KRIs measure revenue, month after month
KPIs predict risk before it happens

cards.q: What is code coverage vs interface testing?
cards.a: Code exercised by tests vs interactions between components
cards.x: Interface testing covers APIs, UIs, and physical interfaces.
wrong: Coverage and interface testing are the same
Coverage tests UIs, clicking every button
Interface counts lines of code in total

cards.q: What is a breach and attack simulation (BAS)?
cards.a: Automated, continuous safe emulation of attacks to validate controls
cards.x: Complements periodic pentests.
wrong: A real breach, with actual data stolen by attackers
A tabletop exercise, talking through the incident plan together as a team
A code review, reading every line by eye carefully

cards.q: Why must audit logs be protected?
cards.a: Attackers alter or delete them to hide activity
cards.x: Centralise, restrict access, and use write-once or integrity checks.
wrong: They use space on the disks, wasting storage
They are public, anyone can read them freely
They slow systems down when writing every entry

cards.q: What does a regression test confirm?
cards.a: A change did not break existing functionality
cards.x: Run the regression suite automatically on every change, so a fix in one place cannot silently break something that used to work.
wrong: New features work exactly as they were designed
Performance improved, pages loading much faster now
Security is perfect, nothing can ever get through

cards.q: An external penetration test is due to start on Monday. What MUST be in place before testing begins?
cards.a: Signed authorisation with scope and rules of engagement
cards.x: Without written permission from someone with authority over the systems, a penetration test is unauthorised access. The scope and rules of engagement also set what is out of bounds and who to call if something breaks.
wrong: Verbal approval from the IT manager who requested the test
A non-disclosure agreement signed by the testers alone
A full network diagram supplied by the testing company

cards.q: Monthly vulnerability scans of the servers report very few issues, yet a breach later exploited missing local patches on those same servers. What is the BEST improvement to the scanning?
cards.a: Credentialed scans that log in and read installed software
cards.x: Unauthenticated scans only see what a host exposes on the network. Credentialed scans read installed packages and patch levels, finding local vulnerabilities the network view cannot.
wrong: Scan more often, moving from monthly to daily network scans
Replace the scanner with another vendor's network scanner
Scan only from outside the firewall, as an attacker would

cards.q: A scan report lists many findings that the server team insists are false positives. What is the BEST next step?
cards.a: Verify them, then track real ones and document the rest
cards.x: Findings should be verified, for example by checking versions and configuration, before they are dismissed or prioritised. Blanket suppression hides real issues; confirmed false positives are documented so they are not re-raised.
wrong: Suppress all of the disputed findings in future scan reports
Escalate every disputed finding to the external auditors
Rescan with the disputed vulnerability checks switched off

cards.q: The board's audit committee wants assurance that key security controls are operating effectively. Who should perform the assessment?
cards.a: An independent party, such as internal or external audit
cards.x: Assurance depends on independence. The team that runs the controls has an interest in the result, so it cannot give the committee objective assurance.
wrong: The security operations team that runs the controls every day
The IT manager responsible for the systems being assessed
The vendor that supplied and configured the security tools

cards.q: A customer wants evidence that a SaaS vendor's security controls actually operated effectively over the past year, not just that they were designed well. Which report should it ask for?
cards.a: A SOC 2 Type II report
cards.x: Type I reports on control design at one point in time; Type II tests operating effectiveness over a period, usually six to twelve months. SOC 1 covers financial reporting controls.
wrong: A SOC 2 Type I report
A SOC 1 Type I report
A SOC 3 general-use seal

cards.q: The server team reports that every critical finding from last quarter's penetration test has been fixed. How should the security manager confirm this?
cards.a: Have the fixes retested, by the testers or a targeted rescan
cards.x: A report of a fix is not evidence of a fix. Retesting each finding confirms it is closed and that the fix did not introduce something new.
wrong: Accept the server team's signed statement that work is done
Close the findings once the change tickets are marked complete
Wait for next year's penetration test to see if they reappear

cards.q: Management wants to know whether security awareness training is actually reducing phishing risk. Which metric BEST answers that?
cards.a: The trend in phishing-simulation click and report rates over time
cards.x: Course completion measures activity, not outcome. A falling click rate and a rising report rate in realistic simulations show whether behaviour changed.
wrong: The percentage of staff who completed the annual training course
The number of training modules the company has published
The average quiz score at the end of each training module

cards.q: A company has a small budget for one week of application penetration testing and wants as many real weaknesses found as possible. Which approach gives the MOST coverage?
cards.a: White-box testing, with source code and design documents
cards.x: With full knowledge, testers spend the week finding flaws rather than mapping the target. Black-box testing better simulates an outsider but covers less in the same time.
wrong: Black-box testing, with no prior knowledge of the application
A vulnerability scan only, run once at the start of the week
Red-team testing, focused on avoiding detection by defenders

cards.q: When is it MOST cost-effective to find security defects in a new application?
cards.a: Early, through design reviews and static analysis during development
cards.x: The cost of fixing a defect rises sharply the later it is found. Threat modelling and static analysis catch issues before they are built into production.
wrong: Just before go-live, in a final penetration test of the release
After release, through the bug bounty programme and user reports
At the yearly audit, when all applications are assessed together

cards.q: A penetration test report will be presented to the executive team. What should its executive summary emphasise?
cards.a: Business risk and prioritised remediation, in plain language
cards.x: Executives decide on risk and funding. Exploit details and raw tool output belong in the technical sections for the teams fixing the issues.
wrong: Step-by-step exploit details for every vulnerability found
Full raw output from every scanning tool that was used
A list of each tester's certifications and experience

cards.q: Database administrators are responsible for reviewing the audit logs of their own administrative activity. What is the main problem with this?
cards.a: It breaks separation of duties: they review their own actions
cards.x: People should not be the sole reviewers of their own activity. Send privileged-activity logs to a central system that an independent team monitors.
wrong: The logs will grow too large for the database to store
Administrators lack the technical skills to read the logs
Reviewing logs slows the database for everyone else

cards.q: An online store wants to find out when checkout breaks at 3 a.m., when almost no real customers are using the site. Which technique fits BEST?
cards.a: Synthetic transactions running a scripted test purchase
cards.x: Real user monitoring only sees problems when users are present. Scripted synthetic transactions exercise the checkout path continuously, whatever the traffic.
wrong: Real user monitoring of the customers who visit the site
A quarterly penetration test of the checkout application
A static code analysis scan of the checkout source code

cards.q: During an authorised penetration test, a tester finds a path into a business partner's network, which is outside the agreed scope. What should the tester do?
cards.a: Stop, take no further action there, and tell the client contact
cards.x: Authorisation covers only the agreed scope: the partner never consented. The finding is reported so the client can address it with the partner.
wrong: Exploit it briefly to prove the risk, then stop and report it
Continue testing, since the path started from in-scope systems
Contact the partner directly and offer to test their network

cards.q: A critical vulnerability in a vendor appliance cannot be patched for three months, until the vendor releases a fix. What is the BEST course of action?
cards.a: A time-limited risk exception with compensating controls
cards.x: When a finding cannot be fixed yet, the risk owner formally accepts it for a limited time, with compensating controls such as isolation and monitoring and a date to revisit it.
wrong: Take no action until the vendor finally releases a fix
Mark the finding as a false positive so it stops reappearing
Remove the appliance from the vulnerability scanning scope

cards.q: An auditor must verify that leavers lose system access promptly. Which evidence is MOST reliable?
cards.a: A sample of HR terminations compared with account disable dates
cards.x: Starting from an independent source (HR's list of leavers) and tracing each one to the system shows whether the control actually worked. A policy or an IT-chosen list only shows intent or a filtered view.
wrong: The written offboarding policy approved by senior management
A list of disabled accounts chosen and supplied by IT
Interviews with IT staff about how offboarding works

decks.title: Domain 7: Security Operations (13%)
decks.summary: Investigations, logging, IR, recovery, and physical safety.

cards.q: What does the ISC2 CISSP incident management process begin with?
cards.a: Detection, then response (containment)
cards.x: Detection, response, mitigation, reporting, recovery, remediation, lessons learned.
wrong: Recovery, restoring systems after the incident
Lessons learned, reviewing what went wrong
Remediation, fixing the root cause

cards.q: What is the best evidence rule?
cards.a: Courts prefer original evidence over copies
cards.x: Forensic images with verified hashes are accepted as duplicates.
wrong: Any evidence is fine, copies or originals
Only witness testimony, what people say in court
Only digital evidence, files and logs alone

cards.q: Which evidence type is hearsay?
cards.a: Second-hand information not from direct knowledge
cards.x: Business records made in the normal course can be an exception.
wrong: Physical evidence, objects found at the scene
Direct testimony, what a witness saw with their own eyes
Forensic images, exact copies of seized disks

cards.q: What are the types of investigation?
cards.a: Administrative, criminal, civil, regulatory
cards.x: Criminal requires "beyond reasonable doubt"; civil "preponderance of evidence".
wrong: Internal and external investigations only
Red and blue
Technical and legal only

cards.q: Full vs incremental vs differential backup restore?
cards.a: Full + last differential, or full + every incremental since
cards.x: Incremental: fast backup, slow restore. Differential: the reverse.
wrong: All equally fast, no matter which backup type
Differential needs all incrementals since the full backup
Incremental needs only one set, the very latest one

cards.q: Which DR test is least disruptive?
cards.a: Read-through / checklist review
cards.x: Then walk-through (tabletop), simulation, parallel, and full interruption.
wrong: Full interruption, shutting everything down for real
Parallel test, recovering live alongside production systems
Simulation, practising recovery without failing over

cards.q: Which DR test is most disruptive (and risky)?
cards.a: Full interruption test
cards.x: Production actually fails over; do it rarely and carefully.
wrong: Parallel test, running the recovery drill beside production
Tabletop, talking through the plan together
Checklist, ticking boxes on a printed page

cards.q: What is entrapment vs enticement?
cards.a: Inducing a crime (illegal) vs luring someone already intent (legal)
cards.x: Honeypots are enticement if used properly.
wrong: Entrapment and enticement are the same offence
Entrapment is legal, the police may do it freely
Enticement is illegal; entrapment is legal

cards.q: What is patch management’s correct sequence?
cards.a: Evaluate, test, approve, deploy, verify
cards.x: Emergency patches still follow an expedited change process.
wrong: Deploy, then test, fixing problems afterwards
Deploy everywhere immediately, then test
Never patch production, leave it as it is

cards.q: What does a SIEM correlation rule do?
cards.a: Links related events into one meaningful alert
cards.x: e.g. failed logons followed by success from a new country.
wrong: Blocks traffic at the firewall edge immediately
Encrypts logs so that only auditors can read them
Deletes duplicates to save disk space

cards.q: What is a key principle of personnel safety during an emergency?
cards.a: Evacuate people first; systems are secondary
cards.x: Doors fail safe (unlocked) for life safety.
wrong: Save the servers first, people can wait
Lock all doors so nobody can get out
Stay at your desk and keep working calmly as usual

cards.q: What is the role of egress monitoring?
cards.a: Detecting data leaving the organisation, e.g. exfiltration
cards.x: DLP, proxy logs, and NetFlow support it.
wrong: Blocking inbound scans at the firewall edge
Monitoring power usage across the data centre
Tracking visitors signing in at the front desk

puzzles.prompt: Order the DR test types from least to most disruptive.
puzzles.x: Only run a full interruption test when you are confident, and with management approval.

decks.title: Domain 8: Software Development Security (10%)
decks.summary: SDLC, DevSecOps, secure coding, and software acquisition.

cards.q: When should security be integrated into the SDLC?
cards.a: From the very start: requirements and design
cards.x: Fixing flaws later costs far more. "Shift left".
wrong: After deployment, once users have found bugs
Only in testing, just before release day
At the end of the project, after everything ships

cards.q: What does the SAMM or BSIMM model measure?
cards.a: Software security programme maturity
cards.x: OWASP SAMM is open; BSIMM is descriptive, based on real firms.
wrong: Code speed, how fast the software runs
CVSS scores, rating each vulnerability found
Cloud costs, what the hosting bill is

cards.q: What is the CMMI maturity level for "optimising"?
cards.a: Level 5
cards.x: 1 Initial, 2 Managed, 3 Defined, 4 Quantitatively Managed, 5 Optimising.
wrong: Level 3
Level 4
Level 1

cards.q: What is DevSecOps?
cards.a: Building automated security into DevOps pipelines
cards.x: SAST, SCA, DAST, IaC scanning, and secrets scanning in CI/CD.
wrong: A separate security team working in isolation
Manual code reviews only, with no automation in the pipeline
A cloud provider hosting the build servers

cards.q: What is software composition analysis (SCA)?
cards.a: Identifying third-party components and their known vulnerabilities
cards.x: Produces or consumes SBOMs.
wrong: Static code review, reading all the source code by eye carefully
Load testing, hammering the app with heavy traffic first
A pentest against the production systems and servers

cards.q: What is a polymorphic object vs polyinstantiation?
cards.a: Same interface, different behaviour; multiple data versions per clearance
cards.x: Polyinstantiation prevents inference in MAC databases.
wrong: Both terms describe exactly the same idea
Two malware types, viruses and trojans together
Two SQL joins, inner and outer, combined together

cards.q: What is an API security top risk?
cards.a: Broken object-level authorisation (BOLA)
cards.x: OWASP API Top 10 #1: check the caller owns each object.
wrong: Slow responses, pages taking too long to load
Too many endpoints, more than anyone can count
JSON format, the way the data is structured

cards.q: What is code escrow?
cards.a: Third party holds source code for vendor failure
cards.x: Protects buyers of critical commercial software.
wrong: Encrypting source code at rest in the repository
Code signing, proving who built the binary file
Open-sourcing code for anyone to use it freely

cards.q: What does an ACID database transaction guarantee?
cards.a: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
cards.x: Ensures integrity of transactions.
wrong: Availability, Confidentiality, Integrity, Durability
Access, Control, Identity, Data
Audit, Compliance, Integrity, Deletion

cards.q: What is the risk of AI coding assistants in the SDLC?
cards.a: Insecure or licence-problematic code accepted without review
cards.x: Keep human review, SAST, and SCA on generated code.
wrong: They type too fast for any human to follow
They cost nothing, completely free to run forever
They cannot write tests, only production code for the application

cards.q: What is a sandbox in software security?
cards.a: A restricted environment for untrusted code
cards.x: Browsers sandbox tabs; mobile apps are sandboxed.
wrong: A test database with copies of production data
A code repo holding every version ever written
A debugger that steps through code

cards.q: What should acquired (third-party) software be assessed for?
cards.a: Security requirements, vendor practices, and contractual obligations
cards.x: Includes SaaS: review SOC 2 reports and data handling terms.
wrong: Only price, whatever the licence costs per year
Only features, whatever the tool can do for us
Nothing if popular — everyone else already uses it, so it must be safe

cards.q: What is the waterfall model?
cards.a: Sequential phases, each completing before the next
cards.x: Requirements, design, implementation, verification, maintenance; revisiting earlier phases is costly.
wrong: Iterative sprints, short cycles with regular demos
Parallel everything, all phases at the same time
Building first and planning as you go

cards.q: What is agile development?
cards.a: Iterative, incremental delivery with close customer collaboration
cards.x: Working software in short cycles; requirements evolve with feedback.
wrong: Development with no documentation of any kind
One big release at the very end
Waterfall with meetings, the same phases renamed

cards.q: What are the Scrum accountabilities (roles)?
cards.a: Product Owner, Scrum Master, and the Developers
cards.x: The Scrum Guide (2020) names three accountabilities: the Product Owner orders the backlog, the Scrum Master removes impediments, and the Developers build each increment.
wrong: Manager, tester, client — the usual project trio
Admin, user, auditor — the operations trio together
CEO, CTO, CISO — the whole executive leadership team together

cards.q: What are the Scrum ceremonies?
cards.a: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective
cards.x: The Scrum Guide (2020) calls these events. All four happen inside the Sprint, which is itself the container event.
wrong: Annual reviews, once a year with the HR team
Change advisory boards, formally approving every production change
Penetration tests, attacking the system for real

cards.q: What is the spiral model?
cards.a: Iterative development with risk analysis each cycle
cards.x: Each loop: plan, assess risk, engineer, evaluate. Good for large, risky projects.
wrong: A backup strategy for restoring lost data quickly
A network topology, how the devices are connected
A malware type that infects office documents silently

cards.q: What is RAD (rapid application development)?
cards.a: Prototype-driven, fast iterations, heavy user involvement
cards.x: Speed comes with a risk of weak security controls if they are not designed in.
wrong: A routing protocol for exchanging network routes
A backup method for copying data every night
A firewall rule set blocking all unwanted traffic at the edge

cards.q: SAST vs DAST?
cards.a: SAST reads source code; DAST tests the running app
cards.x: SAST finds flaws early; DAST finds runtime issues SAST cannot see. Use both.
wrong: SAST and DAST are the same test
SAST tests networks for open ports and services
DAST reads source code; SAST tests the running app

cards.q: Waterfall vs agile: where does security fit?
cards.a: Waterfall: gates per phase; agile: each sprint
cards.x: Either way, security is continuous, not a final phase.
wrong: Only in waterfall, never in any agile project
Only in agile, never in any waterfall project
Security fits neither, it always comes after delivery

cards.q: What is the "definition of done" from a security view?
cards.a: Acceptance criteria including security checks
cards.x: It makes security a release gate in agile teams.
wrong: Code compiles cleanly, no errors from the compiler
Tests exist, at least a few of them
Demo looks good, the screens are polished

cards.q: What is a security champion?
cards.a: A developer promoting secure practices in their team
cards.x: Scales AppSec by embedding security knowledge in every squad.
wrong: The CISO, the executive in charge of security overall
A pentester, attacking systems to find their flaws
A firewall administrator who reviews rule changes

puzzles.prompt: Order the CMMI maturity levels from 1 to 5.
puzzles.x: Maturity grows from ad hoc work to measured, continuously improving processes.

decks.title: D1 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Risk-first decisions: compensating controls, BIA gaps, and policy exceptions.

cards.q: Scenario: A risk assessment finds a critical vulnerability in the order database, but no patch exists and the business cannot take it offline. What is the BEST immediate action?
cards.a: Apply a compensating control and document residual risk
cards.x: When you cannot remediate, you compensate: reduce likelihood or impact another way, record it, and get formal risk acceptance. Doing nothing is not an option.
wrong: Disconnect the database immediately regardless of business impact
Accept the risk informally without documenting it
Wait for the vendor patch before taking any action

cards.q: Scenario: The BIA sets a 4-hour RTO for order processing, but the DR plan restores it in 12 hours. What should you do FIRST?
cards.a: Report the gap to management, review the strategy
cards.x: The BIA defines the requirement; the plan must meet it. The gap is a risk decision for management, not something to quietly accept or unilaterally rebuild.
wrong: Buy faster backup hardware immediately, whatever it costs
Quietly accept the 12-hour RTO and say nothing
Rewrite the entire DR plan yourself over the weekend

cards.q: Scenario: A new privacy regulation takes effect in six months and affects your EU customer data. As security manager, what do you do FIRST?
cards.a: Perform a gap analysis of current controls against the regulation
cards.x: You cannot plan remediation until you know what is missing. Assess first, then roadmap, then implement.
wrong: Hire a data protection officer immediately
Encrypt every database today
Wait for the legal team to tell you exactly what to do about the regulation

cards.q: Scenario: A senior executive requests an exception to the MFA policy for convenience. What is the BEST response?
cards.a: Formal documented risk acceptance, with compensating controls
cards.x: Policy exceptions are legitimate only through the exception process: documented, time-bound, risk-accepted. "Because I am senior" is not a control.
wrong: Grant it — executives are low-risk targets, hardly ever attacked
Grant it quietly to avoid conflict with the boss
Remove MFA for everyone so the policy is "fair"

resources.title: Destination Certification CISSP MindMaps (free videos + PDF)

decks.title: D2 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Data handling under pressure: departing staff, test data, and legal holds.

cards.q: Scenario: An employee with access to customer PII resigns today. From a data-security view, what matters FIRST?
cards.a: Revoke access immediately, then sanitise or reassign devices
cards.x: Containment before cleanup: cut off access so nothing more can leave, then handle data remanence on the hardware.
wrong: Quick-format their laptop for the next hire
Let them keep the laptop until their last day
Only delete their user account next week, never any sooner than that

cards.q: Scenario: Marketing asks to copy production customer data into the test environment to "speed up QA". What is the BEST answer?
cards.a: Refuse — use masked, anonymised, or synthetic data instead
cards.x: Test environments rarely carry production-grade controls. Real PII in test is a breach waiting for an auditor (or an attacker) to find.
wrong: Allow it — faster testing helps the business
Allow a partial copy to limit exposure
Allow it if they promise to delete it afterwards, in writing

cards.q: Scenario: Legal issues a litigation hold covering six months of email. What must happen FIRST?
cards.a: Suspend retention and destruction for the affected data
cards.x: A legal hold overrides the retention schedule. Destroying held data is spoliation, with serious legal consequences.
wrong: Delete old mailboxes to free up space quickly
Archive everything to offline tape for safekeeping off-site
Email all staff the details of the lawsuit

decks.title: D3 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Architecture trade-offs: fail-secure design, layered controls, and key management.

cards.q: Scenario: You are reviewing the design of a new payment application. If a component fails unexpectedly, what is the MOST important design property?
cards.a: Fail-secure (fail closed): failures deny access rather than grant it
cards.x: A failure that opens access turns every bug into a vulnerability. Deny by default, even — especially — when things break.
wrong: Fail open, to protect availability above all else
Log verbose errors to the end user directly on screen
Retry the failed operation indefinitely, forever if it must keep trying

cards.q: Scenario: The team debates firewall versus IPS for the data-centre edge. What is the BEST recommendation?
cards.a: Deploy both: firewall for access, IPS for threats
cards.x: They are different control functions, not substitutes. Layering means one control's miss is another's catch.
wrong: A next-generation firewall alone is sufficient
An IPS inline can replace the firewall
Neither: EDR on every server is enough

cards.q: Scenario: A cloud design stores encryption keys alongside the encrypted data in the same account with the same admins. What is wrong?
cards.a: Keys need their own security domain (KMS/HSM, split duties)
cards.x: Whoever compromises the account gets both lock and key. Keys and data must have different access paths.
wrong: Nothing — it is convenient and cheap, so leave it
Keys belong in application source code instead, hard-coded in plain text
Nothing, as long as the account has MFA enabled

decks.title: D4 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Network defence scenarios: VPNs, evasion, and segmentation.

cards.q: Scenario: Branch-office traffic to headquarters must cross the public internet. What is the MOST appropriate protection?
cards.a: A site-to-site IPsec VPN
cards.x: VPNs provide confidentiality and integrity over untrusted networks — the standard answer for site interconnect.
wrong: VLAN tagging across the internet
Port forwarding on the branch router
MAC address filtering

cards.q: Scenario: Your IDS is missing attacks that use crafted fragmented packets to evade signatures. What is the BEST defence?
cards.a: Normalise and reassemble fragments before inspection
cards.x: Evasion by fragmentation works only if inspection sees fragments. Reassemble first, then match signatures.
wrong: Ignore fragments — they are harmless, just network noise

cards.q: Scenario: Guest Wi-Fi and the corporate LAN will share the same switches and firewall. What is the FIRST design step?
cards.a: Segment them into separate VLANs and firewall zones
cards.x: Guests are untrusted by definition. Segmentation contains lateral movement before anything else is tuned.
wrong: Just give guests a strong Wi-Fi password

decks.title: D5 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Identity decisions: federation, session theft, and exposed secrets.

cards.q: Scenario: A new SaaS HR tool must let staff sign in with corporate credentials, but passwords must never be shared with the vendor. What is the BEST standard to use?
cards.a: SAML (or OIDC) federation against the corporate identity provider
cards.x: Federation delegates authentication to the IdP; the application never sees a password. SAML for enterprise SSO, OIDC for modern web apps.
wrong: Store corporate passwords in the SaaS app itself
Issue one shared service account to all staff
Email temporary passwords to new users directly

cards.q: Scenario: An administrator's session was hijacked even though MFA was enforced at login. Which control would BEST have limited the damage?
cards.a: Short timeouts and step-up re-authentication for privileged actions
cards.x: MFA proves identity at login; session controls bound the blast radius after a theft. The more powerful the session, the shorter its leash.
wrong: Longer, more complex passwords for administrators, rotated every month

Removing MFA to reduce friction for users

cards.q: Scenario: A developer committed a production API key to a public repository an hour ago. What do you do FIRST?
cards.a: Revoke and rotate the key immediately, then investigate
cards.x: A published secret is a compromised secret. Containment (rotation) cannot wait for the investigation to finish.
wrong: Delete the repository and hope nobody saw it
Monitor the key for misuse before revoking it
Schedule rotation for the next maintenance window

decks.title: D6 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Testing triage: pentests, finding prioritisation, and vendor claims.

cards.q: Scenario: Before a major release you want the BEST assurance against vulnerabilities in the running application. Which test do you choose?
cards.a: Penetration testing
cards.x: Pentests simulate real attackers against the running system. SAST examines source; DAST automates black-box checks; neither replaces adversarial testing.
wrong: A source-code review only
A network vulnerability scan
User acceptance testing

cards.q: Scenario: A vulnerability scan returns 500 findings across the estate. How do you prioritise FIRST?
cards.a: By risk: exploitability plus business impact, internet-facing first
cards.x: Scanners report technical severity, not your risk. A critical on an isolated lab box matters less than a high on the payment server.
wrong: Fix them in alphabetical order, A to Z

cards.q: Scenario: A vendor claims SOC 2 compliance during procurement. Before signing, what should you do?
cards.a: Read the SOC 2 report: scope, period, qualifications
cards.x: Third-party risk management runs on evidence, not claims. Check what was audited, when, and what the auditor qualified.
wrong: Take the claim at face value, trusting the vendor completely

Demand ISO 27001 sight unseen as well, blindly

decks.title: D7 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Operations under fire: containment, alert triage, and learning.

cards.q: Scenario: The SOC watches ransomware actively encrypting file shares RIGHT NOW. What is the FIRST action?
cards.a: Isolate the affected systems from the network
cards.x: Incident response runs contain → eradicate → recover. Stopping the spread comes before forensics, backups, or blame.

cards.q: Scenario: A 3am alert reports a single failed login for one user. How should the SOC treat it?
cards.a: Low priority: baseline noise unless corroborated
cards.x: Triage is about fidelity. One failed login is expected background noise; five hundred from one IP is an incident.
wrong: Wake the CISO at once, in the middle of the night
Immediately block the source IP, before checking anything

cards.q: Scenario: An incident is resolved and systems are restored. What is the MOST important step before closing it?
cards.a: Lessons-learned review, then update playbooks and controls
cards.x: Without the post-incident review the same incident will recur. Improvement — not closure speed — is the goal.
wrong: Delete the tickets to keep metrics clean

decks.title: D8 Capstone: Scenario Judgment
decks.summary: Secure development calls: supply chain, secrets, and shift-left.

cards.q: Scenario: Developers want to adopt a popular open-source library. What should happen FIRST?
cards.a: Assess its licence, maintenance health, and known vulnerabilities (SCA)
cards.x: Supply-chain due diligence: licence compatibility, commit activity, and CVE history before a line of it ships.
wrong: Use it — popular open source is inherently safe, that is the whole point
Rewrite the functionality from scratch
Check only the GitHub star count

cards.q: Scenario: A code review finds hardcoded AWS keys in the repository. What is the BEST immediate fix?
cards.a: Revoke keys, move secrets to a vault, add scanning
cards.x: The committed secret is compromised the moment it is pushed. Revoke first, then fix the process so it cannot recur.
wrong: Delete the keys from the latest commit and carry on

cards.q: Scenario: Leadership asks where in the SDLC a security bug is cheapest to fix. What is the correct answer?
cards.a: As early as possible: requirements and design
cards.x: Remediation cost grows exponentially through the lifecycle. Threat modelling in design is orders of magnitude cheaper than an emergency patch in production.

decks.title: Command Line & Filesystem

cards.q: What does `pwd` print?
cards.a: The current working directory as an absolute path
cards.x: pwd = "print working directory". It answers "where am I?", e.g. /home/ana.

The PATH variable
The logged-in username

cards.q: Which command lists files with details, including hidden ones?
cards.a: `ls -la`
cards.x: -l is the long format, -a shows dotfiles (names starting with .).
wrong: `ls`
`ls -R`
`dir /a`

cards.q: What is the difference between an absolute and a relative path?
cards.a: Absolute starts at / (root); relative starts from the current directory
cards.x: /etc/ssh works from anywhere; ../logs only works from the right place.
wrong: Absolute paths are always shorter than relative ones, by definition, in every case
Relative paths always start with ~
There is no difference on Linux

cards.q: What does `cd ~` do?
cards.a: Goes to your home directory
cards.x: ~ expands to $HOME. `cd` alone does the same thing.
wrong: Goes to the root /

Prints the home directory path

cards.q: Which command creates nested directories in one step?

cards.x: -p creates missing parents and does not error if the directory already exists.
wrong: `mkdir -r projects/2026/q1`

`touch -d projects/2026/q1`

cards.a: Recursively force-deletes dir/ with no prompt and no undo
cards.x: -r walks into subdirectories, -f skips confirmation. There is no trash can.
wrong: Moves dir/ to the desktop trash so it can be restored
Renames dir/ to dir.bak
Compresses dir/ first

cards.q: How do you find a file named "app.log" anywhere under /var?
cards.a: `find /var -name "app.log"`
cards.x: find walks the tree; -name matches the basename. Quote the pattern so the shell does not glob it.
wrong: `locate -r /var/app.log`
`grep -r "app.log" /var`, searching file contents for the name
