cards.q: What does `man ls` show you?
cards.a: The manual page documenting ls
cards.x: man pages are the built-in docs: q quits, / searches inside.
wrong: The last 10 lines of ls output
A list of running processes
The ls source code

cards.q: What does pressing Tab do in a shell?
cards.a: Autocompletes the current word
cards.x: Press twice to list candidates. It works for commands, paths, and (often) options.
wrong: Sends SIGINT to the foreground job
Clears the screen
Switches to the previous user

cards.q: How do you re-run the previous command with sudo?
cards.a: `sudo !!`
cards.x: !! expands to the last command, so this is the classic "permission denied, try again" fix.
wrong: `sudo -r`
`!! sudo`
`redo sudo`

decks.title: Permissions & Ownership
decks.summary: rwx, chmod, chown, umask, and the special bits.

cards.q: In `-rwxr-xr--`, what do the three rwx groups mean?
cards.a: Owner, group, others
cards.x: Positions 2-4 are the owner, 5-7 the group, 8-10 everyone else.
wrong: User, admin, root
Read, write, execute — files only
Owner, root, system

cards.q: What numeric mode is `rwxr-xr-x`?
What numeric mode is `rw-r--r--`?
cards.x: rw- = 6, r-- = 4, r-- = 4. The classic default for data files.

cards.q: Which command gives the owner full access, the group read-only, and others nothing on file.sh?
cards.a: `chmod 740 file.sh`
cards.x: 7 = rwx for owner, 4 = r-- for group, 0 = --- for others.
wrong: `chmod 640 file.sh`
`chmod 750 file.sh`
`chmod 704 file.sh`

cards.q: What does `chmod u+x script.sh` do?
cards.a: Adds execute permission for the owner only
cards.x: u = user/owner, g = group, o = others, a = all. Use - to remove: `chmod go-w file`.
wrong: Makes it executable for everyone on the system, all users
Removes execute from the owner
Changes the file owner

cards.q: Which command makes ana the owner and devs the group of file?
cards.a: `chown ana:devs file`
cards.x: Only root (or sudo) can give away ownership. chgrp changes just the group.
wrong: `chmod ana:devs file`
`chgrp ana file`
`usermod ana devs`

cards.q: With umask 022, what permissions does a new file get?
cards.x: Files start at 666 minus the umask (666 - 022 = 644); directories start at 777, giving 755.

cards.q: What does the SUID bit on an executable do?
cards.a: It runs with the file owner's privileges
cards.x: Classic example: /usr/bin/passwd runs as root so normal users can change their own password. Shown as an s: -rwsr-xr-x.
wrong: It makes the file undeletable, even by root, forever
It runs the file at boot
It hides the file from ls

cards.q: What does the sticky bit on /tmp do?
cards.a: Only a file's owner (or root) can delete or rename it
cards.x: Everyone can write to /tmp, but the sticky bit (t in drwxrwxrwt) stops users deleting each other's files.
wrong: It makes /tmp read-only for everyone except root

cards.q: What does SGID on a directory do?
cards.a: New files in it inherit the directory's group
cards.x: Useful for shared project folders: `chmod g+s shared/`. Shown as s in the group execute slot.
wrong: New files inherit the directory's owner instead of the group
The directory becomes read-only
It disables the execute bit

decks.title: Users, Groups & sudo
decks.summary: Accounts, /etc/passwd, groups, and safe privilege escalation.

cards.q: Which file holds one line of account info per user?
cards.a: /etc/passwd
cards.x: Username, UID, GID, home directory, shell. Passwords have not lived here for decades.
wrong: /etc/shadow
/etc/users
/var/lib/users

cards.q: Where are password hashes actually stored?
cards.a: /etc/shadow, readable only by root
cards.x: Shadow also holds ageing policy: expiry, warning days, inactivity lockout.
wrong: /etc/passwd, where every hash sits beside the username
/etc/sudoers
/etc/pam.d/common-password

cards.q: What does UID 0 signify?
cards.a: The superuser (root)
cards.x: Any account with UID 0 has full root privileges, whatever its name.
wrong: A disabled account
The first normal user
A service account

cards.q: Which command creates user ana with a home directory?
cards.a: `useradd -m ana`

wrong: `adduser --no-home ana`
`useradd ana` (home is automatic)
`mkuser ana -home`

cards.q: What does the `id` command show?
cards.a: Your UID, GID, and group memberships
cards.x: `id ana` shows another user's. Handy when debugging "permission denied".
wrong: The machine hostname
Running processes
Disk usage

cards.a: `usermod -aG docker ana`

`addgroup docker ana`

cards.a: sudo grants elevated privileges per the sudoers policy and logs the command under your account, so actions stay attributable to you
cards.x: It asks for YOUR password (not root’s) and logs the command.
wrong: Because sudo switches you to root permanently for the session — once you type your password, every command you run afterwards has root privileges until you log out

Because sudo lists who is allowed to sudo

cards.q: Why must you edit sudoers with `visudo`?
cards.a: It validates the syntax before saving
cards.x: One typo in sudoers can lock every admin out of root access.
wrong: It is faster than other editors, opening instantly every time
It encrypts the file
Normal editors cannot open it

cards.q: What is the practical difference between `su -` and `sudo -i`?
cards.a: `su -` needs the root password; `sudo -i` uses your password and is logged
cards.x: sudo also allows fine-grained rules (e.g. "may restart nginx only") instead of all-or-nothing root.
wrong: They are identical; both prompt for the root password

cards.q: Which command locks ana's account without deleting it?

cards.x: Locking disables password login; -U unlocks. The files and home directory stay put.
wrong: `userdel ana`
`chmod 000 /home/ana`
`killall -u ana`

decks.title: Text Processing Pipelines
decks.summary: grep, pipes, redirection, cut, sort, sed, and awk.

cards.q: What does the pipe `|` do?
cards.a: Feeds one command's stdout into the next command's stdin
cards.x: `dmesg | grep -i usb` searches kernel messages for "usb".
wrong: Runs commands in parallel, all of them at the same time together
Redirects output to a file
Chains commands to run on failure

cards.q: When redirecting output in a shell, how does `>` differ from `>>`?

cards.x: Both create the file if missing. `>` on the wrong file is how data loss happens.
wrong: `>` writes stdout; `>>` writes stderr — the single arrow sends normal output to the file and the double arrow sends error output there instead

`>` only works with root

cards.q: Which command prints lines containing "Failed" in auth.log?

cards.q: What does `grep -ci "error" app.log` print?

wrong: The number of times the word appears

Errors from the last hour

cards.q: What does `2>` redirect?

cards.x: Every process has stdin (0), stdout (1), stderr (2). Plain `>` is shorthand for `1>`.
wrong: Standard input

The exit code

cards.x: /dev/null is the bit bucket; 2>&1 merges stderr into wherever stdout goes.

`command | /dev/null`

cards.q: What does `cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd` print?

cards.x: -d sets the delimiter, -f picks fields; -f1,3 picks fields 1 and 3.
wrong: The whole file unchanged, printed exactly as it sits on disk

The last field of each line

wrong: Sorts and deletes the original file once the counts print

Counts characters per line

cards.q: What does `awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd` do?

wrong: Prints line numbers in front of each line
Prints the whole line

cards.q: How do you replace "foo" with "bar" everywhere in file.txt, in place?

decks.title: Package Management
decks.summary: apt/dnf, repositories, and keeping systems updated.

cards.q: Which package tools belong to which distro family?

cards.x: dpkg/rpm are the low-level tools; apt/dnf resolve dependencies from repositories.

pacman on both families

`ls /usr/bin | ssh`

Kernel modules

Upgrade production before staging

decks.title: systemd & Services

Merge rewrites history

cards.q: The golden rule of rebasing?
cards.a: Never rebase commits that have been pushed/shared — it rewrites others' history
cards.x: Rebase only local, unpushed work.
wrong: Always rebase shared branches so history stays linear
Rebase before every commit
Rebase is never safe

cards.q: What makes a 3-way merge?
cards.a: Git uses both branch tips plus their common ancestor to compute the merge
cards.x: The ancestor helps resolve non-conflicting changes automatically.
wrong: Only the two tips, comparing the branch ends directly without using any common ancestor commit
A single branch
The remote only

cards.q: How can you prevent committing conflict markers?
cards.a: A pre-commit hook / git diff --check that blocks <<<<<<< etc.
cards.x: Committed markers break builds (they did here!).
wrong: Nothing can
Only CI
Rebase removes them, rewriting the branch so any conflict markers disappear from the files

cards.q: What does `git rebase --continue` do?
cards.a: Proceeds after you resolve a conflict mid-rebase (having staged the fix)
cards.x: --abort cancels the whole rebase.
wrong: Starts a new rebase from the current branch onto the latest main, discarding the old one
Pushes the branch
Merges instead

resources.title: Pro Git (the official Git book, free online)
Dangit, Git!? — recovering from common mistakes

puzzles.prompt: Order the steps to resolve a merge conflict.
items: git commit to finish the merge
puzzles.x: You edit to the correct result and delete all three markers, then staging marks it resolved and the commit completes the merge.

decks.title: Undoing Changes
decks.summary: restore, reset, revert, stash and reflog.

cards.q: How do you discard unstaged changes to a file?
cards.a: git restore <file> (older: git checkout -- <file>)
cards.x: This is destructive — the edits are gone.
wrong: git reset <file>, which unstages the file while leaving its working-directory edits untouched
git revert <file>
git clean <file>

cards.q: What does `git revert <commit>` do?
cards.a: Creates a NEW commit that undoes the changes of a given commit
cards.x: Safe for shared history — it adds, never rewrites.
wrong: Deletes the commit from history entirely, removing it and its changes from the log
Resets to it
Edits it in place

cards.q: What does `git reset --soft HEAD~1` do?
cards.a: Undoes the last commit but keeps its changes staged
cards.x: Great for re-committing differently.
wrong: Discards the changes
Reverts on the remote, undoing the commit on origin while keeping your local branch unchanged
Deletes files

cards.q: What does `git reset --hard` do, and the risk?
cards.a: Resets the branch and WIPES working/staged changes — unrecoverable if uncommitted
cards.x: Use with care; prefer stash first.
wrong: Keeps all changes but unstages them, leaving the files untouched
Only unstages files; the branch does not move
Creates a new commit that safely undoes the last one

cards.q: What does `git commit --amend` do?
cards.a: Replaces the last commit (edit its message or add staged changes)
cards.x: Avoid amending commits you have already pushed.
wrong: Creates a second commit alongside the last one, leaving the original commit in history too
Pushes the commit
Reverts it

cards.q: What does `git stash` do?
cards.a: Shelves your uncommitted changes and gives you a clean working tree
cards.x: git stash pop reapplies them later.
wrong: Commits them with a generated message, recording the changes in history before cleaning the tree
Deletes them
Pushes them

cards.q: What is the reflog, and why is it a lifesaver?
cards.a: A log of where HEAD has been — it can recover "lost" commits after a bad reset
cards.x: git reflog shows the history of moves.
wrong: The commit log of the current branch, as shown by git log
A log of every push and pull made against the remote
A merge tool that replays conflicting commits

cards.q: revert vs reset for a commit already pushed?
cards.a: Use revert — it does not rewrite shared history; reset --hard would
cards.x: Rewriting pushed history breaks collaborators.
wrong: Either is fine
reset is safer, since rewriting the branch locally keeps the remote history untouched as well
Neither works

cards.q: How do you throw away ALL local commits back to origin/main?
cards.a: git reset --hard origin/main (destructive)
cards.x: Make sure nothing valuable is uncommitted.
wrong: git revert origin/main, creating a new commit that undoes everything since the remote tip
git clean
git pull

cards.q: What does `git stash pop` do?
cards.a: Reapplies the most recent stash and removes it from the stash list
cards.x: git stash apply keeps it in the list.
wrong: Deletes the stash without applying it, discarding the shelved changes from the list entirely
Commits the stash
Creates a branch

resources.title: Pro Git (the official Git book, free online)
Dangit, Git!? — recovering from common mistakes

decks.title: Workflows & Collaboration
decks.summary: Feature branches, PRs, rebase -i, cherry-pick and tags.

cards.q: What is the feature-branch workflow?
cards.a: Each change is developed on its own branch and merged via review
cards.x: Keeps main releasable and changes isolated.
wrong: Commit everything to main
One branch per person forever, with each developer working only on their own long-lived branch
No branches at all

cards.q: What is a pull request (merge request)?
cards.a: A proposal to merge a branch, with review and discussion before it lands
cards.x: Where code review and CI gates happen.
wrong: A git command that merges two branches
A forced merge
A backup

cards.q: What does `git rebase -i` (interactive) let you do?
cards.a: Reorder, squash, edit or drop commits before sharing them
cards.x: Clean up a messy local history.
wrong: Push to prod, deploying the branch to the production server once the rebase finishes
Merge branches
Resolve remotes

cards.q: What does squashing commits do?
cards.a: Combines several commits into one
cards.x: Gives a tidy, single logical change in history.
wrong: Splits a commit into smaller pieces, so each logical change gets its own commit in history
Deletes history
Creates a tag

cards.q: What does `git cherry-pick <commit>` do?
cards.a: Applies a specific commit from one branch onto your current branch
cards.x: Useful for hotfixes across branches.
wrong: Merges a whole branch, bringing every commit from that branch onto your current branch
Deletes a commit
Reverts it

cards.q: What is a Git tag used for?
cards.a: Marking a specific commit, typically a release (e.g. v1.2.0)
cards.x: Annotated tags store a message and author.
wrong: A branch
A remote
The staging area, marking the set of files staged for the next commit in the repository

cards.q: What is "forking" on a platform like GitHub?
cards.a: Creating your own server-side copy of a repo to contribute via pull requests
cards.x: Common for open-source contributions.
wrong: Deleting a repo from the hosting platform, removing its code and history from the server
A local branch
A merge conflict

cards.q: Trunk-based vs GitFlow — one line?
cards.a: Trunk-based: small, frequent merges to main behind flags; GitFlow: long-lived release/develop branches
cards.x: Trunk-based suits continuous delivery.
wrong: GitFlow: small, frequent merges to main behind flags; trunk-based: long-lived release/develop branches
Both avoid branches
GitFlow has no branches

cards.q: Why keep pull requests small?
cards.a: They are faster to review, lower-risk, and easier to revert
cards.x: Huge PRs hide bugs and stall review.
wrong: To avoid CI
Git requires it
For bigger commits, since large changes need more room to describe what they change

cards.q: What does a CI check on a PR typically do?
cards.a: Runs lint/tests/build so broken code cannot be merged
cards.x: A guardrail against regressions.
wrong: Deploys to prod, shipping the pull request branch straight to production once it opens
Squashes commits
Deletes the branch

decks.title: Internals & Good Practice
decks.summary: The object model, history integrity and security.

cards.q: What identifies a Git commit?
cards.a: A cryptographic hash (SHA-1, moving to SHA-256) of its content
cards.x: Change anything and the hash changes — tamper-evident.
wrong: A sequential number assigned when the commit is created, increasing by one each time
The author name
The branch name

cards.q: What are Git's core object types?
cards.a: blob (file content), tree (directory), commit, and tag
cards.x: Everything is a hashed object in .git/objects.
wrong: Rows and tables
Branches only
Files and folders only, with no commit objects

cards.q: What data structure is Git history?
cards.a: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) of commits linked to their parents
cards.x: Branches/merges are just nodes and edges.
wrong: A linked list only, where each commit points to exactly one parent and nothing ever branches
A single line always
A hash table

cards.q: Why does rewriting shared history cause problems?
cards.a: It changes commit hashes, so collaborators' clones diverge and break
cards.x: Only rewrite local, unpushed commits.
wrong: It never causes problems, since every clone updates its hashes automatically when history changes
It speeds things up
It deletes the remote

cards.q: How do you keep secrets out of a repo?
cards.a: .gitignore + a pre-commit secret scanner (e.g. gitleaks); rotate anything that leaks
cards.x: History makes a committed secret hard to erase.
wrong: Delete the file in a later commit so it no longer appears in the tree
Rely on Git, which encrypts files that look like credentials
Push only to a private repository

cards.q: What are signed commits/tags for?
cards.a: Cryptographically proving who authored them (GPG/SSH signatures)
cards.x: Protects against impersonation in the history.
wrong: Compression, shrinking the commit and its objects so the repository takes up less disk space
Faster merges
Smaller repos

cards.q: What is Git LFS for?
cards.a: Storing large binary files outside normal Git history, via pointers
cards.x: Keeps the repo small and clones fast.
wrong: Encrypting the repo, scrambling file contents so only holders of the key can read them
Linting commits
A branching model

cards.q: Why avoid committing large binaries directly?
cards.a: They bloat every clone's history forever and slow operations
cards.x: Use LFS or keep them out of Git.
wrong: They cannot be committed, since Git refuses files above a fixed size limit on every push
They are encrypted
No downside

cards.q: What does a pre-commit hook enable?
cards.a: Running checks (lint, tests, secret/marker scans) before a commit is recorded
cards.x: Catches problems at the earliest point.
wrong: Deploying the code once the commit is recorded
Pushes automatically
Merges branches

cards.q: Why is a good commit message valuable?
cards.a: It explains WHY a change was made — invaluable when debugging history later
cards.x: Future you (and reviewers) rely on it.
wrong: It is required by Git
It speeds up builds, since a detailed message lets the build system compile the code faster
It has no value

tracks.title: Introduction to Information Technology
tracks.tagline: What computers are, how they work, and how to use them with confidence.

decks.title: What Information Technology Is
decks.summary: Hardware, software, data, networks, and the people who keep them running.

cards.q: What does information technology (IT) cover?
cards.a: The use of computers, networks, software, and data to store, process, and share information.
cards.x: IT is the technology side of handling information — the machines, the networks that connect them, the software that runs on them, and the data they hold.
wrong: Only building websites and mobile apps for clients, plus the hosting and domain names they run on
Only repairing printers and replacing cables
Only writing code for new software

cards.q: What is the difference between hardware and software?
cards.a: Hardware is the physical parts you can touch; software is the instructions that run on them.
cards.x: A laptop's keyboard and screen are hardware. The operating system and the browser are software — they have no weight, but they tell the hardware what to do.
wrong: Hardware is the stored data and documents; software is the cables and ports that connect the parts together
Hardware is the screen and software is the box
There is no difference — the words mean the same thing

cards.q: Which of these is system software?
cards.a: The operating system.
cards.x: System software runs the machine itself: the operating system manages hardware, memory, files, and programs. Applications — browsers, editors, games — sit on top of it.
wrong: A web browser
A spreadsheet app for budgets and tables
A photo editor

cards.q: What does an app (application software) do?
cards.a: It performs a specific task for the user, like writing, browsing, or editing photos.
cards.x: Applications exist to do work you can name: write a document, send a message, edit a photo. They rely on the operating system underneath.
wrong: It manages the computer's hardware directly
It manages the computer's hardware directly, deciding which program gets the CPU and memory next
It writes the firmware on the motherboard

cards.q: What is the input–process–output–storage cycle?
cards.a: Data goes in, the computer works on it, a result comes out, and it can be saved.
cards.x: Every computer job follows the same cycle: input (keyboard, mouse, files), process (the CPU), output (screen, printer, speaker), and storage (the drive) if the result is kept.
wrong: The order a computer boots in, from power-on through firmware and bootloader to the login screen
The steps for installing a new program
The way files are compressed for backup

cards.q: Which kind of computer is built to serve many users at once?
cards.a: A server.
cards.x: Servers stay on, answer requests, and are built for reliability — more memory, redundant disks, and a server operating system. Desktops and laptops serve one person at a time.
wrong: A laptop
A tablet
A smartphone

cards.q: What is the difference between data and information?
cards.a: Data is raw facts; information is data given meaning and context.
cards.x: "23, 24, 22" is data. "The office temperature was 23°, 24°, 22° over three days" is information — the same numbers, now meaningful.
wrong: Data is stored forever and information is deleted once it is used
Information is raw and data is processed
There is no difference between the two

cards.q: What does a network let computers do?
cards.a: Share resources and communicate with each other.
cards.x: A network is a set of connected machines. It lets them share files, printers, and internet access — and lets people on different machines work together.
wrong: Run programs without any software installed on the machines themselves
Store data without a hard drive
Work without an operating system

cards.q: In client–server computing, what does the client do?
cards.a: It requests a service; the server provides it.
cards.x: Your browser is a client: it asks the web server for a page, and the server answers. One server can serve many clients at the same time.
wrong: It stores all the data and answers every request itself
It manages the network cables and switches
It powers the other computers on the network

cards.q: What is the core job of an IT support technician?
cards.a: Help users, fix problems, and keep systems running.
cards.x: Support work is mostly diagnosis and communication: understand the problem, find the cause, fix it, and show the user how to avoid it next time.
wrong: Design new programming languages from scratch for developers
Sell computers to customers
Write the firmware for new devices

puzzles.prompt: Put the input–process–output–storage cycle in order.
items: Process: the CPU works on it
puzzles.x: Every computer job follows the same cycle — in, work, out, keep — whether it is an email or a database query.

decks.title: Binary, Bits & Number Systems
decks.summary: How computers count: bits, bytes, binary, hexadecimal, and text encodings.

cards.q: What is a bit?
cards.a: One binary digit — 0 or 1 — the smallest unit of data.
cards.x: A bit is a single switch state. Everything a computer stores is built from bits: eight of them make a byte.
wrong: Eight binary digits grouped together as the smallest unit a computer can store
A small file stored on a hard drive
A character on a keyboard

cards.q: How many bits are in a byte?
cards.x: A byte is eight bits. It is the unit computers use to represent a single character, a pixel value, or one step of a measurement.

cards.q: How many different values can one byte represent?
cards.x: With eight positions each holding 0 or 1, there are 2^8 = 256 possible patterns — the values 0 through 255.

cards.q: What is binary 1101 in decimal?
cards.x: Read the positions right to left as 1, 2, 4, 8: 1 + 4 + 8 = 13. The leading zero adds nothing.

cards.q: What is binary 1010 in decimal?
cards.x: 8 + 2 = 10. Each position doubles as you move left: 1, 2, 4, 8.

cards.q: What is decimal 255 in hexadecimal?
cards.a: FF.
cards.x: 255 is the largest value one byte can hold, and it is FF in hex — two F digits, each worth 15.
wrong: FE

cards.q: How many bits does a single hexadecimal digit represent?
cards.x: Hex digits run 0–F, sixteen values — exactly 2^4. That is why hex is the shorthand for binary: one hex digit is one nibble.

cards.q: What does the 0x prefix mean?
cards.a: The number that follows is hexadecimal.
cards.x: 0x1F and 31 are the same value written two ways. The prefix removes the ambiguity so code, manuals, and debuggers agree.
wrong: The number is in binary
The number is in decimal
The number is a memory address in octal

cards.q: Why is hexadecimal used as a shorthand for binary?
cards.a: Each hex digit maps to exactly four bits, so long binary strings stay readable.
cards.x: 1101 0010 is hard to scan; D2 says the same thing in two characters. Conversion is a straight grouping, with no arithmetic.
wrong: Hex values are stored more compactly in memory
Hex uses fewer transistors than binary
Hex numbers take less memory than binary numbers, so programs store everything in hexadecimal

cards.q: What is ASCII?
cards.a: A standard that assigns numbers to characters — letters, digits, and symbols.
cards.x: In ASCII, A is 65 and a is 97. One byte holds one character, which is why plain text files are so simple.
wrong: A file system used on Windows drives that stores names in a table at the start of the disk
A programming language for web pages
A compression method for images

cards.q: What is UTF-8?
cards.a: The standard encoding for text on the web, covering every writing system.
cards.x: UTF-8 extends ASCII: ordinary English characters still take one byte, while accented letters, Arabic, Chinese, and emoji take two to four.
wrong: A video compression format used for streaming that encodes each frame in eight-bit blocks
A secure way to store passwords
A protocol for sending email

cards.q: In the binary convention used by Windows and most IT exams, what does 1 KB mean?
cards.a: 1,024 bytes.
cards.x: Strictly, 1,024 bytes is a kibibyte (KiB) and the SI kilobyte (kB) is 1,000 bytes. Windows and most IT courses use KB = 1,024 bytes, while disk makers advertise in powers of ten, which is why a "1 TB" drive shows less in Windows.
wrong: 1,000 bytes
100 bytes
10,240 bytes

puzzles.prompt: Flip the bits to make 13 — the first number in the lesson.
puzzles.x: 1101 is 8 + 4 + 1 = 13. Each position doubles as you move left: 1, 2, 4, 8.

puzzles.prompt: What is binary 1010 in decimal?
puzzles.x: 8 + 2 = 10. Only the 8 and 2 positions hold a 1.

decks.title: Computer Hardware & Components
decks.summary: The CPU, cores, cache, motherboard, chipset, memory, and expansion buses.

cards.q: What does the CPU do?
cards.a: It fetches, decodes, and executes instructions — the work of running programs.
cards.x: The CPU is the computer's worker. It reads an instruction from memory, works out what it means, does it, and moves to the next one — billions of times per second.
wrong: It stores files permanently
It draws images on the screen
It connects the computer to the internet and manages every network connection the programs open

cards.q: What does clock speed, measured in gigahertz (GHz), tell you?
cards.a: How many cycles the CPU runs per second.
cards.x: A 3 GHz CPU runs three billion cycles a second. Clock speed is only part of performance — a newer design does more per cycle than an older one at the same speed.
wrong: How much memory the CPU has built into the chip
How hot the CPU will run
How many programs it can store

cards.q: What is a CPU core?
cards.a: An independent processing unit inside the chip.
cards.x: A quad-core CPU is four processors in one package. Cores let the computer run several things at once instead of queuing them through one worker.
wrong: A slot for extra memory sticks on the motherboard
The fan that cools the processor
A connector for the hard drive

cards.q: What is cache memory (L1, L2, L3)?
cards.a: Very fast, small memory built into or next to the CPU for data it uses constantly.
cards.x: L1 is the fastest and smallest, then L2, then L3 — each a trade-off between speed and size. Cache exists because RAM is too slow to keep a 3 GHz CPU fed.
wrong: The memory on a graphics card
The long-term storage area inside a hard drive that keeps frequently used files ready to open
The buffer on a network card

cards.q: What is the motherboard?
cards.a: The main circuit board that connects every component in the computer.
cards.x: The CPU, RAM, storage, and expansion cards all plug into the motherboard, which carries power and data between them.
wrong: The power supply unit that converts wall power and feeds every part through one cable
The metal case that holds the parts
The software that starts the computer

cards.q: What does the chipset do?
cards.a: It governs which CPUs, memory speeds, and expansion cards the board supports.
cards.x: The chipset is the motherboard's traffic controller and rulebook. Two boards with the same socket can support different CPUs if their chipsets differ.
wrong: It stores the operating system and installed programs so the computer can boot from it
It generates the computer's display
It powers the cooling fans directly

cards.q: What is RAM used for?
cards.a: Fast, temporary working memory for programs that are running right now.
cards.x: When you open a document, it lives in RAM. RAM is fast to read and write — and it forgets everything the moment the power goes off.
wrong: Storing files permanently
Permanent storage for files, which keeps everything safe when the computer is switched off
Cooling the processor

cards.q: What is the difference between RAM and ROM?
cards.a: RAM is volatile working memory; ROM is non-volatile storage that keeps firmware.
cards.x: RAM holds what you are doing now and clears on shutdown. ROM (and its modern flash-based forms) holds the firmware the machine needs to start at all.
wrong: RAM is permanent and ROM is temporary
RAM is on the hard drive and ROM is on the CPU
There is no difference; they are two names for one thing

cards.q: What does PCIe connect?
cards.a: Expansion cards — graphics cards, network cards, and NVMe drives.
cards.x: PCIe slots are the computer's high-speed expansion bus. A graphics card in a PCIe x16 slot has a direct, very fast path to the CPU and RAM.
wrong: Keyboards, mice and other USB devices, plus the power cables that run from the wall socket
Power cables from the wall
The monitor's stand

cards.q: What is the main difference between x86-64 and ARM processors?
cards.a: x86-64 dominates desktops and servers; ARM dominates phones and tablets, built for performance per watt.
cards.x: ARM chips do more work per watt, which is why they rule battery-powered devices. Modern laptops increasingly use ARM for the same reason.
wrong: x86-64 is only for phones and ARM only for servers
ARM cannot run an operating system
x86-64 is used only in phones; ARM only in supercomputers

cards.q: What is the difference between multiprocessing and multitasking?
cards.a: Multiprocessing runs work in parallel on several cores; multitasking switches one core.
cards.x: Multiprocessing is genuinely parallel — two cores, two jobs at once. Multitasking is the OS rapidly switching one core between jobs so they all appear to run together.
wrong: Multitasking runs work in parallel on several cores; multiprocessing switches one core between jobs
Multitasking needs several CPUs to work
They are the same thing with different names

cards.q: What is the maximum RAM a 32-bit system can address?
cards.a: About 4 GB.
cards.x: 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 addresses — roughly 4 GB. A 64-bit system can address far more memory than any machine will hold for decades.
wrong: About 4 TB
About 640 KB
Unlimited memory

puzzles.prompt: What is the maximum RAM a 32-bit system can address, in GB?
puzzles.x: 2^32 addresses is about 4 GB. A 64-bit system can address far more memory than any machine will hold for decades.

puzzles.prompt: Put the CPU cycle in order.
puzzles.x: The CPU repeats fetch → decode → execute billions of times a second. That cycle is what "running a program" means.

decks.title: Storage & Memory
decks.summary: The memory hierarchy, hard drives, SSDs, partitions, and formatting.

cards.q: What is the difference between storage and memory?
cards.a: Storage keeps data after the power goes off; memory (RAM) forgets it.
cards.x: Your files live in storage — SSD or hard drive. When you open one, a copy goes into RAM. Save it, and the changes go back to storage.
wrong: Storage is faster than memory
Memory is permanent and storage is temporary
There is no difference: both keep data after the power goes off and both forget it on restart

cards.q: What is the memory hierarchy?
cards.a: A ladder from the fastest, smallest storage near the CPU down to the slowest, largest storage far away.
cards.x: Registers and cache are fastest but tiny; RAM is the middle; SSDs and hard drives are slowest but huge. Each level holds what the level above is most likely to need next.
wrong: A way of organising files into nested folders, from the root of the drive down to each file
The order in which programs are installed
A list of the fastest internet connections

cards.q: Which is faster to read: RAM or an SSD?
cards.a: RAM — by a wide margin.
cards.x: RAM answers in nanoseconds; an SSD answers in microseconds. That gap is why the CPU keeps its working set in RAM and only goes to the drive when it must.
wrong: An SSD is faster than RAM
They are exactly the same speed
A hard drive is faster than both

cards.q: How is a hard drive (HDD) different from a solid-state drive (SSD)?
cards.a: An HDD stores data on spinning platters; an SSD stores it in flash chips.
cards.x: HDDs are cheaper per gigabyte and hold more, but they are slower and fragile. SSDs are fast and silent, and they survive drops that would kill a hard drive.
wrong: An HDD has no moving parts and stores data in flash chips; an SSD stores it on spinning platters
An SSD can only store music files
An HDD is always faster than an SSD

cards.q: What does HDD speed in RPM measure?
cards.a: How fast the platters spin — usually 5,400 or 7,200 revolutions per minute.
cards.x: Higher RPM means the head reaches data sooner, so a 7,200 RPM drive is noticeably quicker than a 5,400 RPM one — though both are far slower than an SSD.
wrong: How many files the drive can hold
How fast the drive's cable transfers data to the motherboard, in revolutions per minute
How much power the drive uses

cards.q: What is a sector on a disk?
cards.a: The smallest unit the drive can address, traditionally 512 bytes.
cards.x: Data is written in sectors. A file is a chain of sectors — which is why a 1-byte file still takes a whole sector of space.
wrong: A folder on the desktop that groups related files together for the user
A partition table entry
A type of file system

cards.q: What does partitioning a disk do?
cards.a: It divides the disk into separate logical volumes.
cards.x: Partitioning lets one physical disk behave as several: one volume for the system, one for data, or one per operating system on a dual-boot machine.
wrong: It deletes all the files on the disk, wiping it clean
It copies the disk to another drive
It makes the disk spin faster

cards.q: What does formatting a volume do?
cards.a: It writes a file system on it so the operating system can store and find files.
cards.x: Formatting lays down the empty structure — the index of files, free space, and folders. Quick format writes a fresh index; full format also checks every sector.
wrong: It replaces the disk's firmware with a newer version so the drive reads and writes faster
It upgrades the disk to a newer model
It merges two disks into one

cards.q: What is wear levelling on an SSD?
cards.a: The controller spreads writes evenly across the flash cells.
cards.x: Flash cells survive a limited number of writes. Wear levelling, plus TRIM — which tells the drive which blocks are free — is how an SSD lasts for years of daily use.
wrong: A way to make the drive spin more quietly
A backup feature that copies every written block to the cloud as soon as it changes
A security feature that encrypts every file

cards.q: Why should you never defragment an SSD?
cards.a: There is no seek penalty on flash, so defrag gains nothing — and it burns through the drive's limited write cycles.
cards.x: Defrag exists for spinning disks, where reading a scattered file means waiting for the platter. On an SSD every address is equally fast, so defrag is pure wear.
wrong: Defrag would make the SSD's platters spin out of alignment and lose data
Defrag erases the operating system
Defrag is illegal on solid-state drives

cards.q: What is a bad sector?
cards.a: A damaged area of a disk that can no longer hold data reliably.
cards.x: A few bad sectors are normal wear. A count that keeps growing is a warning: the drive is failing — back it up and replace it.
wrong: A file that was deleted by mistake
A partition that was never formatted, so the operating system cannot read it
A virus hiding on the drive

cards.q: Why does a "1 TB" drive show about 931 GB in Windows?
cards.a: Makers count in powers of ten; Windows counts in powers of two.
cards.x: 1 TB on the box is 1,000,000,000,000 bytes. Windows divides by 1,024 three times, which comes out to about 931 GiB — the same bytes, measured with a different ruler.
wrong: The drive is defective and missing space
Windows reserves about 69 GB of every drive for the operating system and its updates
The drive was formatted incorrectly

puzzles.prompt: Order the memory hierarchy from fastest to slowest.
puzzles.x: Each level is faster but smaller than the one below it. Data moves up the ladder when it is needed and down again when it is not.

puzzles.prompt: How many KB are in 1 MB?
puzzles.x: Computers count in powers of two: 1 KB is 1,024 bytes and 1 MB is 1,024 KB.

decks.title: Operating Systems & Booting
decks.summary: What the OS does, the kernel boundary, processes, and the boot sequence.

cards.q: What does an operating system do?
cards.a: It manages the hardware, memory, files, processes, and users of the computer.
cards.x: The OS is the middleman between applications and hardware. It decides who gets CPU time, keeps files organised, and stops one program from breaking another.
wrong: It writes new programs for the user
It manufactures the computer's parts
It connects the computer to the internet and downloads updates for every installed program

cards.q: What is the difference between kernel space and user space?
cards.a: The kernel runs with full hardware access; applications run restricted.
cards.x: This split is the OS's safety boundary. A crashing app can be killed; a crashing kernel takes the whole machine down.
wrong: Kernel space is where user files are stored
User space is faster than kernel space
There is no boundary: applications talk to the hardware directly, just like the kernel does

cards.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
cards.a: A process is a running program with its own memory; a thread shares that memory.
cards.x: A browser is one process per tab; each tab's threads share the tab's memory. Threads are cheap to start, but one thread's crash can take its process with it.
wrong: A process is always faster than a thread, because each process gets a whole CPU core to itself
A thread has its own separate memory
They are the same thing

cards.q: What is virtual memory?
cards.a: Disk space used to extend RAM when physical memory runs short.
cards.x: When RAM fills up, the OS pages the least-used data out to a swap file. It works — but slowly, because the disk is far slower than RAM.
wrong: Memory that only exists in the cloud and is streamed to the computer when it runs short
A second CPU used for graphics
A backup copy of the hard drive

cards.q: What is BIOS, and how is UEFI different?
cards.a: BIOS is the old firmware interface; UEFI is its modern replacement.
cards.x: UEFI replaced BIOS because it can handle large drives, boots in seconds, and can verify that the bootloader is signed before running it.
wrong: BIOS is the newer, faster firmware interface; UEFI is the legacy one it replaced
UEFI is a type of operating system
BIOS and UEFI are the same thing

cards.q: What is POST, and when does it run?
cards.a: The Power-On Self-Test — the first step of boot, checking CPU, memory, and key devices.
cards.x: If POST fails, you hear beeps or see an error code instead of a boot screen. One short beep usually means everything passed.
wrong: The last step of boot, just before the desktop appears
A test run when the computer is shut down
A security scan of installed programs

cards.q: What loads the operating system kernel into memory?
cards.a: The bootloader.
cards.x: The firmware finds the boot device, runs the bootloader (BOOTMGR on Windows, GRUB on Linux), and the bootloader loads the kernel — which then starts the services and the login screen.
wrong: The BIOS battery
The hard drive's motor
The computer's power supply

cards.q: Which bootloader is standard on most Linux systems?
cards.a: GRUB.
cards.x: GRUB (the GRand Unified Bootloader) can list several kernels and operating systems and let you choose at start-up — which is why dual-boot machines show a menu.
wrong: BOOTMGR
UEFI
Systemd

cards.q: What is the difference between MBR and GPT partition tables?
cards.a: MBR is limited to 2 TB disks and four primary partitions; GPT supports huge disks, up to 128 partitions, and keeps backup copies with error checking.
cards.x: MBR dates from 1983 and stores the table in the first sector, with no backup. GPT, part of UEFI, keeps a backup table at the end of the disk and uses CRC checks to detect damage.
wrong: GPT is limited to 2 TB disks and four primary partitions; MBR supports huge disks, up to 128 partitions, and keeps backup copies
GPT cannot boot a computer
MBR supports unlimited partitions

cards.q: How many primary partitions can an MBR disk have?
cards.a: Four.
cards.x: Four entries fit in the MBR table. To have more, one primary becomes an extended partition — a container that holds logical partitions.
wrong: One
Two
Sixteen

cards.q: What is an extended partition?
cards.a: A container partition that holds logical partitions, working around MBR's limit.
cards.x: With one extended partition, you can have three primaries plus as many logical drives as you need — the classic way dual-boot setups fit on an MBR disk.
wrong: A partition that holds a backup copy of the boot sector, used to repair a damaged disk
A backup copy of the boot sector
A partition that only Linux can use

cards.q: What is Secure Boot?
cards.a: A UEFI feature that refuses to run an unsigned bootloader.
cards.x: Secure Boot checks the bootloader's signature against keys stored in the firmware. It stops boot-level malware — and it can block Linux installers that are not signed, which is why some distros ship signed bootloaders.
wrong: A password on the login screen, typed before the desktop loads
An antivirus program
A firewall for the network card

puzzles.prompt: Put the boot sequence in order.
puzzles.x: Booting is a relay race — each stage hands off to the next. A failure at any stage stops the machine there.

puzzles.prompt: How many primary partitions can an MBR disk have?
puzzles.x: Four entries fit in the MBR table. To have more, one primary becomes an extended partition holding logical partitions.

decks.title: Files, Paths & the Command Line
decks.summary: File systems, paths and names, the CLI, and how the OS moves data fast.

cards.q: Which file system is the Windows default, and what does it offer?
cards.a: NTFS — permissions, journaling, encryption, and large files.
cards.x: NTFS replaced FAT32 on Windows because it tracks who may read or change each file, logs changes so a crash does not corrupt the volume, and supports files far larger than 4 GB.
wrong: FAT32 — simple and readable everywhere, with a 4 GB file limit and no permissions
ext4 — the Linux default
exFAT — for camera memory cards

cards.q: Which file system is the Linux default?
cards.a: ext4 — journaled, reliable, and built for Linux permissions.
cards.x: ext4 is the standard Linux file system. It journals changes like NTFS, handles large files, and is the reason a Linux install feels at home on any disk.
wrong: NTFS, the same journaled file system that Windows uses for its system drive
FAT32
APFS

cards.q: What is the key limit of FAT32?
cards.a: A single file cannot exceed 4 GB, and it has no file permissions.
cards.x: FAT32 is universal — every OS can read it — but a 4 GB file cap and no ownership make it a poor choice for a modern system drive. It survives on USB sticks and cameras.
wrong: It only works on Windows
It cannot store text files
It requires an internet connection

cards.q: What is exFAT used for?
cards.a: Flash drives and memory cards that work on Windows and macOS without the 4 GB limit.
cards.x: exFAT is the middle ground: cross-platform like FAT32, but without the 4 GB cap. It has no journaling or permissions, so it is for removable media, not system drives.
wrong: Booting a Linux server from a USB stick that holds the operating system and its logs
Encrypting a system drive
Running a database

cards.q: A script uses `../data/report.csv` and works when run from /home/sam/scripts but fails from /home/sam. Why?
cards.a: It uses a relative path — `../data/report.csv` resolves from the current directory, so it only works from the right place; an absolute path starting at / works from anywhere
cards.x: /home/sam/report.pdf is absolute — it works from anywhere. `../report.pdf` is relative — it means “one folder up from where I am now.”
wrong: Because absolute paths only work on Windows
Because relative paths are always longer
Because a relative path starts at the root; an absolute path starts at the current directory — so `../data/report.csv` works from anywhere, and `/home/sam/scripts` only works from one place

cards.q: Which of these is an absolute path?
cards.a: C:\Users\Sam\report.pdf
cards.x: It starts at the root of the C: drive, so it points to the same file no matter where you are. "..\report.pdf" and "report.pdf" are relative.
wrong: ..\report.pdf
report.pdf
Desktop\report.pdf, sitting right on the user's desktop

cards.q: Why is a file named invoice.pdf.exe dangerous?
cards.a: Windows hides known extensions, so it looks like a harmless PDF but is a program.
cards.x: With "Hide extensions for known file types" on — the default — invoice.pdf.exe shows as invoice.pdf. Double-clicking runs the .exe. Showing extensions is a basic security habit.
wrong: It is not dangerous, because PDF files cannot run code and Windows checks every download
It is a corrupted file that cannot open
It is only dangerous on Linux

cards.q: Are Report.txt and report.txt the same file on Linux?
cards.a: No — Linux file names are case-sensitive.
cards.x: On Linux, Report.txt, report.txt, and REPORT.TXT are three different files. On Windows and macOS they are usually the same file, which is a classic source of "it worked on my machine" bugs.
wrong: Yes — all systems treat them the same
Yes — Linux ignores case in file names
No — because the files are in different folders

cards.q: What is the command line (CLI)?
cards.a: A text interface where you type commands to control the computer directly.
cards.x: The CLI has no buttons or windows — you type, and the shell answers. It is faster for repetitive work, easy to automate, and the native language of servers.
wrong: A graphical desktop with icons and windows, designed for users who do not want to type
A web browser built into the OS
A type of file system

cards.q: Which of these is a Linux shell?
cards.a: Bash.
cards.x: Bash is the default shell on most Linux systems and on macOS before zsh. CMD and PowerShell are the Windows shells.
wrong: CMD
PowerShell
Explorer

cards.q: What does the `cd` command do?
cards.a: It changes the current directory.
cards.x: cd Documents moves you into Documents; cd .. moves you up one level; cd ~ takes you home. Almost every other command depends on knowing where you are.
wrong: It copies a directory
It deletes the current directory and everything inside it
It creates a new directory

cards.q: What is the difference between buffering and caching?
cards.a: A buffer holds data while a slower device catches up; a cache keeps recently used data in fast memory for the next request.
cards.x: A buffer is about timing — smoothing the speed gap between a producer and a consumer. A cache is about reuse — keeping the answer ready in case it is asked again.
wrong: Buffering stores data permanently and caching is temporary
Caching is slower than buffering
A cache holds data while a slower device catches up; a buffer keeps recently used data in fast memory for the next request

puzzles.prompt: What is the maximum size of a single file on FAT32, in GB?
puzzles.x: FAT32 caps a single file at 4 GB and has no permissions — one reason it survives only on USB sticks and cameras.

puzzles.prompt: Order the steps to find and read a file from the terminal.
items: ls to check the file is there
cat the file to read it
puzzles.x: Know where you are, check what is there, then read it. pwd tells you where you are if you ever get lost.

overview: Python is the glue language of IT and security work: short scripts rename a thousand files, parse a firewall log, or call a cloud API. Everything starts with values, the variables that name them, and the operators that combine them.

This lesson covers the core data types (`int`, `float`, `str`, `bool` and `None`), arithmetic including floor division and modulo, converting between types, and working with strings: indexing, immutability and f-strings.

learn.heading: Values, types and variables
body: Every value has a type, and `type(value)` tells you which. `42` is an `int`, `3.0` is a `float` (any literal with a decimal point), `"hi"` is a `str`, `True` and `False` are `bool`, and `None` is the single value that means "nothing here". Functions that do not return anything give back `None`.
A variable is just a name bound to a value: `count = 3`. Python is dynamically typed, so the same name can later refer to a different type, but the value itself always has one definite type.

learn.heading: Operators you will use constantly
body: `+ - * /` work as expected, and `/` always returns a `float` (`7 / 2` is `3.5`). Floor division `//` divides and rounds down (`7 // 2` is `3`), modulo `%` gives the remainder (`7 % 2` is `1`), and `**` raises to a power (`2 ** 3` is `8`).
Modulo is more useful than it looks: `n % 2 == 0` tests for even numbers, and `seconds % 60` turns a duration into the seconds part of minutes:seconds.

learn.heading: Converting types and reading input
body: `input()` always returns a `str`, even if the user types digits. Convert with `int("42")` or `float("3.5")`. If the text is not a valid number, `int()` raises `ValueError`, which you will learn to handle in the Files & Errors lesson.
Going the other way, `str(42)` gives `"42"`. You rarely need that for output, because f-strings convert for you.

learn.heading: Strings: indexing, immutability and f-strings
body: Strings are sequences of characters, indexed from zero: `"abc"[1]` is `"b"`. Negative indices count from the end, so `"hello"[-1]` is `"o"`. `len("hello")` is `5`.
Strings are immutable. Methods such as `.upper()` or `.replace()` return a new string and leave the original unchanged, so you must assign the result: `name = name.strip()`.
To build text from values, use an f-string: `f"Hi {name}, you have {count} alerts"`. Any expression can go inside the braces, including formatting such as `{ratio:.1%}`.

examples.title: Arithmetic and types
examples.code:
print(type(3.0))   # <class 'float'>
print(7 / 2)       # 3.5
print(7 // 2)      # 3  (floor division)
print(7 % 2)       # 1  (remainder)
print(2 ** 3)      # 8
examples.explanation: Run each line in a Python shell (`python` or `python3`) to see the result for yourself.

examples.title: Read a number and report it
examples.code:
raw = input("How many hosts? ")   # always a str
hosts = int(raw)                  # ValueError if not digits
print(f"Scanning {hosts} hosts, about {hosts * 0.5:.0f} seconds")
examples.explanation: Convert input before doing maths with it, then let the f-string format the output.

overview: Programs become useful when they make decisions and repeat work. Control flow is how a script decides what to do with each log line, retries a failed request, or stops when it finds what it was looking for.
This lesson covers `if`/`elif`/`else`, truthiness, `for` and `while` loops with `range`, `break`, `continue` and `pass`, and how to package logic into reusable functions.

learn.heading: Decisions: if, elif, else and truthiness
body: Python delimits blocks with indentation, not braces. PEP 8 recommends 4 spaces per level; mixing tabs and spaces causes errors. The "else if" keyword is `elif`.

Conditions do not have to be booleans. The falsy values are `False`, `None`, `0`, `""` and empty collections; everything else is truthy. That is why `if items:` is the idiomatic way to check that a list is not empty.
Use `==` to compare values and `is` to compare identity. In practice `is` is only for singletons: write `if result is None:`.

learn.heading: Loops
body: A `for` loop walks over any iterable: a list, a string, a file, a dictionary. `range(3)` produces `0, 1, 2`: it starts at 0 and stops before the end value. A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition stays true.

`break` leaves the innermost loop immediately, `continue` skips the rest of the current pass and moves to the next one, and `pass` does nothing: it is a placeholder where the syntax needs a statement.

learn.heading: Functions
body: Define a function with `def name(parameters):` and an indented body. `return` sends a value back; a function without a `return` returns `None`.

Parameters can have default values: `def greet(name="world"):`. Never use a mutable default such as `[]` or `{}`: the default is created once, when the function is defined, and shared by every call. Use `None` and create the list inside the function instead.

learn.heading: Common mistakes: loops and conditions
body: The most common loop bug is the one that never ends. A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition stays true, so the body must make progress toward making it false: increment the counter, consume the next item, or `break` out. If a script seems stuck, the first thing to check is whether the loop variable actually changes.

Off-by-one errors are the second classic. `range(5)` produces `0, 1, 2, 3, 4` — five values, but the last is 4, not 5. When you need each item, loop over the list directly (`for line in lines:`) instead of indexing with `range(len(lines))`; it is shorter and there is no index to get wrong.

Do not change a list while you loop over it: removing items shifts the rest, so the loop skips the next element. Build a new list with the items you want to keep, or loop over a copy (`for item in items[:]:`). And remember `=` assigns while `==` compares — writing `if x = 5:` is a `SyntaxError` in Python, which at least fails loudly instead of silently doing the wrong thing.

examples.title: Classify failed logins
examples.explanation: One function holds the rule; the loop applies it to every user.

examples.title: break, continue and the mutable-default trap
examples.code:
with open("auth.log") as f:     # with: see the Files & Errors lesson
    for line in f:
        if not line.strip():
            continue      # skip blank lines
        if "CRITICAL" in line:
            print(line)
            break         # stop at the first critical entry

def add_tag(tag, tags=None):   # not tags=[]
    tags = [] if tags is None else tags
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags
examples.explanation: With `tags=[]`, every call would append to the same shared list.

overview: Real data comes in groups: a list of IP addresses, a mapping of usernames to roles, a set of blocked domains. Choosing the right collection makes code simpler and often dramatically faster.
This lesson compares the four built-in collections (`list`, `tuple`, `set`, `dict`), then covers slicing, comprehensions, and the looping helpers `enumerate` and `.items()`.

learn.heading: Four collections, four jobs
body: A `list` is ordered and mutable: use it for sequences you add to and change. A `tuple` is ordered but immutable: use it for fixed records such as `(host, port)`. Because tuples cannot change, they are hashable and can be dictionary keys.
A `set` holds unique items only; adding a duplicate does nothing, and membership tests (`x in s`) are O(1) on average. A `dict` maps keys to values and has preserved insertion order since Python 3.7.
Dictionary keys must be hashable, which is why a list cannot be a key: it could change after being stored. Convert it to a tuple first.

learn.heading: Working with lists and dicts
body: `my_list.append(x)` adds one item to the end; `extend` adds every item from another iterable. `d["k"]` raises `KeyError` if the key is missing, whereas `d.get("k", 0)` returns the default instead.
Slices take a range: `nums[1:3]` includes index 1 and excludes index 3, so `[10, 20, 30, 40][1:3]` is `[20, 30]`. `nums[::-1]` reverses a list.

learn.heading: Comprehensions and idiomatic loops
body: A list comprehension builds a list from a loop in one expression: `[x * 2 for x in range(3)]` is `[0, 2, 4]`. Add a filter with `if`: `[ip for ip in ips if ip.startswith("10.")]`. Dict and set comprehensions use `{}`.
Loop over a dict's keys and values together with `for k, v in d.items():`. When you need the position as well as the item, use `for i, item in enumerate(items):` instead of `range(len(items))`.

examples.title: Count hits per IP with a dict
examples.explanation: `get` with a default avoids a KeyError the first time each IP appears.

examples.title: Fast membership with a set
examples.code:
blocked = {"evil.example", "phish.example"}   # set literal
requests = ["docs.python.org", "phish.example"]
flagged = [r for r in requests if r in blocked]
print(flagged)   # ['phish.example']
examples.explanation: Checking membership in a set stays fast even with millions of entries.

overview: Automation lives on files: logs to parse, reports to write, configs to read. It also has to survive the real world, where files go missing and input is malformed. A script that crashes halfway through a batch job is worse than no script.
This lesson covers reading and writing files safely, handling and raising exceptions, organising code into modules, isolating dependencies with virtual environments, and choosing a safe data format.

learn.heading: Files and context managers
body: Open files with `with open(path) as f:`. The `with` block uses a context manager that closes the file automatically when the block ends, even if an error occurs inside it.

The `pathlib` module gives object-oriented paths that work on every operating system: `Path("logs") / "app.log"`, `path.exists()`, `path.read_text()`. For structured data, the `json` module converts between JSON text and Python objects with `json.loads` and `json.dumps`.

learn.heading: Exceptions
body: Errors are raised as exceptions. Opening a missing file raises `FileNotFoundError` (a subclass of `OSError`); bad conversions raise `ValueError`. Handle the ones you expect with `try`/`except SpecificError:`.

Avoid a bare `except:`. It swallows every error, including `KeyboardInterrupt` when you press Ctrl+C, and hides bugs. A `finally` block always runs, whether or not an exception happened, which makes it the place for cleanup.
Signal problems in your own code with `raise ValueError("port must be 1-65535")`, choosing the most specific built-in exception or your own subclass.

learn.heading: Modules, __main__ and virtual environments
body: Every `.py` file is a module you can import. Code under `if __name__ == "__main__":` runs only when the file is executed directly, not when it is imported, so a file can be both a reusable library and a script.

A virtual environment isolates a project's dependencies from the system Python: `python -m venv .venv`, activate it, then `pip install`. List dependencies in `requirements.txt` and pin versions so every install is reproducible.

learn.heading: Safe data formats
body: `pickle` can serialise almost any Python object, but `pickle.load` on untrusted data can execute arbitrary code: an insecure deserialization vulnerability. For anything that crosses a trust boundary, use JSON.

examples.explanation: Each expected failure is handled specifically; anything unexpected still surfaces as an error.

examples.code:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate        # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install requests
pip freeze > requirements.txt
examples.explanation: Anyone can recreate the environment later with `pip install -r requirements.txt`.

Avoid: hides every error, even Ctrl+C
Signal an error from your own code

overview: As scripts grow into tools, you need ways to model things (a host, a finding, a user) and to reuse behaviour without copying code. Object-oriented programming and a few Pythonic features make larger code readable and testable.
This lesson covers classes and `self`, `__init__` and the dunder methods, inheritance, dataclasses, static and class methods, generators, decorators, lambdas, type hints and PEP 8 naming.

learn.heading: Classes, self and dunder methods
body: A class is a blueprint; each object created from it is an instance. `__init__` initialises a new instance's attributes, and every method receives the instance it was called on as its first parameter, named `self` by convention.

Methods with double underscores ("dunder" methods) hook into Python's syntax. `__repr__` controls how an object appears to developers (in the shell and in logs) and should be unambiguous; `__str__` is the friendlier form for end users; `__eq__` defines `==`.
`@dataclass` writes `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` for you from annotated fields, which is ideal for plain data-holding classes.

learn.heading: Inheritance and method types
body: Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend another: `class Admin(User):` gets every `User` method, and `super().__init__(...)` calls the parent's version. Prefer small hierarchies; composition (an object holding another) is often clearer.

`@staticmethod` defines a method that takes neither `self` nor `cls`, a plain function grouped with the class. `@classmethod` receives the class itself as `cls`, which is handy for alternative constructors such as `Host.from_string("10.0.0.1:22")`.

learn.heading: Generators, decorators and lambdas
body: A generator function uses `yield` instead of `return`, producing values lazily, one at a time. It can process a huge file or an endless stream without loading everything into memory.
A decorator is a function that wraps another function to add behaviour: timing, logging, retries, access checks. Writing `@login_required` above a `def` wraps it without editing its body.
`lambda x: x * 2` creates a small anonymous function from one expression, most often as a sort key: `sorted(users, key=lambda u: u.age)`.

learn.heading: Type hints and style
body: Type hints such as `def f(x: int) -> str:` document intent and let tools like mypy and your IDE catch bugs early. They are not enforced at runtime.
PEP 8 naming: `snake_case` for functions and variables, `CapWords` (PascalCase) for classes, `UPPER_CASE` for constants.

overview: This is where Python pays for itself: talking to web APIs, running system commands, pulling indicators out of logs, and turning a one-off script into a tool colleagues can use.
This lesson covers HTTP with `requests`, safe use of `subprocess`, regular expressions, CSV parsing, handling secrets, SSH automation, command-line arguments and proper logging.

learn.heading: Calling APIs
body: `requests` is the de facto library for HTTP: `requests.get(url, timeout=5)` then `.json()` for the body. Always set a timeout, or a hung server can hang your script forever.

Check the status code: 2xx means success, 3xx a redirect, 4xx a client error (bad request, not authorised, not found) and 5xx a server error. `response.raise_for_status()` turns 4xx and 5xx into exceptions.
API keys never belong in code. Read them from an environment variable (`os.environ["API_KEY"]`) or a secrets manager. A key committed to git stays in the history and must be rotated.

learn.heading: Running commands safely
body: `subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host], capture_output=True, text=True)` runs a program with its arguments passed as a list. Each item is one argument, so nothing is interpreted by a shell.
Passing a string with `shell=True` and user input enables command injection: a "hostname" of `8.8.8.8; rm -rf /` becomes two commands. Use the list form, and validate input.

learn.heading: Parsing text: regex and CSV
body: The `re` module finds patterns: `re.findall(r"\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+", log)` pulls IPv4-like strings from a log. Write patterns as raw strings (`r"..."`) so Python does not interpret the backslashes before `re` sees them.
The `csv` module handles quoting and commas inside fields correctly. `csv.DictReader` gives each row as a dictionary keyed by the header, which reads far better than numeric column indexes.

learn.heading: From script to tool
body: `argparse` turns hard-coded values into command-line options and generates `--help` automatically. `logging` replaces `print()` for diagnostics, with levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR) you can filter and handlers that write to files.
For servers and network gear, `paramiko` provides SSH, and `netmiko` builds on it with vendor-specific handling for switches and routers.

examples.title: Query an API with a timeout and a secret from the environment
examples.code:
import os, requests

resp = requests.get(
    "https://api.example.com/v1/alerts",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['API_KEY']}"},
    timeout=5,
)
resp.raise_for_status()           # 4xx/5xx -> exception
for alert in resp.json()["alerts"]:
    print(alert["id"], alert["severity"])
examples.explanation: No key in the code, no request without a timeout, no silent failure on an error status.

examples.title: A small log tool with argparse, regex and logging
examples.code:
import argparse, logging, re

IPV4 = re.compile(r"\b(?:\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}\b")

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="List unique IPs in a log")
    parser.add_argument("logfile")
    parser.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG if args.verbose else logging.INFO)

    with open(args.logfile) as f:
        ips = {ip for line in f for ip in IPV4.findall(line)}
    logging.info("found %d unique IPs", len(ips))
    for ip in sorted(ips):
        print(ip)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
examples.explanation: Run it with `python ips.py auth.log -v`; `python ips.py --help` documents itself.

overview: Scanning a /16, pulling data from 500 APIs or hashing a disk image all hit the same wall: doing things one at a time is slow. Concurrency helps, but only if you pick the right tool for the kind of work.

This lesson explains the GIL, when to use threads, processes or asyncio, how race conditions happen, and how to measure and fix performance with profiling, the right data structures, caching and streaming.

learn.heading: The GIL and the two kinds of work
body: CPython has a Global Interpreter Lock (GIL): only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time. CPython 3.13 and later also offer an experimental free-threaded build without it, but the default build still has the GIL.
I/O-bound work (network requests, disk reads, database calls) spends most of its time waiting, and threads release the GIL while waiting. Threads or `asyncio` therefore speed it up well.

CPU-bound work (hashing, compression, number crunching) is limited by the GIL, so use `multiprocessing` or `ProcessPoolExecutor`: separate processes each have their own interpreter and GIL, so they use multiple cores.

learn.heading: Threads, processes and asyncio in practice
body: `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` gives a pool of worker threads with a simple `submit`/`map` API; `ProcessPoolExecutor` offers the same API with processes. Start with these before reaching for lower-level modules.

`asyncio` runs many tasks on one thread with an event loop. Inside an `async def`, `await` suspends that coroutine until the awaited operation finishes, and the loop runs other tasks meanwhile. It scales to thousands of concurrent connections, but every library in the path must be async-aware.

learn.heading: Race conditions
body: A race condition is when the outcome depends on the unpredictable timing of concurrent access to shared state, for example two threads both reading a counter, adding one, and writing it back. Protect shared state with a `threading.Lock`, or better, avoid sharing: have workers return results and combine them at the end.

learn.heading: Measure, then optimise
body: Profile before changing anything: `python -m cProfile -s cumtime script.py` shows where time actually goes. The fix is often a data structure, not concurrency. `x in my_set` is O(1) on average while `x in my_list` is O(n), so converting a list to a set can turn minutes into milliseconds.

`functools.lru_cache` memoises a pure function's results for repeated arguments. For big inputs, stream with generators: iterating over a file object reads it line by line, so a 10 GB log never has to fit in memory.

overview: A tool other people rely on needs tests that prove it works, a clean way to install it, and dependencies you can trust. Supply-chain attacks against PyPI are real, and untested security tooling fails exactly when it matters.
This lesson covers pytest, fixtures and mocking, coverage, modern packaging with `pyproject.toml` and lock files, and the security checks every Python project should run.

learn.heading: Testing with pytest
body: pytest is the most widely used Python test framework. Tests are plain functions named `test_*` that use ordinary `assert` statements, and pytest explains exactly what differed when one fails. `@pytest.mark.parametrize` runs one test over many inputs.
A fixture is reusable setup code that pytest injects into any test that names it as a parameter. A fixture can `yield` its value and run teardown code after the test finishes.
Mocking replaces a real dependency with a controllable fake. `unittest.mock.patch` stops tests from calling real APIs, databases or clocks, which keeps them fast and repeatable.

learn.heading: Coverage
body: Coverage measures which lines or branches your tests executed. High coverage does not prove the code is correct, since a test can run a line without checking its result, but low coverage clearly shows the blind spots.

learn.heading: Packaging and reproducible installs
body: `pyproject.toml` is the modern standard file for package metadata and build configuration (PEP 517, 518 and 621), replacing most uses of `setup.py`.

A lock file pins the exact version of every dependency, including indirect ones, so installs are reproducible and a compromised new release cannot slip in unnoticed. Tools such as uv, poetry and pip-tools generate them.

learn.heading: Security checks
body: `pip-audit` checks installed packages against the Python Packaging Advisory Database of known vulnerabilities. Typosquatting is a supply-chain attack where malicious packages use names close to popular ones (`reqeusts` instead of `requests`), so check names and publishers.

Bandit is a static security linter (SAST) for Python. It flags insecure patterns such as `eval`, `shell=True` and hard-coded secrets; run it in CI. Never call `eval()` on user input: it executes arbitrary code. Use `ast.literal_eval` to safely parse Python literals.

examples.title: Fixtures, parametrise and mocking
examples.explanation: Assumes `fetch_banner` calls `socket.create_connection(...)` and then `.recv()`. No real network traffic: the fixture patches the socket call, and teardown happens after `yield`.

examples.title: Quality gate for CI
examples.code:
pytest --cov=scanner --cov-report=term-missing
pip-audit
bandit -r scanner/
examples.explanation: Run all three on every pull request: tests with coverage, known-vulnerable dependencies, insecure code patterns.

overview: Security teams build small tools constantly: a port checker, a hash verifier, a log summariser. Python's standard library covers most of it, and a few well-known libraries fill the gaps, but only if you use the security-sensitive parts correctly.

This lesson covers sockets, hashing and password storage, secure randomness, the cryptography library, constant-time comparison, packet crafting, pandas for log analysis, SQL injection prevention, and the ethics of testing.

learn.heading: Networking and integrity
body: The `socket` module opens raw TCP and UDP connections. `socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=2)` succeeding means the port is open, which is the basis of a simple port check. Scapy crafts and sniffs arbitrary packets for deeper protocol work.
`hashlib` computes digests: `hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()` produces the fingerprint you compare against a vendor's published hash to verify a download or preserve evidence integrity.

learn.heading: Passwords, tokens and encryption
body: Never store passwords with a fast hash like plain SHA-256: attackers can try billions of guesses per second. Use a slow, salted algorithm designed for passwords: bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2.
Generate tokens, API keys and passwords with the `secrets` module. The `random` module is predictable and must never be used for security values.
For encryption, use the `cryptography` library. Its Fernet recipe gives authenticated symmetric encryption with sensible defaults, so you do not have to assemble primitives yourself.
When comparing secrets such as tokens or HMACs, use `hmac.compare_digest(a, b)`. A normal `==` stops at the first differing character, and that timing difference can leak the secret byte by byte.

learn.heading: Data and databases
body: pandas is the go-to library for tabular analysis: `pd.read_csv("auth.csv")` then `groupby` and `value_counts` summarise thousands of log rows in a line or two.

Prevent SQL injection with parameterised queries: `cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,))`. The driver sends the value separately from the SQL, so input can never change the query. Never build SQL with f-strings or concatenation.

learn.heading: Authorisation first
body: Scanning or probing systems you do not own or have written permission to test can be illegal, and it violates professional codes of ethics such as ISC2's. Get a written scope before running any of these tools against anything but your own lab.

examples.title: A minimal, polite port check
examples.explanation: A timeout keeps it fast, and the `with` block closes each connection immediately.

examples.title: Tokens, constant-time checks and safe SQL
examples.code:
import hmac, secrets, sqlite3

token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)            # not random.random()

def token_ok(supplied: str) -> bool:
    return hmac.compare_digest(supplied, token)

db = sqlite3.connect("users.db")
name = input("user: ")
rows = db.execute("SELECT id, role FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,)).fetchall()
