overview: Every organization will have incidents. The ones that survive them well are not the ones with the best tools — they are the ones that decided, before the crisis, who does what, in what order, with whose authority. Incident response is that decision, written down and rehearsed.

This lesson covers the NIST SP 800-61 response lifecycle, containment through recovery, the forensics that preserve evidence along the way, and the legal and business realities that shape every response.

learn.heading: The NIST SP 800-61 lifecycle
body: NIST SP 800-61 defines four phases: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery; and Post-Incident Activity. The phases are a cycle, not a line — lessons learned feed back into preparation, and preparation determines how well every other phase performs. NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (April 2025) superseded Rev. 2 and reorganizes incident response around the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 functions; the four-phase lifecycle above remains the model most IR plans and the exam follow.

Preparation is everything built before the incident: the IR team with defined roles, the tooling and access they will need, the playbooks for likely scenarios, and the communication plans for stakeholders, legal, and the public. It also means relationships — an IR retainer, a pre-contracted external response firm for surge support, signed before you need it, because negotiating contracts during a breach is how you lose days you do not have.

Detection and Analysis is the SOC's handoff to the IR process: confirming that an event is an incident, determining scope, and understanding what the attacker did. Analysis quality determines response quality — contain too early and you tip off the attacker before you understand their foothold; contain too late and the damage spreads. A war room — a centralized coordination space or channel with defined roles — keeps the analysis and the decisions in one place instead of scattered across chat threads.

learn.heading: Containment, eradication, recovery
body: When ransomware is confirmed on a host, the first priority is containment: isolate the host from the network immediately. Every minute of delay is lateral movement. Short-term containment isolates the threat quickly — pulling the network cable, disabling the switch port, revoking the cloud account's sessions and access keys. Long-term containment keeps the business running while the threat is neutralized — segmented VLANs, hardened temporary controls — buying time for a thorough response.

Eradication is removing all attacker presence: the malware, the backdoors, the persistence mechanisms, the compromised credentials. Partial eradication is how incidents recur — the attacker's scheduled task or stolen service account survives, and the "recovered" environment is compromised again within days. Eradication must be verified, not assumed, and that verification is what separates a response from a pause.

Recovery restores systems to normal operation from known-good backups and hardened images — never from the compromised state, and never before eradication is confirmed. Systems return in priority order, with enhanced monitoring watching for recurrence. The tension between evidence preservation and business continuity runs through all of this: forensics wants systems frozen, the business wants them back. That tension is resolved in preparation, by deciding in advance which wins and when, not argued during the incident.

learn.heading: Forensics: evidence that holds up
body: Digital forensics is the scientific collection and analysis of digital evidence, and its first rule is that evidence must survive scrutiny — by management, by regulators, and potentially by a court. A forensic image is a bit-for-bit copy of storage media used for analysis; the original is preserved untouched, and all examination happens on the copy. Write-blocking — hardware or software that prevents any writes to the evidence media — guarantees the original cannot be altered during imaging.

Chain of custody is the documented record of who handled evidence, when, and how, from collection to presentation. A gap in the chain is an argument that the evidence was tampered with, and an unbroken chain is what makes digital evidence admissible. Analysts who skip the paperwork have not saved time; they have destroyed the evidence's value.

Collection follows the order of volatility, forensic analysis follows the timeline, and both serve the same goal: a defensible reconstruction of what happened. Know also what forensics is not: analysts should generally avoid definitive attack attribution. Focus on TTPs — what the attacker did and how — because attribution is a political and intelligence judgment that most organizations are not equipped to make, and getting it wrong publicly is worse than not making it.

learn.heading: The legal and business layer
body: Legal counsel's role in incident response is protecting privilege, managing breach notification obligations, and guiding evidence handling so the investigation does not create liability. When counsel directs the investigation, its findings can be protected by attorney-client privilege — which is why involving legal early is a strategic decision, not a courtesy.

An incident is not automatically a breach. A breach is confirmed unauthorized acquisition of data — a higher bar with regulatory consequences. The distinction matters because breach notification laws trigger on breaches, not incidents: what happened, the types of data affected, the steps taken, and what affected individuals should do. Under GDPR, supervisory authorities must be notified within 72 hours of becoming aware of a qualifying breach. The clock starts at awareness, which is why detection and analysis speed is a legal matter as well as a technical one.

Post-Incident Activity closes the loop with the lessons-learned review: a blameless analysis of what happened, what worked, what failed, and what changes, with assigned action items and owners. Blameless is not optional — a review that punishes honesty guarantees the next review hears nothing. Document what went well alongside what did not; it reinforces the controls and decisions that worked and tells the team the review is about improvement, not punishment.

learn.heading: Training, evidence, and closing out (3.3)
body: A plan nobody has practiced is a hope, not a plan. Training takes two forms: tabletop exercises, where the team talks through a scenario around a table and finds the gaps in the plan, and simulations, where the team actually works the incident in a controlled environment. Both test the same things — who decides, who communicates, and whether the playbooks hold up under pressure — and both feed their findings back into preparation.

Evidence handling has one addition the response team must not miss: a legal hold. When litigation or regulatory action is possible, relevant data must be preserved and not deleted, rotated, or overwritten — including backups and logs that would normally age out. Data integrity validation — hashing evidence at collection and re-checking it later — proves nothing changed in between.

Closing out an incident has its own steps. Release from isolation returns systems to normal operation only after verification that the threat is gone — a host released too early is a reinfection waiting to happen. Performing restoration brings services back in priority order with enhanced monitoring. Root cause analysis (RCA) then asks why the incident happened, not just what happened: the missing patch, the unmonitored log source, the process that failed. Corrective action development turns the answer into changes — new detections, new controls, updated playbooks — with owners and deadlines, so the next incident is a different one.

examples.title: Contain a compromised host without losing evidence
examples.code:
1. EDR: network-isolate host FIN-WS-14 (keeps EDR channel)
2. Capture memory: winpmem.exe C:\ir\FIN-WS-14.raw
3. Hash it:         certutil -hashfile C:\ir\FIN-WS-14.raw SHA256
4. Log custody:     who, when, hash, storage location
5. Then image disk, then eradicate
examples.explanation: Isolation stops the spread while keeping the machine powered, so volatile memory (processes, keys, injected code) survives for analysis.

slides.title: Overview
slides.caption: Every organization will have incidents. The ones that survive them well are not the ones with the best tools — they are the ones that decided, before the crisis, who does what, in what order, with whose authority. Incident response is that decision, written down and rehearsed.

slides.title: The NIST SP 800-61 lifecycle
slides.caption: NIST SP 800-61 defines four phases: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery; and Post-Incident Activity. The phases are a cycle, not a line — lessons learned feed back into preparation, and preparation determines how well every other phase performs. NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (April 2025) superseded Rev. 2 and reorganizes incident response around the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 functions; the four-phase lifecycle above remains the model most IR plans and the exam follow.

slides.title: Containment, eradication, recovery
slides.caption: When ransomware is confirmed on a host, the first priority is containment: isolate the host from the network immediately. Every minute of delay is lateral movement. Short-term containment isolates the threat quickly — pulling the network cable, disabling the switch port, revoking the cloud account's sessions and access keys. Long-term containment keeps the business running while the threat is neutralized — segmented VLANs, hardened temporary controls — buying time for a thorough response.

items.def: Short-term isolates immediately; long-term keeps the business running during response.
A bit-for-bit copy of media; analysis happens on the copy, never the original.

slides.title: Forensics: evidence that holds up
slides.caption: Digital forensics is the scientific collection and analysis of digital evidence, and its first rule is that evidence must survive scrutiny — by management, by regulators, and potentially by a court. A forensic image is a bit-for-bit copy of storage media used for analysis; the original is preserved untouched, and all examination happens on the copy. Write-blocking — hardware or software that prevents any writes to the evidence media — guarantees the original cannot be altered during imaging.

overview: Defenders who think in isolated alerts lose to attackers who think in campaigns. Frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK, the cyber kill chain, and the diamond model give analysts a shared language for describing what an attacker is doing — not just which alert fired, but which step of the intrusion it represents.

This lesson covers the three frameworks, how they map to detection and response, and the discipline of threat-informed defense: prioritizing controls against the adversary behaviors that actually threaten you.

learn.heading: MITRE ATT&CK: the adversary playbook
body: MITRE ATT&CK is a knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures, organized as a matrix that has become the industry's common language. A tactic is the adversary's goal — the "why," such as Initial Access, Persistence, or Exfiltration. A technique is how they achieve it — the "how," such as phishing or scheduled tasks. A procedure is the specific implementation — the actual malware, command, or sequence a particular actor uses. Tactic, technique, procedure: goal, method, implementation.

The matrix rewards study because it turns vague alerts into precise statements. Credential dumping via LSASS access is Credential Access (T1003). Scheduled tasks used for persistence are Persistence (T1053). Moving through the environment with WMI or PsExec is Lateral Movement; obfuscating payloads to avoid detection is Defense Evasion. When an analyst says "we have a T1053 detection firing," every defender in the industry knows exactly what behavior is meant.

ATT&CK improves on older models by being non-linear and granular. Real intrusions do not march through phases in order — attackers loop back, skip steps, and pursue multiple tactics simultaneously. ATT&CK describes that reality: a menu of behaviors that can occur in any sequence, each mapped to detection and mitigation guidance. It is a map of the territory, not a script of the journey.

learn.heading: The kill chain and the diamond model
body: The cyber kill chain describes the seven phases of an intrusion in order: Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, and Actions on Objectives. Its strategic insight is that disrupting any single phase defeats the attack — you do not need to stop everything, just one link. Its limitation is linearity: it models the initial compromise well and everything after it poorly.

The diamond model of intrusion analysis complements both by linking four elements of every intrusion event: the adversary, their capability, the infrastructure they use, and the victim. Every event is a diamond connecting who, with what, through which infrastructure, against whom. Pivoting across the diamond — from a malicious IP to the other victims it touched, from a capability to the adversary known to use it — is how analysts expand a single indicator into a full picture of the intrusion.

Use the frameworks together. The kill chain gives you the campaign narrative: where in the intrusion are we? ATT&CK gives you the behavioral detail: exactly what technique is this alert describing? The diamond model gives you the analytic pivots: what else connects to what we just found? An analyst fluent in all three can take one alert and unfold it into the whole operation.

learn.heading: Threat-informed defense
body: Threat-informed defense is the discipline of prioritizing controls against the TTPs most relevant to your sector and threat landscape — not against every technique in the matrix equally. A hospital and a defense contractor face different adversaries; their detection investments should differ accordingly. ATT&CK Navigator visualizes this as heatmaps: technique coverage across your defenses, showing at a glance which adversary behaviors you can detect and which are blind spots.

The durability argument is central. TTP-based detections describe attacker behavior — process injection patterns, unusual authentication sequences — and they survive infrastructure changes because behavior changes slowly. IOC-based detections describe artifacts — a hash, a domain — and they expire the moment the attacker rotates infrastructure. Both have uses, but a detection program built mostly on IOCs is a program that needs constant feeding; one built on TTPs compounds.

MITRE D3FEND extends the picture to the defensive side: a knowledge base of defensive techniques mapped against ATT&CK, so each adversary technique links to the countermeasures that defeat it. And adversary emulation exercises close the loop — simulating a specific threat actor's TTPs against your own environment to test whether the defenses you claim actually work. Mapping incidents to ATT&CK after response standardizes reporting and reveals systemic detection gaps: if every incident involves the same uncovered technique, the gap is the finding.

examples.title: Map an incident to ATT&CK
examples.code:
Observed                                   Tactic              Technique
-----------------------------------------  ------------------  ----------------
VPN login with stolen password             Initial Access      T1078 Valid Accounts
PowerShell download cradle                 Execution           T1059.001
Run key added                              Persistence         T1547.001
LSASS memory read                          Credential Access   T1003.001
Archive files to C:\temp\out.7z            Collection          T1074 Data Staged
examples.explanation: Mapping turns a narrative into gaps: if you had no alert for T1003.001, that is your next detection to build.

overview: The best analysis in the world is worthless if it never changes a decision. Reporting is how security work becomes business action — how an incident becomes funding, a vulnerability trend becomes a policy change, and a SOC's daily grind becomes a board-level conversation about risk.

This lesson covers security metrics and what makes them meaningful, how to communicate with executives and other stakeholders, and the compliance and legal reporting obligations that shape every serious program.

learn.heading: Metrics that mean something
body: Start with the distinction the exam tests: metrics measure activity; KPIs tie measurements to business objectives. "We closed 400 tickets" is a metric. "We reduced mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities from 30 days to 9 days against our 14-day SLA" is a KPI — it connects the work to an objective the business chose. Executives fund KPIs; they skim metrics.

MTTD and MTTR earn their place in reporting as trend metrics: not single numbers but direction over time, showing whether detection and response are getting faster or slower. Trend reporting — alert volume, true positive rate, and MTTR plotted across quarters — is what turns operational data into a story about program health. A single quarter's numbers are trivia; four quarters of movement are evidence.

Vulnerability programs have their own essential metrics: vulnerability aging, how long findings remain open past their remediation SLAs; and scan coverage, the percentage of assets scanned during the period. Unscanned assets are unmeasured risk, and aging shows whether exceptions and delays are accumulating. Together with mean time to remediate by severity, they answer the only question leadership actually asks about vulnerabilities: are we getting safer or not?

learn.heading: Communicating with stakeholders
body: Different stakeholders need different reports from the same facts. An executive incident summary contains business impact, scope, actions taken, and next steps — without technical jargon. Executives need decisions, not packet captures: what happened to the business, what it costs, what is being done, and what they need to approve. The full log dumps and file hashes belong in the technical appendix, not the briefing.

When the board asks "are we secure," the correct answer is risk framing, never a yes. No honest analyst claims absolute security; the professional answer describes residual risk in business terms — what the program covers, where the gaps are, what the trends show, and what investment would change. "Are we secure" is really "are we managing risk acceptably," and the analyst's job is to make that answer concrete.

Technical findings reach non-technical audiences by leading with risk and business impact, then supporting with just enough detail. A stakeholder communication matrix makes this systematic: a plan defining who gets told what, when, and by whom during an incident — executives, legal, public relations, IT, HR, customers — so notification is a procedure, not an improvisation. And the SOC shift handoff note keeps continuity between the people doing the work: open investigations, pending actions, and items to watch, so nothing falls between shifts.

learn.heading: Compliance, legal, and the post-incident record
body: Several compliance frameworks require vulnerability management reporting as a condition of doing business: PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2, and others each demand evidence that vulnerabilities are found, tracked, and remediated on defined timelines. Compliance reporting is therefore not overhead on the security program — for regulated organizations it is one of the program's primary products, and the metrics above are its raw material.

Breach notification has its own formal requirements. A notification must cover what happened, the types of data affected, the steps taken, and what affected individuals should do — and the timelines are law, not courtesy. Under GDPR, supervisory authorities must be notified within 72 hours of becoming aware of a qualifying breach. Attorney-client privilege protects the investigation itself when legal counsel directs it, which is why counsel belongs in the response structure from the start rather than being called after the notifications go out.

The lessons-learned report is the final reporting product of every incident: a blameless post-incident analysis with assigned action items and owners. It differs from a forensic report, which documents evidence and technical findings for potential legal use — the incident report covers timeline and business impact, the forensic report covers artifacts and analysis. Document what went well alongside what failed; it reinforces the controls that worked and keeps the review honest. And responsible disclosure communication — coordinated, factual public statements made after remediation — is how the organization talks about the incident to the outside world without creating new liability.

learn.heading: What the reports contain (4.1 / 4.2)
body: Vulnerability scan reports are the working documents of Domain 2.0: compliance findings against the standard being audited, risk scorecards that rank business units or systems by their exposure, and action plans with owners and dates. The action plan names its dependencies — the patch that needs a maintenance window, the vendor fix that does not exist yet — and its inhibitors to remediation: contractual agreements that limit change, organizational governance, business process interruption, degrading functionality if the fix is applied, legacy or proprietary systems nobody can patch, and patch availability itself. Naming the inhibitor is what turns "not fixed" from an excuse into a managed risk.

Incident and security operations reporting has its own products. Incident declaration and escalation is the formal record that an incident exists and who owns it; the executive summary carries it upward. The communication plan names every audience — stakeholder identification, the legal team, public relations, regulatory reporting agencies, law enforcement, customers — and the channels each one gets. Shift and incident handover keeps the work continuous; the internal threat intelligence report turns what was learned about the adversary into guidance for the next shift and the next detection.

The metrics behind both reports are the same ones the SOC lives by: alert volume, false-positive and true-positive rates, mean time to close, mean time to detect, mean time to respond, and mean time to remediate — plus the phishing campaign click rate, which measures whether the human layer is improving. Post-incident reporting closes the loop: the after action report, the lessons learned, and the root cause analysis, each with its owners and dates. A report that nobody acts on is a filing exercise; a report that changes a decision is the job.

examples.title: An executive incident summary
examples.code:
What happened:  Phishing led to one compromised finance mailbox (12 May).
Impact:         No payments made; 340 customer emails exposed.
Actions:        Account disabled in 20 min; mailbox rules removed; MFA enforced.
Obligations:    Legal assessing GDPR notification (72-hour clock started 12 May 10:00).
Next steps:     Phishing-resistant MFA for finance by 30 June (owner: IT Ops).
examples.explanation: Five lines in business terms, with owners and dates. Hashes, IPs and log excerpts belong in the technical report, not here.

overview: The CISSP is not a technical exam dressed up as a management one; it genuinely asks you to think like a security leader advising the business. Many candidates with deep technical skills fail because they choose the answer an engineer would, not the one a risk advisor would.

This lesson covers the priorities behind CISSP answers, accountability, due care and due diligence, the ISC2 Code of Ethics, cost-justified controls, defence in depth, and the exam format and experience requirements.

learn.heading: The priorities behind every answer
body: Human safety comes first, always. Life safety beats data, systems and money in every scenario, which is why emergency exits fail open.

Senior management is ultimately accountable for security. Responsibility can be delegated to security teams; accountability cannot. CISSP answers favour the viewpoint of a risk advisor to the business, not a technician: pick the option that aligns security with business goals.

Before choosing any control, understand the risk and the business requirements: assess, then treat. Technology is rarely the first answer. In most scenarios the best "first step" is to gather facts or consult policy and stakeholders, not to take a drastic unilateral action.

learn.heading: Due care, ethics and cost
body: Due care is doing the right thing, acting as a prudent person would; due diligence is verifying that it is being done. Failing at due care is negligence.

The ISC2 Code of Ethics has four canons, applied in order when they conflict: protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure; act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally; provide diligent and competent service to principals; advance and protect the profession.

A control should never cost more than the value of the asset it protects. More precisely, its annual cost should be less than the reduction in annualised loss expectancy it delivers. Defence in depth layers administrative, technical and physical controls so no single failure is fatal.

learn.heading: The exam and the credential
body: The English CISSP exam uses computerised adaptive testing (CAT): 100 to 150 items in 3 hours, with a passing score of 700 out of 1000. Full certification needs 5 years of paid work in 2 or more of the 8 domains; a relevant degree or approved certification can waive 1 year. Pass without the experience and you become an Associate of ISC2 while you earn it.

learn.heading: Thinking in risk, not in tools
body: When two answers both look technically right, the exam wants the one that reduces risk the most for the least cost and follows the established process. A technically elegant fix that skips the risk assessment, ignores policy, or acts without the owner’s authority is usually the distractor. Ask yourself: what would a prudent manager responsible for people, legal obligations and the business choose — not what would an engineer reach for first?

The same instinct answers the “what first” questions. The first step is almost always to gather facts, verify what happened, and consult policy and stakeholders — not to reconfigure a system, notify a regulator, or discipline someone on a suspicion. Acting before understanding turns a manageable incident into a second incident, and the exam punishes it consistently.

The credential itself rewards the same long view. Certification must be maintained with continuing professional education — 120 CPE credits over each three-year cycle — plus an annual maintenance fee, and every CISSP attests to the Code of Ethics as a condition of holding the credential. Treat the exam as the start of the professional obligation, not the end of it.

examples.title: Choose the CISSP answer
examples.code:
Scenario: A fire alarm sounds while you are mid-way through
imaging a compromised server for evidence.

A. Finish the image, then leave     (protects evidence)
B. Power the server off and leave   (protects data)
C. Leave immediately                (protects people)   <- answer
D. Call the CISO for a decision     (defers)
examples.explanation: Life safety outranks evidence, data and systems every time. When several options are technically sensible, pick the one a manager responsible for people and the business would choose.

overview: Domain 1 is the largest at 16% of the exam, and it frames everything else: how organisations govern security, analyse and accept risk, meet legal obligations, stay in business through disruption, and manage people.

This lesson covers risk analysis and the NIST Risk Management Framework, residual risk, business continuity and MTD, intellectual property law, personnel controls, supply chain risk, ISO 27001 and STRIDE threat modelling.

learn.heading: Risk
body: Quantitative risk analysis uses monetary values (SLE, ARO, ALE); qualitative analysis uses ratings such as high, medium and low. Most organisations blend both.

The NIST Risk Management Framework (SP 800-37) has seven steps. Authorization is the management decision to accept the residual risk, the risk remaining after controls are applied. Someone with the authority must explicitly accept it.

items.name: Prepare
items.does: Set context, roles and risk strategy before any system work.

items.name: Categorize
items.does: Rate the system by the impact of losing confidentiality, integrity or availability.

items.name: Select
items.does: Choose a baseline of controls and tailor it.

items.name: Implement
items.does: Put the controls in place and document them.

items.name: Assess
items.does: Test that the controls work as intended.

items.name: Authorize
items.does: A senior official explicitly accepts the residual risk.

items.name: Monitor
items.does: Watch controls and risk continuously, and reassess on change.

body: Threat modelling finds design flaws before they are built. Microsoft's STRIDE covers Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege.

learn.heading: Continuity
body: A business continuity plan (BCP) keeps critical business functions running during a disruption; the disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the IT-focused subset that restores systems. Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) is the longest a function can be down before unacceptable damage, and the RTO must be less than or equal to the MTD.

learn.heading: Law and intellectual property
body: A trade secret is protected by keeping it secret with reasonable measures (NDAs, access control); there is no registration, and protection lasts as long as it stays secret. A US utility patent generally lasts 20 years from filing. Copyright lasts the author's life plus 70 years. Trademarks can be renewed indefinitely while in use.

learn.heading: People, suppliers and standards
body: Separation of duties splits critical tasks so no single person can commit fraud alone; collusion becomes necessary. Job rotation and mandatory vacations help detect fraud. When someone leaves, HR and IT act together, revoking access at or before notification and recovering assets.

Supply chain risk management assesses and monitors vendors, including their own suppliers, using SBOMs, contract security requirements and right-to-audit clauses. ISO/IEC 27001 specifies the requirements for an information security management system (ISMS); ISO/IEC 27002 provides the control guidance.

learn.heading: Risk treatments and the governance stack
body: Once a risk is assessed it gets one of four treatments: avoid it by removing the activity, transfer it through insurance or outsourcing, mitigate it with controls, or accept it formally with an owner and a review date. Transfer never transfers accountability: if a vendor fails, the organisation still owns the risk, which is why contracts, service levels and right-to-audit clauses matter. Risk appetite is how much risk leadership is willing to take in pursuit of objectives; risk tolerance is the acceptable variation around that appetite.

Governance turns these decisions into structure. Senior management approves policy and accepts risk; a security steering committee aligns security with business priorities across departments; the CISO advises and implements but does not own the business risk. Policies state mandatory intent, standards give the specifics, procedures give the steps, and guidelines recommend. When a scenario asks who decides, the answer is almost always the business owner, not the security team.

examples.title: Quantitative risk: is the control worth it?
examples.code:
Asset value (AV)            $500,000
Exposure factor (EF)        40%
SLE = AV x EF               $200,000
ARO (once every 4 years)    0.25
ALE = SLE x ARO             $50,000 per year

Control cost                $30,000 per year
ALE after control           $10,000 per year
Value = 50,000 - 10,000 - 30,000 = $10,000 per year  -> justified
examples.explanation: A control is worth buying when the reduction in ALE exceeds its annual cost. Present it to management in exactly these terms.

overview: This deep dive takes Domain 1 further into the governance machinery the exam loves: what business continuity and disaster recovery plans actually contain, how recovery is tested, how controls are classified, how policies are layered, and how people themselves are controlled.

This lesson covers BCP versus DRP plan contents, the Business Impact Analysis, RTO and RPO, DR test types from checklist to parallel, control types and categories, the policy-to-guideline hierarchy, and personnel security controls.

learn.heading: Continuity: plans and analysis
body: The Business Continuity Plan keeps critical business functions running during a disruption; the Disaster Recovery Plan restores IT systems. The DRP is the IT-focused subset of the wider BCP effort, and the BCP is owned by the business, not just IT.

A BCP contains the Business Impact Analysis, recovery strategies, plan invocation procedures, roles and responsibilities, communications plans, and plan maintenance. A DRP contains system recovery procedures, RTO and RPO targets, backup and restore steps, and alternate site details.

The Business Impact Analysis identifies critical functions and their dependencies, the maximum tolerable downtime, RTO and RPO targets, and the financial and operational impacts of disruption. The BIA drives the priorities of both the BCP and the DRP.
RTO is how fast a function must be restored; RPO is how much data loss is tolerable. RTO must sit within the maximum tolerable downtime, and RPO sets how often you back up.

learn.heading: Testing recovery
body: From least to most disruptive: checklist or read-through review, structured walkthrough (tabletop) where the team discusses the plan step by step, simulation where the team practices in a mock scenario, parallel test where recovery systems run alongside production, and full interruption where production actually fails over.

Walkthroughs are cheap and discussion-based, good for finding plan gaps. Simulations add realism without touching production. Parallel tests validate the plan closely but need duplicate capacity. Full interruption is the most realistic and the riskiest, so it is done rarely and carefully.

learn.heading: Controls: types and categories
body: Control types describe intent: preventive controls stop incidents (firewall rules), detective controls spot them in progress (IDS), corrective controls restore afterwards (backups), deterrent controls discourage the attacker (warning signs, policies), recovery controls restore operations (failover), and compensating controls substitute when the primary control is not feasible.

Control categories describe where the control lives: administrative (policies, training, procedures), technical (firewalls, encryption, authentication enforced by systems), and physical (guards, locks, cameras). A single control has both a type and a category.

Policies, standards, procedures, and guidelines form a hierarchy. The policy states mandatory high-level intent and needs senior management sign-off; standards give mandatory specifics; procedures are step-by-step instructions; guidelines are recommended, not mandatory.

learn.heading: Personnel security
body: People are both an asset and a risk. Separation of duties splits critical tasks so fraud needs collusion. Mandatory vacations force someone else to perform a person's duties, which can surface fraud or irregularities. Job rotation reduces both fraud opportunity and single points of knowledge.

These controls work as a set: separation of duties prevents unilateral fraud, mandatory vacations detect ongoing fraud, and job rotation limits how long any one person holds a sensitive position unobserved.

learn.heading: Alternate sites and control assessment
body: Recovery sites trade cost against speed. A hot site is ready to take over immediately, with live data and systems; a warm site has hardware and connectivity but needs data restored; a cold site is empty space and power. Reciprocal agreements, where two organisations host each other’s recovery, are cheap but fragile — the partner may be hit by the same disaster. The choice follows from the BIA numbers, not from budget alone.

The maximum tolerable downtime is the whole recovery budget: it equals the recovery time objective plus the work recovery time, the time needed after systems return before people can actually work again. Controls themselves must be assessed, not just installed: test whether a control is designed correctly and whether it operates effectively over time, because a control that exists on paper and fails in practice is worse than no control — it creates false confidence.

examples.title: From BIA to recovery targets
examples.code:
Function         MTD     RTO     RPO     Strategy
---------------  ------  ------  ------  -------------------------
Order taking     8 h     4 h     15 min  Warm site + log shipping
Payroll          5 days  2 days  24 h    Restore from nightly backup
Intranet wiki    14 days 7 days  1 week  Rebuild from weekly backup
examples.explanation: The BIA sets MTD; RTO must fit inside it and RPO sets backup frequency. The strategy (and its cost) follows from those numbers, not the other way round.

overview: Domain 2 (10%) is about knowing what information you hold, who is responsible for it, how it is classified, how long you keep it and how you destroy it. It sounds administrative, but data that was never inventoried or never destroyed is behind many breaches.
This lesson covers asset inventory, classification and roles, data remanence and sanitisation, retention, GDPR roles and pseudonymisation, scoping and tailoring baselines, and DRM.

learn.heading: Know it, own it, classify it
body: The first step in asset security is to identify and inventory assets: you cannot protect what you do not know you have.

The data owner classifies data and is accountable for it; custodians implement the protections the owner specifies. US government classification, from highest: Top Secret, Secret, Confidential, plus Unclassified. Commercial schemes use levels such as confidential or proprietary, private, sensitive and public.
A data retention policy keeps data only as long as legally and operationally needed. Over-retention increases the impact of a breach and the cost of e-discovery.

learn.heading: Sanitisation
body: Data remanence is residual data left on media after deletion, which is why sanitisation matters. NIST SP 800-88 defines three levels: Clear (overwriting, suitable for reuse inside the organisation), Purge (stronger techniques that defeat laboratory recovery, suitable for reuse outside), and Destroy (physical destruction).
Degaussing does not work on SSDs, because they are not magnetic. Use cryptographic erase, the vendor's secure erase command, or physical destruction.

learn.heading: Privacy roles and techniques
body: Under GDPR, the controller decides the purpose and means of processing personal data; the processor acts on the controller's behalf. A cloud provider is typically a processor.

Pseudonymisation replaces identifiers so data cannot be linked to a person without additional information held separately. Pseudonymised data is still personal data under GDPR; truly anonymised data is not.

learn.heading: Baselines and DRM
body: Scoping selects the controls from a standard baseline (such as NIST SP 800-53) that are relevant to a system; tailoring then adjusts them to the environment. Digital rights management (DRM) protects how content is used after distribution, controlling copying, printing and forwarding.

learn.heading: Handling, labelling and the states of data
body: Classification is only useful when it drives handling. Labelling and marking make the class visible on documents, media and screens, and handling rules follow: restricted data is encrypted, access-controlled and never emailed outside the organisation; internal data stays inside it; public data mainly needs integrity so nobody can alter it unnoticed. The rules must be written, trained and enforced — a classification scheme nobody follows is decoration.

Protection changes with the state of the data. Data at rest is protected with encryption and access control; data in transit with TLS and VPNs; data in use is the hardest, because it must be decrypted to be processed — which is why access control, memory protections and trusted execution matter there. Tokenisation replaces sensitive values with tokens held in a vault, so a stolen database yields nothing usable; masking hides part of a value, such as showing only the last four digits of a card number, for display and test use.

examples.title: A data classification and handling table
examples.code:
Class         Example               Storage           Transmission     Disposal
------------  --------------------  ----------------  ---------------  -----------------
Restricted    Card data, health     Encrypted, MFA    TLS + DLP block  Purge or destroy
Confidential  Contracts, salaries   Encrypted         TLS              Purge
Internal      Policies, org chart   Access-controlled Any internal     Clear
Public        Marketing site        Any               Any              None
examples.explanation: The data owner assigns the class; the custodian applies the handling rules. Classification without handling rules changes nothing.

overview: This deep dive extends Domain 2 beyond classification and sanitisation into the full life of data: the lifecycle phases protection must follow, the roles that govern data, how long data is kept and when destruction must stop, how data loss prevention works across network, endpoint and cloud, and the controls that protect data in cloud environments.

This lesson covers the six data lifecycle phases, owner versus steward versus custodian, retention periods and legal holds, network, endpoint and cloud DLP, data sovereignty and residency, and cloud data controls.

learn.heading: The data lifecycle and its roles
body: Protection must follow the data through every phase of its lifecycle: most breaches exploit the share and archive phases, not the database itself.

items.name: Create
items.does: Data is generated or captured. Classify it here.

items.name: Store
items.does: Committed to storage. Encrypt it and control access.

items.name: Use
items.does: Viewed or processed. Enforce least privilege and log access.

items.name: Share
items.does: Made available to others. Apply DLP and secure transfer.

items.name: Archive
items.does: Moved to long-term storage. Follow retention rules.

items.name: Destroy
items.does: Permanently removed. Sanitise or crypto-shred.

body: The data owner is accountable for the data and classifies it. The data steward manages day-to-day quality and handling according to the owner's policy. The custodian maintains the systems that store and process the data. The owner decides, the steward oversees handling, the custodian operates.

Handling requirements scale with classification: higher classifications need marking, encryption, and strict access control, while public data mainly needs integrity. The rules must be written down, trained, and enforced, or they do not exist.

learn.heading: Retention and legal holds
body: A retention period is set by legal and regulatory requirements plus business need, whichever is longer, and the justification should be documented. Over-retention inflates breach impact and e-discovery costs; under-retention risks non-compliance.

A legal hold, or litigation hold, suspends normal destruction so relevant data is preserved for litigation. Destroying data under a hold can be ruled spoliation of evidence. Holds and retention schedules extend to backups and archives, not just live data.

learn.heading: Data loss prevention
body: Network DLP inspects data in motion at egress points such as email, web uploads, and file transfers. Endpoint DLP controls USB drives, printing, clipboard, and local storage on devices, closing the "sneakernet" exfiltration path. Cloud DLP, often delivered through a CASB, scans uploads, sharing links, and collaboration apps in SaaS.
On a policy violation, DLP can block, quarantine, encrypt, or alert. New deployments should start in monitor and alert mode before enforcing blocks, so legitimate workflows are not broken on day one.

learn.heading: Data in the cloud
body: The customer, not the provider, owns data in a SaaS application; contracts should state ownership, return, and deletion terms explicitly. In IaaS, the customer owns the data and OS layers while the provider owns the hypervisor down, so customer-managed keys (BYOK), storage encryption, and private endpoints are the customer's controls to apply.

Data sovereignty means data is subject to the laws of the country where it is stored or processed, which drives cloud region selection for regulated data. Data residency is only about where data is stored; you can meet residency and still fail sovereignty.

Data discovery and classification tools automatically scan data stores to find and label sensitive data such as PII or card numbers. You cannot apply handling rules to data you have not found, which is why discovery precedes enforcement.

learn.heading: Minimisation and the rights of the data subject
body: Collect only the data you need, keep it only as long as you need it, and give access only to those who need it. Data minimisation is both a privacy principle and a security control: data you never collected cannot leak, and data you deleted on schedule cannot be stolen. Every extra field, copy and retention year is risk carried for no benefit.

Privacy law gives individuals rights over their data, and the exam expects you to know the shape of them. Under GDPR, a data subject can request access to their data, correction of errors, erasure, and portability to another provider. Erasure must reach backups and archives as far as feasible — “we deleted the live record” is not a complete answer when the same data sits in last month’s backup. When a request arrives, the first step is to verify the requester’s identity before disclosing anything.

examples.title: Sanitising media under NIST SP 800-88
examples.code:
Media                      Leaving org?  Method
-------------------------  ------------  --------------------------------
HDD, reused internally     No            Clear  (single overwrite)
HDD, sold to recycler      Yes           Purge  (ATA Secure Erase) or destroy
SSD, any reuse             Either        Purge  (crypto erase / sanitize cmd)
SSD, end of life           Yes           Destroy (shred), with certificate
examples.explanation: The method depends on where the media is going and the data's classification. Degaussing does nothing to SSDs.

overview: Domain 3 (13%) covers how secure systems are designed and built, from formal security models to hardware roots of trust, cryptography choices and the physical protection of facilities.

This lesson covers the classic security models, the trusted computing base and reference monitor, TPMs, Common Criteria, secure design principles, side-channel attacks, ECC versus RSA, and physical security including fire suppression and CPTED.

learn.heading: Security models
body: Bell-LaPadula enforces confidentiality: no read up (you cannot read above your clearance) and no write down (you cannot leak by writing to a lower level). It models military classification.

Biba enforces integrity and is the inverse: no read down (do not trust less reliable data) and no write up (do not contaminate more trusted data). Clark-Wilson enforces integrity through well-formed transactions and separation of duties: users reach data only through programs, the access triple of subject, program and object.

Brewer-Nash, the Chinese Wall model, prevents conflicts of interest: access changes dynamically based on what you have already accessed, so a consultant who viewed Bank A's data cannot then view competitor Bank B's.

learn.heading: Trusted systems
body: The trusted computing base (TCB) is all the hardware, firmware and software that enforces the security policy. The reference monitor is the concept that mediates every access; it must be tamper-proof, always invoked, and small enough to verify.

A TPM (Trusted Platform Module) provides a hardware root of trust for keys, measured boot and attestation; BitLocker uses it to seal disk encryption keys. Common Criteria is the international framework for evaluating security products, with assurance levels EAL1 to EAL7 and protection profiles defining requirements.

learn.heading: Design principles and attacks
body: Secure design principles include fail securely (default to a secure state on failure), secure defaults, least privilege, zero trust and privacy by design.
A side-channel attack extracts secrets from timing, power consumption or emissions rather than breaking the algorithm. Spectre and Meltdown exploited CPU speculative execution.
Elliptic curve cryptography gives equal strength with much shorter keys than RSA: a 256-bit ECC key is roughly as strong as a 3072-bit RSA key.

learn.heading: Physical security
body: For data centres, clean-agent fire suppression (such as FM-200) or pre-action sprinklers are preferred. A pre-action system fills its pipes only after detection, reducing accidental water damage.
CPTED (Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design) uses lighting, sightlines and landscaping to deter crime before any lock or guard is needed.

learn.heading: Key management and the hardware root of trust
body: Cryptography fails far more often in key management than in mathematics. A key’s lifecycle runs generation, distribution, storage, rotation, backup and destruction: generate with a proper random source and sufficient length, distribute without exposing the key, store it separately from the data it protects, rotate it on schedule and immediately on compromise, and destroy it securely when retired. Never hard-code a key in source code, and never let one person hold both the data and its key.

Hardware gives keys a home that software cannot copy. A hardware security module is dedicated hardware that generates and stores keys and performs operations without the key ever leaving the device; a key management service provides the same discipline as a managed cloud service. Validated modules carry a FIPS 140-3 validation, which is the assurance the exam looks for. Secure boot and measured boot extend the same idea to the machine itself: each stage verifies the next before handing over control, and the TPM records the measurements so a changed system can be detected and refused.

examples.title: Bell-LaPadula vs Biba
examples.code:
Subject clearance: SECRET

Bell-LaPadula (confidentiality)
  read  TOP SECRET   -> denied   (no read up)
  write CONFIDENTIAL -> denied   (no write down)

Biba (integrity), subject integrity: MEDIUM
  read  LOW          -> denied   (no read down)
  write HIGH         -> denied   (no write up)
examples.explanation: The two models are mirror images: BLP stops secrets leaking down; Biba stops untrusted data contaminating trusted data.

overview: Domain 4 (13%) is secure network architecture: protecting data as it moves, isolating what should not talk, and giving users access to exactly what they need without trusting the network itself.
This lesson covers IPsec modes and protocols, TLS and DNSSEC, 802.1X with EAP-TLS, segmentation and micro-segmentation, ZTNA, bastion hosts, converged networks, CDNs and IoT risk.

learn.heading: Protecting data in transit
body: IPsec operates at Layer 3. AH (Authentication Header) provides integrity and authentication only; ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) adds confidentiality, and it is what most VPNs use. Transport mode protects the payload between two hosts; tunnel mode encapsulates the entire original packet, which is what site-to-site VPNs use. TLS is usually placed between Layers 4 and 6, depending on the model.
DNSSEC signs DNS responses, providing integrity and authenticity but not confidentiality; DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT) add encryption.

learn.heading: Controlling access to the network
body: EAP-TLS, the strongest common 802.1X method, requires certificates on both the client and the server. PEAP needs only a server certificate and protects a password exchange inside a TLS tunnel.

Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) replaces broad VPN access with per-application, identity-aware access: users reach specific applications and never land "on the network". A bastion or jump host is a single hardened, monitored entry point to a secure zone, increasingly replaced by ZTNA brokers.

learn.heading: Limiting the blast radius
body: Network segmentation mainly limits blast radius and lateral movement, and it is also a PCI DSS scope-reduction technique. Micro-segmentation applies fine-grained policies to individual workloads, a zero trust building block.
IoT devices are often weak and rarely patched, making them ideal pivot points. Put them on isolated segments with strict egress rules.

learn.heading: Converged networks and CDNs
body: Converged networking carries storage (FCoE, iSCSI), voice (VoIP) and other traffic over standard IP and Ethernet. It is convenient, but it widens the attack surface of those services, which once ran on separate media.
A CDN absorbs DDoS attacks and shields origin servers, and is often combined with a WAF at the edge.

learn.heading: Wireless, VPNs and the protocols to retire
body: Wireless security has moved on from shared passwords. WPA3 replaces WPA2’s pre-shared key handshake with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, giving each session forward secrecy so capturing one session does not expose the others; enterprise deployments still use WPA2 or WPA3 with 802.1X and EAP-TLS for per-user certificates. WEP and WPA are broken and open networks offer no protection at all — the exam treats any answer relying on them as wrong.

Remote access is a trust decision, not just a tunnel. A VPN extends the network to the remote user, which is why split tunnelling is risky: traffic that bypasses the tunnel bypasses inspection too. Zero trust access checks identity and device posture for every application instead of trusting the network. And some protocols should simply be retired rather than protected: Telnet, FTP and SNMPv1 send credentials in clear text, so replace them with SSH, SFTP and SNMPv3 instead of monitoring a weakness you could have removed.

overview: Domain 5 (13%) is identity and access management: making sure the right people, and only they, reach the right resources, and that everything they do is attributable to them.
This lesson covers the access control sequence, biometric error rates, Kerberos, federation, just-in-time access, access reviews, modern password guidance, session management and conditional access.

learn.heading: The access control sequence
body: Identification (claim an identity), authentication (prove it), authorisation (receive permissions) and accountability (actions are logged and attributable). Accountability depends on unique identities; shared accounts break it.

learn.heading: Biometrics
body: A Type I error is a false rejection: a valid user is denied. A Type II error is a false acceptance: an impostor gets in, the more serious security failure. Tightening a system trades one for the other. The crossover error rate (CER) is where the two rates are equal, and a lower CER means a more accurate system.

learn.heading: Kerberos and federation
body: Kerberos relies on a trusted third party, the Key Distribution Center (KDC), which contains the Authentication Service and the Ticket-Granting Service. Its main weaknesses are that the KDC is a single point of failure and that it needs synchronised time: clock skew beyond five minutes (the default) breaks authentication.
Federated identity means trusting identities issued by another organisation's identity provider, implemented with SAML, OIDC or WS-Federation.

learn.heading: Keeping access right-sized
body: Just-in-time access grants elevated rights only when needed, for a limited time, eliminating standing privilege. Periodic access reviews, where managers recertify their team's access, remove privilege creep and orphaned accounts.
NIST SP 800-63B favours password length, screening new passwords against lists of breached passwords, and no forced periodic rotation: change a password only on evidence of compromise.

Session management needs timeouts, secure unpredictable tokens, re-authentication for sensitive actions, and invalidation on logout and password change. Risk-based (conditional) access adjusts requirements by context such as device, location and risk score, for example requiring MFA from unknown devices and blocking impossible travel.

learn.heading: Provisioning, roles and the modern authenticator
body: Identity is a lifecycle, and most failures happen in the middle of it. Provisioning should follow HR events automatically: a new hire gets the access their role needs, a transfer triggers a review of old permissions, and a departure triggers immediate removal. The gaps have names the exam uses: privilege creep is access accumulated across role changes, and orphaned accounts are accounts whose owner has left but whose access remains.

Authorisation models answer the same question differently. Role-based access control grants permissions to roles built from job functions; attribute-based access control decides from attributes of the subject, the resource and the environment, such as department, clearance and time of day; rule-based access control applies rules set by an authority, such as mandatory access control labels. The exam contrasts them directly, so know which one fits a scenario rather than which sounds most modern.

Authentication strength is about the factor, not the count. A password plus an SMS code is two factors, but SMS codes can be intercepted and SIM-swapped, so they are the weakest second factor. Phishing-resistant authentication uses FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, where the private key never leaves the device and the signed challenge cannot be replayed on a fake site. Prefer the factor that survives the attack described in the scenario.

examples.title: Biometric error rates
examples.code:
Threshold   FRR (Type I)   FAR (Type II)
---------   ------------   -------------
Low         1%             8%
Medium      3%             3%   <- crossover error rate (CER)
High        9%             0.5%
examples.explanation: Raising sensitivity trades false acceptances for false rejections. The CER compares systems; a lower CER means a more accurate device. For a data-centre door, tune toward low FAR.

overview: Domain 6 (12%) asks how you know your controls actually work. Assessment and testing range from automated scans to independent audits, and their results must reach leadership in terms the business understands.

This lesson covers vulnerability assessments versus penetration tests, audit types and SOC reports, monitoring and testing techniques, breach and attack simulation, security metrics and protecting audit logs.

learn.heading: Assessments and audits
body: A vulnerability assessment finds and ranks weaknesses; a penetration test actively exploits them to prove impact. Both need authorisation.

Internal audits are performed by the organisation's own staff; external audits are performed for external parties such as regulators or customers; third-party audits are performed by an independent firm and carry the most independence.
SOC 1 reports cover controls relevant to financial reporting. SOC 2 reports cover security and the other Trust Services Criteria in detail, for restricted distribution. SOC 3 is a public summary.

learn.heading: Testing techniques
body: Synthetic transaction monitoring runs scripted, simulated user activity to test availability and performance; real user monitoring (RUM) observes actual users. Fuzz testing feeds malformed or random input to find crashes: mutation fuzzing alters valid input, generation fuzzing builds input from a specification. Misuse case testing examines how an attacker might abuse legitimate functionality.

Code coverage measures how much code the tests exercised; interface testing checks interactions between components, including APIs, user interfaces and physical interfaces. A regression test confirms a change did not break existing functionality; automate it in CI.
Breach and attack simulation (BAS) continuously and safely emulates attacks to validate that controls work, complementing periodic penetration tests.

learn.heading: Metrics and evidence
body: KPIs (key performance indicators) report past results; KRIs (key risk indicators) give early warning of rising risk. Report both to leadership in business terms.
Protect audit logs, because attackers alter or delete them to hide activity. Centralise them, restrict access, and use write-once storage or integrity checks.

learn.heading: Vulnerability management and the audit trail
body: Scanning is a programme, not an event. The vulnerability management lifecycle runs discovery, assessment, prioritisation, remediation and verification: find the weaknesses, rank them by risk rather than raw severity, fix them in that order, and re-test to confirm the fix. A critical finding on an internet-facing system outranks a critical finding on an isolated lab box, because risk is exploitability times business impact — and a scanner cannot know your business impact.

How you scan changes what you see. Credentialed scans authenticate to the target and report missing patches and misconfigurations with far fewer false positives; non-credentialed scans see only what an outsider sees. A false positive wastes a fix; a false negative is worse, because it certifies a hole as safe. For assurance reports, remember the difference between Type I and Type II: Type I describes the design of controls at a point in time, while Type II tests whether they operated effectively over a period — and only Type II gives evidence the controls actually worked.

examples.title: Read a SOC 2 Type II report
examples.code:
Scope:     Production SaaS platform (not the mobile app)
Period:    1 Jan - 30 Jun
Criteria:  Security, Availability
Opinion:   Qualified
Exception: CC6.2 - 4 of 25 sampled leavers kept access > 5 days
CUECs:     Customer must manage its own user provisioning
examples.explanation: A 'SOC 2' claim tells you little. The scope, period, exceptions and complementary user entity controls (CUECs) tell you what was tested and what remains your job.

overview: Domain 7 (13%) is security operations: running investigations, handling incidents, patching, backing up and recovering, and keeping people safe. It is where policy meets the 3 a.m. phone call.

This lesson covers the incident management process, evidence rules and investigation types, entrapment versus enticement, backup strategies, DR test types, patch management, SIEM correlation, egress monitoring and personnel safety.

learn.heading: Incident management
body: The ISC2 incident management process runs detection, response (containment), mitigation, reporting, recovery, remediation, and lessons learned. SIEM correlation rules drive detection by linking related events across sources into one meaningful alert, such as repeated failed logons followed by a success from a new country. Egress monitoring (DLP, proxy logs, NetFlow) detects data leaving the organisation.

learn.heading: Evidence and investigations
body: The best evidence rule means courts prefer original evidence over copies; forensic images with verified hashes are accepted as duplicates. Hearsay is second-hand information not from direct knowledge, although business records made in the normal course of business can be an exception.
Investigations are administrative, criminal, civil or regulatory. Criminal cases require proof beyond reasonable doubt; civil cases need a preponderance of evidence.

Entrapment induces someone to commit a crime they would not otherwise have committed, which is illegal. Enticement lures someone already intent on the crime, which is legal. A properly used honeypot is enticement.

learn.heading: Backups, DR tests and patching
body: An incremental backup captures changes since the last backup of any kind: fast to back up, slow to restore (the full backup plus every incremental since). A differential backup captures changes since the last full backup: slower to back up, faster to restore (the full backup plus the latest differential).

DR tests from least to most disruptive: read-through (checklist), walk-through (tabletop), simulation, parallel, and full interruption, where production actually fails over. Do full interruption tests rarely and carefully.
Patch management follows evaluate, test, approve, deploy, verify. Emergency patches still go through an expedited change process.

learn.heading: People first
body: In an emergency, evacuate people first; systems and data are secondary. Doors on escape routes fail safe (unlocked) for life safety.

learn.heading: Order of volatility and the people side of operations
body: Digital evidence disappears in a known order, so collect from the most volatile first: processor registers and cache, then memory, then network state and running processes, then disk, then remote logs and archives. A live memory capture can hold encryption keys and running malware that vanish the moment the machine powers off — which is why the exam penalises powering down a suspect system before imaging its memory.

Operations is also change discipline. Every change, including an emergency patch, goes through a documented change process with approval, testing proportionate to the risk, a backout plan, and verification afterwards; an emergency change is expedited, never skipped. And the human side never leaves the picture: security awareness training and phishing simulations reduce the clicks that start most incidents, duress alarms and safe rooms protect people in a physical emergency, and the first priority in any emergency is always getting people out safely.

examples.title: Chain-of-custody record
examples.code:
Item:      Laptop SN 5CG1234XYZ, image file CASE-17-01.E01
SHA-256:   9f2c...e41a (acquisition) = 9f2c...e41a (verification)
2024-05-12 09:14  Collected by  J. Ortiz   from desk 4.12
2024-05-12 09:40  Imaged by     J. Ortiz   write-blocker WB-2
2024-05-12 10:05  Transferred   J. Ortiz -> evidence locker 3 (K. Lee)
Sealed bag no.  0047812
examples.explanation: Every handover is recorded with who, when and why, and the hash proves the image never changed. A gap in this record can make the evidence inadmissible.

overview: Domain 8 (10%) is software development security. Most vulnerabilities are written, not installed, so the cheapest place to fix them is in requirements and design, long before code reaches production.

This lesson covers security across the SDLC, maturity models, DevSecOps and software composition analysis, API security, database integrity concepts, sandboxing, AI coding assistants, and assessing acquired software.

learn.heading: Security in the SDLC
body: Integrate security from the very start, in requirements and design; flaws fixed later cost far more ("shift left"). DevSecOps builds automated security into DevOps pipelines: SAST, software composition analysis (SCA), DAST, infrastructure-as-code scanning and secrets scanning run in CI/CD.

SCA identifies third-party components and their known vulnerabilities, producing or consuming SBOMs. AI coding assistants add the risk of insecure or licence-problematic code being accepted without review, so keep human review, SAST and SCA on generated code too.

learn.heading: Measuring maturity
body: OWASP SAMM (open) and BSIMM (descriptive, based on what real firms do) measure software security programme maturity. CMMI rates process maturity from 1 to 5.

items.name: Optimising
items.does: Continuous, data-driven process improvement.

items.name: Quantitatively Managed
items.does: Processes are measured and controlled with metrics.

items.name: Defined
items.does: Standard processes documented across the organisation.

items.name: Managed
items.does: Processes are planned and tracked per project.

items.name: Initial
items.does: Ad hoc and unpredictable; success depends on heroics.

learn.heading: Concepts the exam loves
body: Polymorphism is the same interface with different behaviour (an object-oriented concept). Polyinstantiation stores multiple versions of the same data at different classification levels, preventing inference attacks in mandatory access control databases.

An ACID database transaction guarantees Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability, preserving transaction integrity. A sandbox is a restricted environment that limits what code can do; browsers sandbox tabs, and mobile apps are sandboxed from each other.
Broken object-level authorisation (BOLA) is number one in the OWASP API Security Top 10: check that the caller owns every object it requests.

learn.heading: Acquired software
body: Assess third-party software against your security requirements, the vendor's development practices and contractual obligations. For SaaS, review SOC 2 reports and data-handling terms. Code escrow has a third party hold the source code in case the vendor fails, protecting buyers of critical commercial software.

learn.heading: Threat modelling and the OWASP landscape
body: The cheapest security decision happens in design, before a line of code exists. Threat modelling walks through what the system does, what can go wrong, and what to do about it; STRIDE gives the categories of threat, and DREAD scores each one by damage, reproducibility, exploitability, affected users and discoverability. The output is not a document — it is design changes: a control added, a trust boundary moved, a feature rethought.

The OWASP Top 10 is the exam’s shorthand for what goes wrong in web applications, and broken access control sits at number one: functions that fail to check whether the caller may do what they ask. Code review catches what scanners miss, but it has its own limits: automated analysis (SAST) produces false positives that must be triaged by a person, and manual review is slow, so mature teams use both — automation for coverage, humans for judgement on the findings that matter.

examples.title: A DevSecOps pipeline, stage by stage
examples.code:
commit      -> secrets scanning (block pushed keys)
build       -> SAST on source, SCA on dependencies (SBOM)
package     -> container image scan, IaC misconfiguration scan
staging     -> DAST against the running app
release     -> signed artefact, change record
production  -> runtime monitoring, feedback into requirements
examples.explanation: Each stage catches a different class of flaw; failing a gate stops the release, just like a failing unit test.

overview: Domain 1 scenarios test whether you think like a risk advisor, not a technician. The exam rewards the answer that follows the risk process: assess, choose a treatment, document, and get the right owner to accept what remains.

This capstone drills the patterns: compensating controls when remediation is impossible, closing BIA-to-plan gaps through management, assessing before acting on new regulations, and routing policy exceptions through the formal process.

learn.heading: When you cannot fix it, compensate
body: Remediation is not always available: no patch exists, or the business cannot tolerate downtime. The CISSP answer is never "do nothing" and rarely "pull the plug unilaterally" — it is a compensating control that reduces likelihood or impact while the risk is formally tracked.

Compensating controls must be documented, time-bound where possible, and tied to risk acceptance by the appropriate owner. "Temporary" controls without an owner and a review date become permanent shadow controls.

learn.heading: Assess first, exceptions through process
body: New regulation, new threat, new business demand — the first step is almost always to assess the gap between what is required and what exists. Action without assessment is guessing, and the exam punishes guessing.

Policy exceptions are legitimate but only through the exception process: documented business justification, risk analysis, compensating controls, expiry date, and sign-off by the risk owner. Seniority is not a control.

learn.heading: How to approach a D1 scenario
body: Domain 1 questions place you in a governance role and ask what to do first, best or next. The answer is rarely a technical fix. Ask whose decision it is: senior management owns risk acceptance and policy approval, the data owner owns classification, and the security professional advises and implements. An option where the security team accepts risk on the business's behalf is usually wrong.

Next, look for the process step the scenario skipped. If a new regulation applies, a gap assessment comes before buying tools. If a control cannot be applied, a documented exception with compensating controls and an expiry comes before simply ignoring the requirement. Due care means acting as a prudent person would; due diligence means verifying that it actually happened.
Finally, remember the order of priorities that runs through the whole exam: people's safety first, then legal and regulatory obligations, then business objectives, then technology preferences.

learn.heading: The risk register and third-party risk
body: Risk lives in a register, not in people’s heads. Each entry records the risk, its likelihood and impact, the treatment chosen, the residual risk after controls, the owner, and the review date. The register is what lets management see the whole risk picture at once and what makes risk acceptance a real decision instead of a shrug. When a scenario describes a risk nobody documented and nobody owns, the correct answer is usually to record it and escalate it to the owner.

Third parties carry your risk without carrying your accountability. Due diligence happens before the contract: the vendor’s security practices, financial stability, and the sensitivity of the data they will hold. The contract then carries the controls: security requirements, service levels, audit rights, breach notification duties, and return or destruction of data at the end. And diligence does not end at signing — ongoing monitoring, from questionnaires to independent audit reports, is what catches a vendor whose controls decayed after the sale.

examples.title: A formal risk acceptance
examples.code:
Risk:        Unpatched DB server ORDDB01 (CVE-2024-xxxx), no vendor patch
Compensating: Isolated VLAN, IPS signature, access from app tier only
Residual:    Medium
Owner:       VP Operations (signed)
Expiry:      90 days or vendor patch, whichever first
Review:      Monthly by security risk committee
examples.explanation: Acceptance is a documented business decision with an owner, compensating controls and an expiry, never a silent 'we'll live with it'.

overview: Domain 2 scenarios revolve around one truth: data outlives every other asset in the story. The exam tests whether you protect the data through its whole lifecycle — including the awkward moments of departure, testing, and litigation.
This capstone drills data remanence on departure, why production data never belongs in test, and how a legal hold freezes the retention schedule.

learn.heading: Departures and remanence
body: When someone with sensitive access leaves, containment comes before cleanup: revoke access immediately so nothing more can leave, then handle the hardware per the media-handling policy — sanitise, destroy, or reassign based on classification.
A quick format is not sanitisation. Match the method to the classification: cryptographic erase or destruction for the highest tiers, documented and witnessed.

learn.heading: Test data and legal holds
body: Production PII in a test environment is a breach waiting to happen: test systems rarely carry production-grade access controls, logging, or monitoring. The answer is always masked, anonymised, or synthetic data.
A litigation hold suspends the normal retention and destruction schedule for the affected data. Destroying held data is spoliation. When in doubt, preserve and ask legal.

learn.heading: How to approach a D2 scenario
body: Asset security questions turn on who decides and what the data's classification requires. The data owner, a business manager, classifies data and approves access; the custodian, usually IT, implements the controls; users follow the handling rules. When an option asks the custodian to decide classification, or lets a user choose how to handle restricted data, it is usually a distractor.

Follow the data through its lifecycle: creation, storage, use, sharing, archiving and destruction. Most scenarios break one link. Production personal data copied into a test environment breaks 'use' and needs masking or synthetic data. A drive leaving the organisation breaks 'destruction' and needs purging or physical destruction appropriate to the media. A legal hold overrides normal retention and deletion schedules until counsel releases it.
When in doubt, choose the answer that reduces the amount of sensitive data held, because data you do not keep cannot leak.

learn.heading: When classification meets the real world
body: Scenarios test classification at the awkward edges. A document that mixes restricted and public content takes the higher classification; a copy inherits the classification of the original; and declassification needs the owner’s decision, not a user’s judgement that the data “seems old”. When two rules conflict, the stricter handling wins — the exam never rewards the convenient reading.

Shared services make the lifecycle harder. In multi-tenant cloud storage, isolation between tenants is the provider’s job and verifying it is yours, through audit reports and contract terms. Disposal needs the same rigour as collection: media leaving the organisation gets a sanitisation method matched to its classification, a witnessed destruction where required, and a certificate of destruction filed as evidence. An undocumented disposal is an unproven disposal, and an auditor will treat it as no disposal at all.

examples.title: Safe test data
examples.code:
-- copy production structure, not production people
INSERT INTO test.customers (id, name, email, card_last4)
SELECT id,
       'Customer ' || id,
       'user' || id || '@example.test',
       '0000'
FROM prod.customers TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (1);
examples.explanation: Test environments get masked or synthetic values that keep the shape of real data. Real PII in test is a breach waiting for an auditor.
