overview: Domain 3 scenarios test architectural principles under pressure: what the system does when it fails, how controls layer, and where the keys live. The exam loves designs that look reasonable until one principle is violated.
This capstone drills fail-secure defaults, defence in depth as layering of different functions, and the separation of keys from the data they protect.

learn.heading: Fail secure, layer defences
body: Fail-secure (fail closed) means a failure denies access rather than granting it. Any design where a bug becomes a vulnerability has this backwards. Deny by default is the quiet version of the same principle.
Defence in depth is not two firewalls — it is different control functions layered so one miss is another's catch: a firewall for access control plus an IPS for threat prevention, for example.

learn.heading: Keys live apart from data
body: Whoever holds both the ciphertext and the key holds the plaintext. Keys belong in a dedicated security domain — a KMS or HSM with split administrative duties — never next to the data, in source code, or in the same admin's pocket.
Key management questions on the exam almost always reduce to separation and lifecycle: generate securely, store separately, rotate on schedule and on compromise, destroy when retired.

learn.heading: How to approach a D3 scenario
body: Security architecture questions reward principles over products. Look for which design principle the scenario violates: least privilege, defence in depth, fail-safe defaults, separation of duties, economy of mechanism, complete mediation or open design. The right answer usually restores the principle rather than adding a single new tool.

Cryptography scenarios in this domain are mostly about key management. Strong algorithms do not help if the key sits beside the data, never rotates, or is shared across all customers. Prefer answers that move keys into an HSM or key management service, separate duties between key administrators and data users, and plan for algorithm change (crypto agility), including the move to post-quantum algorithms such as ML-KEM.
For physical design questions, life safety outranks asset protection: doors on an escape route fail safe (unlock) on power loss even when that is less secure.

learn.heading: Design traps: the principles behind the distractors
body: The exam hides the violated principle inside a plausible design. Least privilege means a subject gets only the access its task needs; need-to-know is the same idea applied to information. Economy of mechanism says simpler designs are easier to verify and harder to break — a design with three overlapping controls doing one job is a smell, not a strength. And open design, Kerckhoffs’s principle, says security must rest in the key, not in the secrecy of the algorithm: a system that is only secure while nobody understands it is not secure.

Complete mediation is the principle most scenarios violate quietly: every access, by every subject, to every object, must be checked every time. Caching an authorisation decision, trusting a check done earlier in the session, or skipping the check for “internal” callers all break it. When a scenario shows a shortcut around a check, the fix is to restore the check at the point of access — not to add logging that records the unauthorised access after the fact.

examples.title: Fail closed in code
examples.explanation: When a security dependency breaks, the safe default is to deny. Returning True in the except branch would turn every outage into an open door.

overview: Domain 4 scenarios are about moving bits safely across untrusted space and keeping hostile traffic away from trusted assets. The exam tests whether you reach for the right tool: encryption in transit, inspection that cannot be evaded, and segmentation before anything else.
This capstone drills site-to-site VPNs, defeating fragmentation evasion, and segmenting untrusted networks first.

learn.heading: Encrypt the path, inspect honestly
body: Traffic crossing the internet between sites gets a site-to-site IPsec VPN: confidentiality and integrity over untrusted networks. This is the standard answer; exotic alternatives are distractors.
Attackers fragment packets to slip past signature matching. The defence is normalisation: reassemble at the IPS before inspection, so the analyser sees what the endpoint will see.

learn.heading: Segment the untrusted first
body: Guest, IoT, and partner networks are untrusted by definition. The first design step is always segmentation — separate VLANs and firewall zones — before tuning any monitoring or access rules.
Segmentation contains lateral movement. Everything else (monitoring, NAC, passwords) is secondary to not letting the hostile network touch the trusted one.

learn.heading: How to approach a D4 scenario
body: Network security scenarios ask you to protect traffic and limit where an attacker can go. Start by identifying what crosses an untrusted network; that traffic needs encryption and authentication, such as IPsec between sites or TLS for applications. Then look at trust boundaries: guests, contractors, IoT devices and operational technology belong in their own segments with default-deny rules between them and the corporate network.

Many distractors add monitoring where prevention is possible, or add a device without addressing the design. An IDS that alerts on lateral movement is useful, but segmenting the flat network removes the path. A VPN does not help if the remote laptop is already compromised, which is why zero trust checks device posture and identity for every request.
Know the protocols' weaknesses too: Telnet, FTP and SNMPv1 send credentials in clear text, so the best answer replaces them with SSH, SFTP and SNMPv3 rather than merely monitoring them.

learn.heading: When encryption is not the answer
body: Encryption protects data in transit; it does not fix a flat network, a trusted insider, or a compromised endpoint. A scenario that offers TLS as the answer to lateral movement is a trap: the attacker is already inside, and encrypted traffic to the next host is still an attack. Segmentation, least privilege and endpoint controls are what stop movement; encryption is what stops eavesdropping, and the two problems need different answers.

Inspection has the same boundary. TLS interception lets a proxy decrypt and inspect traffic, but it breaks end-to-end trust, needs the private keys or a trusted root on every client, and creates a high-value target in the proxy itself. Use it where the risk justifies it and the law allows it, with the trade-off stated openly. Network access control adds the missing piece at the edge: check device posture and identity before the device joins the network, rather than discovering an unpatched laptop after it has already connected.

examples.title: Segment guest Wi-Fi
examples.code:
VLAN 10  Corporate   10.10.0.0/16   802.1X (EAP-TLS)
VLAN 50  Guest       172.20.0.0/22  WPA3-Personal + captive portal

Firewall policy (zone guest):
  allow  guest -> internet : 80, 443
  deny   guest -> corporate: any   (log)
  deny   guest -> mgmt     : any   (log)
examples.explanation: Guests are untrusted by definition, so the guest zone reaches the internet and nothing else; logging the denies shows anyone probing inward.

overview: Domain 5 scenarios test the identity lifecycle under stress: proving who someone is without sharing secrets, bounding the damage when a session is stolen, and treating an exposed credential as compromised the instant it leaks.
This capstone drills federation for SSO, session controls as the complement to MFA, and immediate rotation of exposed secrets.

learn.heading: Federate, do not share
body: When users need access to a third-party service, federate: SAML for enterprise SSO, OIDC for modern web apps. The identity provider authenticates; the service trusts the assertion. Passwords never cross the boundary.
Shared accounts destroy accountability. Every exam answer that proposes sharing credentials — service or human — is wrong.

learn.heading: Sessions are the second half of authentication
body: MFA proves identity at login; it says nothing about the session afterwards. Short timeouts, idle disconnects, and step-up re-authentication for privileged actions bound the blast radius of a stolen session.
An exposed secret is a compromised secret. Revoke and rotate first, investigate second — the order matters because every minute of delay is attacker opportunity.

learn.heading: How to approach a D5 scenario
body: Identity questions follow the account lifecycle: provisioning, review, change and removal. Many problems come from the middle of it. People change roles and keep old permissions (privilege creep), so the fix is periodic access reviews by the data owner and role-based provisioning tied to HR events. Leavers keep access because deprovisioning is manual, so the fix is automated removal on the termination record.

Prefer federation and single sign-on over shared or duplicated credentials, and phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys) over codes that can be relayed. Remember that authentication is only half the job: session tokens, API keys and service accounts are also credentials, so short session lifetimes, re-authentication for sensitive actions, and vaulted, rotated service credentials appear in many correct answers.

Accountability needs unique IDs. A shared administrator account cannot show who made a change, so replacing it with named accounts and privileged access management is almost always better than adding logging to the shared account.

learn.heading: The lifecycle traps
body: Most identity scenarios fail on a lifecycle transition. Joining is usually well handled; moving is where privilege creep grows, because the new role’s access is added and the old role’s access is forgotten; leaving is where orphaned accounts persist, because deprovisioning is a manual ticket nobody owns. The exam’s fix is always the same shape: tie provisioning to HR events, review access on every role change, and remove access automatically when the HR record closes.

Privileged access deserves its own discipline. Privileged access management vaults administrative credentials, issues them just in time, records the session, and rotates the password after use — so a stolen administrator password is useless an hour later and every privileged action is attributable to a named person. Remember the distinction underneath it all: identity proofing establishes who someone is at enrolment, with documents and checks; authentication verifies that identity later, at each sign-in. A strong authenticator cannot fix weak proofing.

examples.title: Step-up authentication policy
examples.code:
Session: signed in with password + push MFA at 09:00

Action                       Requirement
---------------------------  ------------------------------
Read dashboards              existing session
Change payee bank details    re-authenticate with FIDO2 key
Add an admin role            FIDO2 + approval by second admin
Idle > 15 min                sign in again
examples.explanation: MFA at login proves identity once; step-up and short idle timeouts bound what a stolen session can do, scaled to the risk of each action.

cheatSheet: Revoke and rotate FIRST, then investigate
Proves identity at login; sessions need their own controls

overview: Domain 6 scenarios test whether you choose the right assessment for the question asked — and whether you can tell a finding from a risk. The exam punishes both testing the wrong thing and treating scanner output as a to-do list.
This capstone drills matching test types to targets, prioritising by risk rather than count, and demanding evidence for vendor claims.

learn.heading: Right test, right target
body: Penetration tests simulate attackers against running systems; SAST examines source code; DAST automates black-box checks of running apps; vulnerability scans enumerate known issues. "Best assurance against the running application" points at pentesting.
No single test covers everything. Mature programmes layer them: SAST in the pipeline, DAST in staging, pentests for high-risk releases, scans for continuous hygiene.

learn.heading: Findings are not risks
body: Five hundred scanner findings are a starting point, not a plan. Prioritise by risk: exploitability times business impact. An internet-facing critical system outranks an isolated lab box regardless of raw severity.
Vendor claims are marketing until verified. SOC 2, ISO 27001, pentest letters — read the actual report: scope, period, methodology, and qualifications. Third-party risk management runs on evidence.

learn.heading: How to approach a D6 scenario
body: Assessment questions ask you to match the test to the question being asked. Vulnerability scanning finds known weaknesses broadly; penetration testing proves whether they can be exploited and chained; code review and SAST find flaws before release; a SOC 2 or ISO 27001 audit gives independent assurance about a vendor's controls. Choose the option that answers the scenario's actual question at the right depth.

Testing must be authorised. Before any penetration test, written rules of engagement must define scope, timing, methods and emergency contacts, signed by someone with authority over the systems. An option that starts testing on a verbal request, or tests a third party's systems without their consent, is wrong however efficient it sounds.
Results only matter when they reach decision-makers. Findings should be ranked by risk to the business, assigned owners and dates, reported in management terms, and re-tested after remediation.

learn.heading: What good evidence looks like
body: An assessment is only as good as its evidence. Good evidence is sufficient, meaning enough of it to support the conclusion; appropriate, meaning relevant and reliable for the question asked; and collected independently where it matters. A vendor’s marketing page is none of these; a signed audit report with a defined scope and period is all three. When a scenario offers a claim without evidence, the correct answer is to ask for the evidence, not to accept the claim or to reject it outright.

Sampling and follow-up decide whether findings mean anything. Testing every transaction is rarely possible, so auditors sample — and the sample must represent the population, or the conclusion does not hold. After remediation, the finding is not closed because a ticket says so: re-test the control and confirm the weakness is gone. A finding closed without verification is the most common way a fixed problem quietly returns.

examples.title: Choose the right test
examples.code:
Question                                         Best test
-----------------------------------------------  ----------------------------
Are there flaws in our source before release?    SAST in CI
Is the running app exploitable by an attacker?   Authorised penetration test
Do our detections catch real techniques?         Breach & attack simulation
Did last month's patch still work?               Regression + rescan
examples.explanation: Each test answers a different question. Pick it by what you need to prove, then make sure every finding gets an owner and a date.

overview: Domain 7 scenarios happen at the worst possible time — and the exam checks whether your instincts follow the incident-response order instead of panic. Contain first, think second, learn always.
This capstone drills the contain → eradicate → recover sequence, alert triage by fidelity, and the lessons-learned review that prevents recurrence.

learn.heading: Contain before you cure
body: Active encryption, active exfiltration, active lateral movement: isolate the affected systems from the network first. Every minute of spread multiplies the recovery bill. Forensics, backups, and blame all wait for containment.
Eradication before recovery, or you restore the attacker along with the data. Verify the root cause is gone before bringing systems back.

learn.heading: Triage by fidelity, close with learning
body: Not every alert is an incident. Triage by fidelity and corroboration: a single failed login is noise; the same IP failing five hundred times is a case. Tune the noise, chase the signal.
The most important step is the last one: the lessons-learned review. Update playbooks, controls, and monitoring from what the incident taught, or it will recur on schedule.

learn.heading: How to approach a D7 scenario
body: Operations scenarios often describe an incident in progress and ask for the next step. Use the incident response sequence: detect and analyse, then contain, then eradicate, then recover, then learn. If the attack is active, containment comes before investigation is finished; if it is contained, preserving evidence comes before rebuilding systems. Recovery before eradication invites the attacker back.

Evidence handling has firm rules: collect in order of volatility, work on verified copies (hash before and after), and keep a chain of custody for anything that may go to court. Notify according to the plan; legal counsel and management decide on external notification, not the analyst on shift.

For continuity questions, the priority is people's safety, then restoring the most critical business functions in the order set by the business impact analysis, not the order in which IT happens to find them.

learn.heading: Communication and the legal clock
body: An incident is a communications problem as much as a technical one, and the exam tests who decides what. Legal counsel and senior management decide on external notification — to regulators, customers and law enforcement — not the analyst on shift. Notification duties are set by law and contract, and they carry clocks: under GDPR, a personal data breach must be reported to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of it. Miss the clock and the incident becomes a compliance failure on top of a security failure.

Keep the response itself off the compromised network: use out-of-band channels for coordination, because an attacker in the mail system reads the incident bridge. After the incident, the lessons-learned review is the step that prevents the next one — update the playbook, fix the control that failed, and test the fix. Tabletop exercises do the same work before an incident: walk the team through a scenario on paper so the first real test is not the first time anyone has opened the plan.

examples.title: First hour of a ransomware incident
examples.code:
00:00  Declare incident; open bridge; assign IC and scribe
00:05  Isolate affected subnets (EDR network containment)
00:15  Preserve: memory from 2 hosts, firewall + EDR logs
00:20  Notify legal and leadership via out-of-band channel
00:30  Scope: which accounts, which data, is exfiltration seen?
00:45  Confirm backups are intact and offline
examples.explanation: Contain first, preserve evidence, communicate out of band, then scope. Restoring before scoping usually brings the attacker back with the data.

Speed of closure < quality of learning

overview: Domain 8 scenarios test whether security is built in or bolted on: what happens before a dependency is adopted, what happens the instant a secret leaks, and where in the lifecycle a bug is cheapest to kill.
This capstone drills supply-chain due diligence, secret-spill response, and the economics of shift-left.

learn.heading: Trust, but verify the supply chain
body: Every dependency is code you did not write running with your privileges. Before adopting: licence compatibility, maintenance health (commits, maintainers, issue response), and known vulnerabilities via SCA. Popularity is not diligence.
Generate and keep an SBOM so that when the next Log4Shell lands, you know in minutes whether you are exposed instead of discovering it in weeks.

learn.heading: Secrets spill: revoke first, shift left always
body: A secret in version control is compromised the moment it is pushed — repositories are copied, backed up, and mirrored. Revoke and rotate immediately, move to a vault, and add pre-commit scanning so it cannot recur.
Bugs are cheapest where they are born: threat modelling in design beats a pentest finding, which beats an emergency production patch. Shift-left is economics, not ideology.

learn.heading: How to approach a D8 scenario
body: Software security questions reward building security in early. A flaw found in requirements or design costs far less to fix than one found in production, so answers that add threat modelling, secure coding standards and automated testing in the pipeline usually beat answers that rely on a final penetration test.

Third-party code is part of your software. Maintain a software bill of materials, scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities, pin and verify versions, and evaluate a new library's maintenance and licence before adopting it. For acquired software or SaaS, ask for evidence such as security test results or an attestation rather than a vendor's assurance.

When something goes wrong, contain first: a leaked secret is revoked and rotated before the history is cleaned, and a vulnerable release is patched or rolled back before the root cause analysis is written.

learn.heading: The dependency decision, step by step
body: Adopting a dependency is adopting someone else’s code, maintainers and vulnerabilities. Before it enters the build, check the licence for compatibility with your product, the maintenance health — recent commits, responsive maintainers, a path for security fixes — and the known vulnerabilities in it and everything it pulls in. Pin versions and keep a lockfile so the build you tested is the build you ship; an unpinned dependency can change under you between test and release.

Integrity does not stop at the source. Sign release artefacts so consumers can verify what they received, and prefer reproducible builds, where the same source always produces the same binary. Runtime protections such as a web application firewall or runtime application self-protection can compensate for a known weakness, but they are compensating controls, not fixes: the vulnerability is still in the code, and the correct long-term answer is still to patch it.

examples.title: Respond to a committed secret
examples.code:
$ git log -p | grep -n 'AKIA'
  commit 3f9a... +AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIA...
1. Revoke the key in IAM now (assume it is compromised)
2. Review CloudTrail for its use since the commit time
3. Move secrets to a vault; inject at runtime
4. Add gitleaks as a pre-commit hook and in CI
examples.explanation: Deleting the line does not help: the key is in history and any clone. Revoke first, investigate second, then fix the process so it cannot recur.

overview: C++ is a compiled language: your source code is translated to native machine code before it ever runs, which is why it powers game engines, operating systems, and high-frequency trading — anywhere speed is non-negotiable.

This lesson covers what compilation means, the three build stages (preprocess, compile, link), the `main()` entry point, basic console output with `std::cout`, and compiling your first program with `g++`.

learn.heading: Compiled, not interpreted
body: C++ programs do not run line by line. A compiler — `g++`, `clang++`, or MSVC — translates your entire source into machine code ahead of time and produces a native executable. The payoff is raw speed; the price is that you must build before you can run, and a single missing semicolon stops the whole process.

That build happens in three stages. First the preprocessor expands `#include` directives and macros, essentially stitching your source together. Then the compiler translates each source file into an object file of machine code. Finally the linker combines the object files (plus any libraries) into one executable. When a build fails, knowing which stage complained tells you where to look.

learn.heading: Hello, world — anatomy of a program
body: Every C++ program starts at `main()`. Execution enters there, and `return 0;` signals success to the operating system — any non-zero value means something went wrong. The classic first program prints a line: `#include <iostream>` brings in the input/output declarations, and `std::cout << "Hello, world!";` sends text to the console, where `<<` is the stream insertion operator.

The `std::` prefix is a namespace qualifier — it says "this name comes from the standard library." You will see `using namespace std;` in tutorials; it pulls every standard name into scope so you can write `cout` instead of `std::cout`. Convenient, but in real projects it invites name clashes, so prefer the explicit `std::` form.

To build a single file into an executable named `app`, the command is `g++ main.cpp -o app`. Add `-std=c++20` to choose the language standard — C++ evolves, and modern features (smart pointers, `auto`, lambdas) require telling the compiler which era of the language you are writing in.

learn.heading: Building real projects with CMake
body: Calling the compiler by hand works for one file. Real projects use a build system, and CMake is the de facto standard for C++. A minimal `CMakeLists.txt` declares `cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)`, `project(hello CXX)`, `set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)` and `add_executable(hello main.cpp)`. Then `cmake -S . -B build` configures the project and `cmake --build build` compiles it, using whichever compiler and generator the platform provides.

Build in two configurations. A Debug build (`-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug`) keeps symbols and turns off optimisation so a debugger can step through code. A Release build turns on optimisation for speed. Add warnings to every build, for example `target_compile_options(hello PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic)` with GCC and Clang, and treat new warnings as bugs.

examples.title: Compile and run a first program
examples.explanation: Turn on warnings (-Wall -Wextra) from day one; the compiler catches many mistakes before they become bugs.

overview: C++ is statically typed: every variable has a fixed type decided at compile time, which lets the compiler catch a whole class of bugs before your program ever runs.
This lesson covers the fundamental types (`int`, `double`, `char`, `bool`), `const` correctness, type deduction with `auto`, integer division pitfalls, and safe conversions with `static_cast`.

learn.heading: The fundamental types
body: The workhorses are `int` for whole numbers (commonly 4 bytes — `sizeof(int)` tells you the actual size on your platform), `double` for decimals, `char` for a single byte or character, and `bool` for `true`/`false`. A character literal uses single quotes (`'a'`); a string literal uses double quotes (`"a"`), which is actually a null-terminated array of characters — a different beast entirely.

Mark anything that should not change as `const`: `const int x = 5;` makes `x` read-only, and the compiler will reject any accidental reassignment. `const` is cheap insurance — it turns runtime mistakes into compile-time errors, which is always the better trade.

`auto` deduces a type from the initializer: `auto x = 3.0;` makes `x` a `double`. The variable is still statically typed — `auto` just saves you from writing it out. It does not make C++ dynamically typed; nothing does.

learn.heading: Operators, division, and the traps
body: Two traps catch every beginner. First, `7 / 2` is `3`, not `3.5` — when both operands are integers, C++ does integer division and truncates. Write `7.0 / 2` when you want the decimal result. Second, `=` assigns while `==` compares; writing `if (x = 5)` assigns 5 and is always true, a classic bug that compilers now warn about.

Signed integer overflow is undefined behaviour in C++ — not "wraps around," not "throws an exception," but literally anything-goes. (Unsigned overflow does wrap, by definition.) Never write code that depends on what signed overflow does.
For conversions, prefer `static_cast<double>(x)` over the old C-style `(double)x`. The named cast is explicit, greppable, and checked at compile time — a small habit that keeps conversions honest.

learn.heading: Initialisation and conversions
body: C++ has several ways to initialise a variable, and brace initialisation is the safest default: `int count{0};` or `double rate{0.05};`. Braces refuse narrowing conversions, so `int n{3.7};` is a compile error rather than a silent truncation to 3. An uninitialised local such as `int total;` holds an indeterminate value, and reading it is undefined behaviour, so always initialise.

Mixing signed and unsigned types causes surprising results: `-1 < 1u` is false, because `-1` converts to a huge unsigned value. Compare sizes with `std::ssize()` or cast deliberately, and turn on `-Wsign-compare`. Use `static_cast<int>(x)` when you mean a conversion so it is visible in review; avoid C-style casts such as `(int)x`, which can silently perform more dangerous conversions.

examples.title: Integer overflow and safe conversion
examples.explanation: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour; unsigned arithmetic wraps. Use fixed-width types when size matters and static_cast to make conversions visible.

overview: Programs are decisions and repetition. C++ gives you the classic control structures — `if`, `switch`, `for`, `while` — and functions to package logic into reusable, testable units.

This lesson covers the loop flavors (including the do-while that always runs once), `break` vs `continue`, function definitions, pass-by-value vs pass-by-reference, overloading, and default arguments.

learn.heading: Decisions and loops
body: The `do { ... } while (cond);` loop is the odd one out: its condition is checked after the body, so it always executes at least once. Every other loop — `while`, `for`, range-based `for` — may execute zero times. Inside any loop, `break` exits the innermost loop immediately, while `continue` skips to the next iteration.

`switch` matches an integral or enumeration value against `case` labels with exact equality — no strings, no ranges. And every `case` needs its own `break;`, because without one execution falls through into the next case. Forgetting `break` is one of the oldest bugs in the language.

learn.heading: Functions: the unit of reuse
body: A function declared `void` returns nothing — you call it for its side effects. Parameters are passed by value by default, meaning the function receives a copy; changes to it never reach the caller. To let a function modify the caller's variable, take the parameter by reference (`void f(int& x)`) or by pointer.

For large objects you do not want to modify, the idiom is `const T&`: pass by const reference. It avoids an expensive copy while promising the function will not touch the object. This is the default way to pass big read-only parameters in modern C++.

Two functions can share a name if their parameter lists differ — that is overloading, and the compiler picks the best match by the arguments you pass. You can also give parameters defaults (`int f(int x, int y = 0)`), so callers may omit them. And remember: a function must be declared — by its definition or a forward declaration (prototype) — before its first use, which is why headers exist.

learn.heading: Overloading, default arguments and returning results
body: Functions can share a name if their parameter lists differ: `int area(int side)` and `double area(double w, double h)` are overloads, and the compiler picks one from the argument types. Default arguments supply values the caller may omit: `void log(const std::string& msg, int level = 1);`. Keep defaults in the declaration in the header, not repeated in the definition.

Return results by value: modern compilers elide the copy, and moves make it cheap even when they cannot. To return several values, return a struct or use structured bindings with `std::pair` or `std::tuple`: `auto [min, max] = std::minmax(a, b);`. For a value that may be missing, return `std::optional<T>` rather than a magic number such as -1, so the caller has to check.

examples.title: Pass by value, reference and const reference
examples.code:
void byValue(std::string s)        { s += "!"; }   // copies; caller unchanged
void byRef(std::string& s)         { s += "!"; }   // modifies caller's string
std::size_t len(const std::string& s) { return s.size(); } // no copy, read-only

std::string msg = "hi";
byValue(msg);  // msg == "hi"
byRef(msg);    // msg == "hi!"
examples.explanation: Pass large objects by const reference to avoid copies, and use a non-const reference only when the function is meant to change the argument.

overview: Pointers are C++'s superpower and its most notorious footgun: direct access to memory addresses, with no safety net. Understanding them is understanding how C++ actually works.

This lesson covers what pointers are, the address-of and dereference operators, `nullptr`, the stack vs the heap, `new`/`delete`, and the classic failure modes: leaks, dangling pointers, and mismatched array deletes.

learn.heading: Addresses, pointers, and references
body: A pointer is a variable that stores a memory address. `&x` gives you the address of `x` — `int* p = &x;` makes `p` point at `x` — and `*p` dereferences the pointer, reaching the object it points to. On the left side of an assignment, `*p = 5;` writes through the pointer.

A pointer that points to nothing should be `nullptr`, the modern null-pointer constant. Dereferencing `nullptr` — or a wild, uninitialized pointer — is undefined behaviour. A reference, by contrast, is an alias that must bind at creation, can never be null, and can never be reseated: safer, but less flexible.

learn.heading: Stack, heap, and the ways memory dies
body: Local variables live on the stack and are freed automatically when their scope ends. Heap memory — obtained with `new` — is yours to manage: `new` returns a pointer, and you must `delete` it, or the memory is lost until the program exits. That loss has a name: a memory leak.

Worse than a leak is a dangling pointer: one that points to memory already freed or out of scope. Using it is undefined behaviour and a favorite exploit primitive. And arrays allocated with `new[]` must be freed with `delete[]` — mismatching the forms is undefined behaviour. The modern answer to all of this is smart pointers (see the RAII lesson), but you must understand the raw mechanics first, because every abstraction leaks eventually.

learn.heading: Choosing between references, pointers and smart pointers
body: Use a reference when the object must exist and you only need to use it: `void print(const Order& o)`. Use a raw pointer when 'nothing' is a valid value and the function does not own the object: `Node* find(int key)` returns `nullptr` when the key is missing. Never use a raw pointer to own memory in modern code; that is the job of `std::unique_ptr` or `std::shared_ptr`.

For a view of a contiguous range, `std::span<int>` (C++20) carries a pointer and a length together, so the function knows the size and cannot be handed a mismatched one. Similarly `std::string_view` views characters without copying. Views must not outlive the data they point to, which is the same dangling risk as a raw pointer.

examples.title: Dangling pointer
examples.explanation: Returning the address of a local variable leaves a dangling pointer; reading it is undefined behaviour. Return by value or a smart pointer instead.

overview: C++ invented much of what the world now calls object-oriented programming — and then kept the escape hatches. Classes bundle data with the functions that operate on it, and the access system decides who may touch what.
This lesson covers `class` vs `struct`, constructors and destructors, encapsulation, `virtual` functions and runtime polymorphism, abstract classes, and constructor initializer lists.

learn.heading: Classes, construction, destruction
body: In C++, `class` and `struct` are nearly identical — the only difference is the default access: `class` members are private unless stated otherwise, `struct` members are public. That default is why `class` signals "encapsulated abstraction" and `struct` signals "plain data."

A constructor is the special member function that initializes an object at creation — same name as the class, no return type. Its counterpart, the destructor (`~ClassName()`), runs automatically when the object dies and handles cleanup: freeing resources, closing handles. Prefer initializing members in the constructor's initializer list — `ClassName() : member(value) {}` — rather than assigning in the body: it is more efficient, and it is required for `const` and reference members.

Access specifiers are the encapsulation machinery: `private` means class-only, `protected` extends to derived classes, `public` is open to everyone. The discipline is to keep internals private and expose a deliberate public interface — clients depend on the interface, not the implementation.

learn.heading: Inheritance and polymorphism
body: Declaring a member function `virtual` makes it overridable: calling it through a base-class pointer or reference dispatches at runtime to the derived class's override, via the virtual table. That is runtime polymorphism — one interface, many behaviors, chosen by the actual object type.

Two rules follow. First, a polymorphic base class needs a virtual destructor, so that deleting a derived object through a base pointer runs the derived destructor; without it, you get undefined behaviour and likely a leak. Second, a pure virtual function (`virtual void f() = 0;`) has no base implementation and makes the class abstract — it cannot be instantiated, and derived classes must override the function. Inside any member function, `this` is a pointer to the current object.

learn.heading: The rule of zero, three and five
body: If a class manages a resource directly, such as raw memory or a file handle, it needs a destructor, and then almost certainly a copy constructor and copy assignment operator too (the rule of three), plus a move constructor and move assignment for efficiency (the rule of five). Getting any of these wrong causes double frees or leaks.

The better design is the rule of zero: hold resources in members that already manage themselves, such as `std::vector`, `std::string` and `std::unique_ptr`, and write none of the five. The compiler-generated versions then do the right thing. Mark single-argument constructors `explicit` to stop accidental conversions, and mark overriding functions `override` and classes not meant for inheritance `final`.

examples.title: Virtual functions and a virtual destructor
examples.explanation: override lets the compiler check the signature, and the virtual destructor ensures Circle's destructor runs when deleted through a Shape pointer.

overview: The Standard Template Library is the part of C++ you will use every day: containers that manage their own memory, iterators that traverse them, and algorithms that operate on ranges.
This lesson covers `std::vector` (your default container), `std::map` and `std::set`, `std::string`, iterators, range-based for loops, and the `<algorithm>` header — `sort`, `find`, and friends.

learn.heading: Containers: vector first, the rest on demand
body: `std::vector` is a dynamic, contiguous array — it grows as needed, and because its elements sit side by side in memory it is cache-friendly and fast to iterate. It is the default container: reach for anything else only when you need its specific behavior. Add elements with `push_back` (or `emplace_back`), check `size()` and `empty()`.

`std::map` stores sorted, unique key→value pairs; `std::set` stores sorted unique elements. Their hash-based cousins, `std::unordered_map` and `std::unordered_set`, trade ordering for average O(1) lookup. And `std::string` is a managed, resizable string that owns its memory — no manual null-termination, no buffer sizing, none of the C-string anxiety.
`std::pair` holds two values together (a map entry exposes `.first` and `.second`); `std::tuple` generalizes the idea to any number of values.

learn.heading: Iterators and algorithms
body: An iterator is an object that points into a container and can be advanced to traverse it — a generalization of the pointer idea. `begin()` and `end()` delimit the range, and `end()` is the past-the-end sentinel: `std::find` returns `end()` when the value is absent, so always compare against it before using the result.

The modern way to traverse is the range-based for loop: `for (const auto& x : container)`. The `&` avoids copying each element; `const` promises read-only. For everything else there is `<algorithm>`: `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end())` sorts ascending by default (pass a comparator for custom order), and dozens of siblings — `find`, `count`, `transform`, `any_of` — turn raw loops into named intent.

learn.heading: Choosing a container and watching iterator invalidation
body: Start with `std::vector`: its elements sit in contiguous memory, which makes iteration fast and cache-friendly. Use `std::unordered_map` for average constant-time lookups by key, `std::map` when you need keys in sorted order, `std::deque` for cheap insertion at both ends, and `std::array` for a fixed size known at compile time. `std::list` is rarely the best choice despite its cheap middle insertion.

Modifying a container can invalidate iterators, pointers and references into it. A `push_back` that grows a vector reallocates its storage, so any pointer to an element becomes dangling. Erasing inside a loop must use the iterator that `erase` returns: `it = v.erase(it);`. Calling `reserve()` when you know the final size avoids repeated reallocations.

examples.explanation: Standard algorithms are tested and state intent clearly. The erase-remove idiom (or C++20 std::erase_if) is how you delete matching elements from a vector.

overview: RAII — Resource Acquisition Is Initialization — is the single most important idiom in C++: tie a resource's lifetime to an object's scope, and the destructor releases it automatically, even when exceptions fly.
This lesson covers the RAII principle, `unique_ptr` and `shared_ptr` (and why `weak_ptr` exists), `make_unique`, move semantics, the Rule of Five, and the Rule of Zero.

learn.heading: Ownership, expressed in types
body: The idea is disarmingly simple: acquire the resource in the constructor, release it in the destructor. Because destructors run automatically when an object leaves scope — including during stack unwinding when an exception propagates — resources are released on every path, with no manual cleanup to forget. This is why RAII beats manual `new`/`delete` so completely: the correct behavior is the default behavior.

`std::unique_ptr` expresses exclusive ownership of a heap object; it cannot be copied, only moved, and it frees the object when it dies. `std::shared_ptr` expresses shared ownership through reference counting — copying increments the count, destruction decrements it, and the object is freed when the last owner goes away. Two `shared_ptr`s pointing at each other would never release, which is why `std::weak_ptr` exists: it observes a `shared_ptr` without owning, breaking the cycle.

Always prefer `std::make_unique<T>(...)` over raw `new`: it is exception-safe (no leak if construction throws) and you never write the type twice. After `auto p2 = std::move(p1);`, `p1` is left empty — ownership transferred, not duplicated.

learn.heading: Move semantics and the rules
body: Move semantics transfer resources instead of copying them: `std::move` casts to an rvalue so the move constructor (not the copy constructor) is chosen. Moving a vector hands over its buffer pointer rather than duplicating every element — the difference between O(1) and O(n).

The Rule of Five says: if you define any of the destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, or move assignment, consider all five — managing a resource usually means handling them as a set. But the better rule is the Rule of Zero: design classes so you need none of them, letting members like smart pointers and vectors manage resources for you. The safest special member function is the one you never write.

learn.heading: Exception safety and custom deleters
body: RAII is what makes code exception-safe. If a function acquires two resources by hand and the second acquisition throws, the first leaks unless every path cleans it up. With each resource owned by an object, stack unwinding runs the destructors automatically. Aim for the strong guarantee where it matters: an operation either succeeds completely or leaves the object unchanged, often by doing the work on a copy and swapping it in.

Smart pointers can manage resources other than memory through custom deleters: `std::unique_ptr<FILE, decltype(&fclose)> f(fopen("log.txt", "r"), &fclose);` closes the file when `f` goes out of scope. Create shared objects with `std::make_shared` and unique ones with `std::make_unique`, and break `shared_ptr` reference cycles with `std::weak_ptr`.

examples.explanation: Resources tied to object lifetimes are released on every exit path, including exceptions, with no cleanup code to forget.

overview: Modern C++ — roughly C++11 onward — is almost a different language from the C++ of the 1990s: type-safe generics, lambdas, compile-time computation, and a standard library that finally feels complete.
This lesson covers templates and when they instantiate, lambdas and captures, `constexpr`, namespaces, the header/source split, `nullptr`, and `std::optional`.

learn.heading: Templates and lambdas
body: A template is a blueprint: `template<typename T> T max(T a, T b)` generates a separate function for every type actually used — at compile time, not runtime. That is why templates mostly live in headers: the compiler needs the full definition visible wherever instantiation happens.

A lambda is an inline anonymous function object: `[](int x){ return x*2; }`. The capture list in brackets decides what surrounding state it can see — `[&]` captures everything by reference, `[=]` by value. Capturing by reference is powerful and dangerous in equal measure: if the lambda outlives the captured variable, you have a dangling reference.

learn.heading: The modern toolkit
body: `constexpr` asks the compiler to evaluate something at compile time when possible, turning runtime computation into compile-time constants. Namespaces group related names to avoid collisions — `std` is just the most famous one, accessed as `ns::name`.

The header/source split is C++'s compilation model made concrete: the `.h`/`.hpp` declares the interface so callers can compile against it, while the `.cpp` defines the implementation. (Templates are the exception — they usually stay header-only.) Two small modernizations punch above their weight: `nullptr` is a real null-pointer type, so overload resolution is unambiguous where `NULL`-as-zero could silently pick the wrong function; and `std::optional<T>` represents "a value that may not be present" — a type-safe alternative to sentinels and null pointers.

learn.heading: Ranges and compile-time programming
body: C++20 ranges let you compose operations without writing loops or managing iterator pairs: `for (int x : v | std::views::filter([](int n) { return n % 2 == 0; }) | std::views::transform([](int n) { return n * n; }))` visits the squares of the even numbers lazily, without creating intermediate containers. Algorithms in `std::ranges` take the whole container: `std::ranges::sort(v);`.

Work can move from run time to compile time. A `constexpr` function can be evaluated by the compiler when its arguments are constants, and `consteval` (C++20) requires it. `if constexpr` chooses a branch at compile time inside templates, discarding the other. Combined with concepts, these replace most of the template tricks older C++ code relied on.

examples.title: A constrained template (C++20 concepts)
examples.explanation: Concepts state requirements up front, so misuse produces a short, readable error instead of pages of template instantiation messages.

overview: C++ gives you no guardrails: out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, and signed overflow are not errors the language catches — they are undefined behaviour, meaning the compiler is allowed to do literally anything.

This lesson covers what undefined behaviour means, why buffer overflows are a security catastrophe, the safe alternatives (`vector`, `.at()`), and the tooling that catches what the compiler cannot: warnings, sanitizers, and Valgrind.

learn.heading: Undefined behaviour: the contract you cannot break
body: Undefined behaviour (UB) means the C++ standard assigns no meaning to your code — the compiler may do anything, including appearing to work today and exploding after an unrelated change. Out-of-bounds array access, signed integer overflow, and use-after-free are all UB, not "an exception" or "a crash you can rely on." Treating UB as merely a bug understates it: it voids every assumption your program rests on.

The most consequential UB is the buffer overflow: writing past an array corrupts adjacent memory, and C++ performs no bounds checking on raw arrays or `operator[]`. Attackers have turned this into decades of exploits. The defences are straightforward — use `std::vector` or `std::array` instead of raw arrays, iterate with range-based for loops, and reach for `.at(i)` instead of `[i]` when the index is uncertain: `.at()` throws `std::out_of_range` rather than invoking UB.

A use-after-free — accessing memory through a pointer after it was freed — is UB with the same exploit potential. Null pointers after freeing, or better yet smart pointers that make the question moot, are the way out. And the single highest-leverage habit in modern C++: never write raw `new`/`delete` when RAII and smart pointers will do.

learn.heading: The tooling safety net
body: The compiler is your first line of defence: build with `-Wall -Wextra` to enable warnings that catch likely bugs, and consider `-Werror` in CI so warnings cannot be ignored into production. Warnings are the cheapest bugs you will ever fix.

What warnings miss, sanitizers catch at runtime. AddressSanitizer (`-fsanitize=address`) detects use-after-free, buffer overflows, and leaks during testing with modest slowdown — run your test suite under it routinely. Valgrind finds the same class of memory errors without recompilation, at the cost of much slower execution. Between strict warnings, sanitizers, RAII, and bounds-checked access, modern C++ is far safer than its reputation — but every layer is opt-in, and the language will never force you to use them.

learn.heading: Writing safer C++ day to day
body: Many memory-safety bugs disappear with a few habits. Prefer containers and views (`std::vector`, `std::array`, `std::span`, `std::string_view`) over raw arrays and pointer arithmetic; use `.at()` where an out-of-range index is possible; own memory only through smart pointers; and initialise every variable. The C++ Core Guidelines collect these rules, and clang-tidy checks many of them automatically.

Treat compiler and tool output as part of the build. Enable warnings and make them errors in CI, run tests under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, fuzz code that parses untrusted input, and add static analysis. Hardening options such as `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3`, stack protectors and the standard library's hardened mode catch some remaining errors at run time.

examples.title: Catch memory bugs with sanitizers
examples.code:
$ g++ -std=c++20 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined bug.cpp -o bug && ./bug
==1234==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x602000000014
WRITE of size 4 at 0x602000000014 thread T0
    #0 0x401234 in main bug.cpp:7
examples.explanation: AddressSanitizer and UBSan turn silent memory corruption into an exact file and line. Run tests with them in CI; prefer std::vector::at, std::span and smart pointers in code.

overview: Before containers, shipping software meant shipping hope: it worked on the developer’s laptop, and everyone crossed their fingers it would work in production. A container ends that gamble by bundling the application with everything it needs — code, runtime, libraries — into a single portable unit that behaves identically everywhere it runs.

This lesson covers what containers actually are, how they differ from virtual machines, and the image/container model at the heart of Docker: a read-only template, and the runnable instances created from it.

learn.heading: Containers, not virtual machines
body: A virtual machine virtualizes hardware: each one carries a full guest operating system, its own kernel, its own memory footprint — heavy, slow to boot, expensive to run many of. A container virtualizes the operating system instead. Containers are isolated processes on the host, separated by Linux namespaces and resource-limited by cgroups, all sharing the host’s kernel. The result starts in milliseconds and sips memory where a VM gulps it.

That lightness is the whole point. Because containers share the kernel, you can run dozens on a host that would struggle with a handful of VMs. And because each container carries its own dependencies, the application that passed tests on a laptop is byte-for-byte the same artifact that ships to production. “Works on my machine” stops being a joke and starts being a guarantee.

learn.heading: Images and containers: template and instance
body: A Docker image is a read-only template — a stack of filesystem layers plus metadata describing how to run them. Nothing in an image changes at runtime; it is the recipe, frozen. A container is a runnable instance of an image: Docker adds a thin writable layer on top and starts the defined process inside its own isolated namespaces.

One image can spawn many containers, each independent. Run `docker run nginx` and Docker pulls the image if it is not local, creates the container, and starts it — that single command is the entire deployment story for simple cases. `docker ps` shows what is running; `docker images` shows the templates waiting on disk. The engine itself is two parts: the dockerd daemon that does the work, and the CLI that talks to it over an API.

learn.heading: How containers are isolated
body: A container is an ordinary Linux process with restricted views of the system. Namespaces give it its own process IDs, network interfaces, mount points and hostname, so it sees only its own processes and files. Control groups (cgroups) limit how much CPU, memory and I/O it can use. Because containers share the host's kernel, they start in milliseconds and use little memory, but they are not as strongly isolated as virtual machines.

That shared kernel matters for security and portability. A kernel vulnerability can let a process escape its container, and Linux containers need a Linux kernel: Docker Desktop on Windows and macOS runs them inside a lightweight Linux VM. When strong isolation between tenants is required, use VMs, or sandboxed runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers.

examples.title: Image vs container
examples.code:
$ docker pull nginx:1.27            # download an image (read-only template)
$ docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27   # start a container from it
$ docker ps
CONTAINER ID  IMAGE       STATUS        PORTS                  NAMES
3f1c2a...     nginx:1.27  Up 5 seconds  0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp   web
$ docker stop web && docker rm web
examples.explanation: One image can start many containers. Removing a container deletes its writable layer, not the image.

overview: Every Docker image begins life as a text file. The Dockerfile is a recipe — a short list of instructions that Docker executes top to bottom, each one adding a layer to the image. Learn to write a good Dockerfile and you control everything about how your application is built, cached, and shipped.

This lesson walks through the essential instructions, how layer caching makes builds fast, and the small disciplines — ordering, .dockerignore, WORKDIR — that separate a Dockerfile that works from one that works well.

learn.heading: The Dockerfile: a recipe in layers
body: It starts, almost always, with FROM: the base image everything else builds on — a language runtime, a minimal Linux, whatever your app needs. After that, each instruction adds a layer: RUN executes a command during the build (installing packages, compiling code), COPY moves files from the build context into the image, and the pair of ENTRYPOINT and CMD defines what actually runs when a container starts — ENTRYPOINT names the executable, CMD supplies its default arguments.

Two instructions deserve special attention because beginners misread them. EXPOSE documents which port the container listens on, but it is metadata only — it opens nothing and publishes nothing; you still map the port at run time with -p. And WORKDIR sets the working directory for everything after it, creating the directory if needed, so your COPY and RUN steps land somewhere sane instead of the filesystem root.

learn.heading: Layer caching: build fast by building smart
body: Docker caches the result of every layer. Rebuild, and any instruction whose inputs have not changed is skipped — which is why instruction order matters enormously. Put the steps that change rarely first and the ones that change constantly last: COPY the dependency manifest and install before copying the source, so a one-line code change does not trigger a full dependency reinstall.

Two more habits complete the picture. A .dockerignore file keeps .git, node_modules and other build-irrelevant bulk out of the build context, so less data crosses to the daemon and images stay lean. And remember that each RUN creates a layer — the cache is your friend during development, but a bloated layer history is your enemy in production, a theme the optimization lesson takes further.

learn.heading: Writing a good Dockerfile
body: Pin the base image to a specific version, such as `python:3.12-slim`, rather than `latest`, so builds are reproducible. Add a `.dockerignore` file listing `.git`, `node_modules`, test data and secrets, so they are never sent to the build or copied into the image. Combine related commands into one `RUN` and clean up in the same step, for example `apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`, because files deleted in a later layer still take up space in an earlier one.

Know the difference between `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT`: `ENTRYPOINT` sets the executable and `CMD` supplies default arguments that `docker run` can override. Use the exec form (`["python", "app.py"]`) so the process receives signals and stops cleanly. Never pass secrets with `ARG` or `ENV`, which are visible in the image history; use BuildKit secret mounts (`RUN --mount=type=secret`) instead.

examples.title: A cache-friendly Dockerfile
examples.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt   # cached until requirements change
COPY . .                                            # code changes only rebuild from here
USER 1000
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
examples.explanation: Copy the dependency file and install before copying source code, so editing code does not reinstall every package.

slides.caption: It starts, almost always, with FROM: the base image everything else builds on — a language runtime, a minimal Linux, whatever your app needs. After that, each instruction adds a layer: RUN executes a command during the build (installing packages, compiling code), COPY moves files from the build context into the image, and the pair of ENTRYPOINT and CMD defines what actually runs when a container starts — ENTRYPOINT names the executable, CMD supplies its default arguments.

items.def: Adds files from the build context into the image
Default command / executable run when the container starts
Documents the listening port (metadata only — does not publish it)

slides.title: Layer caching: build fast by building smart
slides.caption: Docker caches the result of every layer. Rebuild, and any instruction whose inputs have not changed is skipped — which is why instruction order matters enormously. Put the steps that change rarely first and the ones that change constantly last: COPY the dependency manifest and install before copying the source, so a one-line code change does not trigger a full dependency reinstall.

items.def: Unchanged steps are skipped on rebuild — order slow-changing first

slides.title: Writing a good Dockerfile
slides.caption: Pin the base image to a specific version, such as `python:3.12-slim`, rather than `latest`, so builds are reproducible. Add a `.dockerignore` file listing `.git`, `node_modules`, test data and secrets, so they are never sent to the build or copied into the image. Combine related commands into one `RUN` and clean up in the same step, for example `apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`, because files deleted in a later layer still take up space in an earlier one.

overview: Building the image is half the craft; running it well is the other half. The `docker run` command looks simple, but its flags are the steering wheel for everything a container does: where it runs, how it is reached, what it can see, and what happens when it stops.

This lesson covers the flags you will use daily, how to get inside a running container, read its logs, and manage its lifecycle — plus the one truth about containers that surprises everyone exactly once.

learn.heading: The flags that matter
body: Most containers run detached with -d, in the background, rather than holding your terminal. Ports are published with -p 8080:80 — host port first, container port second — which is how the outside world reaches in. Give the container a name with --name web so you can address it by something friendlier than a hex id, pass configuration with -e KEY=value, and add --rm for throwaway runs so the container cleans itself up on exit instead of littering your system.

For interactive work, -it combines -i (keep stdin open) and -t (allocate a terminal): `docker run -it ubuntu bash` drops you into a shell inside a fresh Ubuntu container, perfect for exploring an image. These flags compose freely — `-d -p 8080:80 --name web --rm -e MODE=prod` is a perfectly ordinary production-ish invocation.

learn.heading: Inside, around, and after
body: A running container is not a black box. `docker exec -it <container> sh` starts a new shell inside the existing container — exec runs alongside the main process, it does not replace it. `docker logs` (with -f to follow) shows what the main process has printed, which is where every debugging session begins. And `docker stop` followed by `docker rm` ends the lifecycle; `docker rm -f` does both at once.

Here is the truth that surprises everyone once: anything written inside the container — outside a volume — dies with it. The container’s writable layer is deleted on removal, by design. Containers are ephemeral; they are cattle, not pets. If the data matters, it belongs in a volume, which is exactly where the next lesson begins.

learn.heading: Container lifecycle and cleanup
body: A container moves through created, running, paused, stopped and removed states. `docker stop` sends SIGTERM and, after a grace period (10 seconds by default), SIGKILL, so applications should handle SIGTERM and shut down cleanly. `docker kill` sends SIGKILL immediately. A stopped container keeps its writable layer until you remove it, which is why `docker ps -a` often shows a long list of exited containers.

Clean up regularly: `docker container prune` removes stopped containers, `docker image prune` removes dangling images, and `docker system df` shows how much space images, containers, volumes and build cache use. `docker system prune -a --volumes` removes everything unused, including volumes, so read its warning before running it on a machine with data you need.

examples.title: Common run options
examples.code:
docker run -d \
  --name api \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 \
  -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://db:5432/app \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --memory 512m --cpus 1 \
  myorg/api:1.4.2
examples.explanation: Binding to 127.0.0.1 keeps the port off the public interface; limits stop one container starving the host; pin an image tag rather than latest.

overview: Two problems appear the moment containers get serious: data must outlive the container that created it, and containers must talk to each other. Docker answers the first with volumes and the second with networks — and both have one more subtlety than beginners expect.
This lesson covers persistent storage, the volume/bind-mount distinction, container networking from bridge to none, and the golden rule of secrets.

learn.heading: Volumes: data that survives
body: A volume is Docker-managed storage that lives independently of any container. Mount a named volume with -v myvol:/data and Docker creates it if needed; delete every container and the data remains, ready for the next one. That is the correct home for databases, uploads, anything you would mourn losing. Writing into the container’s own layer instead is the classic beginner mistake — fast, easy, and gone the moment the container is removed.

Bind mounts are the sibling: they map a specific host path into the container, which makes them perfect for development — mount your source tree and edit live while the container runs your code. The rule of thumb: volumes for production data Docker manages, bind mounts for files you edit on the host. And never bake secrets into either the image or the Dockerfile; configuration arrives at runtime through environment variables, mounted files, or a secrets manager.

learn.heading: Networks: containers that talk
body: The default bridge network gives containers a private subnet where they can reach each other — and on a user-defined bridge, they do it by name, thanks to Docker’s built-in DNS. Your web container simply connects to “db”, no IP addresses memorized. That name resolution is the reason to prefer user-defined networks over the default bridge for anything real.

Two special modes complete the picture. `--network host` shares the host’s network stack outright — no port mapping needed, slightly faster, but the container gives up network isolation (and it behaves differently on non-Linux hosts). `--network none` is the opposite: no networking at all, for untrusted or fully offline workloads. Most of the time, though, you will live on a bridge network and let DNS do the work.

learn.heading: Backing up volumes and publishing ports safely
body: Volumes live outside the container, so they need their own backups. A common method mounts the volume into a temporary container and archives it: `docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata.tgz -C /data .`. For databases, prefer the database's own dump tool (`pg_dump`, `mysqldump`) so the backup is consistent rather than a copy of files being written.

Publishing a port with `-p 8080:80` binds to every host interface by default, making the service reachable from the network. Bind to `127.0.0.1:8080:80` for services only the host should reach. Also note that Docker writes its own iptables rules for published ports, which can bypass host firewall rules such as ufw; check what is actually exposed with `ss -tlnp` and a scan from another machine.

examples.title: Named volume and user-defined network
examples.code:
docker network create appnet
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d --name db --network appnet -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/pg postgres:16
docker run -d --name api --network appnet myorg/api:1.4.2
# inside api, the database is reachable at host name 'db'
examples.explanation: Containers on a user-defined network resolve each other by name (the default bridge does not), and the named volume keeps data when the db container is replaced.

overview: Real applications are rarely one container. A web app needs its database, its cache, maybe a queue — and starting them by hand, in order, with the right flags, is toil that begs to be automated. Docker Compose replaces a folder of shell scripts with a single declarative YAML file.
This lesson covers the compose file, the service/network/volume model, the daily lifecycle commands, and how services find and configure each other.

learn.heading: One file for the whole stack
body: The compose.yaml file declares services — each one a container definition with its image or build context, ports, environment, and volumes — plus the networks and volumes they share. `docker compose up` reads it and brings the entire stack to life; add -d to run detached. When you are done, `docker compose down` stops everything and removes the containers and networks it created, a clean teardown in one command.

Services reach each other by name over the network Compose creates for them: the app connects to “db:5432” and never cares which host or IP the database landed on. Dependencies are declared with depends_on — with one caveat worth memorizing: it waits for the container to start, not for the database inside to be ready. Pair it with a healthcheck when startup order truly matters.

learn.heading: Day-to-day Compose
body: Configuration lives with the service, not in the image: the environment: mapping (or env_file:) keeps secrets and settings out of built artifacts, where they belong. When code changes, `docker compose up --build` rebuilds the images that have a build context before starting. And when one service needs muscle, `docker compose up --scale web=3` runs three copies — Compose handles the replicas while something upstream spreads the traffic.

Compose is deliberately single-host: it orchestrates containers on one machine beautifully, and that covers development, CI, demos, and small production deployments. When you outgrow one host — true clustering, self-healing across machines — that is the moment Kubernetes enters the picture, and the next track is waiting.

learn.heading: Environments, overrides and secrets in Compose
body: Compose reads variables from a `.env` file in the project directory and substitutes them into `compose.yaml`, for example `image: myapp:${APP_VERSION}`. Per-environment differences go in override files: `compose.override.yaml` is merged automatically for local development, and `docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d` applies production settings. `docker compose config` prints the final merged configuration, which is the quickest way to check what will run.

Keep secrets out of the YAML and out of version control. Compose supports a `secrets:` section that mounts files at `/run/secrets/<name>` inside the container, which many official images read through `_FILE` variables such as `POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE`. Profiles (`profiles: [debug]`) let optional services such as admin tools start only when requested with `--profile debug`.

examples.title: A compose file with a health check
examples.code:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    volumes: [pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    depends_on:
      db: { condition: service_healthy }
volumes:
  pgdata:
examples.explanation: depends_on with service_healthy waits until the database actually accepts connections, not just until its container has started.

overview: An image sitting on your laptop helps no one. Registries — Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR — are the distribution layer: the place images live so any host, CI runner, or cluster can pull exactly the artifact you built.
This lesson covers tagging and the treachery of `latest`, immutable digests, pushing and pulling, private registries, and why you scan everything you did not build yourself.

learn.heading: Tags, digests, and the lie of `latest`
body: A tag like app:1.2.0 names a version of a repository — human-readable, convenient, and mutable: you can push a different image under the same tag tomorrow. `latest` is the most misunderstood tag of all; it is merely the default when you omit a tag, not a promise of newness. Nothing updates it for you. In production, pin explicit versions, because “latest” today and “latest” next month may be different software.

The digest — that sha256:... string — is the antidote. It content-addresses the exact image bytes: immutable, tamper-evident, reproducible. Pin by digest for the deployments where certainty matters, and re-tag freely with `docker tag local:tag registry/repo:tag` when preparing an image for its journey to a registry.

learn.heading: Push, pull, and trust
body: The lifecycle is simple: `docker login` once, `docker push` to upload, `docker pull` to download (and `docker run` pulls automatically when the image is missing locally). Organizations run private registries to keep proprietary images internal and control exactly what flows into their clusters — standard practice in any serious CI pipeline.

But a registry is a shelf, not a guarantee. Base images and their dependencies carry known vulnerabilities, and pulling blindly is how CVEs enter production. Scan images — with Trivy, Docker Scout, or your registry’s built-in scanner — before they run, ideally as a gate in CI that fails the build. Trust the pipeline, verify the artifact.

learn.heading: Signing, scanning and retention
body: Before deployment, scan images for known vulnerabilities with tools such as Trivy, Grype or the registry's built-in scanner, and fail the pipeline on critical findings that have a fix. Generate a software bill of materials (SBOM) so you can answer 'which images contain this vulnerable library?' when the next major CVE is announced.

Signing proves an image came from your pipeline and has not been altered. Sigstore's cosign signs an image digest and stores the signature in the registry, and admission policies in Kubernetes can refuse unsigned images. Set retention rules in the registry to delete old untagged images, and make release tags immutable where the registry supports it, so `app:1.4.2` always means the same image.

examples.title: Tag and push to a registry
examples.code:
docker build -t myorg/api:1.4.2 .
docker tag myorg/api:1.4.2 ghcr.io/myorg/api:1.4.2
echo $GHCR_TOKEN | docker login ghcr.io -u myorg --password-stdin
docker push ghcr.io/myorg/api:1.4.2
docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/myorg/api:1.4.2   # shows the digest
examples.explanation: The registry host is part of the image name. Deploy by digest (@sha256:...) for an immutable reference; tags can be moved.

overview: A container image is a shipping manifest for your attack surface: every package in it is something to patch, every layer a place for secrets to hide, every root process a prize for an attacker. Small, least-privilege, scanned images are not aesthetic preferences — they are security controls.
This lesson covers building small with multi-stage builds, running least-privilege, keeping secrets out of layers, and proving your images are what they claim to be.

learn.heading: Build small
body: Multi-stage builds are the single biggest win: use one stage with the full toolchain to compile your app, then COPY only the resulting artifact into a second, slim runtime stage. The compiler, the headers, the build cache — none of it ships. Pair that with a minimal base like Alpine or a distroless image and you have cut most of the CVEs before they ever existed, because fewer packages means fewer vulnerabilities to patch.

Layer discipline compounds the gain. Order your Dockerfile from least- to most-frequently-changing so the build cache does maximum work. Combine related RUN commands with && and clean up package caches in the same layer — otherwise the deleted files still exist in an earlier layer, bloating the image and, worse, potentially recoverable.

learn.heading: Run least-privilege, prove integrity
body: Then shrink the runtime blast radius. Run as a non-root USER — a one-line instruction that limits what a compromised process can do. Consider --read-only so the app cannot write to its own filesystem, mounting a writable volume only where it truly needs one. And treat layers as public: anything baked into a layer, even deleted later, remains recoverable from image history. Secrets go in at runtime, never in the build.

Finally, verify. Scan every image for known CVEs with Trivy or Docker Scout and gate the pipeline on the results. Sign images with a tool like cosign so clusters can verify authenticity before deploying — in a supply-chain-attack world, “this exact image came from our CI” is a claim worth proving, not assuming.

learn.heading: Hardening at run time
body: Image hardening is half the job; the run options decide what a compromised container can do. Drop all Linux capabilities and add back only what is needed (`--cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE`), prevent privilege escalation with `--security-opt no-new-privileges`, make the root filesystem read-only with a tmpfs for scratch space, and set memory, CPU and PID limits. Never use `--privileged` for application containers.

Never mount the Docker socket (`/var/run/docker.sock`) into an application container: whoever controls the socket controls the host. Rootless mode runs the Docker daemon itself as an unprivileged user, and user namespace remapping maps root inside the container to an unprivileged user on the host. Docker Bench for Security checks a host against the CIS Docker Benchmark.

examples.title: Multi-stage build to a minimal image
examples.code:
FROM golang:1.23 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/app .

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
USER nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
examples.explanation: The compiler and source stay in the build stage; the final image holds only the binary, runs as non-root and has no shell, so it is tiny with few CVEs to scan.
